title: Spanish B2
description: The fourth step in Latin American Spanish, from B1 to CEFR level B2, the level of the Instituto Cervantes DELE B2 exam. Lessons cover the past tenses as Mexico and Spain use them, the perfect and pluperfect subjunctive, past counterfactuals with si and de + infinitive, opinion and value judgments in both moods, feelings about the past, the full range of concessive, causal, consecutive, purpose, time and condition connectors, probability in the present, past and future, relative clauses with el cual and cuyo, reported speech with every tense, the passive and impersonal sentences, the uses of se and object pronouns, verbal periphrases, discourse markers, the nominal style of formal writing, describing data and trends, debating and proposing solutions, word formation and diminutives, por and para, and the letters, opinion articles and spoken tasks the DELE B2 asks for. About 580 new words build on the roughly 2,550 from Spanish A1 to B1, with Mexican usage as the standard and Spain's words noted. Conjugation drills keep all eleven forms of the earlier courses, and a reading list suggests graded readers, podcasts, magazines and stories for this level. Unlocks when Spanish B1 is complete.
author: Erudior

modules.title: Lo que pasó y lo que pudo pasar (what happened and what could have happened)
Opinar y matizar (giving and nuancing opinions)
Contar lo que se dice (reporting, the news and the media)
Los matices de la lengua y el DELE B2 (the fine points of the language and the B2 exam)
Honors: Literatura, arte y lenguas de México (literature, art and the languages of Mexico)

lessons.title: Así fue: the past tenses at B2, in Mexico and in Spain
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Welcome to Spanish B2. This first module is about the past: what happened, how people tell it,
and, by lesson 04, what *could* have happened. You know every **[[indicative]]** past tense from
A1–B1: the **[[preterite]]** (*viví*), the **[[imperfect]]** (*vivía*), the **[[present perfect]]** (*he
vivido*) and the **[[pluperfect]]** (*había vivido*). This lesson sets them side by side at B2 depth
and shows a difference you'll hear in any series from Spain: the present perfect is used
differently there. The theme is lives: biographies, memoirs and family stories.

## Four pasts, one life

![A timeline titled Una vida en cuatro tiempos, for the grandmother in Text 1. Green bars above the line show the imperfect: vivía en el pueblo (1931 to 1947) and trabajaba (1947 to 1958). Blue dots on the line show the preterite: nació (1931), se fue a Puebla (1947), falleció (2009). A dashed purple box, su padre había muerto, sits above the early years, with a dashed arrow pointing back to it from 1947: the pluperfect. An orange arrow runs from 2009 to AHORA under a box reading desde entonces la he abierto muchas veces: the present perfect. A legend names the four tenses.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Tense | What it does in a life story | Example |
|---|---|---|
| preterite | events, and periods seen as closed (with a start and an end) | *Vivió veinte años en París.* |
| imperfect | the scene, habits, what was going on, plans that didn't happen | *Vivía en París cuando conoció a su esposa.* |
| pluperfect | what had already happened before the story's moment | *Su padre ya había muerto.* |
| present perfect | (Mexico) a period or repetition that reaches now | *He vuelto al pueblo muchas veces.* |

Three B2 points need more care than "preterite for actions, imperfect for descriptions".

A long period can take the preterite. What matters is not how long something lasted but
whether you present it as closed. *Vivió veinte años en París* (He lived in Paris for twenty
years) is a finished chapter, so it is preterite, even though twenty years is a long time.
*A lo largo de su vida escribió cuarenta libros* (Over the course of her life she wrote forty books)
sums up a whole closed life. Compare *Cuando vivía en París, escribía todas las mañanas* (When he
lived in Paris, he wrote every morning): now Paris is the background and writing is a habit.

The imperfect for plans that didn't happen. *Iba a* + infinitive, or the imperfect alone, tells
what was about to happen or was planned, often followed by *pero*:

- *Iba a llamarte, pero se me acabó la batería.* — I was going to call you, but my battery died.
- *Mi abuela se casaba en junio, pero la boda se canceló.* — My grandmother was getting married in
  June, but the wedding was called off.

The polite imperfect softens a request by placing the wish a moment in the past:

- *Quería pedirle un favor.* — I wanted to ask you a favor.
- *Venía a preguntar si todavía hay lugar en el taller.* — I came to ask whether there's still room
  in the workshop.

## The present perfect and the preterite: Mexico and Spain

![A chart titled México y España: el pretérito perfecto, with a column for Mexico (and much of Latin America) and one for Spain (in large part). For something finished today, the rows differ: Hoy me levanté a las seis beside Hoy me he levantado a las seis, and ¿Ya comiste? beside ¿Ya has comido? For something that reaches now, they are the same: He vivido aquí desde 2019 in both. A note at the bottom: for yesterday, last week or 2009, both use the preterite.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In Mexico and most of Latin America, the preterite covers anything finished, even if it
happened five minutes ago:

- *Hoy me levanté a las seis.* — Today I got up at six.
- *¿Ya comiste?* — Have you eaten yet?
- *Esta mañana vi a tu hermano.* — I saw your brother this morning.

The present perfect is kept for what continues or repeats up to now, and for "ever" and "not
yet":

- *He vivido aquí desde 2019.* — I've lived here since 2019.
- *Últimamente he dormido mal.* — I've been sleeping badly lately.
- *¿Has estado en Oaxaca?* — Have you ever been to Oaxaca?
- *Todavía no ha llegado el resultado.* — The result hasn't arrived yet.

Even for "ever", Mexicans often use the preterite with *ya*: *¿Ya fuiste a Oaxaca?* is everyday
Mexican Spanish.

In most of Spain, the present perfect is the usual tense for what happened today and in the
very recent past, even when it is completely finished:

- *Hoy me he levantado a las seis.* — Today I got up at six.
- *¿Ya has comido?* — Have you eaten yet?
- *Esta mañana he visto a tu hermano.* — I saw your brother this morning.

For yesterday and earlier, Spain uses the preterite too: *Ayer me levanté a las seis.*
The *Nueva gramática de la lengua española* of the RAE and ASALE (2009, §23.7) describes these
regional differences, and the picture is not uniform: some areas of Spain (in the northwest and the
Canary Islands) use the preterite much as Latin America does, and in some Andean areas the present
perfect often appears where other regions would use the preterite. This course writes the Mexican pattern. Learn to recognize
Spain's: when a speaker from Madrid says *Hoy he comido con mi madre*, nothing is wrong.

## The historical present

Biographies, timelines and history books often tell the past in the present tense, the
**[[historical present]]**. It makes events feel close and lists dates quickly:

- *En 1910 estalla la Revolución.* — In 1910 the Revolution breaks out. (*estallar* = to break out)
- *En 1936 se muda a la Ciudad de México.* — In 1936 he moves to Mexico City.

Background moves into the present too: *En 1950 la familia se muda a Monterrey, donde ya viven
sus tíos* (where her aunts and uncles already live). Two rules: keep it consistent (don't jump back
to the preterite without a reason), and mark the time clearly, because the verb itself no longer says "past". Spoken anecdotes use it
at the exciting moment: *Y entonces abro la puerta y ¿quién crees que está ahí?* (And then I open
the door and who do you think is there?)

## Words that steer the tense

| Expression | Meaning | Usual tense | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *en aquel entonces* | back then | imperfect (the scene) | *En aquel entonces no había metro.* |
| *a lo largo de* | throughout | preterite (a closed whole) or imperfect (a habit) | *A lo largo de su vida viajó mucho.* |
| *a raíz de* | as a result of | preterite (the change it caused) | *A raíz del accidente, dejó de manejar.* |
| *desde entonces* (B1) | since then | present perfect or present (up to now) | *Desde entonces he vuelto cada año. / Desde entonces vive en Mérida.* |

These are tendencies, not rules: *a lo largo de los noventa trabajaba de noche* (a habit) is as
correct as *…trabajó en tres países* (a summary).

## Talking about a life

Biographies use a small set of words again and again, many of them formal (in conversation,
*murió* and *famoso*).

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *Nace en 1902 y fallece en 1988.* (*el fallecimiento* = the death, formal) | He is born in 1902 and passes away in 1988. |
| *Destacó en matemáticas desde niña; fue una destacada científica.* | She stood out in math from childhood; she was a prominent scientist. |
| *Fue una de las pioneras de la radio en México.* | She was one of the pioneers of radio in Mexico. |
| *Alcanzó la fama a los cuarenta; hoy es célebre en todo el mundo.* | She became famous at forty; today she is celebrated all over the world. |
| *Es un arquitecto reconocido; el reconocimiento le llegó tarde.* | He's a renowned architect; recognition came to him late. |
| *Se exilió en 1939 y murió en el exilio.* | He went into exile in 1939 and died in exile. |
| *Sus antepasados eran campesinos de Zacatecas.* | Her ancestors were farmers from Zacatecas. |

*La biografía* is written by someone else, *la autobiografía* tells the writer's own life, and
*las memorias* (plural in this sense) collect the writer's memories of a period or of other
people. *Un testimonio* is a first-hand account of events the speaker lived through.

When you evaluate a life story, ask what kind of source it is: an autobiography is a testimony,
not a neutral record. *Según su autobiografía…* (according to his autobiography) keeps the source
visible.

## Text 1: a memoir

An excerpt from the memoirs of Elena Ruiz, an invented writer, about her grandmother.

> Mi abuela Carmen nació en 1931 en un pueblo de la sierra de Puebla. En aquel entonces no había
> carretera, y para ir a la ciudad la gente caminaba dos días. Su padre había muerto cuando ella
> tenía tres años, así que creció entre mujeres: su madre, dos tías y una bisabuela que solo hablaba
> náhuatl. A raíz de esa infancia, decía, aprendió a no esperar nada de nadie.
>
> A los dieciséis años se fue sola a Puebla. Trabajó once años en una fábrica de textiles y estudió
> de noche. Fue la primera de su generación que terminó la secundaria, una hazaña que nadie en el
> pueblo había imaginado. Cuando yo era niña, me contaba esa anécdota cada domingo, siempre con los
> mismos detalles: el camión que no llegaba, los zapatos prestados, la maestra que le regaló un
> diccionario.
>
> A lo largo de su vida guardó todo: cartas, boletos, recibos. Iba a escribir sus memorias, pero
> nunca encontró el tiempo. Falleció en 2009, y su legado está en una caja de cartón que hoy tengo
> en mi escritorio. Desde entonces la he abierto muchas veces. Cada papel evoca una época que ya no
> existe, y cada vez encuentro algo que no había visto.

Translation:

> My grandmother Carmen was born in 1931 in a village in the mountains of Puebla. Back then there was
> no road, and to get to the city people walked for two days. Her father had died when she was three,
> so she grew up among women: her mother, two aunts and a great-grandmother (*la bisabuela*) who
> spoke only Nahuatl. As a result of that childhood, she used to say, she learned not to expect
> anything from anyone.
>
> At sixteen she went to Puebla on her own. She worked for eleven years in a textile factory and
> studied at night. She was the first of her generation to finish middle school, a feat nobody in the
> village had imagined. When I was a girl, she told me that story every Sunday, always with the same
> details: the bus that didn't come, the borrowed shoes, the teacher who gave her a dictionary.
>
> Throughout her life she kept everything: letters, tickets, receipts. She was going to write her
> memoirs, but she never found the time. She passed away in 2009, and her legacy is in a cardboard
> box that I now keep on my desk. Since then I have opened it many times. Every piece of paper
> evokes an era that no longer exists, and every time I find something I hadn't seen.

*Trabajó once años* is a closed period; *me contaba … cada domingo* is a habit; *iba a escribir…,
pero* is a plan that didn't happen; *había muerto* steps back before the story. *La he abierto
muchas veces* reaches the present, while *falleció en 2009* is dated and finished: preterite
everywhere, Spain included.

## Text 2: a biography in the historical present

> Luis Barragán nace en Guadalajara en 1902. Estudia ingeniería y, en los años veinte, viaja por
> Francia y España; en 1931 asiste en París a conferencias de Le Corbusier. En 1936 se muda a la
> Ciudad de México, donde vive hasta su muerte. Entre 1945 y 1952 trabaja en los Jardines del
> Pedregal, y a partir de 1948 construye su propia casa en Tacubaya. En 1957 le encargan el símbolo
> de la nueva Ciudad Satélite: las Torres de Satélite, que diseña con el escultor Mathias Goeritz.
> En 1980 recibe el Premio Pritzker, uno de los reconocimientos más importantes de la arquitectura.
> Fallece en su casa el 22 de noviembre de 1988. En 2004 la UNESCO inscribe la Casa Estudio Luis
> Barragán en la Lista del Patrimonio Mundial.

Translation:

> Luis Barragán is born in Guadalajara in 1902. He studies engineering and, in the 1920s, travels in
> France and Spain; in 1931 he attends lectures by Le Corbusier in Paris. In 1936 he moves to Mexico
> City, where he lives until his death. Between 1945 and 1952 he works on the Jardines del Pedregal,
> and from 1948 he builds his own house in Tacubaya. In 1957 he is commissioned to create the symbol
> of the new Ciudad Satélite: the Satélite Towers, which he designs with the sculptor Mathias
> Goeritz. In 1980 he receives the Pritzker Prize, one of the most important awards in architecture.
> He dies at his home on November 22, 1988. In 2004 UNESCO adds the Luis Barragán House and Studio
> to the World Heritage List.

Every verb is in the present, and every sentence carries a date. Retold in the preterite (*nació,
estudió, viajó*), nothing else would change.

## Pronunciation

- *época, anécdota, célebre*: all stressed on the third syllable from the end, so all carry an
  accent: É-po-ca (three syllables), a-NÉC-do-ta (four), CÉ-le-bre (three).
- *a raíz de*: *raíz* has two syllables, ra-ÍZ; the accent breaks the diphthong. Its plural is
  *raíces* (ra-Í-ces).
- *fallecer, fallezco*: *ll* sounds like *y*, and *z* and *ce* like *s*: fa-ye-SER, fa-YES-ko.
- *exiliarse*: e-ksi-LIAR-se, four syllables; *-lia-* is one syllable, and there is no accent in
  *me exilio* (me e-KSI-lio).

## Common mistakes

- The imperfect for a measured, closed period: ~~Vivía veinte años en París~~ → *Vivió veinte años
  en París* (also *toda su vida, de 1990 a 2000*).
- Calling Spain's present perfect wrong: *Hoy he desayunado tarde* is standard there. In your own
  Spanish, keep one pattern.
- The present perfect with a past date: ~~Ha fallecido en 2009~~ → *Falleció en 2009* (Spain too).
- Mixing tenses in a historical-present biography: ~~Nace en 1902 y estudió ingeniería~~ → *Nace
  en 1902 y estudia ingeniería*.

## Key points

- Preterite: events and closed periods, however long (*Vivió veinte años en París*). Imperfect:
  scene, habits, what was going on, and plans that didn't happen (*Iba a llamarte, pero…*); also
  polite requests (*Quería pedirle un favor*). Pluperfect: the past before the story.
- Mexico and most of Latin America: preterite for anything finished, today included (*Hoy me
  levanté a las seis*); present perfect for what reaches now (*He vivido aquí desde 2019*), "ever"
  and "not yet". Most of Spain: present perfect also for today (*Hoy me he levantado a las seis*).
- The historical present tells history and biographies with dates: *En 1910 estalla la
  Revolución.* Keep it consistent.
- *En aquel entonces* (back then), *a lo largo de* (throughout), *a raíz de* (as a result of) and
  *desde entonces* (since then) frame a life story.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Espero que hayas aprobado: the perfect subjunctive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 reviewed the past in the **[[indicative]]**, the **[[mood]]** of facts. This lesson adds the
past to the **[[subjunctive]]**, the mood of wishes, doubts, feelings and the not-yet-real. In B1 you
met one sentence of it: *Me alegra que hayas venido* (I'm glad you came). That is the **perfect
subjunctive**, and here it gets the full treatment: forms, uses, and how it differs from the
present subjunctive. The theme is university life in Mexico, from the entrance exam to the thesis
defense. This lesson also unlocks the perfect-subjunctive drill in your conjugation practice.

## The forms

The perfect subjunctive is the present subjunctive of *haber* + a **[[participle]]**:

| | *haber* | + participle |
|---|---|---|
| yo | haya | terminado |
| tú | hayas | aprobado |
| él, ella, usted | haya | leído |
| nosotros, nosotras | hayamos | escrito |
| (vosotros, vosotras) | (hayáis) | (hecho) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | hayan | vuelto |

As in every compound tense, the participle never changes, nothing goes between *haya* and the
participle, and pronouns go before *haya*: *No creo que lo haya leído; Espero que te hayas
titulado*. The irregular participles are the ones you know: *hecho, dicho, escrito, visto, puesto,
vuelto, abierto, roto, muerto, resuelto, descubierto*.

![A grid titled Los cuatro tiempos del subjuntivo. Rows: main verb in the present (espero, no creo, me alegra) and main verb in the past (esperaba, no creía, me alegró). Columns: same time or later, and earlier. Top left: present subjunctive, que vengas (B1). Top right, highlighted in green: perfect subjunctive, que hayas venido (lesson 02). Bottom left: imperfect subjunctive, que vinieras (B1). Bottom right, dashed and gray: pluperfect subjunctive, que hubieras venido (lesson 03).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Use 1: something already done, seen from now

The main verb is in the present, the present perfect, the future or a command, and it triggers
the subjunctive for any of the reasons you know from B1 (a wish, a doubt, a feeling, a value
judgment). If the event in the *que* clause is already over, use the perfect subjunctive:

- *Espero que hayas entregado la tesis.* — I hope you've handed in your thesis.
- *No creo que lo haya leído.* — I don't think she's read it.
- *Me sorprende que no hayan llamado.* — I'm surprised they haven't called.
- *Es increíble que te hayas titulado en cuatro años.* — It's amazing that you got your degree in
  four years.

English often uses a simple past here ("that you got your degree"), and in Mexico the event may
well be told in the preterite in the indicative (*Te titulaste en cuatro años*). Don't let either
fool you: after a present main verb, a finished event in the subjunctive is *haya* + participle.

### Present or perfect subjunctive?

| Sentence | What it says |
|---|---|
| *No creo que estudie.* | I don't think he's studying / will study. (now or later) |
| *No creo que haya estudiado.* | I don't think he studied / has studied. (before now) |
| *Me alegra que vengas.* | I'm glad you're coming. |
| *Me alegra que hayas venido.* | I'm glad you came. |

The main verb says *when you are speaking* (now); the subjunctive tense says *when the event is*
compared with that: at the same time or later (present), or earlier (perfect).

## Use 2: done before a point in the future

After *cuando, en cuanto, hasta que, después de que* and other time words, B1 taught the present
subjunctive for the future: *Cuando termines, avísame.* The perfect subjunctive stresses that one
thing will be finished before the other happens:

- *Cuando hayas terminado, avísame.* — When you've finished, let me know.
- *Te llamo en cuanto haya salido el resultado.* — I'll call you as soon as the result is out.
- *No te vayas hasta que hayan firmado el acta.* — Don't leave until they've signed the record.
  (*El acta*, the official record of the exam, is feminine, like *el agua*.)

Both *cuando termines* and *cuando hayas terminado* are correct; the second just makes "finished
first" explicit.

## Use 3: in relative clauses and after superlatives

B1 taught the subjunctive in a relative clause when the person or thing may not exist or isn't
known. If the description is about the past, use the perfect subjunctive:

- *Busco a alguien que haya hecho un posgrado en el extranjero.* — I'm looking for someone who has
  done a graduate degree abroad.
- *No conozco a nadie que haya reprobado ese examen.* — I don't know anyone who has failed that exam.
- *¿Hay alguien aquí que haya presentado el examen profesional?* — Is there anyone here who has
  already had their thesis defense?

After a superlative or *el único / la primera*, Spanish allows both moods, with little difference
in meaning; the subjunctive sounds a little more emphatic or formal:

- *Es el mejor curso que he tomado. / Es el mejor curso que haya tomado.* — It's the best course
  I've taken. (Both correct.)
- *Eres la única que se ha titulado. / Eres la única que se haya titulado.* — You're the only one
  who has gotten her degree.

## A guess about the past

*Es posible que* and *puede que* take the subjunctive, so a guess about something already done uses
the perfect subjunctive: *Es posible que ya haya salido* (It's possible she's already left). B1 also
taught a shorter way, the future perfect: *Ya habrá salido* (She must have left by now). Lesson 08
compares them on a scale from certain to doubtful.

## University life in Mexico

![A university campus seen from above around a central lawn and crossing paths, with six labels: la rectoría (a tall building with a clock and a flag), la biblioteca (a building with an open book on its front), la facultad (a long building with columns), el aula (a classroom with a board and rows of desks), la cafetería (a small building with a steaming cup) and el estacionamiento (a parking lot with cars and a P).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A typical path at a Mexican public university:

1. After *el bachillerato* (high school, often called *la prepa*), you take *el examen de admisión*.
   The UNAM and other public universities hold one, and places in popular programs are scarce.
2. You enroll (*la matrícula* = enrollment) in a *facultad* (school) and follow its *plan de
   estudios* (curriculum), earning *créditos*. Your *promedio* (average, usually out of 10) matters for scholarships.
3. With enough credits you start *el servicio social*, work for the public that students must do
   before they can get their degree. At the UNAM it is at least 480 hours over six months to two
   years, and you usually need at least 70% of your credits to begin (some programs set a different
   share).
4. When you have passed every course, you *egresas* (finish your studies) and become *un egresado*
   or *una egresada*.
5. Then you *te titulas* (get your degree), often by writing *una tesis* and defending it in *el
   examen profesional*, an oral exam before a panel (*el jurado*). Many universities also offer
   other ways to get the degree.
6. Finally, the SEP's Dirección General de Profesiones issues *la cédula profesional*, the license
   that lets you practice; today it is usually processed online.

At private universities students pay *una colegiatura* (tuition) every month or semester; at the
UNAM fees are very low. Other people *en el campus*: *el rector* or *la rectora* (the university
president, whose office is *la rectoría*), *el catedrático* (a full professor, though in Mexico
the word is often used for any university professor), and your *asesor* or
*asesora* (thesis advisor), who may see you during *tutorías* (office hours). Two words every
student fears: *el plagio* (plagiarism) and *la fecha de entrega* (the due date).

## Congratulating and consoling

| To congratulate | To console |
|---|---|
| *¡Felicidades! Me alegra mucho que hayas aprobado.* | *Siento mucho que no hayas quedado. Hay otra convocatoria en febrero.* |
| *¡Qué bueno que te hayan dado la beca!* | *Es una lástima que te hayan pedido tantos cambios.* |
| *Estoy muy orgulloso de que te hayas titulado.* | *No creo que hayas hecho nada mal: el examen era difícil.* |

In everyday Mexican speech you'll also hear the indicative after *¡Qué bueno que…!* (*¡Qué bueno
que aprobaste!*), as B1 noted; in writing, the subjunctive is the safe choice. *Quedar* here means
"to get in" (*Quedé en Medicina* = I got into medicine).

## Text: the thesis defense

A WhatsApp thread between classmates in Mexico City. Daniela's thesis defense is the next day.

> Daniela: Mañana a las diez es mi examen profesional. No he dormido nada.
>
> Iván: ¡Tranquila! Espero que hayas descansado aunque sea un poco. ¿Ya te confirmaron el jurado?
>
> Daniela: Sí: mi asesora y dos catedráticos. Ojalá no hayan leído el capítulo tres con mucha atención, jaja.
>
> Rosa: Cuando hayas terminado, avísanos. Te esperamos afuera de la facultad.
>
> Daniela (next day, 13:40): ¡Aprobé! ¡Y con mención honorífica!
>
> Rosa: ¡Felicidades! Me alegra muchísimo que te haya ido tan bien.
>
> Iván: ¡Qué orgullo! Eres la primera de la generación que se titula.
>
> Daniela: Gracias. Todavía me falta la cédula profesional, pero eso ya es puro trámite.
>
> Rosa: Oigan, ¿y Pablo? Es raro que no haya escrito.
>
> Iván: Es posible que no haya visto los mensajes. Hoy tenía su examen de admisión al doctorado.
>
> Pablo: Perdón, acabo de salir. ¡Felicidades, Daniela! No creo que me haya ido muy bien, pero ya veremos.
>
> Daniela: ¡Seguro que te fue mejor de lo que crees! Cuando salgan los resultados, festejamos los dos.

Translation:

> Daniela: Tomorrow at ten is my thesis defense. I haven't slept at all.
>
> Iván: Relax! I hope you've rested at least a little. Have they confirmed your panel yet?
>
> Daniela: Yes: my advisor and two full professors. I hope they haven't read chapter three very closely, haha.
>
> Rosa: When you've finished, let us know. We'll wait for you outside the school.
>
> Daniela: I passed! And with honors!
>
> Rosa: Congratulations! I'm so glad it went so well for you.
>
> Iván: So proud of you! You're the first in our class to get your degree.
>
> Daniela: Thanks. I still need my professional license, but that's just paperwork now.
>
> Rosa: Hey, what about Pablo? It's strange that he hasn't written.
>
> Iván: Maybe he hasn't seen the messages. He had his entrance exam for the PhD today.
>
> Pablo: Sorry, I just got out. Congratulations, Daniela! I don't think it went very well, but we'll see.
>
> Daniela: I'm sure it went better than you think! When the results come out, we'll both celebrate.

Notes: *la mención honorífica* is a distinction given for an outstanding defense; *la generación*
here means one's class or cohort; *festejar* = to celebrate (very common in Mexico). *Ojalá* +
perfect subjunctive (*Ojalá no hayan leído…*) hopes about something that may already have happened.
Iván's *la primera … que se titula* uses the indicative; *que se haya titulado* would also be right.

## Pronunciation

- *haya, halla, allá*: with yeísmo, *haya* (of *haber*) and *halla* (of *hallar*, to find) sound the
  same: A-ya. *Allá* (over there) is stressed on the last syllable: a-YÁ.
- *hayamos*: a-YA-mos, three syllables, stress on the second.
- *el posgrado*: pos-GRA-do; *la tesis*: TE-sis, two syllables, the same in the plural.
- *el catedrático*: ca-te-DRÁ-ti-co, five syllables, stressed on the third from the end.

## Common mistakes

- The indicative of *haber* after a subjunctive trigger: ~~Espero que has descansado~~ → *Espero
  que hayas descansado*.
- *Haiga* for *haya*: it is heard in some rural and informal speech, but it is not standard; write
  *haya*.
- The perfect subjunctive after a past main verb: *Esperaba que hayas llegado bien* is heard in
  Latin American speech, but the standard sequence, and the safe choice in writing, is *Esperaba
  que hubieras llegado bien* (lesson 03) or *Esperaba que llegaras bien* (B1). After a present main
  verb, both *Espero que hayas llegado bien* and *Espero que llegues bien* are correct, with different
  times.
- Making the participle agree: ~~Espero que las hayas entregadas~~ → *Espero que las hayas
  entregado*.
- *Egresar* and *titularse* aren't the same: you can *egresar* in 2024 (finish your courses) and
  *titularse* in 2026 (receive the degree).

## Key points

- Perfect subjunctive: *haya, hayas, haya, hayamos, hayan* + participle; pronouns before *haya*.
- After a present, future or command main verb, for something already done: *Espero que hayas
  entregado la tesis; No creo que lo haya leído.*
- For something finished before a future point: *Cuando hayas terminado, avísame.*
- In relative clauses about the past: *Busco a alguien que haya hecho un posgrado.* After a
  superlative or *el único*, both *he tomado* and *haya tomado* are correct.
- Present subjunctive = same time or later; perfect subjunctive = earlier.
- Mexico's degree path: *examen de admisión → créditos → servicio social → egresar → tesis y examen
  profesional → titularse → cédula profesional*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Me dolió que no me lo hubieras dicho: the pluperfect subjunctive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 02 completed the subjunctive seen from the present: *que vengas, que hayas venido*. This
lesson completes it seen from the past. B1 taught the imperfect subjunctive (*que vinieras*), and
B1's honors lesson 16h1 previewed the **[[pluperfect subjunctive]]** (*que hubieras venido*); here
everyone learns it fully, together with the whole **[[sequence of tenses]]**, the rule that matches the
tense of the main verb with the tense of the subjunctive. The theme is friendship: trust, betrayal,
jealousy and making up. This lesson unlocks the pluperfect-subjunctive drill (both *-ra* and *-se*
forms are accepted).

## The forms

The pluperfect subjunctive is the imperfect subjunctive of *haber* (from *hubieron*) + a
participle:

| | *-ra* (taught) | *-se* (recognize) | + participle |
|---|---|---|---|
| yo | hubiera | hubiese | dicho |
| tú | hubieras | hubieses | invitado |
| él, ella, usted | hubiera | hubiese | mentido |
| nosotros, nosotras | hubiéramos | hubiésemos | hablado |
| (vosotros, vosotras) | (hubierais) | (hubieseis) | (visto) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | hubieran | hubiesen | traicionado |

The *-ra* forms are the usual ones in Mexico and the ones this course writes; the *-se* forms mean
the same, are heard more in Spain and seen more in writing than in Mexican speech (though *-ra* is
the more common form everywhere), and are accepted in every answer. Note the
accent on *hubiéramos / hubiésemos*. Pronouns go before *hubiera*: *que no me lo hubieras dicho*.

## Use 1: an earlier event, seen from the past

When the main verb is in a past tense or the conditional and the event in the subjunctive clause
happened *before* it, use the pluperfect subjunctive:

- *Me dolió que no me hubieras invitado.* — It hurt me that you hadn't invited me.
- *No podía creer que me hubiera mentido.* — I couldn't believe he had lied to me.
- *Me sorprendió que se hubieran distanciado tanto.* — I was surprised they had drifted so far apart.
- *Me habría gustado que me lo hubieras contado.* — I would have liked you to have told me.

It is the subjunctive twin of the pluperfect indicative: *Sabía que me había mentido* (fact) →
*No podía creer que me hubiera mentido* (disbelief).

When the order of events is obvious, Spanish speakers often use the imperfect subjunctive instead:
*Me dolió que no me invitaras* is also correct and very common. The pluperfect makes "before"
explicit, and you need it when the difference matters:

| Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *Me molestó que llegara tarde.* | It annoyed me that she arrived (or was arriving) late. |
| *Me molestó que ya se hubiera ido.* | It annoyed me that she had already left (before I got there). |

## Use 2: *ojalá* for regrets

B1 taught *ojalá* with the present (a possible wish) and the imperfect subjunctive (an unlikely or
impossible one now). With the pluperfect subjunctive it looks back at a past that can't be changed:
a regret.

| *Ojalá* + | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| present | a hope for now or later | *Ojalá venga.* I hope she comes. |
| perfect (02) | a hope about something that may have happened | *Ojalá haya llegado bien.* I hope she got there OK. |
| imperfect | an unlikely or impossible wish now | *Ojalá estuviera aquí.* I wish she were here. |
| pluperfect | a regret about the past | *Ojalá no le hubiera dicho nada.* I wish I hadn't told him anything. |

- *Ojalá hubieras venido a la fiesta.* — I wish you had come to the party.
- *Ojalá nos hubiéramos reencontrado antes.* — If only we'd met again sooner.

## Use 3: *como si*

*Como si* (as if) always takes a past subjunctive, even when the main verb is in the present. The
choice is about time:

![A two-panel picture titled Como si: ¿al mismo tiempo o antes? Top panel: a man gives orders in a speech bubble (¡Haz esto! ¡Y esto!) to an unhappy woman; caption Me habla como si fuera mi jefe, imperfect subjunctive, at the same time as he talks. Bottom panel: on the left, a dashed gray box shows the two arguing earlier (antes: la pelea); on the right, they greet each other smiling (después: el saludo); a dashed arrow points back from the greeting to the argument; caption Me saludó como si no hubiera pasado nada, pluperfect subjunctive, earlier than the greeting.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *Me habla como si fuera mi jefe.* — He talks to me as if he were my boss. (same time)
- *Me saludó como si no hubiera pasado nada.* — She greeted me as if nothing had happened. (earlier)
- *Actúa como si nunca nos hubiéramos conocido.* — He acts as if we had never met.

## The sequence of tenses

Put lessons 02 and 03 together and you have the whole system:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the subjunctive tense
  accDescr: First look at the main verb. If it is present, present perfect, future or a command, use the present subjunctive for an event at the same time or later, and the perfect subjunctive for an earlier event. If it is a past tense or the conditional, use the imperfect subjunctive for the same time or later, and the pluperfect subjunctive for an earlier event.
  A{"Main verb?"} -->|"present, perfect, future, command"| B{"The event in the que clause is..."}
  A -->|"past or conditional"| C{"The event in the que clause is..."}
  B -->|"same time or later"| D["present subjunctive: que vengas"]
  B -->|"earlier"| E["perfect subjunctive: que hayas venido"]
  C -->|"same time or later"| F["imperfect subjunctive: que vinieras"]
  C -->|"earlier"| G["pluperfect subjunctive: que hubieras venido"]
```

| Main verb | Same time or later | Earlier |
|---|---|---|
| *Espero / He pedido / Pediré / Pide* | *que vengas* | *que hayas venido* |
| *Esperaba / Esperé / Había esperado / Esperaría* | *que vinieras* | *que hubieras venido* |

The table is a strong default, not a law. A present main verb can take a past subjunctive when the
event itself is in the past, especially a dated one:

- *No creo que lo dijera ayer.* — I don't think he said it yesterday. (Correct; *No creo que lo
  haya dicho* is also fine.)
- *Es raro que no llamara anoche.* — It's strange that he didn't call last night.

And after *me gustaría*, the imperfect is the usual choice (*Me gustaría que vinieras*), though the
present (*que vengas*), common in Latin America, can't be called wrong, as B1 noted.

## Reproaching, regretting, describing a reaction

A reproach (*un reproche*) can be blunt or soft; the subjunctive tenses let you choose:

- *¿Cómo es posible que no me lo hayas dicho?* — How could you not have told me? (present main
  verb → perfect subjunctive)
- *Me molestó muchísimo que no me hubieras llamado.* — It really bothered me that you hadn't called.
- *Me habría gustado que confiaras en mí.* — I'd have liked you to trust me. (softer)
- *Me arrepiento de no haberte llamado.* — I regret not calling you. (same subject: infinitive)
- *Me quedé helada, como si me hubieran echado un balde de agua fría.* — I froze, as if someone had
  thrown a bucket of cold water on me.

## Words for trust and betrayal

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *ser leal / fiel; la lealtad* | to be loyal / faithful; loyalty |
| *traicionar a alguien; la traición* | to betray someone; betrayal |
| *engañar a alguien; el engaño; la infidelidad* | to deceive (or cheat on) someone; deception; infidelity |
| *decepcionar: Me decepcionó.* | to disappoint: He disappointed me. |
| *herir; estar dolido* | to hurt (feelings); to be hurt |
| *ofenderse; la ofensa* | to take offense; an insult, offense |
| *el reproche; el rencor; ser rencoroso; estar resentido* | reproach; resentment; to hold grudges; to be bitter |
| *tener celos; darle celos a alguien* | to be jealous; to make someone jealous |
| *distanciarse; romper con alguien* | to drift apart; to break up with someone |
| *reencontrarse; el reencuentro* | to meet again; a reunion |
| *la complicidad; el cómplice* | closeness, understanding; partner in crime |

Two false friends: *decepcionar* is "to disappoint" (to deceive is *engañar*), and *estar
resentido* describes the hurt after one wrong, while *ser rencoroso* is a trait.

## Text: the misunderstanding

Lucía and Mariana have been friends since middle school. Lucía has just seen photos of a reunion
of their old class on social media.

> Lucía: Vi las fotos del reencuentro de la secundaria. Me dolió mucho que no me hubieras avisado.
>
> Mariana: Ay, Lucía, ¿de verdad? Pensé que no querías ir. Andrés iba a estar ahí.
>
> Lucía: ¿Y qué? Rompí con él hace tres años. Me habría gustado que me lo preguntaras, por lo menos.
>
> Mariana: Tienes razón. Pero no fue una traición: lo hice para no herirte.
>
> Lucía: Lo sé… Es que me sentí como si todos se hubieran puesto de acuerdo sin mí.
>
> Mariana: Nadie se puso de acuerdo. Ojalá te hubiera llamado antes de ir; nos habríamos ahorrado este drama.
>
> Lucía: Y yo, ojalá no te hubiera escrito ese mensaje tan feo anoche. Perdón.
>
> Mariana: Ya pasó. No te guardo rencor. ¿Sabes qué me preguntó todo el mundo? Que dónde estaba mi cómplice.
>
> Lucía: ¿En serio? Bueno, para el próximo reencuentro, vamos juntas.

Translation:

> Lucía: I saw the photos of the middle-school reunion. It really hurt that you hadn't told me.
>
> Mariana: Oh, Lucía, really? I thought you didn't want to go. Andrés was going to be there.
>
> Lucía: So what? I broke up with him three years ago. I'd have liked you to at least ask me.
>
> Mariana: You're right. But it wasn't a betrayal: I did it so as not to hurt you.
>
> Lucía: I know… It's just that I felt as if everyone had agreed on something without me.
>
> Mariana: Nobody agreed on anything. I wish I'd called you before I went; it would have saved us this drama.
>
> Lucía: And I wish I hadn't sent you that nasty message last night. Sorry.
>
> Mariana: It's over. I don't hold a grudge. You know what everybody asked me? Where my partner in crime was.
>
> Lucía: Really? Well, for the next reunion, we're going together.

Notes: *ponerse de acuerdo* = to agree, to arrange something together; *ahorrarse algo* = to spare
oneself something (*nos habríamos ahorrado* = we would have spared ourselves); *feo* here = nasty, unkind; *Ya pasó* = it's over, never mind. Lucía's *Me
habría gustado que me lo preguntaras* uses the imperfect subjunctive (she would have liked a
question *at that time*); *que me lo hubieras preguntado* would also be correct.

### Lucía tells her sister

> Al principio me ofendí: no podía creer que Mariana hubiera ido sin decirme nada. Pensé que me
> había traicionado. Luego me explicó que no quería que me encontrara con Andrés, y entendí que lo
> había hecho por lealtad, no para engañarme. Ojalá le hubiera preguntado antes de mandarle ese
> mensaje. Al final nos reímos, como si nunca nos hubiéramos peleado.

Translation:

> At first I took offense: I couldn't believe Mariana had gone without telling me anything. I
> thought she had betrayed me. Then she explained that she didn't want me to run into Andrés, and I
> understood she had done it out of loyalty, not to deceive me. I wish I had asked her before
> sending her that message. In the end we laughed, as if we had never fought.

Notice the pairs: *pensé que me había traicionado* (indicative, what she believed) and *no podía
creer que hubiera ido* (subjunctive, disbelief); *no quería que me encontrara* (imperfect: at the
same time as the wish).

## Pronunciation

- *hubiéramos*: u-BIÉ-ra-mos, four syllables, stressed on the third from the end, so it needs the
  accent. *Hubiera* (u-BIE-ra) has none.
- *la traición*: trai-CIÓN, two syllables, since *ai* is one syllable.
- *reencontrarse*: re-en-con-TRAR-se, five syllables; the two *e*s are separate, though they blend
  in fast speech. *El reencuentro*: re-en-CUEN-tro.
- *los celos*: SE-los. *Leal*: le-AL, two syllables.

## Common mistakes

- The conditional after *ojalá*: ~~Ojalá no le habría dicho nada~~ → *Ojalá no le hubiera dicho
  nada*.
- The perfect subjunctive after a preterite main verb: *Me dolió que no me hayas invitado* is
  often heard in Latin America, especially about something recent, but it breaks the usual
  sequence of tenses. In writing, and in this course's answers, use *que no me hubieras invitado*
  (or *que no me invitaras*).
- The present or perfect subjunctive after *como si*: ~~como si no haya pasado nada~~ → *como si no
  hubiera pasado nada*.
- Forgetting the accent: ~~hubieramos~~ → *hubiéramos*.
- *Hubiese* for *habría* in a main clause: lesson 04 shows that *hubiera* can replace *habría*
  (*Me hubiera gustado*). You'll also see *me hubiese gustado*, more often in Spain; the RAE's
  *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* admits it in the result of a condition but prefers *hubiera*.
  In Mexico it is rare, so this course writes *habría* or *hubiera*.

## Key points

- Pluperfect subjunctive: *hubiera, hubieras, hubiera, hubiéramos, hubieran* + participle (*-se*:
  *hubiese…*, accepted).
- After a past or conditional main verb, for an earlier event: *Me dolió que no me hubieras
  invitado; Me habría gustado que me lo hubieras contado.* The imperfect subjunctive is also common
  when the order is clear.
- *Ojalá* + pluperfect subjunctive = a regret: *Ojalá no le hubiera dicho nada.*
- *Como si* + imperfect subjunctive (same time) or pluperfect subjunctive (earlier): *Me saludó como
  si no hubiera pasado nada.*
- Sequence of tenses: present-type main verb → present or perfect subjunctive; past or conditional
  → imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. A present main verb can take a past subjunctive for a past
  event: *No creo que lo dijera ayer.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Si hubiera salido antes…: past and mixed conditions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

With the pluperfect subjunctive from lesson 03 you can now say the sentence every language needs
for regret and relief: "If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the flight." B1 taught two
kinds of **[[si clause]]** (*si llueve, nos quedamos*; *si tuviera tiempo, viajaría*) and the
**[[conditional perfect]]** in phrases (*Con más tiempo, lo habría terminado*). This lesson joins them:
past conditions, **[[mixed conditionals]]** that cross from the past to the present, and the compact
*de* + infinitive. The theme is decisions, chance and turning points. This lesson unlocks the
conditional-perfect drill.

## Past conditions: what didn't happen

To imagine a different past, use *si* + pluperfect subjunctive, and the conditional perfect for
the result:

| *si* + pluperfect subjunctive | conditional perfect | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Si hubiera salido antes,* | *no habría perdido el vuelo.* | If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have missed the flight. |
| *Si me lo hubieras dicho,* | *te habría ayudado.* | If you had told me, I would have helped you. |
| *Si no hubiéramos revisado el pronóstico,* | *nos habría agarrado la tormenta.* | If we hadn't checked the forecast, the storm would have caught us. |

Either clause can come first. When the *si* clause comes first, put a comma after it: *Te habría
ayudado si me lo hubieras dicho* / *Si me lo hubieras dicho, te habría ayudado.*

### *Hubiera* in the result

In the result clause you will very often hear, and read, *hubiera* + participle in place of
*habría*: *Si hubiera salido antes, no hubiera perdido el vuelo.* It is very common, especially in
the Americas, and the RAE and ASALE's *Nueva gramática* accepts it. The *-ra* form is the one that
usually does this job. *Hubiese* is normal in the *si* clause (*si hubiese salido*); in the result it
is much rarer, especially in Mexico, and the RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* admits it there
but prefers *hubiera*. This course writes *habría* in the result and accepts *hubiera*.

## Mixed conditionals

The past and the present don't have to match. A mixed conditional joins a condition in one
time with a result in another:

- Past condition → present result: *si* + pluperfect subjunctive, then the conditional.
  - *Si hubiera estudiado medicina, ahora sería médica.* — If I had studied medicine, I would be a
    doctor now.
  - *Si no nos hubiéramos mudado, hoy viviríamos en Toluca.* — If we hadn't moved, we'd be living
    in Toluca today.
- Lasting condition → past result: *si* + imperfect subjunctive (something that is generally
  true, now and before), then the conditional perfect.
  - *Si fuera más prudente, no habría tenido el accidente.* — If he were more careful, he wouldn't
    have had the accident.
  - *Si no tuviera tanto miedo a volar, habría ido a tu boda.* — If I weren't so afraid of flying,
    I would have gone to your wedding.

Ask two questions: *When is the condition?* and *When is the result?* Then choose each tense
separately.

![A chart titled Las condiciones con si, with columns tipo, si + … and resultado, and an example under each row. Real (A2): present, then present, future or command; Si llueve, nos quedamos. Hypothetical (B1): imperfect subjunctive, then conditional; Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría. Past (lesson 04, highlighted): pluperfect subjunctive, then conditional perfect or hubiera; Si hubiera salido antes, no habría perdido el vuelo. Mixed, past to now: pluperfect subjunctive, then conditional; Si hubiera estudiado medicina, ahora sería médica. Mixed, always to past: imperfect subjunctive, then conditional perfect; Si fuera más prudente, no habría tenido el accidente.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## *De* + infinitive

In writing and careful speech, *de* + infinitive can replace a *si* clause. It works when the
subject is clear from the rest of the sentence:

- *De ser así, te aviso.* — If that's the case, I'll let you know. (= *Si es así…*)
- *De seguir así, vamos a llegar tarde.* — If this goes on, we'll be late.
- *De haberlo sabido, te habría avisado.* — Had I known, I would have told you. (B1 honors' *de
  haberlo sabido*; = *Si lo hubiera sabido…*)
- *De no haber llovido, habríamos ido a la playa.* — If it hadn't rained, we'd have gone to the
  beach.

The compound form, *de haber* + participle, is the past condition; the simple infinitive covers
real or hypothetical conditions about now or later. Pronouns attach to *haber*: *de haberlo
sabido*.

*De no haber sido por* + a noun or pronoun means "if it hadn't been for":

- *De no haber sido por ti, me habría perdido.* — If it hadn't been for you, I would have gotten lost.
- *De no haber sido por el GPS, habríamos llegado a otro pueblo.* — If it hadn't been for the GPS,
  we would have ended up in another town.

In speech, *si no hubiera sido por ti* is more usual; both are correct.

## Two things not to copy

- The conditional in an "if" clause. In some regions people say *si habría sabido* or *si
  tendría tiempo* in casual speech. It isn't standard: after *si* meaning "if", use the subjunctive
  (*si hubiera sabido*). A *si* that means "whether" is different and can take the conditional: *No
  sé si habría venido* (I don't know whether she would have come).
- The present subjunctive after "if" (~~si tenga~~): standard Spanish never uses it.

## Speculating, regretting, justifying

- *¿Qué habría pasado si no hubieras aceptado el trabajo?* — What would have happened if you hadn't
  taken the job?
- *Si lo hubiera previsto, habría hecho otra reservación.* — If I had foreseen it, I would have
  made another reservation.
- *No me arrepiento: si no me hubiera arriesgado, hoy no tendría mi negocio.* — I don't regret it:
  if I hadn't taken the risk, I wouldn't have my business today.
- *Hice lo que pude. De lo contrario, habría sido peor.* — I did what I could. Otherwise, it would
  have been worse.
- *¡Menos mal que llevabas paraguas!* — Thank goodness you had an umbrella!

## Words for decisions and chance

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *estar en una encrucijada; tener un dilema* | to be at a crossroads; to have a dilemma |
| *no tener alternativa; una decisión arriesgada* | to have no choice; a risky decision |
| *seguir la intuición / el instinto* | to follow one's intuition / instinct |
| *prever; la previsión; un imprevisto* | to foresee; foresight; something unexpected |
| *acertar; fue un acierto* | to get it right; it was a good choice |
| *desaprovechar una oportunidad; evitar un error* | to waste an opportunity; to avoid a mistake |
| *la suerte; un golpe de suerte; al azar* | luck; a stroke of luck; at random |
| *un punto de inflexión; el efecto dominó* | a turning point; the domino effect |
| *salir bien / mal; me fue fatal* | to turn out well / badly; it went terribly for me |
| *desgraciadamente; menos mal* | sadly; thank goodness |

*Prever* is conjugated like *ver*: *preveo, prevé, previsto, prevea*; the imperfect is *preveía*.
There is no verb "preveer".

## Three "what if" stories

### 1. *Un efecto dominó* (a past condition)

> La noche antes de la boda de su hermana, Tomás no puso el despertador. Si lo hubiera puesto, se
> habría levantado a tiempo; si se hubiera levantado a tiempo, no habría perdido el vuelo de las
> seis a Mérida. Fue un efecto dominó: tomó el siguiente vuelo, que salió con retraso,
> y llegó a la iglesia cuando los novios ya estaban saliendo. Desgraciadamente, se perdió la
> ceremonia. Pero en el aeropuerto compartió taxi con Paula, una ingeniera que también iba a la boda
> y que también había tenido un imprevisto. De no haber sido por ese retraso, nunca se habrían
> conocido. Hoy tienen una empresa juntos. ¿Fue el azar o un golpe de suerte? Tomás dice que las
> dos cosas.

### 2. *La encrucijada de Alma* (past condition → present result)

> A los dieciocho años, Alma estaba en una encrucijada: estudiar medicina, como quería su padre, o
> música, como quería ella. Era una decisión arriesgada, pero siguió su intuición y eligió la
> música. Si hubiera estudiado medicina, hoy sería médica y seguramente ganaría más dinero. Pero si
> no hubiera entrado al conservatorio, hoy no tocaría el violín en la orquesta de Xalapa, que es lo
> que más le gusta en el mundo. ¿Desaprovechó una carrera segura? Ella cree que no. Para Alma,
> aquella decisión fue el mayor acierto de su vida y el punto de inflexión que la convirtió en la
> persona que es.

### 3. *Raúl y su instinto* (lasting condition → past result)

> Raúl no es una persona prudente: nunca revisa el pronóstico, nunca lleva agua y confía demasiado
> en su instinto. El sábado pasado salió a caminar por el bosque, y le fue fatal: se quedó
> sin batería y sin agua a mitad del camino. Si fuera más prudente, habría cargado el celular antes
> de salir. Si no fuera tan orgulloso, habría regresado cuando empezó a llover. Al final todo salió
> bien: otros caminantes lo encontraron y lo acompañaron al pueblo. Menos mal. Ahora promete que va
> a prever todo, aunque sus amigos no le creen. "Llévate agua la próxima vez", le dijeron. "De lo
> contrario, no te esperamos."

Translation:

> (1) The night before his sister's wedding, Tomás didn't set the alarm clock. If he
> had set it, he would have gotten up on time; if he had gotten up on time, he
> wouldn't have missed the six o'clock flight to Mérida. It was a domino effect: he took the next
> flight, which left late, and got to the church as the bride and groom were walking out. Sadly, he
> missed the ceremony. But at the airport he shared a taxi with Paula, an engineer who was also going
> to the wedding and who had also had something unexpected happen. If it hadn't been for that delay,
> they would never have met. Today they run a company together. Was it chance or a stroke of luck?
> Tomás says both.
>
> (2) At eighteen, Alma was at a crossroads: study medicine, as her father
> wanted, or music, as she wanted. It was a risky decision, but she followed her intuition and chose
> music. If she had studied medicine, she would be a doctor today and would probably earn more money.
> But if she hadn't gotten into the conservatory, she wouldn't be playing the violin in the Xalapa
> orchestra today, which is what she loves most in the world. Did she waste a safe career? She thinks
> not. For Alma, that decision was the best choice of her life and the turning point that made her
> the person she is.
>
> (3) Raúl isn't a careful person: he never checks the forecast, never
> carries water and trusts his instinct too much. Last Saturday he went walking in the forest, and
> it went terribly for him: his battery died and he ran out of water halfway. If he were more careful, he
> would have charged his phone before leaving. If he weren't so proud, he would have turned back when
> it started to rain. In the end everything turned out fine: other hikers found him and walked with
> him to the village. Thank goodness. Now he promises he's going to plan for everything, although his
> friends don't believe him. "Take water next time," they told him. "Otherwise, we won't wait for you."

In story 2, *si hubiera estudiado* (past) leads to *sería* and *tocaría* (now). In story 3, *si
fuera más prudente* describes Raúl in general, and the results (*habría cargado, habría regresado*)
are about last Saturday.

![A branching diagram titled Una mañana, dos caminos. At the top: La noche antes: ¿pongo el despertador? The left branch, in solid boxes, is what happened (lo que pasó): No lo puse; Perdí el vuelo de las seis; Compartí taxi con Paula; Hoy tenemos una empresa (preterite, present). The right branch, in dashed boxes, is what would have happened (lo que habría pasado): Si lo hubiera puesto…; …habría tomado el vuelo; …no habría conocido a Paula; …hoy no tendría la empresa (pluperfect subjunctive with the conditional perfect or conditional).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *habría, habríamos*: a-BRÍ-a, a-BRÍ-a-mos; the *í* is a separate syllable.
- *hubiéramos*: u-BIÉ-ra-mos. In *si hubiera* the two vowels often link into one syllable in speech: siu-BIE-ra.
- *la encrucijada*: en-cru-ci-JA-da, five syllables; the *j* is usually softer in Mexico than in
  Spain.
- *prever, prevé, prevén*: pre-BER, pre-BÉ, pre-BÉN; *b* and *v* sound the same.

## Common mistakes

- The conditional after *si* ("if"): ~~Si habría sabido~~ → *Si hubiera sabido*.
- The simple conditional for a past result: ~~Si hubiera salido antes, no perdería el vuelo~~ → *no
  habría perdido* (unless you mean a present result, as in a mixed conditional).
- *Hubiese* in the result: you may see *no hubiese perdido*, more often in Spain; the DPD admits
  it but prefers *hubiera*, and it is rare in Mexico. Say *no habría perdido* or *no hubiera
  perdido*.
- "Preveer": the verb is *prever* (*preveo, previó, previsto*).
- *De* + infinitive with a pronoun in the wrong place: ~~De lo haber sabido~~ → *De haberlo sabido*.

## Key points

- Past condition: *si* + pluperfect subjunctive + conditional perfect: *Si hubiera salido antes, no
  habría perdido el vuelo.* *Hubiera* is also used in the result (very common in the Americas);
  *hubiese* there is rare in Mexico.
- Mixed: past → present (*Si hubiera estudiado medicina, ahora sería médica*); lasting → past (*Si
  fuera más prudente, no habría tenido el accidente*).
- Either clause first; a comma after a *si* clause that comes first.
- *De* + infinitive: *de ser así, de haberlo sabido*; *de no haber sido por ti*.
- After *si* meaning "if": no conditional, no present subjunctive.

lessons.title: Honors: Una vida en pocas líneas: obituaries, death notices and tributes
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 told lives in four past tenses and in the historical present. Some of the most carefully
written life stories in any newspaper are the ones published when a life ends. This honors lesson
reads three genres you will meet in Mexican newspapers, websites and ceremonies: the short paid
death notice (*la esquela*), the journalistic obituary (*la necrológica*, more often called
*el obituario* in Mexico) and the spoken tribute (*las palabras de despedida*, a farewell
speech). You'll see their set formulas, how the tenses work in each, the register that shows
respect, and the customs that surround a death in much of Mexico. Everything here uses grammar you
already have; the new skill is reading and writing a genre with strict rules.

## The death notice (*la esquela*)

An *esquela* is a short notice, paid for by the family, colleagues or an institution, that
announces a death and the arrangements. In Mexico it is often framed in a black border and topped
by a cross or another symbol, though many families now choose none. Its language is fixed and
formal:

| Part | Typical wording | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| opening | *Con profundo pesar…* / *Con profundo dolor…* | With deep sorrow… |
| the news | *…comunicamos el sensible fallecimiento de la señora…* | …we announce the sad death of Mrs.… |
| a blessing | *…acaecido el día 3 de mayo. Descanse en paz.* | …which occurred on May 3. May she rest in peace. |
| the family | *Sus hijos, nietos y demás familiares…* | Her children, grandchildren and other relatives… |
| arrangements | *Sus restos serán velados en…; el sepelio se llevará a cabo en el panteón…* | The wake will be held at… (literally, her remains will be watched over); the burial will take place at the cemetery… |

Three features stand out. First, the death is a noun, not a verb: *el sensible fallecimiento*
(*sensible* here = sad, regrettable, as in many Mexican notices), not *murió*. Second, the
arrangements are in the passive and the future (*serán velados, se llevará a cabo*), the language
of official announcements. Third, the dead person is treated with titles: *la señora*, *el
licenciado*, *la maestra*, *el ingeniero*, or *don* / *doña* before the first name.

Colleagues and institutions publish their own *esquelas* to share the family's grief: *La
dirección y el personal de… lamentan el fallecimiento de…* and *nos unimos a la pena de su
familia* (we share the sorrow of his family). B1's *que en paz descanse* (may he / she rest in
peace) is the spoken version of *descanse en paz*; in writing you'll also see the initials *Q.E.P.D.*

![A newspaper death notice in a thick black border. At the top, a small cross. Then: Con profundo pesar comunicamos el sensible fallecimiento de la señora Rosa María Treviño Garza (1938–2026), acaecido el 3 de mayo en Monterrey, N. L. Descanse en paz. Sus hijos Jorge y Elena, sus nietos y demás familiares. Below a line: Velorio: Capillas San José, sala 4, a partir de las 17:00. Sepelio: 4 de mayo, 11:00, Panteón del Carmen.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: writing an esquela

Ana's grandfather, Héctor Salinas, has died in Puebla at 91. The family wants a short notice.
Build it part by part.

1. Opening and news, with a title and the formal noun: *Con profundo pesar comunicamos el sensible
   fallecimiento del señor Héctor Salinas Ortega, acaecido el 12 de octubre en Puebla, Pue.*
2. A blessing: *Descanse en paz.*
3. The family as the subject of a second sentence: *Sus hijos Ana y Luis, sus nietos y demás
   familiares agradecen sus muestras de cariño.* (thank you for your expressions of affection)
4. Arrangements in the future, with the passive or *se*: *Sus restos serán velados hoy en Funerales
   del Sur. La misa de cuerpo presente se celebrará mañana a las 10:00.* (*la misa de cuerpo
   presente* = the funeral Mass with the body present)

Notice what is missing: no life story, no adjectives about his character, no first person singular.
That is the job of the next genre.

## The obituary (*la necrológica*, *el obituario*)

An obituary is journalism: a short life story of a known person, written by the newspaper. It
starts with the news (who, when, where, at what age), then tells the life, often in the historical
present or the preterite, and ends with the *legado*. Typical moves:

- the news, in the preterite: *Falleció ayer en la Ciudad de México, a los 84 años, la arquitecta…*
  (subject after the verb, as in many news openings);
- the life, with dates: *Nace en Oaxaca en 1942; estudia en la UNAM; en 1970 funda…*;
- background in the imperfect: *En aquel entonces, pocas mujeres trabajaban en la construcción.*
- earlier events in the pluperfect: *Ya había recibido el Premio Nacional cuando…*
- recognition, including posthumous honors: *una obra póstuma* (published after death), *un
  homenaje póstumo*;
- the closing, often about her legacy: *Su legado sigue vivo en…*

Obituaries are respectful but not always solemn. A good one includes an anecdote and lets the
person's own words speak, in quotation marks.

### Example 2: an obituary of a fictional teacher

> Falleció el pasado domingo en Xalapa, a los 79 años, la maestra Teresa Ochoa Luna, fundadora de la
> primera biblioteca pública de su colonia. Nacida en 1947 en Coatepec, Teresa se tituló como
> profesora de primaria en 1966 y durante cuarenta años dio clases en escuelas de la región. En
> aquel entonces muchas familias no tenían libros en casa, así que en 1979 convirtió la sala de su
> propia casa en una biblioteca abierta a los vecinos. A lo largo de los años, la biblioteca prestó
> más de veinte mil libros. Sus exalumnos la recuerdan como una maestra exigente y generosa. "No hay
> niño que no lea; hay niños que no han encontrado su libro", solía decir. El próximo sábado, la
> colonia le rendirá homenaje con una lectura en voz alta. Descanse en paz.

Translation:

> Teacher Teresa Ochoa Luna, founder of the first public library in her neighborhood, died last
> Sunday in Xalapa at the age of 79. Born in 1947 in Coatepec, Teresa qualified as a primary school
> teacher in 1966 and for forty years taught in schools in the region. Back then many families had no
> books at home, so in 1979 she turned the living room of her own house into a library open to the
> neighbors. Over the years, the library lent more than twenty thousand books. Her former students
> remember her as a demanding and generous teacher. "There's no child who doesn't read; there are
> children who haven't found their book," she used to say. Next Saturday, the neighborhood will pay
> tribute to her with a reading aloud. May she rest in peace.

Look at the structure: news (*falleció*), life (preterite for events, *tenían* and *solía decir*
for background and habit), a quotation, and the tribute in the future (*le rendirá homenaje*). Her
quotation contrasts the moods: *no hay niño que no lea* (subjunctive: no such child exists) and *hay
niños que no han encontrado su libro* (indicative: those children do exist).

## A real life in brief: Lola Beltrán

A dated summary of the kind you'll find in an anniversary article, in the historical present.
(Facts as reported by the news agency EFE in 2021.)

> María Lucila Beltrán Ruiz, conocida como Lola Beltrán, nace en Sinaloa el 7 de marzo de 1931
> (algunas fuentes dicen 1932). En los años cincuenta trabaja como secretaria en la XEW, la radio
> más influyente de la época, y allí conoce a productores y artistas que le abren el camino. Graba
> más de setenta discos, protagoniza al menos sesenta películas y la llaman "la Reina de la canción
> ranchera" y "Lola la Grande". Según EFE, es la primera cantante de música folclórica que se
> presenta en el Palacio de Bellas Artes. Fallece el 24 de marzo de 1996, a los 65 años.

Translation:

> María Lucila Beltrán Ruiz, known as Lola Beltrán, is born in Sinaloa on March 7, 1931 (some
> sources say 1932). In the 1950s she works as a secretary at XEW, the most influential radio station
> of the time, and there she meets producers and artists who open the way for her. She records more
> than seventy albums, stars in at least sixty films and is called "the Queen of ranchera song" and
> "Lola the Great". According to EFE, she is the first folk singer to perform at the Palacio de
> Bellas Artes. She dies on March 24, 1996, at the age of 65.

The hedges are part of the genre done well: *algunas fuentes dicen*, *según EFE*, *al menos*.

## The tribute (*las palabras de despedida*)

At a funeral, a memorial or a later homage, a family member or colleague may say a few words. The
register is warmer: first person, direct address to the dead person, and the full range of the
subjunctive for feelings and regrets you learned in lessons 02 and 03.

### Example 3: a granddaughter's words

> Buenas tardes a todos, y gracias por acompañarnos. Mi abuela Rosa María nos enseñó a cocinar, a
> discutir sin pelearnos y a no dejar nunca a nadie solo en un velorio. Me alegra que tantos de
> ustedes hayan venido desde lejos: ella habría estado feliz de verlos juntos. Ojalá le hubiera
> preguntado más sobre su juventud; siempre pensé que habría tiempo. Abuela, gracias por todo.
> Te vamos a extrañar.

Translation:

> Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for being with us. My grandmother Rosa María taught us to
> cook, to argue without fighting and never to leave anyone alone at a wake. I'm glad that so many of
> you have come from far away: she would have been happy to see you together. I wish I had asked her
> more about her youth; I always thought there would be time. Grandma, thank you for everything. We're
> going to miss you.

The grammar map: *me alegra que hayan venido* (present + perfect subjunctive, lesson 02); *habría
estado feliz* (conditional perfect, an unreal past); *ojalá le hubiera preguntado* (a regret, lesson
03).

## Customs around a death in Mexico

Customs vary by region, religion and family, so read this as a description of what is often done,
not as rules.

- *El velorio* (the wake): the family and friends keep watch over the body, at home or in a
  funeral home (*una funeraria*, *unas capillas de velación*), often through the night, with coffee,
  sweet bread and quiet conversation. Spain usually says *el velatorio*. Many people consider it
  important to go *dar el pésame* (B1: to offer condolences) in person.
- *El sepelio* (formal) or *el entierro* (everyday): the burial, often the day after the death,
  in *el panteón* (the usual Mexican word for a cemetery; *el cementerio* is general). Cremation is
  also common.
- *El novenario*: in Catholic families, nine days of prayers, usually including the rosary, after
  the death; a Mass is often celebrated when it ends.
- *El luto* (mourning): the outward signs and period of mourning, such as wearing black (*vestirse
  de luto*); *estar de luto* = to be in mourning. *El duelo* is the grief itself and the process of
  living through it (*vivir el duelo*).
- Later, *la lápida* (the headstone) is placed on the grave, and on the Día de Muertos (A1's
  honors theme) many families visit the *panteón* with flowers and food.

## Register and respect

- Use *usted* and titles with the family you don't know well: *Mi más sentido pésame, señora.*
- Avoid euphemisms that sound flippant (*se fue al otro mundo*) in writing; *falleció* and *nos dejó*
  are respectful.
- In a notice, keep the formulas; in a tribute, be personal and short.
- Say *el difunto / la difunta* (B1) or the person's name; *el muerto* sounds blunt in a formal text.

## Common mistakes

- A verb where the genre wants a noun: in an esquela, *comunicamos el sensible fallecimiento de…*,
  not ~~comunicamos que murió…~~ (correct Spanish, but not the genre's style).
- Mixing the historical present and the preterite in one life summary: choose one.
- *Póstumo* and *póstuma* agree with the noun: *una obra póstuma, un homenaje póstumo*.
- *El duelo* vs *el luto*: you *vives el duelo* (grief), and you *estás de luto* (mourning, with its
  outward signs).
- The present perfect for the dated death in a Mexican text: *falleció ayer*, not ~~ha fallecido
  ayer~~.

## Key points

- *La esquela*: a paid notice with fixed formulas (*Con profundo pesar…, el sensible fallecimiento
  de…, Descanse en paz*), titles, and arrangements in the future and passive (*serán velados, el
  sepelio se llevará a cabo*).
- *La necrológica / el obituario*: journalism; news in the preterite, the life in the preterite or
  historical present, the *legado* at the end; hedge facts that sources disagree on.
- The tribute: first person, warm, with the subjunctive of feelings (*Me alegra que hayan venido*)
  and regret (*Ojalá le hubiera preguntado…*).
- Customs (often, not always): *el velorio*, *el sepelio* in *el panteón* or cremation, *el
  novenario*, *el luto*; *rendir homenaje* to someone later.
