lessons.title: Honors: Tenses you'll only read: the pretérito anterior, the literary -ra and the future subjunctive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 01–04 gave you every past tense that Mexicans use in speech and in ordinary writing. Open a
nineteenth-century novel, a colonial chronicle, a law or a contract, though, and you will meet
three forms that no one uses in conversation:

- the **[[pretérito anterior]]**: *hubo terminado* (had finished, just before);
- the *-ra* form used as a pluperfect indicative: *la casa que construyera su abuelo* (the house
  his grandfather had built);
- the **[[future subjunctive]]**: *fuere, hubiere, tuviere*.

This honors lesson teaches you to recognize them and to translate them into modern Spanish. You
won't need to produce them: in your own Spanish, always use the modern equivalent. They are useful
for reading the classics (*los clásicos*), historical novels and legal Spanish, and for
understanding a handful of set phrases that are still alive today.

## The pretérito anterior

### Form and meaning

It is the preterite of *haber* + a participle:

| | *haber* (preterite) | + participle |
|---|---|---|
| yo | hube | terminado |
| tú | hubiste | llegado |
| él, ella, usted | hubo | salido |
| nosotros, nosotras | hubimos | comido |
| (vosotros, vosotras) | (hubisteis) | (visto) |
| ellos, ellas, ustedes | hubieron | dicho |

It says that one past action ended *immediately* before another. It almost always follows a time
word: *apenas* (B1: as soon as, barely), *no bien* (no sooner), *en cuanto, luego que, así que,
tan pronto como, cuando, después que*.

- *Apenas hubo terminado la misa, el pueblo salió a la plaza.* — As soon as Mass had ended, the
  townspeople went out into the square.
- *No bien hubieron llegado los soldados, comenzó la lluvia.* — No sooner had the soldiers arrived
  than the rain began.

### Modern equivalents

Today, educated speakers replace it with the preterite (most often) or the pluperfect:

| Literary | Modern |
|---|---|
| *Apenas hubo terminado, se fue.* | *Apenas terminó, se fue.* / *En cuanto terminó, se fue.* |
| *Cuando hubieron comido, salieron.* | *Cuando terminaron de comer, salieron.* / *Después de comer, salieron.* |
| *No bien hubo llegado, empezó a llover.* | *En cuanto llegó, empezó a llover.* |

The pretérito anterior is practically absent from speech today and uncommon even in writing. You'll find it in the prose of the nineteenth and early twentieth
centuries and in writers who imitate an older style.

## The literary *-ra* with pluperfect meaning

The *-ra* form (*construyera, dijera*) comes from the Latin pluperfect indicative, and for centuries
it kept that meaning. That old use survives in literature and in some journalism, mostly in
relative clauses:

- *Vivía en la casa que construyera su abuelo.* = *…que había construido su abuelo.* — He lived in
  the house his grandfather had built.
- *El escritor, que naciera en Puebla en 1890, murió en el exilio.* = *…que había nacido…* — The
  writer, who had been born in Puebla in 1890, died in exile.

Here the form is **[[indicative]]** in meaning: nothing triggers a subjunctive. Read it as "had" +
participle. In news writing, some style guides advise against it and recommend the pluperfect or the
preterite; in literature it is a recognized stylistic choice, not a mistake.

Don't confuse it with two everyday uses of *-ra* you already know: the imperfect subjunctive
(*Quería que vinieras*) and the polite *quisiera* (I'd like).

## The future subjunctive

### Form

Take the *ellos* preterite, drop *-ron*, and add *-re, -res, -re, -remos, -ren* (the *nosotros*
form has an accent, as in the imperfect subjunctive):

| infinitive | *ellos* preterite | future subjunctive (yo / él) | nosotros |
|---|---|---|---|
| *ser, ir* | *fueron* | *fuere* | *fuéremos* |
| *haber* | *hubieron* | *hubiere* | *hubiéremos* |
| *tener* | *tuvieron* | *tuviere* | *tuviéremos* |
| *hacer* | *hicieron* | *hiciere* | *hiciéremos* |
| *ver* | *vieron* | *viere* | *viéremos* |

It looks like the *-ra* subjunctive with an *e*: *fuera* → *fuere*. That makes it easy to spot.

### Where it lives

It once referred to a possible future event in conditions and relative clauses. Historians of the
language generally agree that by the eighteenth century it had largely disappeared from speech, and the present subjunctive (or the present
indicative after *si*) took its place. It survives in three places:

1. Old texts and solemn style: chronicles, the classics, a formal oath.
2. Some legal and administrative writing, especially older laws and contracts: *El que
   incumpliere esta disposición será sancionado* = *El que incumpla…* (Whoever breaks this rule
   will be penalized). Modern Mexican laws usually prefer the present subjunctive, but older wording
   is still quoted and kept.
3. Set phrases that are still in use: *sea cual fuere* beside the modern *sea cual sea* (whatever
   it may be); *venga de donde viniere* (wherever it may come from); and the proverb *Adonde fueres,
   haz lo que vieres*, the Spanish "When in Rome, do as the Romans do", which keeps its old verbs
   only because it is a fixed saying.

| Old | Modern |
|---|---|
| *Si alguien preguntare por mí, díganle que…* | *Si alguien pregunta por mí, díganle que…* |
| *El que tuviere hambre, que coma.* | *El que tenga hambre, que coma.* |
| *Sea cual fuere el resultado…* | *Sea cual sea el resultado…* |

Note *sea cual sea* agrees in the plural: *sean cuales sean las razones* (whatever the reasons may
be).

![A three-row chart titled Leer en literario, escribir en moderno. Each row has an arrow from what you read (recognize) to what you write (produce). Pretérito anterior: apenas hubo terminado, to apenas terminó. -ra with pluperfect meaning: la casa que construyera su abuelo, to la casa que había construido su abuelo. Future subjunctive: sea cual fuere, el que incumpliere, to sea cual sea, el que incumpla. A note at the bottom: reconocer, no producir; in your Spanish, use the modern form.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Where you'll meet them: some dated facts

- *El Siglo de Oro* (Spain's Golden Age of literature) is usually placed in the sixteenth and
  seventeenth centuries; scholars date its start and end differently. Its prose (*la prosa*) and plays use
  the future subjunctive freely.
- The chronicles of the conquest of Mexico: Hernán Cortés wrote his *Cartas de relación* to
  Charles V between 1519 and 1526. Bernal Díaz del Castillo, who had fought with Cortés, wrote his
  *Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España* in old age in Guatemala; he probably
  finished it around 1568, and the manuscript was first printed in Madrid in 1632. Modern editions
  usually keep the old verb forms and modernize the spelling.
- Historical novels (*la novela histórica*) written today sometimes imitate this style for flavor, and their authors
  mix old forms with modern ones.

## Worked examples

The passages below are original, written to imitate an old style. Each is followed by a modern
version and an English translation.

### Example 1: a chronicle

> No bien hubimos desembarcado, vinieron a nosotros unos señores de aquella tierra, y nos trajeron
> maíz y frutas. El capitán, que antes hablara con ellos por medio de una intérprete, les dio
> cuentas de vidrio. Y apenas hubo anochecido, mandó que nadie saliese del real, so pena de que
> el que saliere fuese castigado.

Modern Spanish: *En cuanto desembarcamos, vinieron unos señores de aquella tierra y nos trajeron
maíz y frutas. El capitán, que antes había hablado con ellos por medio de una intérprete, les dio
cuentas de vidrio. Y en cuanto anocheció, ordenó que nadie saliera del campamento: quien saliera
sería castigado.*

Translation: No sooner had we come ashore than some lords of that land came to us and brought us
corn and fruit. The captain, who had spoken with them earlier through an interpreter, gave them
glass beads. And as soon as night had fallen, he ordered that no one leave the camp, on pain of
punishment for anyone who did.

What to notice: *hubimos desembarcado, hubo anochecido* (pretérito anterior after *no bien,
apenas*); *hablara* = *había hablado* (literary *-ra*); *saliese* (an ordinary imperfect
subjunctive after *mandó que*, in its *-se* form); *el que saliere* (future subjunctive in a
relative clause about a possible future case). *El real* is an old word for an army camp, and *so
pena de* means "on pain of". Words like these are archaisms (*arcaísmos*), and the whole passage
sounds archaic (*arcaico*) to a modern reader.

### Example 2: a legal clause

> Artículo 12. El arrendatario que no pagare la renta dentro de los primeros cinco días de cada mes
> deberá cubrir un recargo del cinco por ciento. Si hubiere controversia, sea cual fuere su causa,
> las partes se someterán a los tribunales de esta ciudad.

Modern Spanish: *El arrendatario que no pague la renta…; Si hay alguna controversia, sea cual sea
su causa, las partes se someterán…*

Translation: Article 12. A tenant who does not pay the rent within the first five days of each month
must pay a five percent surcharge. Should any dispute arise, whatever its cause, the parties will
submit to the courts of this city.

What to notice: legal Spanish keeps the future subjunctive because it describes possible future
cases (*no pagare, hubiere*); the main verbs are future (*deberá, se someterán*). *El arrendatario*
= the tenant. Honors lesson 12h1 reads a modern regulation, where the present subjunctive is more
usual.

### Example 3: a historical novel

> Doña Inés abrió el arcón que le dejara su madre. Dentro, entre papeles amarillos, encontró el
> manuscrito: unas memorias que nadie había leído en cien años. Lo leyó de pie, sin respirar, y no
> bien hubo llegado a la última página, comprendió por qué su madre lo había escondido.

Modern Spanish: *…el arcón que le había dejado su madre… y en cuanto llegó a la última página,
comprendió…*

Translation: Doña Inés opened the chest her mother had left her. Inside, among yellowed papers, she
found the manuscript: a memoir no one had read in a hundred years. She read it standing up, holding
her breath, and no sooner had she reached the last page than she understood why her mother had
hidden it.

What to notice: a modern writer imitating an older, more solemn (*solemne*) prose: literary *-ra*
(*le dejara*), the pretérito anterior (*hubo llegado*) and, beside them, the ordinary pluperfect
(*había leído, había escondido*). *El arcón* = a large chest.

## Register: why these forms survive

They belong to *la lengua culta escrita*, educated written language. Writers use them to sound
historical, solemn or legal; readers recognize them as signs of a genre. In conversation they would
sound as odd as "whosoever" or "ere" in English.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *construyera* in *la casa que construyera su abuelo* as a subjunctive ("would build"): in
  this literary use it means *había construido*.
- Producing the pretérito anterior in your own writing: write *en cuanto terminó*, not *en cuanto
  hubo terminado*, unless you are deliberately imitating an old style.
- Mixing up *fuere* (future subjunctive) and *fuera* (imperfect subjunctive): *sea cual fuere* is a
  fixed formula; *sea cual fuera* is also found, but *sea cual sea* is the safe modern choice.
- Forgetting the plural: ~~sea cual sea las razones~~ → *sean cuales sean las razones*.
- Taking *no bien* as "not well": in *no bien llegó…* it means "no sooner".

## Key points

- Pretérito anterior: *hube, hubiste, hubo, hubimos, hubieron* + participle, after *apenas, no
  bien, en cuanto*; = an action just before another. Modern: the preterite (*en cuanto terminó*).
- Literary *-ra* = pluperfect indicative in relative clauses: *la casa que construyera su abuelo* =
  *que había construido*.
- Future subjunctive: *ellos* preterite minus *-ron* + *-re* (*fuere, hubiere, tuviere*); in old
  texts, some legal writing and set phrases (*sea cual fuere, Adonde fueres, haz lo que vieres*).
  Modern: the present subjunctive or, after *si*, the present indicative.
- Recognize all three; produce the modern equivalents.

lessons.title: No es que no me guste: opinions, value judgments and neuter lo
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 gave you all four subjunctive tenses. This module uses them to give opinions, judge,
soften claims, concede and guess.

You already know the basic rule from B1 lesson 04: *creo que* + indicative, *no creo que* +
subjunctive. At B2 you need three more things:

- **[[value judgments]]** (*es absurdo que, me parece lógico que…*), which take the subjunctive even
  when the fact is true;
- *no es que…, sino que…*, the standard way to correct a wrong idea about you;
- the **[[neuter lo]]** (*lo bueno, lo caro que es*), which turns an adjective into a topic.

The theme is consumer society: fashion, fast fashion (*la moda rápida*), minimalism and
secondhand clothes.

## Opinions: the B1 rule and its edges

An opinion verb that presents something as true takes the indicative; the same verb negated
takes the subjunctive:

- *Creo que el consumo de ropa es excesivo.* — I think clothing consumption is excessive.
- *No creo que el minimalismo sea para todos.* — I don't think minimalism is for everyone.
- *Me parece que esta chamarra es de segunda mano.* — I think this jacket is secondhand.
- *No me parece que sea un derroche.* — I don't think it's an extravagance.

Two places where the rule loosens (for recognition: you don't need to produce both):

- Questions. *¿Crees que es caro?* asks for an opinion; *¿Crees que sea caro?* sounds more
  doubtful. Both are correct, and you'll hear both.
- Negative commands. *No pienses que es fácil* and *No pienses que sea fácil* (Don't think
  it's easy) both occur. With the indicative, the speaker is usually telling you it isn't easy.

## Value judgments take the subjunctive

A **[[value judgment]]** is an expression that says how you rate a fact: logical, normal,
unfair, outrageous. In English the fact keeps its ordinary verb (*It's unfair that they earn so
little*), so learners keep the indicative. Spanish doesn't. After a value judgment the verb goes
into the subjunctive, even when everyone agrees the fact is true:

- *Es lógico que la ropa barata dure poco.* — It's logical that cheap clothes don't last long.
- *Es injusto que los trabajadores ganen tan poco.* — It's unfair that the workers earn so little.
- *Es absurdo que tiren ropa nueva.* — It's absurd that they throw away new clothes.
- *Es indignante que nadie haga nada.* — It's outrageous that nobody does anything.
- *Me parece razonable que pidan un descuento.* — I think it's reasonable that they ask for a
  discount.

The message is the judgment, not the fact, which the subjunctive marks as background. That's why
*me parece* changes mood: *Me parece que es caro* (an opinion: indicative) but *Me parece normal
que sea caro* (a judgment: subjunctive).

Other common judgments: *es normal, es raro, es una pena, es una vergüenza, está bien, está mal,
es mejor, es increíble que…*, also after *me parece*.

Expressions of certainty assert the fact, so they keep the indicative: *Es evidente que
consumimos demasiado.*

Two more patterns:

- Same subject or nobody in particular → infinitive. *Es absurdo gastar tanto* (It's absurd
  to spend so much). Add *que* + subjunctive only when someone specific does it: *Es absurdo que
  gastes tanto.*
- A past judgment → past subjunctive. The sequence of tenses from lesson 03 applies: *Era
  injusto que ganaran tan poco* (It was unfair that they earned so little); *Me pareció absurdo
  que lo hubieran tirado* (I thought it was absurd that they had thrown it away); and for
  something already done, the perfect subjunctive from lesson 02: *Es lógico que hayan subido los
  precios.*

![A chart titled "Opinion, certainty or value judgment?" in three columns. Left column, green, headed Opinion or certainty, indicativo: Creo que es caro. Me parece que es caro. Es evidente que es caro. Middle column, yellow, headed Opinion denied or doubted, subjuntivo: No creo que sea caro. No me parece que sea caro. No es verdad que sea caro. Right column, purple, headed Value judgment, subjuntivo even for facts: Es lógico que sea caro. Me parece normal que sea caro. Es injusto que sea caro. Along the bottom: same subject or general → infinitive: Es absurdo gastar tanto.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## *No es que…, sino que…*

To reject an explanation and give the real one, Spanish uses *no es que* + subjunctive (the idea
you deny) and *sino que* + indicative (the real reason, which you assert):

- *No es que no me guste la moda, sino que no tengo dinero.* — It's not that I don't like
  fashion; it's that I don't have any money.
- *No es que derroche, sino que todo está carísimo.* — It's not that I squander money; it's that
  everything is really expensive.

The *sino que* half is optional (*No es que no me guste…*, trailing off, is a polite refusal),
and in conversation *es que* often replaces it: *No es que no quiera, es que no puedo.*

## A *que* clause as the subject

When a *que* clause comes first as the subject of the sentence, it usually takes the
subjunctive, even when it states a fact. The speaker turns the fact into a topic and then
comments on it:

- *Que la ropa sea desechable me parece absurdo.* — That clothes are disposable seems absurd to me.

*El hecho de que* (the fact that) is similar, but both moods are used after it: the
subjunctive is the more frequent choice, especially at the start of the sentence, and the
indicative appears when the speaker stresses the fact as information. *El hecho de que sea
barato no significa que sea bueno* (The fact that it's cheap doesn't mean it's good).

## Neuter *lo*: turning an adjective into a topic

The **[[neuter lo]]** is *lo* used before an adjective or an adverb to talk about a quality or an
idea, not a thing. It has two patterns at B2.

### 1. *Lo* + adjective = "the … thing"

- *Lo bueno es que no cuesta mucho.* — The good thing is that it doesn't cost much.
- *Lo malo de la moda rápida es la calidad.* — The bad thing about fast fashion is the quality.

The adjective after *lo* is always masculine singular (*lo bueno*, never ~~lo buena~~). When *lo
bueno es que* presents a fact, the verb is indicative, as above. When the expression says what
would be best, it's a value judgment and takes the subjunctive: *Lo mejor es que la devuelvas*
(The best thing is for you to return it); *Lo lógico es que te reembolsen el dinero* (The logical thing is for them to refund your money).

### 2. *Lo* + adjective or adverb + *que* = "how …"

This is the B2 way to say "how expensive it is", "how fast it changes":

- *No sabes lo caro que es.* — You have no idea how expensive it is.
- *Me sorprende lo rápido que cambia la moda.* — It surprises me how fast fashion changes.
- *¡Lo ostentosa que es esa bolsa!* — How showy that bag is!

Here the adjective agrees with the noun it describes, even though *lo* stays the same: *lo
cara que es la ropa, lo caros que son los tenis, lo ostentosa que es*. An adverb doesn't change
(*lo rápido que cambia*, where *rápido* means "fast(ly)"). The verb after this *que* is normally
indicative, even after a feeling verb like *me sorprende*, because *lo … que* names a degree you
can see, not a separate event to react to.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the mood in opinions and judgments
  accDescr: Start with the main expression. If it is an opinion or a statement of certainty such as creo que, me parece que or es evidente que, use the indicative. If it is a negated opinion such as no creo que or no me parece que, use the subjunctive. If it is a value judgment such as es lógico que, es injusto que or me parece normal que, use the subjunctive even for a true fact, or the infinitive when no one in particular is meant. If it is no es que, use the subjunctive, and the indicative after sino que. If it is lo plus adjective plus que, meaning how, use the indicative.
  A{"What is the main expression?"} --> B["opinion or certainty: creo que, me parece que, es evidente que"]
  B --> B2["indicative"]
  A --> C["negated opinion: no creo que, no me parece que"]
  C --> C2["subjunctive"]
  A --> D["value judgment: es lógico que, es injusto que, me parece normal que"]
  D --> D2["subjunctive, even for facts; infinitive if no one in particular"]
  A --> E["no es que … sino que …"]
  E --> E2["subjunctive, then indicative"]
  A --> F["lo + adjective + que (how …)"]
  F --> F2["indicative"]
```

## Radio: *Línea abierta*

An invented call-in show on a Mexican radio station. Today's question: is secondhand clothing a
good idea? *La ropa de paca* is a common name in Mexico for used clothing that arrives in large
bales (*pacas*) and is sold at street markets (A1's *el tianguis*).

> LOCUTORA: Buenas tardes. Hoy hablamos de ropa de segunda mano. Tenemos la primera llamada.
>
> DANIELA: Hola, soy Daniela, de Monterrey. Yo compro casi todo en el tianguis, ropa de paca. Lo
> bueno es que encuentras prendas únicas. No sabes lo barata que es: una chamarra me costó 120
> pesos.
>
> LOCUTORA: ¿Y no te preocupa la calidad?
>
> DANIELA: Al contrario. Me parece absurdo que la gente tire ropa casi nueva. Prefiero
> reutilizar.
>
> LOCUTORA: Gracias, Daniela. Segunda llamada.
>
> ERNESTO: Buenas, habla Ernesto, de Puebla. No es que esté en contra, sino que no me da
> confianza. Y la verdad, mucha gente compra de marca para aparentar, por el estatus. Les importa
> más la apariencia que la calidad.
>
> LOCUTORA: ¿Usted cree que la ropa nueva da estatus?
>
> ERNESTO: No creo que dé estatus, pero así piensan muchos. Es comprensible que los jóvenes
> quieran verse bien.
>
> LOCUTORA: Tercera llamada.
>
> SOFÍA: Hola, soy Sofía, estudiante en la Ciudad de México. Me hice minimalista hace dos años:
> tengo treinta prendas. Lo difícil fue prescindir de las compras por impulso. Es lógico que
> cueste trabajo, porque todo el sistema te invita a consumir. Para mí, el minimalismo es un estilo
> de vida, y la moda rápida es un derroche.

Translation:

> HOST: Good afternoon. Today we're talking about secondhand clothes. We have the first call.
>
> DANIELA: Hi, I'm Daniela, from Monterrey. I buy almost everything at the street market,
> *ropa de paca*. The good thing is that you find unique pieces. You have no idea how cheap it is:
> a jacket cost me 120 pesos.
>
> HOST: And doesn't the quality worry you?
>
> DANIELA: On the contrary. I think it's absurd that people throw away almost new clothes. I'd
> rather reuse.
>
> HOST: Thank you, Daniela. Second call.
>
> ERNESTO: Hello, this is Ernesto, from Puebla. It's not that I'm against it; it's that I don't
> trust it. And honestly, a lot of people buy designer brands to keep up appearances, for the
> status. They care more about appearance than quality.
>
> HOST: Do you think new clothes give you status?
>
> ERNESTO: I don't think they give you status, but that's how a lot of people think. It's
> understandable that young people want to look good.
>
> HOST: Third call.
>
> SOFÍA: Hi, I'm Sofía, a student in Mexico City. I became a minimalist two years ago: I have
> thirty garments. The hard part was giving up impulse buying. It's logical that it's hard,
> because the whole system invites you to consume. For me, minimalism is a lifestyle, and fast
> fashion is an extravagance.

Notes: *la prenda* = garment, item of clothing; *habla Ernesto* = this is Ernesto (on the phone);
*de marca* = brand-name, designer; *no me da confianza* = I don't trust it; *verse bien* = to look
good; *hacerse* = to become (by choice); *costar trabajo* = to be hard (to do).

Notice *lo barata que es*, agreeing with *la ropa*. The host uses *usted* with Ernesto (*¿Usted
cree…?*) and *tú* with Daniela.

A fact behind the debate, from the UN Environment Programme (November 8, 2021): the fashion
industry is responsible for between 2% and 8% of global carbon emissions, and the number of times
a garment is worn before it is thrown away has fallen by 36%.

![A wooden closet with its doors open. On the shelf, a pair of folded jeans and a sign that reads Segunda mano, todo a 100 pesos. On the rail hang a dress, a jacket with buttons, a T-shirt and a sweater; a belt hangs from a hook on the left door; a pair of sneakers sits on the floor of the closet.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *superfluo*: three syllables, su-PER-fluo; the *uo* is a diphthong.
- *reutilizar*: in the present the stress falls on *-li-*: *reutilizo, reutiliza* (reuti-LI-za),
  never on the *u*, so no accent mark.
- *desechable*: de-se-CHA-ble, four syllables.
- *indignante*: in-dig-NAN-te; the *g* ends the syllable *dig*, as in *digno*, and never sounds like English *j*.
- *estatus*: es-TA-tus, stress on the middle syllable, unlike English "STAY-tus".

## Common mistakes

- Indicative after a judgment because the fact is true: ~~Es injusto que ganan poco~~ → *Es
  injusto que ganen poco.*
- Subjunctive after an affirmative opinion: ~~Creo que sea caro~~ → *Creo que es caro.* (*Me
  parece que* is an opinion; *me parece lógico que* is a judgment.)
- The adjective after *lo … que* not agreeing: ~~lo caro que son los tenis~~ → *lo caros que son
  los tenis.* But after plain *lo* it's always masculine singular: *lo bueno, lo malo.*
- Calquing English "how": ~~Me sorprende cómo caro es~~ → *Me sorprende lo caro que es.*
- *Sino* vs *sino que*: before a full clause with a verb it's *sino que* (*sino que no tengo
  dinero*); before a word or phrase it's *sino* (*No es caro, sino justo*).

## Key points

- Opinions and certainty (*creo que, me parece que, es evidente que*) take the indicative; their
  negatives take the subjunctive. In questions and negative commands both moods occur.
- Value judgments (*es lógico / normal / absurdo / injusto / comprensible / indignante que, me
  parece razonable que*) take the subjunctive even for true facts; with no particular subject,
  the infinitive.
- *No es que* + subjunctive, *sino que* + indicative.
- A *que* clause at the start usually takes the subjunctive; *el hecho de que* takes either.
- Neuter *lo*: *lo bueno es que* + indicative for a fact; *lo + adjective / adverb + que* = "how
  …", with the adjective agreeing and the indicative.
