lessons.title: No soportaba que…: feelings, attitudes and character in the past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In B1 lesson 03 you reacted to things with *gustar*-type verbs + *que* + subjunctive: *Me molesta
que no llames.* Those sentences were in the present. Real complaints are often about the past (the
roommate who never washed up, the neighbor who played music at two in the morning), so this lesson
puts feelings into every tense with the four subjunctive tenses from module 1. It also adds three
tools for talking about people: *caer bien / mal / gordo*, *ser* vs *estar* for character and
behavior, and *es de los que…*.

The theme is living together (*la convivencia*): roommates, family, neighbors and house rules.

## Feelings in every tense

The feeling verb sets the time; the verb after *que* follows the sequence of tenses from lesson
03.

| Main verb | Same time or later | Earlier |
|---|---|---|
| present: *me molesta, no soporto, me hace gracia* | present subjunctive: *que grite* | perfect subjunctive: *que haya gritado* |
| past: *me molestaba, no soportaba, me sentó mal, me hizo gracia* | imperfect subjunctive: *que gritara* | pluperfect subjunctive: *que hubiera gritado* |

- *Me molesta que dejes los trastes sucios.* — It bothers me that you leave the dishes dirty.
- *Me molesta que no me hayas avisado.* — It bothers me that you didn't let me know.
- *Me molestaba que dejara los trastes sucios.* — It used to bother me that he left the dishes
  dirty.
- *No soportaba que pusiera la música a todo volumen.* — I couldn't stand her playing music at
  full volume.
- *Me sentó mal que no me invitaran.* — It upset me that they didn't invite me.
- *Me sentó mal que se hubieran comido mi pastel.* — It upset me that they had eaten my cake.
- *Me hizo gracia que el perro se escondiera en la regadera.* — I found it funny that the dog hid
  in the shower.
- *Me daba igual que llegaran tarde.* — I didn't care if they came home late.

*Los trastes* is a very common everyday word for the dishes in Mexico (*lavar los trastes*); *los
platos* is understood everywhere.

Imperfect or preterite in the main verb? The same as always: the imperfect for an ongoing or
repeated feeling (*Me molestaba que…*, every time), the preterite for a reaction to one event
(*Me molestó que…*, that time). After both, the past subjunctive.

![A two-row chart titled "Feelings: the main verb sets the time". Top row, now: Me molesta que, then an arrow to two boxes: que grites (present subjunctive, same time) and que hayas gritado (perfect subjunctive, earlier). Bottom row, then: Me molestaba que / Me molestó que, then an arrow to two boxes: que gritaras (imperfect subjunctive, same time) and que hubieras gritado (pluperfect subjunctive, earlier). A note at the bottom: same subject → infinitive: No soporto gritar.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The new phrases

Three phrases from this lesson work exactly like *gustar*: the thing or person that causes the
feeling is the subject, and the person who feels it is an indirect-object pronoun.

- *sentar mal / bien* (to go down badly / well): *Le sentó mal que nadie le diera las gracias.*
  (It upset her that nobody thanked her.) *Sentar* is a stem changer: *me sienta, me sentó.*
- *hacer gracia* (to amuse): *Me hace gracia su acento* (I find his accent funny). *No me hace
  gracia* often means "I'm not thrilled": *No me hace gracia que traigas a tu novio todos los
  días.*
- *fastidiar* (to annoy) also works like *gustar*: *Me fastidia que…*

### Same subject: the infinitive

As with every feeling verb, when the person who feels and the person who acts are the same, use
the infinitive: *No soporto llegar tarde* (I can't stand being late; I'm the one who's late).
Compare *No soporto que llegues tarde* (you're the one who's late).

## *Caer bien, caer mal, caer gordo*

To say you like or dislike a person (not their actions), Spanish usually says the person *falls*
well or badly on you:

- *Me cae bien tu compañero de cuarto.* — I like your roommate. (Informally in Mexico: *tu
  roomie*.)
- *Mis vecinos me caen bien.* — I like my neighbors. (The verb agrees with *mis vecinos*.)
- *¿Te cayó mal mi hermana?* — Did you not like my sister?
- *El nuevo jefe me cae gordo.* — The new boss rubs me the wrong way.

*Caer gordo* is colloquial and stronger than *caer mal*; it's very common in Mexico, and the RAE's
student dictionary lists it without a regional mark. Notice that *gordo* agrees with the person
you dislike: *me cae gordo* (him), *me cae gorda* (her), *me caen gordos* (them). It says nothing
about anyone's weight.

*Caer bien* is the natural way to say you like someone as a person; *Me gusta Ana* can suggest
you're attracted to her.

## Character with *ser*, behavior with *estar*

*Ser* + adjective describes what someone is like; *estar* + the same adjective describes how
they're behaving or how they seem now, often against their usual character:

- *Memo es muy tranquilo.* — Memo is a very calm person.
- *Hoy Memo está insoportable.* — Today Memo is being unbearable.
- *Andrea es ordenada.* — Andrea is a tidy person. / *Su cuarto está ordenado.* — Her room is tidy
  (right now).
- *Es generosa, pero hoy está muy quisquillosa.* — She's generous, but today she's being very
  picky.
- *Lucía es tolerante, pero con la limpieza es terca.* — Lucía is tolerant, but she's stubborn
  about cleaning. (*Terco* describes character, so *ser*.)

B1's informal *estar de malas* (to be in a bad mood) has a "becoming" partner: *ponerse de malas*
(to get in a bad mood): *Se pone de malas cuando no hay café.*

## *Es de los que…*: describing someone by type

To describe a person by the group they belong to, Spanish says *es de los que* (he's one of those
who…) or *es de las que* for a woman, + the indicative:

- *Es de las que nunca llegan a tiempo.* — She's the kind of person who's never on time.
- *Memo es de los que lavan los trastes en cuanto terminan de comer.* — Memo is the type who
  washes the dishes as soon as he finishes eating.
- *Yo soy de los que piensan que hay que ceder un poco.* — I'm one of those people who think you
  have to give in a little.

The verb is usually plural, agreeing with *los que*; that's the form the RAE's *Diccionario
panhispánico de dudas* (*concordancia*, 4.11–4.12) prefers. The singular (*Es de las que nunca llega a
tiempo*) is also heard and accepted, though less recommended. What the DPD advises against is a first- or
second-person verb: ~~Yo soy de los que pienso~~, ~~Tú eres de los que nunca cedes~~.

## Group chat: *Depa 302*

Three roommates in Guadalajara share an apartment. Lucía has just found a problem in the
kitchen.

> Lucía: Chicos, ¿quién dejó la olla con frijoles en la estufa desde el viernes?
>
> Memo: Fui yo, perdón. Iba a lavarla, pero se me olvidó.
>
> Lucía: No es la primera vez. La semana pasada me sentó fatal que nadie sacara la basura.
>
> Andrea: A mí también me molestó, la verdad. Y no soportaba que el perro de Memo durmiera
> en el sillón.
>
> Memo: Oigan, tampoco es para tanto… Pero tienen razón, soy bastante desordenado.
>
> Lucía: No es que no me caigas bien, Memo, me caes muy bien. Pero así la convivencia no
> funciona.
>
> Andrea: Propongo un pacto. Repartimos la limpieza por días y lo pegamos en el refri.
>
> Memo: Va. Pero que conste que Lucía es de las que lavan un vaso a las tres de la mañana.
>
> Lucía: Jajaja, ok, tengo mis manías. Me hizo gracia que lo notaras.
>
> Andrea: Entonces el sábado lo escribimos. Hay que tener paciencia los tres.

Translation:

> Lucía: Guys, who left the pot of beans on the stove? It's been there since Friday.
>
> Memo: It was me, sorry. I was going to wash it, but I forgot.
>
> Lucía: It's not the first time. Last week it really upset me that nobody took out the trash.
>
> Andrea: It bothered me too, honestly. And I couldn't stand Memo's dog sleeping on the couch.
>
> Memo: Hey, it's not that big a deal… But you're right, I'm pretty messy.
>
> Lucía: It's not that I don't like you, Memo, I really like you. But living together doesn't
> work like this.
>
> Andrea: I propose a pact. We divide up the cleaning by days and stick it on the fridge.
>
> Memo: OK. But let it be on record that Lucía is the kind who washes a glass at three in the
> morning.
>
> Lucía: Hahaha, OK, I have my quirks. I found it funny that you noticed.
>
> Andrea: So we'll write it on Saturday. All three of us need to be patient.

Notes: *el depa* = informal for *el departamento* (apartment) in Mexico; *sentar fatal* = to go
down really badly (*fatal* = awful, informal: lesson 04); *tampoco es para tanto* = it's not that
big a deal; *¡Va!* = OK, deal (Mexico, informal); *que conste que…* = let it be noted that…; *el
refri* = the fridge (informal for *el refrigerador*).

## The house pact

On Saturday they wrote it and stuck it on the fridge.

> Pacto de convivencia del depa 302
>
> 1. La limpieza se reparte por días: lunes y jueves, Memo; martes y viernes, Andrea; miércoles y
> sábado, Lucía.
> 2. Quien cocina no lava los trastes, siempre que deje la cocina en orden.
> 3. Nada de música fuerte después de las once, a menos que haya fiesta y todos estén invitados.
> 4. El perro puede subir al sillón solo si tiene su cobija.
> 5. Si alguien no cumple, paga las pizzas del viernes.
> 6. Si algo te molesta, dilo pronto. Ceder un poco no es perder.

Translation:

> The apartment 302 living-together pact
>
> 1. The cleaning is divided up by days: Monday and Thursday, Memo; Tuesday and Friday, Andrea;
> Wednesday and Saturday, Lucía.
> 2. Whoever cooks doesn't wash the dishes, as long as they leave the kitchen tidy.
> 3. No loud music after eleven, unless there's a party and everyone is invited.
> 4. The dog can get on the couch only if it has its blanket.
> 5. If someone doesn't keep to it, they pay for Friday's pizzas.
> 6. If something bothers you, say so soon. Giving in a little isn't losing.

*Siempre que* (as long as) and *a menos que* (unless) are B1's condition connectors, both with the
subjunctive; *la cobija* = blanket (Mexico).

![A white refrigerator door covered with notes held by magnets. A large sheet at the top headed Pacto de convivencia lists the days: L y J Memo, M y V Andrea, Mi y S Lucía. Smaller sticky notes say: ¡Nada de música después de las 11!, ¿Quién se comió mi yogur?, and El perro solo con cobija. A small drawing of a dog and a pizza magnet are at the bottom.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *convivencia*: con-vi-VEN-cia, four syllables; both *v*s sound like a soft *b*.
- *quisquilloso*: quis-qui-YO-so; *qu* is a plain *k* sound and *ll* sounds like *y* in most of
  Mexico.
- *maniático*: ma-NIÁ-ti-co, four syllables; *manía*: ma-NÍ-a, three (the accent breaks the
  diphthong).
- *impuntual*: im-pun-TUAL, three syllables.

## Common mistakes

- A present subjunctive after a past feeling: ~~Me molestaba que dejes los trastes~~ → *Me
  molestaba que dejaras los trastes.*
- The indicative after a feeling verb: ~~No soportaba que ponía la música~~ → *No soportaba que
  pusiera la música.*
- *Que* + subjunctive with the same subject: ~~No soporto que yo llegue tarde~~ → *No soporto
  llegar tarde.*
- *Caer* not agreeing: ~~Me cae bien tus amigos~~ → *Me caen bien tus amigos.*
- *Gustar* for liking a person in a friendly way: *Me cae bien tu hermana* (I like her as a
  person) is safer than *Me gusta tu hermana*.
- A first-person verb after *soy de los que*: ~~Soy de los que pienso~~ → *Soy de los que
  piensan.*

## Key points

- Feeling verb in the present → present or perfect subjunctive; in the past (imperfect or
  preterite) → imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive. Same subject → infinitive.
- *Caer bien / mal / gordo, sentar mal, hacer gracia, fastidiar* work like *gustar*; the verb and
  *gordo* agree with the person or thing.
- *Ser* + adjective for character, *estar* + adjective for behavior now.
- *Es de los / las que* + indicative, preferably plural.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Por más que lo intente: concession at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A **[[concessive clause]]** admits a fact or a possibility that might seem to stop something, and
then says it doesn't: *Although I'm scared, I'll do it.* B1 lesson 17 taught the basics: *aunque*
with the indicative or the present subjunctive, *a pesar de (que)*, *por mucho que* and *aun así*.
At B2 you need *aunque* with the past subjunctives from module 1, and a set of other concessive
**[[connectors]]** (words that link two ideas and show how they relate), each with its own mood,
position and register.

The theme is risk sports (*el alpinismo, la escalada, el buceo, el paracaidismo*), fears and
phobias (*las fobias*, like *el vértigo*).

## *Aunque* with four moods and tenses

The mood after *aunque* tells the listener how you see the obstacle.

| *aunque* + | The obstacle is… | Example |
|---|---|---|
| indicative | a fact you're telling the listener | *Aunque tengo vértigo, voy a subir.* |
| present subjunctive | possible, unknown, or a fact you treat as unimportant | *Aunque llueva, vamos a subir.* |
| imperfect subjunctive | unlikely or imaginary (now or later) | *Aunque me pagaran, no haría paracaidismo.* |
| pluperfect subjunctive | imaginary, in the past | *Aunque hubiera llovido, habríamos subido.* |

- *Aunque tengo vértigo, voy a subir.* — Although I'm afraid of heights, I'm going to climb up.
  (I'm telling you: I do have vertigo.)
- *Aunque llueva, vamos a subir.* — Even if it rains, we're going to climb. (Maybe it will.)
- *Aunque sea peligroso, me encanta.* — It may be dangerous, but I love it. (We both know it's
  dangerous; I'm not arguing.)
- *Aunque me pagaran, no haría paracaidismo.* — Even if they paid me, I wouldn't go skydiving.
- *Aunque hubiera llovido, habríamos subido.* — Even if it had rained, we would have climbed.
  (It didn't rain.)

The last two match the conditions of B1 lesson 14 and lesson 04: imperfect subjunctive with a
conditional, pluperfect subjunctive with a conditional perfect (or *hubiera*). After a past main
verb, the imperfect subjunctive can also simply follow the sequence of tenses: *Me dijo que
subiría aunque lloviera* (She told me she'd climb even if it rained).

## *Por más que* and *por muy… que*: "no matter how"

### *Por más que, por mucho que, por poco que*

"No matter how much". B1's *por mucho que* and this
lesson's *por más que* mean the same; *por poco que* means "however little".

- *Por más que lo intente, no puedo mirar hacia abajo.* — No matter how hard I try, I can't look
  down.
- *Por mucho que entrenes, siempre hay riesgo.* — However much you train, there's always a risk.
- *Por poco que entrenes, notarás la diferencia.* — However little you train, you'll notice the
  difference.

Usually the subjunctive. The indicative is used for a real, known fact, often a repeated one: *Por
más que lo intento, no me sale* (I keep trying, and it doesn't work).

### *Por (muy)* + adjective + *que*

"No matter how" + adjective or adverb. *Muy* is
optional, and the verb is usually in the subjunctive:

- *Por muy difícil que sea, lo voy a intentar.* — No matter how difficult it is, I'm going to try.
- *Por cansada que estuviera, nunca se quitaba el arnés antes de bajar.* — However tired she was,
  she never took off her harness before getting down.
- *Por muy lejos que esté la cima, llegaremos.* — However far away the summit is, we'll get there.

The adjective agrees: *por muy cansadas que estén*.

## Other connectors: register and mood

### *A pesar de (que), pese a (que)*

Despite, in spite of. *Pese a* is the formal twin of
B1's *a pesar de*, common in the news. Both take a noun, an infinitive or *que* + a clause, with the
mood choices of *aunque*:

- *Pese al mal tiempo, la expedición siguió adelante.* — Despite the bad weather, the expedition
  carried on.
- *Pese a que el curso es caro, siempre está lleno.* — Although the course is expensive, it's
  always full.

### *Si bien*

Although, while; formal, mostly written; + indicative. It concedes a point before an
argument:

- *Si bien el riesgo existe, es muy bajo con un buen equipo.* — Although the risk exists, it's very
  low with good equipment.

This *si* is not "if": never translate *si bien* word for word.

### *Aun cuando*

Even if, even though; formal. With the subjunctive it means "even if", with the
indicative "even though":

- *Aun cuando haga buen tiempo, llevaremos cuerda.* — Even if the weather is good, we'll take rope.
- *Aun cuando conocía el riesgo, decidió bucear.* — Even though she knew the risk, she decided to
  dive.

### *Y eso que*

Even though, and that's despite…; spoken; + indicative. It's an afterthought,
added after the main clause, often with surprise:

- *No se cansó nada, y eso que subió cinco horas.* — He wasn't tired at all, even though he
  climbed for five hours.
- *Le dio pánico, y eso que es instructora.* — She panicked, and she's an instructor!

### *Aun* + gerund

Even + -ing:

- *Aun sabiéndolo, fue.* — Even knowing it, she went.
- *Aun teniendo miedo, saltó.* — Even though he was scared, he jumped.

*Aun* without an accent means "even" (*aun así, aun cuando, aun sabiéndolo*); *aún* with an accent
means "still, yet" (*Aún no llegan*).

![A chart titled "Concessive connectors by register" in three bands. Spoken band: y eso que + indicative, placed after the main clause; aunque, all registers. Neutral band: a pesar de (que), por más que / por mucho que + subjunctive (indicative for a known fact), por muy + adjective + que + subjunctive, aun + gerund. Formal and written band: pese a (que), si bien + indicative, aun cuando + subjunctive (even if) or indicative (even though).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Encouraging and objecting

Concessive sentences are the natural way to encourage someone (the obstacle is real, but it
doesn't matter) and to object politely (your point is real, but it doesn't change mine):

- *Aunque no llegues a la cima, ya es un logro.* — Even if you don't reach the summit, it's
  already an achievement.
- *Por más miedo que tengas, puedes hacerlo paso a paso.* — However scared you are, you can do it
  step by step.
- *Tienes razón, es extremo. Aun así, quiero probarlo.* — You're right, it's extreme. Even so, I
  want to try it.
- *Si bien entiendo tu miedo, no creo que sea peligroso con un instructor.* — While I understand
  your fear, I don't think it's dangerous with an instructor.

*Por más* can go before a noun (*por más miedo que tengas*); with an adjective *por muy* is the usual choice, though *por más difícil que sea* is also common and correct.

## Interview: *El miedo también sube*

An invented interview from a sports magazine. Itzel Garza is a fictional climbing instructor in
Nuevo León.

> —Itzel, ¿una instructora de escalada también tiene miedo?
>
> —Claro. Por más experiencia que tengas, el miedo no desaparece. Yo tengo vértigo, y eso que
> escalo desde los quince años.
>
> —¿Y cómo se controla?
>
> —Con técnica y con equilibrio. Si bien la fuerza ayuda, lo más importante es confiar en la
> cuerda y en el arnés. Aunque una pared parezca imposible, siempre hay un camino.
>
> —¿Qué les dice a los alumnos que entran en pánico?
>
> —Que respiren. Por muy alto que estén, no deben mirar el precipicio, sino la siguiente piedra.
> Aun sabiéndolo, todos miramos abajo alguna vez.
>
> —¿Y los temerarios?
>
> —Me preocupan más que los cobardes. Aunque me ofrecieran mucho dinero, no llevaría a nadie sin
> casco. La adrenalina es buena, pero la cima no vale una vida.
>
> —¿Practica otros deportes extremos?
>
> —Buceo. Aun cuando el mar está tranquilo, reviso todo dos veces. Pese a lo que piensa la gente,
> los deportes extremos son para personas muy prudentes.

Translation:

> "Itzel, does a climbing instructor get scared too?"
>
> "Of course. No matter how much experience you have, fear doesn't go away. I'm afraid of heights,
> even though I've been climbing since I was fifteen."
>
> "And how do you control it?"
>
> "With technique and with balance. Although strength helps, the most important thing is to trust
> the rope and the harness. Even if a wall seems impossible, there's always a way up."
>
> "What do you tell students who panic?"
>
> "To breathe. However high up they are, they shouldn't look at the drop, but at the next rock.
> Even knowing that, we all look down sometimes."
>
> "And the reckless ones?"
>
> "They worry me more than the cowards. Even if they offered me a lot of money, I wouldn't take
> anyone up without a helmet. Adrenaline is good, but the summit isn't worth a life."
>
> "Do you do other extreme sports?"
>
> "Scuba diving. Even when the sea is calm, I check everything twice. Despite what people think,
> extreme sports are for very careful people."

Notes: *por más experiencia que tengas* shows that *por más* can take a noun (no matter how much
experience); *entrar en pánico* = to panic; *la piedra* = stone, rock (here a hold on the wall);
*el casco* = helmet (B1); *prudente* = careful, sensible. Itzel's *aun cuando el mar está
tranquilo* uses the indicative because it's a real, repeated situation (even when it's calm).

![A climber on a rock wall near the top of a cliff. She wears a harness around her waist and a helmet; a rope runs from her harness up to an anchor and down to an instructor standing at the bottom. Above her is the summit of the rock with a small flag; to the right of the wall the ground drops away into a deep cliff edge over a valley.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Pronunciation

- *vértigo*: VÉR-ti-go, stressed on the first syllable, as in English, but with Spanish vowels; the accent mark shows the stress.
- *paracaidismo*: pa-ra-cai-DIS-mo, five syllables; *ai* is one syllable here (but *paracaídas*,
  with an accent, has a separate *í*: pa-ra-ca-Í-das).
- *arnés*: ar-NÉS; plural *arneses* (ar-NE-ses), without the accent.
- *temerario*: te-me-RA-rio, four syllables.
- *y eso que*: run together in speech, *yeso-que*.

## Common mistakes

- *Si bien* with the subjunctive: ~~Si bien sea caro~~ → *Si bien es caro…*
- *Y eso que* at the start: it follows the main clause: *No se cansó, y eso que subió cinco horas.*
- An accent on *aun* = "even": ~~aún cuando, aún así~~ → *aun cuando, aun así*.
- *Por muy* with a noun: ~~por muy experiencia~~ → *por mucha experiencia que tengas* or *por más
  experiencia que tengas*.
- *A pesar* without *de*: ~~a pesar el frío~~ → *a pesar del frío*.

## Key points

- *Aunque* + indicative (a fact you assert), present subjunctive (possible, or conceded), imperfect
  subjunctive (imaginary), pluperfect subjunctive (imaginary past).
- *Por más / mucho / poco que* and *por (muy)* + adjective + *que* usually take the subjunctive;
  the indicative for a known, real fact.
- *Pese a (que)* is formal *a pesar de (que)*; *si bien* + indicative is formal and written; *aun
  cuando* is formal; *y eso que* + indicative is spoken and comes last.
- *Aun* + gerund = even + -ing; *aun* = even, *aún* = still.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Habrá perdido el vuelo: probability and hypotheses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

English guesses with words: *probably, must, I wonder*. Spanish has those words too, but it can
also guess with the tense itself: *Estará en el aeropuerto* (She's probably at the airport).
A2's honors lesson 16h2 introduced this for the present, and B1 lesson 11 showed the future
perfect making a guess about the recent past. This lesson puts the whole system together: four
tenses for guessing about four times, *deber de*, and a scale of words from "almost sure" to "who
knows".

The theme is travel mishaps, expeditions and getting lost. This lesson also opens the
future-perfect drill (*habré, habrás, habrá… + participle*).

## Guessing with tenses

Take what you would say if you were sure, and move the verb one step "further away": present →
future, preterite or imperfect → conditional, perfect → future perfect, pluperfect → conditional
perfect.

| You're sure | You're guessing | Time of the guess |
|---|---|---|
| *Está en el aeropuerto.* | *Estará en el aeropuerto.* | now |
| *Ha perdido la conexión.* / *Perdió la conexión.* | *Habrá perdido la conexión.* | the recent past |
| *Eran las tres cuando llegamos.* | *Serían las tres cuando llegamos.* | the past |
| *Ya había salido cuando llamaste.* | *Ya habría salido cuando llamaste.* | before a past moment |

### The future of probability: now

The **[[future of probability]]** is the simple future used for a guess about the present:

- *¿Dónde está Pablo? —Estará en la fila de migración.* — Where's Pablo? —He's probably in the
  immigration line.
- *Tendrá unos treinta años.* — He must be about thirty.
- *¿Qué hora será en Madrid?* — I wonder what time it is in Madrid.

### The future perfect: the recent past

The future perfect (*habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habrán* + participle) guesses about something
that has probably just happened, the way Mexicans would use the preterite if they were sure:

- *No contesta. Habrá perdido el vuelo.* — He's not answering. He must have missed the flight.
- *Se le habrá acabado la batería.* — Her battery must have died.
- *¿Qué habrá pasado?* — I wonder what's happened.

### The conditional of probability: the past

The **[[conditional of probability]]** is the conditional used for a guess about the past, where you'd
use the preterite or imperfect if you were sure:

- *Serían las tres de la mañana cuando aterrizamos.* — It must have been about three in the
  morning when we landed.
- *Tendría unos veinte años cuando hizo su primera expedición.* — She must have been about twenty
  when she went on her first expedition.
- *¿Por qué no vendría?* — I wonder why he didn't come.

The conditional perfect does the same for a moment before another past one (*Ya habría salido
cuando llamaste* = she had probably already left when you called). You'll meet it in reading;
you don't need to produce it.

Context decides. *Estará en Puebla* can mean "She'll be in Puebla" (with *mañana*) or "She's
probably in Puebla" (now). *Llegaría tarde* can mean "He'd arrive late" (a condition) or "He
probably arrived late". Time words and the situation make it clear.

### Conceding with the future

The future of probability often concedes a point, like *aunque* in lesson 07: *Será muy bonito,
pero está carísimo* (It may well be beautiful, but it's very expensive); *Habrá viajado mucho,
pero no sabe leer un mapa* (He may have traveled a lot, but he can't read a map).

## *Deber de* and *deber*

A2's *deber de* + infinitive is another way to guess; *deber* + infinitive gives an obligation:

- *Debe de estar cansada: lleva doce horas viajando.* — She must be tired: she's been traveling
  for twelve hours. (a guess)
- *Debe llamar a la aerolínea.* — She has to call the airline. (an obligation)
- *Deben de haber cerrado la carretera.* — They must have closed the highway. (a guess about the
  past: *deber de haber* + participle)

That's the distinction grammars recommend, and it's the one to use in writing. In real speech the
line is blurred. The RAE's *Nueva gramática* (2009) recommends *deber* without *de* for obligation,
but says that *deber* alone for probability (*Debe estar cansada*) is so widespread at every level
that it can't be considered incorrect. So *Debe estar cansada* is fine; *Debes de pagar la renta*
for an obligation is the use to avoid.

## The probability scale

![A vertical ladder titled "How likely?" with seven rungs from top to bottom. At the top, Casi seguro: seguramente, debe de + infinitive, the future: estará. Next, Lo más probable es que + subjunctive. Next, Es probable que + subjunctive. Middle rung, Puede que / Es posible que + subjunctive. Next, Quizás / Tal vez + either mood. Next, A lo mejor + indicative; capaz que, usually indicative. Lower, ¿Será? Next to the bottom, ¡Quién sabe! / ¡A saber!. A side note: Spain, colloquial: igual + indicative.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Expression | Mood | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *seguramente* | indicative | *Seguramente se quedó dormido.* |
| *lo más probable es que* | subjunctive | *Lo más probable es que llegue mañana.* |
| *es probable / es posible que* | subjunctive | *Es posible que hayan cancelado el vuelo.* |
| *puede que* | subjunctive | *Puede que esté varado en Monterrey.* |
| *quizás, tal vez* | either | *Quizás llega / llegue en la noche.* |
| *a lo mejor* | indicative | *A lo mejor perdió la conexión.* |
| *capaz que* | usually indicative | *Capaz que llueve en la tarde.* |
| *igual* (Spain) | indicative | *Igual llega mañana.* |

Notes on the last three:

- *Capaz que* (maybe, it could be that) is colloquial in many Latin American countries, Mexico
  among them, according to the RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (*capaz*). It usually
  takes the indicative, though the subjunctive also occurs; *es capaz que* is the same thing.
  Don't add *de*: ~~es capaz de que~~.
- *Igual* meaning "maybe" + indicative belongs to colloquial Spain, as the DPD (*igual*) notes:
  *Igual necesita ayuda* (Maybe she needs help). In Mexico you'll understand it; you don't need to
  use it.
- *A lo mejor* and *capaz que* both sound relaxed; in an e-mail to a client, prefer *es posible
  que* or *probablemente*.

For "who knows", Spanish has *quién sabe* and *a saber*: *¿Cuándo saldrá el vuelo? —¡Quién sabe!*
/ *¡A saber!* (*A saber* also means "namely" in formal writing: *tres causas, a saber: …*.)

### *Suponer que* and *suponiendo que*

A2 honors' *suponer* (to suppose) takes the indicative: *Supongo que el vuelo saldrá tarde* (I
suppose the flight will leave late). Its gerund, *suponiendo que* (assuming that), sets up a
hypothesis and takes the subjunctive: *Suponiendo que lleguemos a las diez, todavía alcanzamos el
último camión* (Assuming we arrive at ten, we'll still make the last bus).

## Phone call: *¿Dónde estará Rodrigo?*

Valeria and her brother Toño are at Mexico City's airport waiting for their friend Rodrigo, a
backpacker coming back from Lima. The plane landed an hour ago.

> Valeria: Toño, ¿dónde estás? El vuelo aterrizó hace una hora y Rodrigo no sale.
>
> Toño: Estoy en el estacionamiento. ¿No te ha escrito?
>
> Valeria: Nada. Se le habrá acabado la batería, como siempre.
>
> Toño: O estará en la fila de migración. A esta hora hay muchísima gente.
>
> Valeria: Capaz que le extraviaron la mochila. Con su suerte…
>
> Toño: No especules. Lo más probable es que esté esperando el equipaje.
>
> Valeria: ¿Y si perdió la conexión en Bogotá? Me dijo que tenía solo cuarenta minutos.
>
> Toño: Si la hubiera perdido, nos habría avisado. Debe de estar adentro.
>
> Valeria: ¡Ahí viene! Trae la mochila… pero sin zapatos.
>
> Toño: ¿Sin zapatos? ¿Qué le habrá pasado?
>
> Valeria: A saber. Viene riéndose, así que no habrá sido nada grave.

Translation:

> Valeria: Toño, where are you? The flight landed an hour ago and Rodrigo isn't coming out.
>
> Toño: I'm in the parking lot. Hasn't he texted you?
>
> Valeria: Nothing. His battery must have died, as usual.
>
> Toño: Or he's probably in the immigration line. At this time of day there are tons of people.
>
> Valeria: Maybe they lost his backpack. With his luck…
>
> Toño: Don't speculate. Most likely he's waiting for his luggage.
>
> Valeria: And what if he missed the connection in Bogotá? He told me he only had forty minutes.
>
> Toño: If he had missed it, he would have told us. He must be inside.
>
> Valeria: Here he comes! He's got his backpack… but no shoes.
>
> Toño: No shoes? What could have happened to him?
>
> Valeria: Goodness knows. He's laughing, so it can't have been anything serious.

Notes: *aterrizar* = to land; *el estacionamiento* = parking lot (Mexico); *escribir* = to text
(here); *la fila* = line (of people); *traer* = to have with you (here). Toño's *Si la hubiera
perdido, nos habría avisado* is a past condition from lesson 04. *No habrá sido nada grave* is a
future perfect guess in the negative: "it can't have been anything serious".

![An airport departures board titled Salidas, Departures, with four columns: Hora, Destino, Vuelo, Estado. 14:05 Bogotá 712 Retrasado 15:30. 14:20 Cancún 1204 Abordando. 14:45 Lima 2471 Cancelado. 15:10 Monterrey 318 A tiempo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The board above is invented. Looking at it, you could guess: *El vuelo a Lima está cancelado: los
pasajeros estarán furiosos. Habrá habido una tormenta. Capaz que quedan varados hasta mañana.* (The Lima flight is canceled: the passengers must be
furious. There must have been a storm. Maybe they'll be stranded until tomorrow.)

## A walk that went wrong

Guessing about the past is what you do when someone's late from a hike. Read this voice message
from a park ranger to a colleague.

> Oye, Rafa, la expedición de los mochileros todavía no regresa al campamento. Salieron a las
> siete; serían las dos cuando los vio el guía en el refugio. Mi hipótesis: habrán tomado el
> sendero viejo, que es más largo. Tampoco tenían brújula, así que capaz que se perdieron en el
> trayecto del río. No creo que sea un percance serio: llevaban cantimploras y repelente, y lo
> peor que les habrá pasado es alguna picadura. Pero es solo una suposición. Lo más probable es
> que lleguen antes de que oscurezca, cansados de la caminata. Si a las seis no han llegado, salimos
> a buscarlos. Un contratiempo así pasa cada semana.

Translation:

> Hey, Rafa, the backpackers' expedition still hasn't come back to the campsite. They left at
> seven; it must have been about two when the guide saw them at the mountain hut. My hypothesis:
> they must have taken the old trail, which is longer. They didn't have a compass either, so maybe
> they got lost on the stretch along the river. I don't think it's a serious mishap: they had
> canteens and insect repellent, and the worst that's probably happened to them is a bite or
> two. But it's only a guess. Most likely they'll get here before dark, tired from the hike. If
> they haven't arrived by six, we'll go out and look for them. A setback like this happens every
> week.

*Serían las dos* is a past guess (conditional); *habrán tomado* and *les habrá pasado* are recent
past guesses (future perfect); *capaz que se perdieron* guesses with the preterite.

## Pronunciation

- *habrá, habrás*: stress on the last syllable, a-BRÁ; *habría*: a-BRÍ-a, three syllables.
- *brújula*: BRÚ-ju-la, stressed on the first syllable (an accent three from the end).
- *hipótesis*: i-PÓ-te-sis, four syllables; the *h* is silent.
- *extravío*: ex-tra-VÍ-o, four syllables: the accent splits *ío*.
- *percance*: per-CAN-ce; *cantimplora*: can-tim-PLO-ra.

## Common mistakes

- The present when you're only guessing: *Está en la fila* states it as a fact; *Estará en la
  fila* or *Debe de estar en la fila* makes it a guess.
- The future for a past guess: ~~Serán las tres cuando llegamos~~ → *Serían las tres cuando
  llegamos.*
- The subjunctive after *a lo mejor*: ~~A lo mejor esté~~ → *A lo mejor está.*
- The indicative after *puede que* or *lo más probable es que*: ~~Puede que está~~ → *Puede que
  esté.*
- *Deber de* for an obligation in careful Spanish: ~~Debes de llamar~~ → *Debes llamar.*
- *Es capaz de que*: → *es capaz que* or *capaz que*.

## Key points

- Guessing with tenses: future (now), future perfect (recent past), conditional (past),
  conditional perfect (before a past moment, recognition).
- *Deber de* + infinitive guesses, *deber* + infinitive obliges; *deber* alone for guesses is
  accepted (*Nueva gramática*).
- Subjunctive: *lo más probable es que, es probable / posible que, puede que*; either: *quizás, tal
  vez*; indicative: *seguramente, a lo mejor, capaz que* (usually), Spain's *igual*.
- *Supongo que* + indicative; *suponiendo que* + subjunctive.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Todos los mexicanos…: stereotypes and careful generalizations
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 05 taught you to give and judge opinions; lesson 07 to concede a point. This honors lesson
puts both to work on one of the hardest things to discuss politely in any language: what people
"are like". You'll learn to soften a generalization so it stays true, to answer a stereotype
without sounding aggressive, and to talk about identity and diversity in Mexico.

Nothing here is presented as fact about any group. The stereotypes in this lesson appear as
examples of claims people make, so you can learn to answer them.

## Why generalizations go wrong

A stereotype (*el estereotipo*) is a fixed, simplified image of a group: *Todos los
mexicanos llevan sombrero.* A *prejuicio* (prejudice) is a judgment made before knowing the
person, often based on a stereotype. *Un tópico* and *un cliché* are worn-out ideas or images;
*tópico* is a false friend: "topic" is *el tema*.

Most stereotypes break down in one of three ways:

1. All or nothing: *todos, nadie, siempre, nunca*. One counterexample ruins the claim.
2. No source: the speaker reports an impression as a fact.
3. One part for the whole: what is true of one region, class or generation is said of a
   whole country. Mexico had more than 126 million people in 2020; what one Mexican does tells you
   little about the rest.

The cure is not to stop generalizing (we need generalizations to think), but to generalize
carefully.

## Hedges: softening a generalization

A **[[hedge]]** is a word or phrase that limits a claim so it stays true: "usually", "in many
cases", "some people". Spanish has a full set.

| Hedge | Example | English |
|---|---|---|
| *por lo general, en general* | *Por lo general, se come tarde.* | Generally, people eat late. |
| *soler* + infinitive (A2) | *Los domingos suelen comer en familia.* | On Sundays they usually eat with family. |
| *tender a* + infinitive | *Los jóvenes tienden a mudarse a las ciudades.* | Young people tend to move to cities. |
| *en muchos casos* | *En muchos casos, la familia ayuda.* | In many cases, the family helps. |
| *muchos, la mayoría de* | *La mayoría de los encuestados dijo que sí.* | Most respondents said yes. |
| *no todos…* | *No todos los chilangos manejan mal.* | Not all people from Mexico City drive badly. |
| *hay quien* + verb | *Hay quien piensa / piense que…* | Some people think that… |
| *se suele decir que, se dice que* | *Se dice que los regios son tacaños.* | People say that… |

Notes:

- *Tender a* is a stem changer like *entender*: *tiendo, tiende, tienden*.
- After *la mayoría de* + plural noun, the verb can be singular (agreeing with *la mayoría*) or
  plural (agreeing with the people): *La mayoría de los mexicanos vive / viven en ciudades.* Both are
  correct.
- *Hay quien* (there are those who, some people) can take either mood. The indicative is very
  common and presents the people as real (*Hay quien dice que…*); the subjunctive keeps them
  vaguer (*Hay quien piense que…*). The plural *hay quienes* works the same way.
- *Chilango* is an informal word for someone from Mexico City; *regio*, for someone from
  Monterrey; *tacaño*, stingy (in Mexico also, informally, *codo*). Many people use them
  affectionately, but they can sting: know your audience.

### Example 1: Hedging a sweeping statement

Start: *Los mexicanos siempre llegan tarde.*

1. Remove the all-or-nothing word: *siempre* → *a veces* or nothing at all.
2. Limit the group and the situation: not all Mexicans, and not every event. A party is not a
   job interview.
3. Use a hedge and, if you can, a source.

Result: *En muchos casos, a las fiestas se llega más tarde de la hora de la invitación, pero eso
no significa que la gente sea impuntual en el trabajo.* (In many cases, people arrive at parties
later than the time on the invitation, but that doesn't mean people are unpunctual at work.)

Notice *no significa que* + subjunctive: denying a conclusion works like *no creo que* (B1).

## Answering a stereotype

A good answer (1) concedes what is true, (2) limits it, and (3) gives a counterexample or a fact.
Lesson 07's concessive connectors do step 1; lesson 05's *no es que…, sino que…* does step 2.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Three steps for answering a stereotype
  accDescr: Start from the claim, for example Los mexicanos siempre llegan tarde. Step one, concede what is true, with si bien es cierto que or puede que. Step two, limit it, with no es que plus subjunctive and sino que plus indicative, or no todos. Step three, give a counterexample or a fact with its source and date, such as según el INEGI, en 2020. The result is a careful generalization with a hedge.
  A["Claim: Los mexicanos siempre llegan tarde."] --> B["1. Concede: si bien es cierto que…, puede que…"]
  B --> C["2. Limit: no es que + subjunctive, sino que…; no todos…"]
  C --> D["3. Counterexample or fact: según el INEGI, en 2020…"]
  D --> E["A careful generalization, with a hedge"]
```

- *Si bien es cierto que en algunas regiones se come muy picante, no todo el mundo aguanta el
  chile.* — While it's true that very spicy food is eaten in some regions, not everyone can take
  chili.
- *Puede que algunos lo hagan, pero generalizar es injusto.* — Some people may do it, but
  generalizing is unfair.
- *No es que no exista ese tipo de persona, sino que no representa a todo un país.* — It's not that
  that kind of person doesn't exist; it's that they don't represent a whole country.
- *Por más que lo repitan en las películas, no es verdad que todos vivamos en el desierto.* —
  However much the movies repeat it, it isn't true that we all live in the desert.

### Example 2: Answering with data

Claim: *México es un país rural: la mayoría vive en pueblos pequeños.*

1. Concede: *Es cierto que hay muchos pueblos pequeños, y que la vida en el campo forma parte de
   nuestra identidad.*
2. Give the fact, with its source and date: INEGI, Mexico's statistics institute, reports that in
   2020, 21% of the population lived in localities of fewer than 2,500 inhabitants, the size it
   counts as rural. *Según el INEGI, en 2020 el 21 % de la población vivía en localidades de menos
   de 2500 habitantes.*
3. Draw the conclusion carefully: *Es decir, alrededor de cuatro de cada cinco personas vivían en
   localidades más grandes.*

Step 3 is a calculation (100% − 21% = 79%), so the answer says *alrededor de* (about). Notice
the Spanish number style: *el 21 %* with a space before the sign, *2500* without a space in a
four-digit number (RAE).

### Example 3: Mood after *hay quien* and *no todos*

Complete: *Hay quien ___ (creer) que en México se duerme la siesta todos los días, pero no todos
los que lo dicen ___ (haber) visitado el país.*

- After *hay quien*, either mood: *cree* or *crea*.
- After *no todos los que*, the relative clause describes real people: indicative, *han
  visitado*. (*Hayan visitado* is also possible here, making the group vaguer.)

So: *Hay quien cree que en México se duerme la siesta todos los días, pero no todos los que lo
dicen han visitado el país.* (*La siesta* = afternoon nap.)

## The other direction

Stereotypes travel both ways. Inside Mexico, people trade regional ones (*los regios son
tacaños, los chilangos son prepotentes*, arrogant), and Mexicans hold images of other countries
too. The same tools apply: *Se dice mucho que…, pero en mi experiencia…* When you discuss these
in class or online, three habits keep the conversation respectful:

- Present the stereotype as a claim (*se dice que, hay quien piensa que*), never in your own
  voice as a fact.
- Prefer people's own names for themselves. If you aren't sure a word is friendly, don't use it.
- Talk about diversity inside each group: *la diversidad* is often the strongest answer to a
  stereotype.

## Forum thread: *¿Es verdad que los mexicanos…?*

An invented thread on a travel forum (*el foro*). A user called *viajera_ca* from Canada asks a
question; *Rulo_mty*, from Monterrey, answers.

> viajera_ca: Hola. Voy a vivir seis meses en Querétaro. Me dijeron que los mexicanos nunca
> dicen "no" directamente y que siempre llegan tarde. ¿Es verdad? No quiero ofender a nadie.
>
> Rulo_mty: ¡Bienvenida! Buena pregunta, y gracias por preguntar en vez de suponer. Te
> contesto con cuidado, porque es fácil generalizar.
>
> Sobre el "no": es cierto que mucha gente tiende a suavizar un rechazo. En lugar de "no puedo",
> a veces vas a oír "a lo mejor" o "luego vemos". No es que la gente mienta, sino que, por lo
> general, se valora no herir al otro. Si no entiendes la respuesta, pregunta otra vez con
> amabilidad.
>
> Sobre la puntualidad: depende muchísimo de la situación. A una fiesta en casa, lo normal es
> llegar un rato después de la hora; a una cita de trabajo o al médico, se espera que llegues a
> tiempo. Hay quien es impuntual en todo, como en cualquier país, pero no me gusta que nos
> etiqueten así a todos.
>
> Y un consejo: Querétaro no es Monterrey ni Oaxaca. México es enorme, y su diversidad es parte de
> su identidad. La idiosincrasia de un país no cabe en un cliché. ¡Disfruta!

Translation:

> viajera_ca: Hi. I'm going to live in Querétaro for six months. I was told that Mexicans never
> say "no" directly and that they're always late. Is it true? I don't want to offend anyone.
>
> Rulo_mty: Welcome! Good question, and thanks for asking instead of assuming. I'll answer
> carefully, because it's easy to generalize.
>
> About "no": it's true that a lot of people tend to soften a refusal. Instead of "I can't", you'll
> sometimes hear "maybe" or "we'll see". It's not that people lie; it's that, in general, not
> hurting the other person is valued. If you don't understand the answer, ask again kindly.
>
> About punctuality: it depends a great deal on the situation. For a party at someone's home, the
> normal thing is to arrive a while after the time; for a work appointment or the doctor, you're
> expected to be on time. Some people are late for everything, as in any country, but I don't like
> all of us being labeled that way.
>
> And a piece of advice: Querétaro isn't Monterrey or Oaxaca. Mexico is huge, and its diversity is
> part of its identity. A country's character doesn't fit into a cliché. Enjoy!

Glosses: *suavizar un rechazo* = to soften a refusal; *luego vemos* = we'll see (later); *herir
al otro* = to hurt the other person (lesson 03's *herir*); *se espera que llegues* = you're
expected to arrive; *no cabe en* = doesn't fit into.

## Pronunciation

- *estereotipo*: es-te-re-o-TI-po, six syllables: *e-o* are two vowels in separate syllables.
- *idiosincrasia*: i-dio-sin-CRA-sia, five syllables; *dio* and *sia* are one syllable each.
- *prejuicio*: pre-JUI-cio, three syllables; the *j* is the strong Spanish *j*.
- *generalización*: ge-ne-ra-li-za-CIÓN, six syllables, with seseo: *za* sounds like *sa*.

## Common mistakes

- Turning a hedge into a fact: *Se dice que los regios son tacaños* reports a claim; *Los regios
  son tacaños* asserts it.
- *Tópico* for "topic": ~~el tópico de mi presentación~~ → *el tema de mi presentación*.
- *Idiosincracia* with *c*: the spelling is *idiosincrasia*.
- The indicative after a denied conclusion: *Eso no significa que la gente sea impuntual* is the
  usual and safe choice, like *no creo que*.
- A data claim with no date or source: say *según el INEGI, en 2020…*

## Key points

- Hedges: *por lo general, suele, tiende a, en muchos casos, la mayoría de, no todos, hay quien*.
- Answer a stereotype in three steps: concede (*si bien, puede que*), limit (*no es que…, sino
  que…*), give a counterexample or a sourced, dated fact.
- *Hay quien* takes either mood; *la mayoría de* + plural noun takes a singular or plural verb.
- Present stereotypes as claims, not facts, and talk about diversity.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Bitácora de una expedición: an original travel diary
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 08 taught you to guess with tenses: the future and future perfect for now and the recent
past, the conditional for the past. A diary is where those guesses live naturally, because the
writer doesn't know yet what happened to everyone else. This honors lesson is one long original
text: the logbook of a four-day trek in a Mexican canyon that goes wrong, followed by the rescue
report, written impersonally. You'll practice reading a long text without a full translation,
and turning personal narrative into an official report.

The trek and the people are invented. The setting is real: the Barrancas del Cobre (Copper
Canyon) in the Sierra Tarahumara, Chihuahua, which a 2025 Meteored México article describes as a
complex of seven canyons. The same article gives the rainy season as June to September, and warns
that in April, May and the first half of June the bottoms of the canyons can pass 25 or 30 °C
while the high sierra is much cooler. That mix of heat and sudden storms is the background of the
story.

*La barranca* is the usual Mexican word for a deep canyon or ravine.

## The diary: *Bitácora de la barranca*

Mariana, a nurse from Chihuahua city, kept this logbook during a trek with two friends and a
local guide in early June.

> *Lunes 3.* Salimos de Creel a las seis de la mañana, Joaquín, Paulina y yo, con Chayo, la
> guía. La idea es una travesía de cuatro días: bajar a la barranca, seguir el río y subir del
> otro lado. Llevamos tres litros de agua cada uno, el botiquín que preparé en el hospital y las
> bolsas de dormir. Arriba hacía fresco, pero conforme bajábamos el calor se volvía insoportable.
> Serían las dos cuando Joaquín empezó a quejarse de dolor de cabeza. Había dejado el sombrero en
> la camioneta, claro. Chayo le prestó su sombrero y lo hizo descansar a la sombra; le dimos agua poco a poco. Creo que
> fue el principio de una insolación. Esta noche prendimos una fogata junto al río y cenamos
> frijoles. Joaquín ya está mejor; dice que mañana no se quita el sombrero de Chayo ni para dormir.
>
> *Martes 4.* Mal día. Para ganar tiempo, Chayo propuso un atajo por la ladera, más corto pero
> sin sombra. A media mañana Paulina se mareó. No había tomado casi nada de agua porque, según
> ella, no tenía sed. Así es como uno se deshidrata sin darse cuenta. Le preparé suero oral del
> botiquín y esperamos dos horas bajo una roca. Perdimos medio día. Mientras Paulina dormía, Chayo nos contó que
> su abuelo cruzaba estas barrancas a pie para vender manzanas, y que nunca caminaba al mediodía.
> "El sol de aquí no perdona", dijo. Ojalá hubiéramos seguido esa regla desde el lunes.
> Chayo estaba seria; me imagino
> que estaría calculando cuánta agua nos quedaba. Llenamos las cantimploras en un arroyo y las
> purificamos con pastillas. En la noche, mientras escribo, se ven relámpagos muy lejos, hacia el
> norte. Chayo dice que la temporada de lluvias apenas empieza, y que la primera tormenta a veces llega
> de golpe.
>
> *Miércoles 5.* Llegó. A las cuatro de la tarde el cielo se puso negro y empezó a llover como
> nunca había visto. Los relámpagos caían sobre la sierra y el trueno sonaba dentro de la barranca
> como un tambor. Chayo nos hizo subir de inmediato a una terraza de piedra, lejos del río. Tenía
> razón: en menos de una hora el río creció tanto que el sendero de la orilla desapareció. Serían
> las cinco cuando vimos pasar troncos enteros. Estamos bien, mojados pero a salvo, y sin camino
> para seguir ni para regresar. No hay señal. Pienso en mi mamá: ya habrá visto las noticias de
> la tormenta y estará preocupadísima. Chayo dice que el grupo de Creel ya se habrá dado cuenta
> de que no llegamos al punto de control. Ojalá. Esta noche no hay fogata: todo está empapado.
> Cenamos galletas y una lata de atún entre cuatro. Paulina, que
> ya se sentía mejor, nos hizo reír imitando a Joaquín con el sombrero de Chayo. Dormimos los cuatro
> pegados, dentro de las bolsas de dormir, sobre las mochilas. Cada relámpago iluminaba la barranca
> entera, y después todo volvía a quedar negro.
>
> *Jueves 6.* Amaneció despejado. El río sigue alto y café. Chayo subió con Joaquín a una cresta
> para buscar señal, y a las nueve, por fin, consiguieron una raya. Llamaron al 911 y explicaron
> dónde estábamos. Nos pidieron que no nos moviéramos, que nos quedáramos visibles y que
> ahorráramos batería. Pusimos la ropa más brillante sobre las rocas y una lona
> naranja en el punto más alto de la terraza. Después solo quedaba esperar. Joaquín contaba los
> minutos; yo revisaba el botiquín por tercera vez, aunque ya sabía lo que tenía. A las doce oímos un
> helicóptero, pero pasó de largo; habrá estado buscando a otro grupo, o no nos vio. Fue la peor
> hora del viaje. Paulina lloró un poco; yo también. A las dos y media llegó por la ladera una
> brigada de rescate a pie: cinco personas con cuerdas, agua y radio. El jefe nos revisó uno por
> uno. Si no hubiéramos subido a la terraza el miércoles, nos habría alcanzado el río; eso nos lo
> dijo él, muy tranquilo, y no lo voy a olvidar.
>
> *Viernes 7.* Escribo desde Creel. La brigada nos sacó por una vereda alta que nunca habríamos
> encontrado solos; tardamos seis horas en subir, despacio, con descansos cada media hora. Llegamos
> de noche, y en la plaza nos esperaban el grupo de Creel y un médico. Anoche dormimos en una cama
> de verdad. Hoy hablé con mi
> mamá, que efectivamente no había dormido en dos días. Releo esta bitácora y me sorprende lo
> rápido que cambió todo: el lunes nos quejábamos del calor y el miércoles casi nos lleva el
> agua. Lo bueno es que nadie salió herido. Lo que aprendí: el agua se toma aunque no tengas
> sed, el sombrero no se deja en la camioneta, y si el cielo se pone negro, se sube, no se
> espera. Chayo dice que el próximo año volvemos, pero en octubre.

Summary in English (the diary is about 810 words; read the Spanish first and use this to
check):

- *Monday.* Mariana, Joaquín and Paulina leave Creel at dawn with Chayo, their guide, for a
  four-day crossing: down into the canyon, along the river, up the other side. It gets hotter as
  they descend; at about two Joaquín, who left his hat in the truck, gets a headache: the start of
  sunstroke. Chayo lends him her hat and they rest him in the shade. Campfire and beans by the river.
- *Tuesday.* A shortcut across a sunny slope; Paulina, who had barely drunk, gets dizzy and
  dehydrated. Mariana gives her oral rehydration solution; they lose half a day. That night,
  lightning far to the north.
- *Wednesday.* A violent storm. Chayo makes them climb to a rock terrace; within an hour the
  river rises and the riverside trail disappears. No signal; no way forward or back. Mariana
  guesses that her mother must have seen the news and that the group in Creel must have noticed
  they're missing. They sleep huddled together,
  soaked.
- *Thursday.* Clear sky. From a ridge, Chayo and Joaquín get one bar of signal and call 911,
  who tell them to stay put, stay visible and save battery. A helicopter passes without seeing
  them; at 2:30 a rescue team arrives on foot. Its leader tells them the river would have caught
  them if they hadn't climbed up.
- *Friday.* Writing from Creel: the team had led them out the day before by a high path; after a
  six-hour climb they reached Creel at night, safe. Lessons learned: drink even if you aren't thirsty, keep your
  hat, and when the sky turns black, climb; don't wait.

Glosses: *conforme bajábamos* = as we went down; *se mareó* = she got dizzy; *el atajo* = shortcut;
*la ladera* = hillside, slope; *el suero oral* = oral rehydration solution; *el arroyo* = stream;
*la orilla* = bank (of a river); *el tronco* = tree trunk; *a salvo* = safe; *el punto de
control* = checkpoint; *empapado* = soaked; *la cresta* = ridge; *una raya* = one bar (of signal);
*pasó de largo* = it went straight past; *la brigada* = team, squad; *casi nos lleva el agua* =
the water nearly carried us away.

Tuesday night's camp, as Mariana might have sketched it in the logbook, with lightning in the
distance:

![A campsite between two canyon walls. A bolt of lightning flashes in the sky. On the ground, from left to right: a blue sleeping bag, a campfire of crossed logs ringed with stones, a white first-aid kit with a red cross, a green canteen with a cap and a strap, and in front a small compass with a red needle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## How the diary uses tense

The diary shows almost every past tense together, plus guesses.

| Form | Example from the diary | Why |
|---|---|---|
| preterite | *Salimos de Creel a las seis.* | events, in order |
| imperfect | *Arriba hacía fresco.* | background, description |
| pluperfect | *Había dejado el sombrero en la camioneta.* | before the story's moment |
| conditional of probability | *Serían las dos cuando Joaquín empezó…* | a guess about the past |
| conditional of probability | *Estaría calculando cuánta agua nos quedaba.* | a guess about someone's thoughts then |
| future perfect | *Ya habrá visto las noticias.* | a guess about the recent past |
| future of probability | *Estará preocupadísima.* | a guess about now |
| pluperfect subjunctive + conditional perfect | *Si no hubiéramos subido…, nos habría alcanzado el río.* | an imaginary past (lesson 04) |

### Example 1: Changing facts into guesses

Mariana doesn't know what the helicopter was doing. Rewrite each sure statement as a guess,
keeping the time.

1. *El helicóptero buscaba a otro grupo.* (past background) → *El helicóptero buscaría a otro
   grupo.*
2. *No nos vio.* (just happened) → *No nos habrá visto.*
3. *Mi mamá está preocupada.* (now) → *Mi mamá estará preocupada.*
4. *El grupo de Creel ya se dio cuenta.* (just happened) → *Ya se habrá dado cuenta.*

The rule from lesson 08: one step "further away" for each tense. Item 1 could also be *habrá
estado buscando*, the form the diary uses, if Mariana thinks of it as recent.

### Example 2: Reported instructions

On the phone, 911 told them: *No se muevan. Quédense visibles. Ahorren batería.* Mariana reports
it the next day: *Nos pidieron que no nos moviéramos, que nos quedáramos visibles y que
ahorráramos batería.* The commands become *que* + imperfect subjunctive after the past *pidieron*
(B1 lesson 15).

## The rescue report

An official report doesn't say *I* or *we*. It uses the impersonal and passive *se* (B1), the
passive with *ser*, and nouns instead of verbs. Here is the same story as an invented report
from a municipal civil protection office.

> *Informe de rescate.* El 6 de junio, a las 9:05 horas, se recibió una llamada al 911 de un
> grupo de cuatro excursionistas que había quedado aislado en la barranca por la crecida del
> río. Se envió una brigada de rescate a pie y se solicitó apoyo aéreo. El grupo fue localizado
> a las 14:30 horas en una terraza rocosa. Se realizó una revisión médica: dos personas
> presentaban síntomas leves de deshidratación e insolación de días anteriores. No se reportaron
> heridos. Los cuatro fueron trasladados a Creel. Se recomienda consultar el pronóstico antes de
> cualquier travesía y no acampar cerca de los cauces durante la temporada de lluvias.

Translation:

> *Rescue report.* On June 6, at 9:05, a 911 call was received from a group of four hikers who
> had been cut off in the canyon by the rising river. A rescue team was sent on foot and air
> support was requested. The group was located at 14:30 on a rocky terrace. A medical check was
> carried out: two people showed mild symptoms of dehydration and sunstroke from previous days.
> No injuries were reported. All four were taken to Creel. It is recommended that the weather
> forecast be checked before any trek and that people not camp near riverbeds during the rainy
> season.

Glosses: *aislado* = cut off; *la crecida* = rising water, flood; *el excursionista* = hiker;
*trasladar* = to take, to transfer; *el cauce* = riverbed. Notice *el rescate* (the operation) vs
*rescatar* (the verb), and the 24-hour clock (*14:30 horas*), common in official
writing.

### Example 3: From diary to report

| Diary (personal) | Report (impersonal) |
|---|---|
| *Llamaron al 911.* | *Se recibió una llamada al 911.* |
| *Llegó una brigada de rescate.* | *Se envió una brigada de rescate.* |
| *Nos encontraron a las dos y media.* | *El grupo fue localizado a las 14:30 horas.* |
| *El jefe nos revisó uno por uno.* | *Se realizó una revisión médica.* |
| *Nadie salió herido.* | *No se reportaron heridos.* |

The report removes feelings (*Paulina lloró*), guesses (*habrá estado buscando*) and the first
person, and keeps times, numbers and actions.

## Safety, as language

This lesson teaches the language of safety, not safety itself. Before any trip to a canyon or
mountain in Mexico, check the official guidance of the Coordinación Nacional de Protección Civil
and your state's civil protection office, and the weather forecast. In an emergency, Mexico's
emergency number is 911 (introduced in October 2016 and extended to the rest of the country in January 2017). Useful phrases
from the story: *¿Hay pronóstico de lluvia?*, *¿Dónde está el punto de control?*, *Estamos
aislados y sin camino*, *Tenemos una persona deshidratada*.

## Common mistakes

- The future for a past guess: ~~Serán las cinco cuando vimos los troncos~~ → *Serían las cinco
  cuando vimos los troncos.*
- First person in a report: ~~Encontramos al grupo~~ → *El grupo fue localizado* / *Se localizó al
  grupo.*
- A plural *se* passive that doesn't agree: ~~Se reportó heridos~~ → *No se reportaron heridos.*
  (With a person introduced by *a*, the verb stays singular: *Se localizó al grupo.*)
- *Insolación* for any heat illness: it's caused by the sun; for heat in general, Spanish also
  says *el golpe de calor* (heatstroke).

## Key points

- A diary mixes the four pasts with guesses: *serían* (past), *habrá visto* (recent past),
  *estará* (now).
- Past instructions: *Nos pidieron que no nos moviéramos.*
- A report is impersonal: *se recibió, se envió, fue localizado, no se reportaron heridos*,
  official times (*14:30 horas*), no feelings.
- For real trips: Protección Civil guidance, the forecast, and 911 in an emergency.

lessons.title: El inventor cuyo nombre nadie recuerda: relative clauses at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A **[[relative clause]]** describes a noun, the way an adjective does: *el invento que cambió el
mundo* (the invention that changed the world). The noun it describes is its **[[antecedent]]**
(*el invento*), and the word that links them is a **[[relative pronoun]]** (*que*). You have used
*que, quien, lo que, donde* since A2, and B1's lesson 08 added *el que* after prepositions and the
subjunctive for an unknown antecedent (*Busco un celular que tenga buena cámara*). B1 also showed
*el cual* in passing, for recognition.

This lesson is about the relatives of careful speech and writing: *el cual* and *lo cual*, *quien*
in its proper places, *cuyo* (whose), and *donde, como, cuando* as relatives. These are what make
a museum label, a news story or a DELE B2 essay sound like B2 rather than B1. The theme is
inventions and inventors around the world.

## Two kinds of relative clause

A **[[restrictive clause]]** picks out which one you mean. It has no commas:

- *Los inventores que patentaron sus ideas se hicieron ricos.* — The inventors who patented their
  ideas got rich. (only those; the others didn't)

A **[[non-restrictive clause]]** adds information about something already identified. It goes
between commas:

- *Los inventores, que patentaron sus ideas, se hicieron ricos.* — The inventors, who patented
  their ideas, got rich. (all of them patented and all of them got rich)

The commas change the meaning, so they matter in writing and show as small pauses in speech. This
difference also decides which relative pronoun you may use, as the next sections show.

## *El cual, la cual, los cuales, las cuales*

*El cual* agrees in gender and number with its antecedent. It has two main jobs.

First, after a preposition. After short prepositions (*a, con, de, en, por*), both *el que* and *el
cual* are correct; *el cual* sounds more formal:

- *el laboratorio en el que / en el cual trabajó* — the lab she worked in
- *la razón por la que / por la cual renunció* — the reason he resigned

After longer prepositions and prepositional phrases (*frente a, a pesar de, gracias a, debajo de,
según, durante, mediante*), *el cual* is the usual choice:

- *Es un prototipo gracias al cual ganaron el concurso.* — It's a prototype thanks to which they
  won the contest.
- *Este es el edificio frente al cual estaba la primera imprenta de la ciudad.* — This is the
  building opposite which the city's first printing press stood.

Remember that *a* + *el* and *de* + *el* contract: *al cual, del cual*.

Second, in a non-restrictive clause, after a comma, in formal writing:

- *La patente, la cual se concedió en 1880, protegía el foco de Edison.* — The patent, which was
  granted in 1880, protected Edison's light bulb.

Here *que* is also correct and more common. *El cual* helps when there are two possible
antecedents, because its gender and number point to the right one: *la colaboradora del
inventor, la cual vivía en Boston* (the woman collaborator, not the inventor, lived in Boston).

What *el cual* can't do is start a restrictive clause with no preposition: *el invento que cambió
el mundo*, not ~~*el invento el cual cambió el mundo*~~.

## *Lo que* and *lo cual*: a whole idea

When the antecedent is a whole idea rather than a noun, use the neuter *lo que* or *lo cual*,
after a comma:

- *Bell registró la patente antes que nadie, lo que / lo cual provocó años de juicios.* — Bell
  registered the patent before anyone else, which led to years of lawsuits.

Only *lo que* can be a **[[free relative]]** (one with no antecedent: "what, whatever"):

- *No entiendo lo que dices.* — I don't understand what you're saying. (not ~~*lo cual dices*~~)
- *Haz lo que quieras.* — Do whatever you want.

## *Quien, quienes*

*Quien* (one person) and *quienes* (several) refer only to people. Use them:

- after a preposition: *la científica con quien trabajó* (= *con la que / con la cual*);
- in a non-restrictive clause: *Hedy Lamarr, quien también fue actriz, patentó un sistema de
  comunicación* (*que* is fine here too);
- as a free relative, "whoever, the person who": *Quien inventa algo útil merece un premio*
  — Whoever invents something useful deserves a prize. (Don't confuse it with the question
  word *quién*, with an accent: *No sabemos quién inventó el microscopio*.)

Not in a restrictive clause without a preposition: *la mujer que inventó el aparato*, not
~~*la mujer quien inventó el aparato*~~. English "who" pushes learners toward that mistake.

## *Cuyo*: whose

*Cuyo* is a relative adjective meaning "whose". It agrees with the thing possessed, not with
the owner:

- *el inventor cuyas ideas cambiaron la medicina* — the inventor whose ideas changed medicine
  (*cuyas* agrees with *ideas*)
- *la empresa cuyo prototipo ganó* — the company whose prototype won (*cuyo* with *prototipo*)

Never put an article after it (~~*cuyo el nombre*~~), and put any preposition before it: *el
científico en cuyo laboratorio se hizo el descubrimiento* (the scientist in whose lab the
discovery was made). *Cuyo* is formal and mostly written; in conversation people rephrase: *el
inventor que tenía ideas raras*. You'll also hear *que su* (*el señor que su hijo es ingeniero*):
it is very common in speech but nonstandard, so don't write it. For the question "whose?" use *¿de
quién?*: *¿De quién es esta idea?*

| Relative | Refers to | After a preposition | Non-restrictive (commas) | Restrictive, no preposition |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *que* | anything | mostly no: use *el que* (but *el día en que, la forma en que*) | yes | yes |
| *el que* | anything | yes | rare without a preposition | no |
| *el cual* | anything | yes (preferred after long ones) | yes (formal) | no |
| *quien* | people | yes | yes | no |
| *lo que, lo cual* | a whole idea | yes | yes | — |
| *cuyo* | an owner (but agrees with the thing possessed) | before it: *en cuyo* | yes | yes |

The chart below asks the same questions in order.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a relative pronoun
  accDescr: A decision chart. First question, is the antecedent a whole idea? If yes, use lo que or lo cual after a comma. If no, does the clause say whose? If yes, use cuyo, cuya, cuyos or cuyas, agreeing with the thing possessed. If no, is there a preposition? If yes, use el que or el cual, the latter preferred after a long preposition, or quien for a person. If no preposition, is the clause between commas? If yes, use que, or formal el cual or quien. If no, use que.
  A["Antecedent = a whole idea?"] -->|yes| B["lo que / lo cual (after a comma)"]
  A -->|no| C["Does it say whose?"]
  C -->|yes| D["cuyo, cuya, cuyos, cuyas (agree with the thing owned)"]
  C -->|no| E["Is there a preposition?"]
  E -->|yes| F["el que / el cual (el cual after long ones); quien for people"]
  E -->|no| G["Between commas?"]
  G -->|yes| H["que (formal: el cual, quien)"]
  G -->|no| I["que"]
```

## *Donde, adonde, como, cuando*

These adverbs work as relatives too:

- *donde* (place): *la ciudad donde nació* = *en la que nació*. With movement toward a place,
  *adonde*: *el país adonde emigró*. (You'll also see it written *a donde*.)
- *como* (manner), mostly after *la forma, la manera, el modo*: *la forma como funciona* = *la
  forma en que funciona*.
- *cuando* (time), mostly non-restrictive: *En 1876, cuando Bell patentó el teléfono, otros
  trabajaban en lo mismo.* In a restrictive clause after a time noun, *en que* is more usual: *el
  día en que lo presentaron*.

## Mood in relative clauses: a review

The B1 rule still decides the mood: a known antecedent takes the indicative, an unknown or
nonexistent one the subjunctive.

- *Tengo un colega que trabaja en un laboratorio.* (he exists: indicative)
- *Buscan a alguien que sepa programar robots.* (anyone who can: subjunctive)
- *No hay ningún invento que no tenga riesgos.* (nonexistent: subjunctive)

Free relatives about the future or about "anyone" also take the subjunctive: *Los que lleguen
tarde no podrán entrar; Quien tenga una idea, que la presente.*

After a superlative or *el único, el primero*, both moods are correct. The subjunctive (often the
perfect subjunctive from lesson 02) sounds more emphatic, "that has ever been made":

- *Es el invento más útil que se ha hecho / que se haya hecho.* — It's the most useful invention
  ever made.
- *Fue la primera mujer que patentó / que patentara un aparato así* (the second is literary).

## Five inventions on a timeline

![A horizontal timeline from 1400 to 2000. Five dated markers, with boxes above and below the line: about 1450, Gutenberg's printing press in Mainz; about 1590, the compound microscope, attributed to the Janssens in the Netherlands, with a note that the attribution is disputed; 1876, Bell's telephone patent in the United States; 1880, Edison's patent for an incandescent light bulb; 1942, the frequency-hopping patent of Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: an audio guide

This is the script of an audio guide in an imaginary science museum. Listen for every relative.

> Bienvenidos a la sala Mentes brillantes, en la cual presentamos cinco inventos que cambiaron la
> vida diaria. Empezamos por la imprenta de tipos móviles, que Johannes Gutenberg desarrolló en
> Maguncia hacia 1450. Siglos antes ya se imprimía con tipos móviles en China y Corea, pero fue su
> máquina, gracias a la cual los libros se volvieron más baratos, la que transformó Europa.
>
> A su derecha está el microscopio. Nadie sabe con certeza quién lo inventó: se suele atribuir a
> los Janssen, unos fabricantes de lentes holandeses cuyo taller funcionaba a finales del siglo XVI,
> pero la atribución se discute. Lo que sí sabemos es que, en la década de 1670, Antonie van
> Leeuwenhoek observó con sus lentes seres diminutos que nadie había visto antes, lo cual abrió
> el camino a la microbiología.
>
> Siga hasta la vitrina del teléfono. En 1876 Alexander Graham Bell registró una patente sobre la
> cual todavía se discute: el italiano Antonio Meucci, quien había trabajado en un aparato
> parecido, es para muchos el verdadero pionero.
>
> Frente a usted, el foco. Thomas Edison obtuvo en 1880 la patente de un foco incandescente, pero
> el británico Joseph Swan, cuyas lámparas se parecían mucho a las suyas, ya las había presentado
> en Inglaterra.
> Edison, quien tenía un gran laboratorio y muchos colaboradores, logró un foco que duraba horas.
>
> Por último, una actriz. Hedy Lamarr, quien trabajaba en Hollywood, obtuvo en 1942, con el
> compositor George Antheil, la patente de un sistema de salto de frecuencia cuya idea muchos
> consideran un antecedente de las tecnologías inalámbricas actuales. Quien piense que el ingenio es solo cosa de científicos no
> conoce esta historia. Gracias por su visita.

Summary: the guide welcomes visitors to a room on five inventions. Gutenberg developed his
movable-type press in Mainz around 1450; movable type already existed in China and Korea, but his
machine made books cheaper. The microscope is usually credited to the Janssens, Dutch lens makers
of the late 16th century, though this is disputed; in the 1670s Leeuwenhoek saw tiny living
things. Bell's 1876 telephone patent is still debated because of Antonio Meucci. Edison patented
an incandescent bulb in 1880 while Joseph Swan was doing similar work. Hedy Lamarr and George
Antheil received a 1942 patent for frequency hopping, an idea many see as a forerunner of today's
wireless technology.

(*los tipos móviles* — movable type; *la vitrina* — display case; *el salto de frecuencia* —
frequency hopping; *inalámbrico* — wireless; *diminuto* — tiny; *el pionero* — pioneer, lesson 01; *atribuir* — to attribute; *se
suele atribuir* — it is usually attributed; *el antecedente* — forerunner, precedent.) Notice *una
patente sobre la cual todavía se discute* (a patent that is still argued about), *cuyo taller* and *cuyas lámparas* agreeing with the thing possessed, and *Quien piense…* (whoever thinks), a free
relative with the subjunctive.

## Pronunciation

- *Cuyo*: two syllables, *CU-yo*; with Mexican *yeísmo*, the *y* sounds like the *y* of *yo*.
  *Cuales* is two syllables too: *CUA-les*.
- *Microscopio* has four syllables: *mi-cros-CO-pio* (the final *io* is one syllable).
- *Ingenioso*: four syllables, *in-ge-NIO-so*; the *g* before *e* is the throaty *j* sound.
- *Revolucionar*: five syllables, *re-vo-lu-cio-NAR*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*la mujer quien inventó*~~ → *la mujer que inventó*. No *quien* in a restrictive clause
  without a preposition.
- ~~*el inventor cuyo ideas*~~ → *el inventor cuyas ideas*. *Cuyo* agrees with the thing owned.
- ~~*cuyo el laboratorio*~~ → *cuyo laboratorio*. No article after *cuyo*.
- ~~*No entiendo lo cual dices*~~ → *lo que dices*. *Lo cual* needs an antecedent and a comma.
- ~~*el laboratorio que trabajé*~~ → *el laboratorio en el que / en el cual trabajé*. The
  preposition can't be dropped or moved to the end as in English.
- ~~*el señor que su hijo es ingeniero*~~ in writing → *el señor cuyo hijo es ingeniero*.

## Key points

- Restrictive clauses pick out (no commas); non-restrictive clauses add information (commas).
- *El cual* agrees with its antecedent: after prepositions (preferred after long ones: *gracias al
  cual, frente a la cual*) and, formally, after a comma; never alone in a restrictive clause.
- *Lo que / lo cual* for a whole idea after a comma; only *lo que* means "what".
- *Quien, quienes*: people, after a preposition, after a comma, or as "whoever".
- *Cuyo, cuya, cuyos, cuyas* agree with the thing possessed; formal; *que su* is nonstandard.
- *Donde, adonde, como, cuando* work as relatives.
- Subjunctive for an unknown or nonexistent antecedent; either mood after a superlative.
