lessons.title: Como sube la renta, se van: cause and consequence
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

B1's lesson 17 gave you the everyday ways to give a reason (*porque, ya que, puesto que, dado
que, debido a*) and a result (*así que, por eso, por lo tanto, de modo que*). At B2 you need to
argue about a social issue: to say which cause matters, reject the wrong one and draw a
conclusion in a formal register. This lesson adds the **[[causal clause]]** with *como* and *debido a
que*, the cause that brings good or bad results, the pattern *no porque… sino porque*, and the
**[[consecutive clause]]** with *en consecuencia, por ende, así pues, de ahí que* and *tan… que*. All
of these are **[[connectors]]**: words that join two ideas and show how they relate.

The theme is cities and housing: rising rents, gentrification, digital nomads, and families
moving to the outskirts. It's a debated topic, and the lesson gives the language for every side
of the argument rather than taking one.

## Giving a cause: position matters

*Porque* normally follows the main clause. *Como* (since, as) gives a cause that comes first,
before the main clause, and takes the indicative:

- *Nos mudamos porque subió la renta.* — We moved because the rent went up.
- *Como subió la renta, nos mudamos.* — Since the rent went up, we moved.

Put *como* after the main clause and it stops meaning "since": ~~*Nos mudamos como subió la
renta*~~ is not Spanish. To start with the cause, use *como*, *ya que* or *dado que*; to end with
it, use *porque*, *ya que* or *dado que*.

*Debido a que* (because, owing to the fact that) is the formal partner of B1's *debido a* + noun,
and *a causa de* takes a noun:

- *La obra se detuvo debido a que no tenía permisos.* — The construction stopped because it
  didn't have permits.
- *Cerraron el mercado a causa de las lluvias.* — They closed the market because of the rain.

Spanish also likes to say whether a cause was good or bad news:

- *gracias a (que)* for a good result: *Gracias a que los vecinos se organizaron, el mercado
  sigue abierto.* — Thanks to the residents getting organized, the market is still open.
- *por culpa de* + noun or infinitive for a bad one: *Por culpa del tráfico, llego tarde todos
  los días.* — Because of the traffic, I'm late every day.

*Gracias a* with a bad result is ironic: *Gracias a ti, perdimos el departamento* (Thanks a lot to
you, we lost the apartment).

## Rejecting a cause: *no porque… sino porque*

To deny one reason and give the real one, put the rejected cause in the subjunctive and the real
one in the indicative:

- *Se fue no porque quisiera, sino porque no podía pagar.* — She left not because she wanted to,
  but because she couldn't pay.
- *No vendo la casa porque necesite dinero, sino porque ya no reconozco la colonia.* — I'm not
  selling the house because I need money, but because I no longer recognize the neighborhood.

The subjunctive marks a cause the speaker says isn't true. (B2's lesson 05 showed the same logic
with *no es que* + subjunctive.) Follow the sequence of tenses: present main verb, present
subjunctive (*necesite*); past main verb, imperfect subjunctive (*quisiera*).

## Drawing a consequence

The connectors of consequence sit on a scale of register:

| Connector | Register | Mood | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *así que, por eso* | everyday | indicative | *Subió la renta, así que nos mudamos.* |
| *de modo que, de manera que* | neutral | indicative | *No había nada disponible, de modo que buscamos en las afueras.* |
| *por lo tanto, en consecuencia* | written | indicative | *La oferta es escasa; en consecuencia, los precios suben.* |
| *por ende, así pues* | formal | indicative | *Así pues, el problema no es solo económico.* |
| *de ahí que* | written | usually subjunctive | *Los precios suben; de ahí que mucha gente se mude.* |

*En consecuencia* and *por ende* go after a semicolon or a period, or between commas inside a
sentence: *Subió el predial y, en consecuencia, subieron las rentas* (*el predial* = property
tax). *Así pues* usually opens a concluding sentence.

*De ahí que* (hence, which is why) is the odd one: although it introduces a result, it is
normally followed by the subjunctive, because the result is presented as something already known
that the first sentence explains:

- *El centro es carísimo; de ahí que tantos estudiantes vivan lejos.* — Downtown is very
  expensive, which is why so many students live far away.
- *Las rentas se encarecieron; de ahí que muchas familias se hayan ido.* — Rents went up, which
  is why many families have left.

You'll occasionally read *de ahí que* with the indicative; the subjunctive is the norm to
produce.

## *Tan… que, tanto… que*

For a consequence that comes from an intensity, Spanish uses a pair:

- *tan* + adjective or adverb + *que*: *La renta subió tan rápido que no nos dio tiempo de
  ahorrar.*
- *tanto, tanta, tantos, tantas* + noun + *que* (agreeing with the noun): *Hay tantos
  departamentos vacíos que la calle parece abandonada.*
- verb + *tanto que*: *La colonia ha cambiado tanto que ya no la reconozco.*

Don't mix them: *tan caro* (adjective) but *tanto dinero* (noun) and *subió tanto* (verb).

## A chain of causes

![A cause-and-consequence chain drawn as six boxes joined by arrows from top to bottom, with a long arrow beside them from causa to consecuencia. Box 1: llegan nuevos residentes y rentas de corto plazo. Arrow labeled por eso. Box 2: sube la demanda de vivienda. Arrow labeled en consecuencia. Box 3: la vivienda se encarece. Arrow labeled por lo tanto. Box 4: las familias se mudan a la periferia. Arrow labeled así que. Box 5: aumentan los desplazamientos largos al trabajo. Arrow labeled por ende. Box 6: más tráfico y menos tiempo libre.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each arrow is a connector you could use between the two boxes. In a text you'd vary them:
*Llegan nuevos residentes; por eso sube la demanda y, en consecuencia, la vivienda se encarece. De
ahí que muchas familias se muden a la periferia.*

## Words for the city

- *la periferia* and *las afueras* (plural only) are the outskirts; *el suburbio* is a false
  friend: it usually means a poor outlying district, not a well-off suburb. In Mexico a planned
  development of houses, often gated, is *un fraccionamiento*.
- *la urbanización* is urbanization, the growth of a city (in Spain it's also a housing estate);
  *el hacinamiento* is overcrowding.
- *el auge* is a boom (*las rentas de corto plazo están en auge*); *la especulación
  inmobiliaria* is property speculation; *la inmobiliaria* is a real estate agency or developer.
- *desalojar* is to evict (or to clear a building: *desalojaron por el sismo*); *el desalojo* is
  an eviction.
- *encarecerse* (to become more expensive, *se encarece*) and *el encarecimiento*; *desplazar*
  (*desplacé*: to displace) and *el desplazamiento*, which also means a commute in formal style;
  *el éxodo* (exodus).
- *el nómada digital, la nómada digital*: someone who works online while living in different
  places, often for an employer or clients in another country.

For scale: the Ciudad de México had 9,209,944 residents and 2,756,319 inhabited private
dwellings, about 3.3 people per home, in the 2020 census of INEGI (Mexico's statistics
institute).

## Text: a news feature

> *La colonia que cambió de cara*
>
> Hace diez años, en la colonia Jardines del Río, en la Ciudad de México, casi todos los negocios
> eran de vecinos: la tortillería, la papelería, la fonda de doña Ofelia. Hoy, en la misma
> cuadra, hay tres cafeterías de especialidad y un edificio de departamentos amueblados que se
> rentan por noche. ¿Qué pasó?
>
> Como la zona tiene parques, metro y edificios antiguos, empezó a atraer a nuevos residentes,
> entre ellos nómadas digitales que cobran en dólares o en euros. La demanda creció tanto que las
> rentas se dispararon; en consecuencia, muchos inquilinos de toda la vida no pudieron renovar sus
> contratos. "No me fui porque quisiera", explica Ofelia, que ahora vive en un fraccionamiento a
> hora y media del centro, "sino porque me pidieron el doble". Como ella, muchas familias se
> fueron a las afueras, a municipios vecinos donde la vivienda es más barata, aunque los
> desplazamientos al trabajo son mucho más largos.
>
> Para los nuevos vecinos, el cambio también tiene ventajas. Gracias a que llegaron negocios, hay
> más empleo y las calles están más iluminadas. Algunos propietarios, además, pudieron arreglar
> sus casas por primera vez en años, y hay quien dice que, como la colonia está de moda, sus
> propiedades valen hoy mucho más que antes.
>
> Los especialistas que consultamos no coinciden en todo. Una urbanista explica que la
> gentrificación no tiene una sola causa: influyen la especulación inmobiliaria, el auge de las
> rentas de corto plazo y la falta de vivienda asequible. Un economista añade que el
> encarecimiento expulsa a quienes ganan menos; de ahí que la periferia crezca más rápido que el
> centro. Así pues, concluyen ambos, el debate no es si la ciudad debe cambiar, sino cómo
> conseguir que los vecinos de siempre puedan quedarse.

Summary: in a (fictional) Mexico City neighborhood, local shops have given way to specialty
cafés and furnished apartments rented by the night. Because the area has parks, the metro and
old buildings, it attracted newcomers, including digital nomads paid in foreign currency; rents
shot up and many long-time tenants couldn't renew. Doña Ofelia now lives in a development an
hour and a half from downtown: she left because her rent doubled, not by choice; many families
moved to cheaper towns nearby and now commute much farther. Newcomers point to jobs, better
lighting, repaired houses and rising property values. An urban planner says gentrification has several
causes; an economist says rising costs push lower earners out, which is why the outskirts grow
faster. Both conclude that the question is how to let long-time residents stay.

(*cambiar de cara* — to change its face; *la fonda* — small family restaurant; *de
especialidad* — specialty; *dispararse* — to shoot up; *de toda la vida* — lifelong; *el
urbanista* — urban planner; *coincidir* — to agree; *asequible* — affordable; *expulsar* — to
push out; *hay quien dice* — some people say; *estar de moda* — to be in fashion, lesson
05.) Find the connectors: *como* (cause, first), *tanto que* and *en consecuencia*
(consequence), *no… porque quisiera, sino porque* (rejected cause), *gracias a que* (good cause),
*de ahí que crezca* (subjunctive), *así pues* (conclusion).

## Pronunciation

- *Gentrificación*: five syllables, *gen-tri-fi-ca-CIÓN*; the *g* before *e* is the *j* sound.
- *Hacinamiento*: five syllables, *a-ci-na-MIEN-to*: the *h* is silent and *ci* is *si*.
- *Éxodo*: *É-xo-do*, stressed on the first syllable; the *x* is *ks*.
- *Periferia*: four syllables, *pe-ri-FE-ria*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*Nos mudamos como subió la renta*~~ → *Nos mudamos porque subió la renta* or *Como subió la
  renta, nos mudamos*. Causal *como* comes first.
- ~~*debido a que la lluvia*~~ → *debido a la lluvia* (noun) or *debido a que llovió* (clause).
- *No me fui porque quería, sino porque…* when you reject the cause: the indicative is heard,
  but it can also be read as "wanting to was the reason I didn't leave". Use the subjunctive,
  *porque quisiera*, which can only mean a rejected cause.
- ~~*tan dinero que*~~ → *tanto dinero que*; ~~*tanto caro que*~~ → *tan caro que*.
- *el suburbio* for a well-off suburb: say *una zona residencial* or *un fraccionamiento*.

## Key points

- *Como* + indicative gives a cause and always comes first; *porque* normally follows the main
  clause; *ya que, dado que, puesto que* go either way.
- *Debido a que* + clause (formal), *debido a / a causa de* + noun; *gracias a (que)* for a good
  result, *por culpa de* for a bad one.
- *No porque* + subjunctive, *sino porque* + indicative rejects one cause and gives the real one.
- Consequence by register: *así que, por eso* → *de modo que* → *por lo tanto, en consecuencia* →
  *por ende, así pues*; *de ahí que* usually + subjunctive.
- *Tan* + adjective / adverb, *tanto/a/os/as* + noun, verb + *tanto*, then *que*.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Una vez que te den de alta: purpose and time at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In B1 you learned that *para que* takes the subjunctive (lesson 06) and that *cuando, en cuanto,
hasta que* take the subjunctive when they point to the future (lesson 07): *Cuando llegues,
llámame.* This lesson takes both ideas to B2. It adds the formal **[[purpose clause]]** connectors
(*a fin de que, con el fin de que*), the precaution *no vaya a ser que*, and the **[[time clause]]**
connectors that instructions and explanations need: *una vez que, a medida que, cada vez que,
desde que* and *al* + infinitive. Purpose and time clauses are two kinds of **[[adverbial clause]]**:
a clause that works like an adverb, telling you why, when, how or on what condition.

The theme is health and medical treatment: a diagnosis, a prescription, surgery and recovery. The
lesson gives language, not medical advice: for your own health, ask a doctor.

## Purpose: from everyday to formal

The rule from B1 still holds: the same subject takes an infinitive, a different subject takes
*que* + subjunctive.

- *Vine para hacerme unos análisis.* — I came to get some tests done. (same subject; *los
  análisis* = lab tests, lesson 18)
- *Te dejo la receta para que compres el medicamento.* — I'm leaving you the prescription so you
  can buy the medicine. (different subject)

Formal speech and writing replace *para* with *a fin de* or *con el fin de*, and add *con la
intención de* (with the intention of). The infinitive / *que* + subjunctive rule is the same:

| Same subject | Different subject | Register |
|---|---|---|
| *para* + infinitive | *para que* + subjunctive | all |
| *a fin de* + infinitive | *a fin de que* + subjunctive | formal |
| *con el fin de* + infinitive | *con el fin de que* + subjunctive | formal |
| *con la intención de* + infinitive | *con la intención de que* + subjunctive | all |

- *Se suspendieron las visitas con el fin de evitar contagios.* — Visits were suspended in order
  to avoid infections. (*evitar* = to avoid, lesson 04; *el contagio* = infection)
- *Le pedimos llegar en ayunas a fin de que los resultados sean confiables.* — We ask you to
  arrive without eating so that the results are reliable. (*en ayunas* = on an empty stomach;
  *confiable* = reliable)

After a past main verb, the subjunctive moves to the imperfect: *La doctora me dio una hoja con
las indicaciones para que no se me olvidara nada.*

### A precaution: *no vaya a ser que*

*No vaya a ser que* (literally "may it not turn out that") and its shorter form *no sea que* add a
precaution: "in case, so that… doesn't happen". They always take the subjunctive and usually come after
the main clause:

- *Lleva la receta, no vaya a ser que te pidan verla.* — Take the prescription in case they ask
  to see it.
- *Tómate la temperatura en la noche, no sea que vuelva la fiebre.* — Take your temperature at
  night, in case the fever comes back.

The subjunctive here is in the present for a present or future main verb; after a past one, it's
the imperfect: *Llevé la receta, no fuera a ser que me la pidieran.*

## Time clauses: one mood rule for all

B1's rule for *cuando* covers almost every time connector: the **[[indicative]]** for the past and
for habits, the **[[subjunctive]]** for the future.

- *Una vez que te den de alta, descansa una semana.* — Once they discharge you, rest for a week.
  (future: subjunctive)
- *Una vez que me dieron de alta, me fui a casa de mi mamá.* — Once they discharged me, I went to
  my mom's. (past: indicative)

The same goes for:

- *a medida que* (as, as gradually), for two things that change together. Its synonym *conforme*
  is common in Mexico and works the same way: *A medida que / Conforme baje la inflamación,
  podrás doblar la rodilla.* — As the swelling goes down, you'll be able to bend your knee.
  (*la inflamación* = swelling)
- *cada vez que* and *siempre que* (whenever): *Cada vez que me pongo de pie, me duele* (habit);
  *Cada vez que sientas dolor, tómate el analgésico* (future). Remember from B1 that *siempre que*
  + subjunctive can also mean "as long as": lesson 12 returns to it.
- *en cuanto, tan pronto como, apenas* (as soon as), from B1: *En cuanto tengamos el diagnóstico,
  le avisamos.*

Two exceptions:

- *desde que* (since) is about a real starting point, so it usually takes the indicative: *Desde
  que empecé la rehabilitación, camino mejor.* (For a starting point still in the future, Spanish
  usually says *a partir de que* + subjunctive: *A partir de que empieces la terapia, vas a venir dos
  veces por semana* — From the time you start therapy, you'll come twice a week.)
- *antes de que* always takes the subjunctive, even in the past, because the event hadn't happened
  yet at that point: *Me pusieron la anestesia antes de que entrara el cirujano.* (*el cirujano* =
  surgeon)

With the same subject, use an infinitive: *antes de comer, después de operarse* (to have surgery), and *al* +
infinitive for "when, on doing": *Al salir del quirófano, me sentía mareado* (When I came out of
the operating room, I felt dizzy).

### *Hasta que no*: an extra *no*

You'll hear *hasta que* with an extra *no* that doesn't make the clause negative: *No te vas
hasta que no te baje la fiebre* (You're not leaving until your fever goes down). Grammars call it
an expletive *no*; it is common in speech, especially when the main clause is negative. You never
need it: *hasta que te baje la fiebre* says the same thing.

In Spain you'll also meet *nada más* + infinitive for "as soon as": *Nada más llegar, me
llamó* (As soon as he arrived, he called me). Recognize it; in Mexico, say *En cuanto llegó, me
llamó*.

## A treatment over time

![A timeline of a treatment after knee surgery. Day 0: surgery in the operating room. Day 2: Alta: reposo, with the phrase una vez que te den de alta. Day 10: Te quitan los puntos, with the phrase en cuanto te los quiten. Weeks 2 to 8: physical therapy, a bar that grows from light to dark, labeled a medida que avances, más ejercicios. Week 8: a follow-up appointment with the specialist, labeled antes de que vuelvas a correr: consulta. Below the line, a row of pills labeled cada vez que te duela: analgésico, no más de una dosis cada ocho horas.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Words for treatment

- *el diagnóstico* (diagnosis) and *diagnosticar* (*diagnostiqué*); *el especialista, la
  especialista*; *la consulta* (a doctor's appointment, or the doctor's office hours: *Tengo
  consulta el martes*).
- *recetar* (to prescribe): *la receta* is both the prescription and a recipe. In Mexico,
  antibiotics may be sold only with a prescription: a 2010 agreement published in the *Diario
  Oficial de la Federación* requires pharmacies to stamp the prescription and keep it once the
  prescribed amount has been dispensed.
- *el tratamiento* (treatment), *la dosis* (dose; same form in the plural), *el analgésico*
  (painkiller), *el efecto secundario* (side effect).
- *la cirugía* (surgery), *la anestesia*, *el quirófano* (operating room); *dar de alta* (to
  discharge: *Me dieron de alta el lunes*).
- *contagioso, crónico; prevenir* (to prevent, conjugated like *venir*: *prevengo, previne*) and
  *la prevención*; *la recaída* (relapse); *la rehabilitación* (physical therapy, rehab).

## Dialogue: the day of discharge

Héctor had knee surgery two days ago. Dr. Salinas comes to see him before he leaves.

> Dra. Salinas: Buenos días, Héctor. Todo salió muy bien, así que hoy lo damos de alta.
>
> Héctor: ¡Qué bueno! ¿Y cuándo puedo volver a jugar futbol?
>
> Dra. Salinas: No tan rápido. Una vez que le quitemos los puntos, empieza la rehabilitación, a fin de que la rodilla recupere fuerza.
>
> Héctor: ¿Y el dolor? Anoche me dolió bastante.
>
> Dra. Salinas: Le receté un analgésico. Tómelo cada vez que lo necesite, pero no más de una dosis cada ocho horas.
>
> Héctor: ¿Tiene efectos secundarios?
>
> Dra. Salinas: Puede darle sueño, así que no maneje mientras lo tome. Y no deje la rehabilitación antes de que el especialista lo autorice, no vaya a ser que tenga una recaída.
>
> Héctor: Entendido. ¿Cuándo sabré si ya estoy bien?
>
> Dra. Salinas: A medida que pasen las semanas, va a notar la diferencia. Cuando vaya a su cita con el especialista, llévele esta hoja.
>
> Héctor: Muchas gracias, doctora. Al llegar a casa, me voy a dormir una semana entera.

> Dr. Salinas: Good morning, Héctor. Everything went very well, so we're discharging you today.
>
> Héctor: Great! And when can I play soccer again?
>
> Dr. Salinas: Not so fast. Once we take out your stitches, physical therapy starts, so that your knee gets its strength back.
>
> Héctor: And the pain? Last night it hurt quite a lot.
>
> Dr. Salinas: I've prescribed a painkiller. Take it whenever you need it, but no more than one dose every eight hours.
>
> Héctor: Does it have side effects?
>
> Dr. Salinas: It can make you sleepy, so don't drive while you're taking it. And don't stop therapy before the specialist says so, in case you have a relapse.
>
> Héctor: Got it. When will I know I'm all right?
>
> Dr. Salinas: As the weeks go by, you'll notice the difference. When you go to your appointment with the specialist, take this sheet along.
>
> Héctor: Thank you very much, doctor. When I get home, I'm going to sleep for a whole week.

(*los puntos* — stitches; *autorizar* — to authorize.) Every future time clause has a
subjunctive (*le quitemos, lo necesite, lo tome, lo autorice, pasen, vaya*); *mientras* +
subjunctive here means "while" about the future, as in B1.

## The discharge sheet

![A hospital discharge sheet from the invented Hospital Los Cedros. Heading: Hoja de alta. Rows: Paciente: Héctor Ruiz Treviño. Fecha de ingreso: 3 de marzo de 2026. Fecha de alta: 5 de marzo de 2026. Diagnóstico: lesión de menisco, rodilla derecha. Procedimiento: cirugía artroscópica. Tratamiento: paracetamol 500 mg, una tableta cada 8 horas si hay dolor, máximo 5 días. Indicaciones: reposo; no mojar la herida; iniciar rehabilitación una vez que se retiren los puntos. Próxima consulta: 13 de marzo de 2026: retiro de puntos. Acuda a urgencias si presenta: fiebre, sangrado o dolor que no cede.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Discharge sheets use the infinitive for instructions (*no mojar la herida* — don't get the wound
wet) and the formal *usted* command (*Acuda a urgencias si presenta…* — Go to the emergency room
if you have…). *Que no cede* means "that doesn't let up"; *la lesión de menisco* is a
meniscus injury (*la lesión*, lesson 16); *el sangrado* is bleeding; *el retiro de puntos* is
the removal of stitches. The medication on this sheet is
invented for the example; only a doctor can say what you should take.

## Pronunciation

- *Quirófano*: four syllables, *qui-RÓ-fa-no*; *qu* is a *k* sound.
- *Diagnóstico*: four syllables, *diag-NÓS-ti-co* (*ia* is one syllable).
- *Cirugía*: four syllables, *ci-ru-GÍ-a*: the accent breaks *ía* into two.
- *Analgésico*: five syllables, *a-nal-GÉ-si-co*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*Una vez que te dan de alta, descansa*~~ for the future → *te den de alta*.
- ~~*antes de que entró el cirujano*~~ → *antes de que entrara*. *Antes de que* is always
  subjunctive.
- ~~*Desde que empiece la terapia, camino mejor*~~ → *Desde que empecé la terapia, camino mejor*.
  *Desde que* about a real, past starting point takes the indicative.
- ~~*a fin de que los resultados son confiables*~~ → *sean*. Every purpose clause with *que* is
  subjunctive.
- ~~*Lleva la receta, no vaya a ser que te la piden*~~ → *te la pidan*.
- Translating "as" with *como* for two changes over time: *A medida que pasa el tiempo* (as time
  goes by), not ~~*Como pasa el tiempo*~~, which would mean "since time passes".

## Key points

- Purpose: *para, a fin de, con el fin de, con la intención de* + infinitive (same subject) or
  + *que* + subjunctive (different subject); *a fin de* and *con el fin de* are formal.
- *No vaya a ser que / no sea que* + subjunctive: a precaution, "in case".
- Time: *una vez que, a medida que (conforme), cada vez que, siempre que, en cuanto, tan pronto
  como, apenas* + indicative for the past and habits, subjunctive for the future.
- *Desde que* + indicative (for a real starting point); *antes de que* + subjunctive always; *al* + infinitive = when, on
  doing.
- *Hasta que no* (expletive *no*) and Spain's *nada más* + infinitive: recognize them.

lessons.title: Siempre y cuando firmes: conditions beyond si at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

B1's lesson 18 introduced the conjunctions of condition that take the subjunctive (*con tal de
que, a menos que, en caso de que, siempre y cuando*), and B2's lesson 04 took *si* into the past
(*Si hubiera firmado, no habría perdido*). This lesson completes the picture: it sorts the
condition connectors by what they mean, adds the formal ones of contracts and courts (*a
condición de que, en el supuesto de que, salvo que, excepto que*), and shows three more ways to
make a condition without *si*: *como* + subjunctive, *de* + infinitive and the gerund. It also
puts all of them in the past.

The theme is law and citizens' rights: lawsuits, courts, contracts and human rights in Mexico.
Everything here is general information for learning Spanish, not legal advice.

## Four jobs, one mood

Almost every connector in this lesson takes the subjunctive, because a condition is something that
hasn't happened yet. What changes is the job the condition does.

![A chart of condition connectors sorted by meaning, in four boxes. Box 1, Requisito mínimo (minimum requirement): siempre y cuando, siempre que, con tal (de) que, a condición de que. Box 2, Excepción (unless): a no ser que, a menos que, salvo que, excepto que. Box 3, Caso posible (in case): en caso de que, en el supuesto de que, por si (acaso). Box 4, Otras formas: como + subjuntivo (advertencia), de + infinitivo, gerundio. A note across the bottom: las conjunciones llevan subjuntivo, salvo por si (indicativo o imperfecto de subjuntivo) y excepto que + indicativo (= except that).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 1. A minimum requirement

As long as, provided that, on condition that:

- *Te rento el local siempre y cuando lo dejes como estaba.* — I'll rent you the space as long as
  you leave it as it was.
- *Acepto el acuerdo a condición de que quede por escrito.* — I accept the agreement on condition
  that it's put in writing.
- *Firmo con tal de que me paguen a tiempo.* (B1; also *con tal que*)

*Siempre que* + subjunctive means the same here; with the indicative it means "whenever", and
with the subjunctive it can also mean "whenever" about the future (B1 18, lesson 11): context
decides. *Siempre y cuando* has only the condition meaning.

### 2. An exception

Unless:

- *El juicio será en marzo, a no ser que lleguen a un acuerdo.* — The trial will be in March,
  unless they reach an agreement.
- *El contrato se renueva solo, salvo que una de las partes avise por escrito.* — The contract
  renews automatically unless one of the parties gives written notice.

*A no ser que* and *a menos que* mean the same; *salvo que* is more formal. *Excepto que* changes
with the mood:

- + subjunctive = unless: *Firmo mañana, excepto que cambien las condiciones.*
- + indicative = except that (a fact): *El contrato era bueno, excepto que no decía nada del
  depósito.* — The contract was good, except that it said nothing about the deposit.

### 3. A possible case

In case, in the event that:

- *En caso de que no le devuelvan el depósito, puede demandar.* (B1)
- *En el supuesto de que el arrendatario incumpla el contrato, pagará una indemnización.* — In the
  event that the tenant breaches the contract, he or she will pay damages. (*el arrendatario* =
  tenant in legal language)

*En el supuesto de que* belongs to contracts and laws; in conversation, *en caso de que* or *si*.

*Por si* and *por si acaso* (just in case; *por si acaso* is also listed in lesson 22) are
different: they are built on *si*, so they never
take the present subjunctive. Use the indicative, or the imperfect subjunctive for a less likely
case:

- *Guarda todos los recibos, por si hay un problema.* — Keep all the receipts, just in case
  there's a problem.
- *Llevé una copia del contrato, por si me la pidieran.* — I took a copy of the contract in case
  they asked me for it.

## Three ways to make a condition without a conjunction

### *Como* + subjunctive

At the start of the sentence, *como* + subjunctive makes a warning or a threat:

- *Como no pagues la renta, te demandan.* — If you don't pay the rent, they'll sue you.
- *Como vuelvas a llegar tarde, hablo con tu jefe.* — If you're late again, I'm talking to your
  boss.

Compare lesson 10's causal *como* + indicative: *Como no pagaste la renta, te demandaron* (Since
you didn't pay the rent, they sued you). The mood tells you which one you're hearing. The chart above calls it *advertencia*
(warning, lesson 13). This *como*
is colloquial and usually sounds like a warning or a threat; for a neutral condition use *si*.

### *De* + infinitive

This is a compact, slightly formal "if":

- *De seguir así, perderán el juicio.* — If they carry on like this, they'll lose the case.
- *De no presentar la apelación a tiempo, la sentencia queda firme.* — If the appeal isn't filed
  in time, the ruling becomes final.

Lesson 04's compound form works the same way for the past: *De haberlo sabido, no habría firmado.*

### The gerund

The gerund can carry a condition, mostly in ads and instructions. Recognize it:

- *Firmando hoy, recibe un descuento del 10 %.* — If you sign today, you get a 10% discount.

## Conditions in the past

After a past or conditional main verb, the subjunctive moves into the imperfect (or the
pluperfect, for something completed before), following the sequence of tenses:

- *Me dijo que firmaría siempre y cuando le pagaran por adelantado.* — He told me he would sign as
  long as they paid him in advance.
- *El juez aceptó a condición de que el acusado se presentara cada semana.* — The judge agreed on
  condition that the defendant report every week.
- *No habrían ganado a no ser que hubieran tenido un buen abogado.* — They wouldn't have won unless
  they'd had a good lawyer.

## Courts and rights in Mexico

![A courtroom seen from the public seats. At the back, on a raised bench, a judge. In front of the bench, at the left table, the prosecutor and at the right table the defense lawyer beside the defendant. To one side, a witness stand with a seated witness. A Mexican flag stands behind the judge.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- In a criminal trial, *el fiscal* (the prosecutor, *la fiscal*) accuses. Mexico's Constitution
  calls the prosecuting authority *el Ministerio Público*, and people often say *el ministerio
  público* or *el MP* for the prosecutor's office or a prosecutor (*el agente del Ministerio
  Público*). *El abogado defensor* defends *el
  acusado*; *el juez* (B1) issues *la sentencia* (the ruling), which can be appealed (*apelar*).
  *El testigo* (A2) is a witness.
- In a civil case you *demandar* (sue) someone: *poner una demanda*. If a court finds that a
  contract was breached (*incumplir, el incumplimiento*), it can order *una indemnización*
  (damages).
- *El notario* is not what a US notary public is. In Mexico a *notario público* must be a lawyer
  who has done an internship and passed an exam, and notaries handle deeds, wills and company
  papers.
- *El amparo*, or *juicio de amparo*, is a Mexican lawsuit that protects a person against an act
  of an authority that violates his or her rights: a resident can ask a federal judge for an
  *amparo* against a decision of a government office, for example. It is set out in articles 103
  and 107 of the Constitution.
- *Los derechos humanos*: a constitutional reform published on June 10, 2011, changed article 1 so
  that everyone enjoys the human rights recognized in the Constitution and in the international
  treaties Mexico is party to, and replaced the older phrase *garantías individuales* with
  *derechos humanos*. The Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos (CNDH), created on June 6,
  1990, receives complaints against authorities; it was given constitutional rank in 1992 and
  autonomy in 1999.
- *legal / ilegal*; *acusar a alguien de algo* (to accuse someone of something); *la defensa*
  (the defense).

## Dialogue: a broken contract

Raúl hired a company to remodel his kitchen. The work stopped halfway. He sees a lawyer, the
*licenciada* Treviño (in Mexico, lawyers are usually addressed as *licenciado / licenciada*).

> Lic. Treviño: Cuénteme, Raúl. ¿Qué dice exactamente el contrato?
>
> Raúl: Que terminarían en ocho semanas, siempre y cuando yo pagara la mitad por adelantado. Y la pagué.
>
> Lic. Treviño: Entonces ellos incumplieron. ¿Hay alguna cláusula sobre retrasos?
>
> Raúl: Sí: en el supuesto de que la obra se retrase, me devuelven una parte del dinero, salvo que el retraso sea por lluvia.
>
> Lic. Treviño: ¿Y llovió?
>
> Raúl: Dos días, nada más. Llevan tres semanas sin venir.
>
> Lic. Treviño: Bien. Primero les mandamos una carta. A no ser que respondan en diez días, ponemos la demanda.
>
> Raúl: ¿Y si dicen que fue culpa mía?
>
> Lic. Treviño: Tendrían que probarlo. Usted guarde todos los recibos y mensajes, por si los necesitamos.
>
> Raúl: ¿Cuánto tardaría un juicio?
>
> Lic. Treviño: Meses, a menos que acepten un acuerdo. De llegar a un acuerdo, usted recuperaría su dinero mucho antes.
>
> Raúl: Acepto cualquier acuerdo, con tal de que terminen mi cocina.

> Lic. Treviño: Tell me what happened, Raúl. What exactly does the contract say?
>
> Raúl: That they'd finish in eight weeks, as long as I paid half in advance. And I paid it.
>
> Lic. Treviño: Then they're in breach. Is there a clause about delays?
>
> Raúl: Yes: in the event that the work is delayed, they give me back part of the money, unless the delay is due to rain.
>
> Lic. Treviño: And did it rain?
>
> Raúl: Two days, that's all. They haven't come for three weeks.
>
> Lic. Treviño: Fine. First we send them a letter. Unless they reply within ten days, we file the lawsuit.
>
> Raúl: And what if they say it was my fault?
>
> Lic. Treviño: They'd have to prove it. Keep all the receipts and messages, in case we need them.
>
> Raúl: How long would a trial take?
>
> Lic. Treviño: Months, unless they accept a settlement. If we reach a settlement, you'd get your money back much sooner.
>
> Raúl: I'll accept any settlement, provided they finish my kitchen.

(*la obra* — the construction work; *por adelantado* — in advance; *probar* — to prove; *el
recibo* — receipt; *el acuerdo* — here, a settlement.) Notice the past condition in Raúl's report
of the contract (*terminarían… siempre y cuando yo pagara*) and *De llegar a un acuerdo* (If we
reach a settlement).

## Pronunciation

- *Indemnización*: five syllables, *in-dem-ni-za-CIÓN*; the *m* and *n* are both pronounced.
- *Incumplimiento*: five syllables, *in-cum-pli-MIEN-to*.
- *Tribunal* is stressed on the last syllable: *tri-bu-NAL*.
- *Supuesto*: three syllables, *su-PUES-to* (*ue* is one syllable).

## Common mistakes

- ~~*a no ser que llegan a un acuerdo*~~ → *lleguen*. These connectors take the subjunctive.
- ~~*por si llueva*~~ → *por si llueve* or *por si lloviera*. *Por si* follows the rules of *si*.
- ~~*Como no pagas, te demandan*~~ as a warning → *Como no pagues…* (with the indicative, *como*
  gives a cause: "since you don't pay").
- ~~*Me dijo que firmaría siempre y cuando le paguen*~~ in careful speech → *le pagaran*: a past
  main verb takes the imperfect subjunctive when the condition is seen from the past.
- *excepto que* + indicative is not "unless": *excepto que llegamos tarde* = except that we arrived
  late.

## Key points

- Requirement: *siempre y cuando, siempre que, con tal (de) que, a condición de que* +
  subjunctive.
- Exception: *a no ser que, a menos que, salvo que, excepto que* + subjunctive; *excepto que* +
  indicative = except that.
- Possible case: *en caso de que, en el supuesto de que* (formal) + subjunctive; *por si (acaso)*
  + indicative or imperfect subjunctive.
- Without a conjunction: *como* + subjunctive (warning), *de* + infinitive, the gerund
  (recognition).
- After a past verb: imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive.
- Law: *la demanda, el tribunal, la sentencia, apelar, el fiscal, el acusado, el abogado defensor,
  el notario, el amparo, los derechos humanos*.

lessons.title: Honors: El lenguaje jurídico: reading a regulation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 12 gave you the condition connectors of contracts (*siempre y cuando, en el supuesto de
que, salvo que*) and the basic words of courts and rights. Sooner or later, if you live, rent or
work in Mexico, you'll have to read the rules themselves: a building's regulations, a lease, the
terms of a service, a consumer law. Legal Spanish has its own habits. Sentences are long, the
subject often comes late, obligations are in the future tense, and old texts use a tense you'll
almost never hear, the future subjunctive.

This honors lesson shows how Mexican laws and regulations are laid out, explains the five habits
of legal style, walks through an original condominium regulation, and ends with a plain-language
summary of a consumer's rights under Mexico's federal consumer law. It teaches you to read like a
lawyer, not to act as one: nothing here is legal advice.

## How a Mexican law is laid out

Mexican laws and regulations follow a fixed hierarchy. Big laws are divided into *títulos* and
*capítulos*; the unit you'll cite is the *artículo*. An article can have several *párrafos*
(paragraphs) and a list of numbered parts called *fracciones*, written in Roman numerals; a
fracción can be divided into *incisos*, marked with letters. At the end come the *artículos
transitorios*, which say when the law comes into force and what it repeals.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The parts of a Mexican law
  accDescr: A hierarchy from top to bottom. A ley o reglamento is divided into títulos and capítulos. These contain artículos, numbered 1, 2, 3. An artículo can have párrafos and fracciones, numbered with Roman numerals I, II, III. A fracción can have incisos, lettered a), b), c). At the end of the law, separate artículos transitorios say when it comes into force and what it repeals.
  A["Ley o reglamento"] --> B["Títulos y capítulos"]
  B --> C["Artículos: 1, 2, 3…"]
  C --> D["Párrafos"]
  C --> E["Fracciones: I, II, III…"]
  E --> F["Incisos: a), b), c)…"]
  A --> G["Artículos transitorios: entrada en vigor, derogación"]
```

So a precise reference reads *artículo 8, fracción III, inciso b)*. In Mexico, *la fracción*
(subsection) is the usual word for these numbered parts; in Spain and other countries you'll more
often see *el apartado* or *el numeral*.

Official texts are published in the *Diario Oficial de la Federación* (DOF) for federal laws and
in each state's official gazette for state laws; the Cámara de Diputados keeps the current text of
every federal law on its website. A law *entra en vigor* (comes into force) on the date its
transitorios give, and a later law can *derogar* (repeal) it, in whole or in part.

## Five habits of legal style

### 1. The future for obligations

Where a contract in English says "shall" or "must", Spanish
legal texts use the simple future or *deberá*:

- *El condómino pagará la cuota de mantenimiento dentro de los primeros diez días de cada mes.*
  — The unit owner shall pay the maintenance fee within the first ten days of each month.
  (*el condómino* = unit owner in a condominium; *la cuota* = fee)
- *El arrendatario deberá dar aviso por escrito.* — The tenant must give written notice.

This isn't a prediction; it's a duty. *Podrá* gives a right or permission (*podrá tener
mascotas*), and *queda prohibido* or *se prohíbe* forbids.

### 2. The impersonal and the passive

Rules rarely say who does the action. They use *se*
(*Se sancionará a quien…* — Anyone who… will be penalized) and the *ser* passive (*será
sancionado*).

### 3. Long subjects and nominal style

Legal Spanish turns actions into nouns and stacks them in
front of the verb: *La falta de pago de dos o más cuotas consecutivas dará lugar a la suspensión
del servicio de agua.* — Failure to pay two or more consecutive fees will result in the water
service being suspended. Find the verb (*dará lugar*), then everything before it is the subject.

### 4. Relatives that define who

Rules are written for categories of people, so they use free
relatives (lesson 09): *Quien / El que estacione en un lugar ajeno…* (Whoever parks in someone
else's space…), and the formal relatives: *el área común en la cual*, *el condómino cuyo
vehículo*.

### 5. Conditions and exceptions

Lesson 12's connectors are everywhere: *en el supuesto de que,
salvo que, siempre y cuando, a condición de que*. A rule usually states the obligation first and
the exceptions after it.

## An old tense: the future subjunctive

Honors lesson 04h2 introduced the **[[future subjunctive]]** for recognition: forms like *fuere,
hiciere, infringiere*, built from the ellos preterite (*fueron → fuere, hicieron → hiciere*). It
has almost disappeared from everyday Spanish, but it survives in older laws, in legal formulas
and in a few fixed phrases. You don't need to produce it; you need to recognize it and replace it
in your head with a modern tense:

| You read | Modern equivalent | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *el que infringiere esta disposición* | *el que infrinja* | whoever breaks this provision |
| *si así no lo hiciere* | *si así no lo hace* | if he or she doesn't do so |
| *cualquiera que fuere su causa* | *cualquiera que sea su causa* | whatever its cause may be |
| *en los casos en que hubiere lugar* | *en los casos en que haya lugar* | in the cases where it applies |

Most recent Mexican laws use the present subjunctive or the present indicative in these places,
but older texts, notarial formulas and some regulations copied from them keep the future
subjunctive. If you read an *-re* ending where you expected *-ra*, think "future subjunctive" and
read it as a present subjunctive (after *si*, as a present indicative: *si así no lo hace*).

## An original regulation

This is an invented internal regulation for an invented condominium, written in the style of
real ones.

> *Reglamento interno del Condominio Jardines de Coyoacán*
>
> *Capítulo II. De las obligaciones de los condóminos*
>
> *Artículo 7.* Todo condómino deberá pagar la cuota ordinaria de mantenimiento dentro de los
> primeros diez días naturales de cada mes. La falta de pago de dos o más cuotas consecutivas
> dará lugar a un recargo del 3 % mensual sobre el monto adeudado.
>
> *Artículo 8.* Queda prohibido a los condóminos y a sus visitantes:
>
> I. Producir ruido que moleste a los vecinos entre las 22:00 y las 7:00 horas, salvo que la
> Asamblea autorice un evento con anticipación;
>
> II. Ocupar las áreas comunes con objetos personales;
>
> III. Estacionar vehículos en lugares ajenos o en las entradas del condominio.
>
> *Artículo 9.* Los condóminos podrán tener mascotas, siempre y cuando:
>
> a) estén registradas ante la Administración;
>
> b) circulen con correa en las áreas comunes, y
>
> c) sus dueños recojan sus desechos.
>
> *Artículo 10.* En el supuesto de que un condómino rente su departamento, el arrendatario
> quedará obligado a cumplir el presente Reglamento, del cual el condómino le entregará una copia.
>
> *Artículo 11.* Se sancionará con una multa equivalente a una cuota mensual al infractor de
> cualquiera de las disposiciones del artículo 8. En caso de reincidencia, la multa se duplicará.
> El infractor cuya multa no se pague en treinta días perderá su derecho a voto en la Asamblea
> hasta que regularice su situación.
>
> *Artículo 12.* Las obras de remodelación en los departamentos solo podrán realizarse de lunes
> a sábado, de 9:00 a 18:00 horas, a condición de que el condómino avise a la Administración con
> cinco días hábiles de anticipación.
>
> *Transitorio único.* El presente Reglamento entrará en vigor al día siguiente de su aprobación
> por la Asamblea y deroga el reglamento anterior.

Summary: owners must pay the monthly fee within ten calendar days, with a 3% monthly surcharge
after two missed fees (art. 7). Night noise, clutter in common areas and parking in others' spaces
are banned (art. 8). Pets are allowed if registered, leashed and cleaned up after (art. 9).
Tenants must follow the rules (art. 10). Breaking article 8 costs one month's fee, doubled for a
repeat offense, and unpaid fines cost the vote (art. 11). Remodeling is limited to set hours with
five business days' notice (art. 12). The rules take effect the day after approval and repeal the
old ones.

(*días naturales* — calendar days, as opposed to *días hábiles*, business days; *el monto
adeudado* — the amount owed; *la Asamblea* — the owners' meeting; *con anticipación* — in advance;
*la correa* — leash; *los desechos* — droppings, waste; *la reincidencia* — a repeat offense;
*regularizar su situación* — to settle one's debt; *el presente Reglamento* — these regulations;
*las obras de remodelación* — remodeling work.)

## Worked examples

### Example 1: unpacking an article

Take article 11's last sentence: *El infractor cuya multa no se pague en treinta días perderá su
derecho a voto en la Asamblea hasta que regularice su situación.*

1. Find the main verb: *perderá* (the future of rules: "shall lose").
2. Find its subject, everything before it: *El infractor cuya multa no se pague en treinta días*.
   The core is *el infractor*; the relative clause with *cuya* (agreeing with *multa*) says which
   offender.
3. Notice the moods: *se pague* is subjunctive because the clause describes any offender who might
   be in that situation (an unknown antecedent, lesson 09); *hasta que regularice* is subjunctive
   because it points to the future (lesson 11).
4. Say it in plain Spanish: *Si alguien no paga la multa en treinta días, no puede votar en la
   Asamblea hasta que pague.* In English: anyone who doesn't pay a fine within thirty days loses
   the vote until they pay.

### Example 2: applying the rules to a case

*Situation:* Mariana rents apartment 302. On Saturday she has a party until 1 a.m. without asking
anyone, and her dog walks around the garden without a leash. It's the first time.

1. Is Mariana bound by the rules? Yes: article 10, *el arrendatario quedará obligado a cumplir el
   presente Reglamento*.
2. The noise: article 8, fracción I, forbids it between 22:00 and 7:00 *salvo que la Asamblea
   autorice un evento con anticipación*. Nobody authorized it, so the exception doesn't apply.
3. The dog: article 9, inciso b), requires a leash in common areas. That's a breach of a
   condition, but article 11 fines only breaches of article 8, so the regulation as written sets no
   fine for the leash.
4. The fine: one month's fee for the noise (article 11); *En caso de reincidencia, la multa se
   duplicará*, but this is her first time.

Written as an administrator's notice: *Se le informa que, por infringir el artículo 8, fracción I,
del Reglamento, y conforme a su artículo 11, se le sancionará con una multa equivalente a una cuota mensual. Le recordamos que,
de acuerdo con el artículo 9, inciso b), las mascotas deben circular con correa.* (*conforme a* =
in accordance with.)

## A consumer's rights, in plain language

Mexico's federal consumer law, the *Ley Federal de Protección al Consumidor* (LFPC), was
published in the DOF on December 24, 1992, and has been reformed many times since; it replaced a
first consumer law of 1975. Profeco (the Procuraduría Federal del Consumidor) applies it. Three of
its rules are worth knowing, summarized here in plain language from the current text:

- Advertising must be truthful, verifiable and clear; an ad can be misleading even if each fact
  in it is true, when it is partial or exaggerated (article 32).
- When a product or service is sold with a warranty, the warranty can't be shorter than 90 days
  from delivery (article 77).
- When a product doesn't match what was offered (quantity, quality, specifications or official
  standards), or a repair under warranty leaves it unusable, the consumer can choose a
  replacement or a refund and is also owed a *bonificación* (a partial refund or credit) of at
  least 20% of the price paid (articles 92 and 92 TER).

In legal style, the core of the second point reads: *La garantía no podrá ser inferior a noventa días.*
In a letter of complaint you might write: *Conforme al artículo 77 de la Ley Federal de
Protección al Consumidor, la garantía no podrá ser inferior a noventa días, salvo que…* Read the
current article on the Cámara de Diputados site before you cite it: laws change.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *pagará* in a regulation as a prediction. It's an obligation: "shall pay".
- Taking the first noun of a long sentence as the subject when it's part of a nominal phrase: in
  *La falta de pago de dos cuotas dará lugar a…*, the subject is *la falta de pago*, not *dos
  cuotas*.
- Treating *fuere, hubiere* as typos for *fuera, hubiera*. They are future subjunctives; read them
  as *sea, haya*.
- Writing the future subjunctive yourself. In a modern letter, write *cualquiera que sea*, not
  ~~*cualquiera que fuere*~~ (not wrong, but stiff and old-fashioned).
- Confusing *la fracción* (a numbered part of an article, in Mexico) with *el párrafo*.

## Key points

- Laws: *título, capítulo, artículo, párrafo, fracción* (Roman numerals), *inciso* (letters),
  *artículos transitorios*.
- Obligations in the future (*pagará, deberá*); permissions with *podrá*; bans with *queda
  prohibido, se prohíbe*.
- Impersonal *se*, the passive, long nominal subjects, free relatives (*quien, el que*), *cuyo*
  and *el cual*, and condition connectors are the backbone of legal style.
- The future subjunctive (*fuere, hiciere, hubiere*) survives in old formulas: recognize it and
  read it as a present subjunctive (after *si*, a present indicative).
- *Entrar en vigor, derogar, la disposición, la sanción, sancionar, el infractor, estipular, el
  decreto, el reglamento*.

lessons.title: Honors: Ciencia latinoamericana: lives told with relatives and the passive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 09 told the stories of inventions from Europe and the United States with *el cual, cuyo*
and *quien*. This honors lesson turns to Latin America: six scientists and engineers from Mexico
and Argentina, from a 1940 patent for color television to a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995. Their
short biographies are the kind of text you'll meet in a museum, an encyclopedia or a DELE reading
task, and they lean on two structures: relative clauses that pack facts into one sentence, and the
**[[passive voice]]**, which puts the discovery before the person.

It also deals with a problem every science writer has: claims of "the first" and "the inventor
of". Sources don't always agree, so the lesson shows how to report a claim exactly as a source
makes it.

## Two tools for a dense biography

### Relatives

A biography joins facts that a beginner would write as separate sentences:

- *Mario Molina nació en la Ciudad de México. Sus estudios sobre el ozono le valieron el premio
  Nobel.* → *Mario Molina, cuyos estudios sobre el ozono le valieron el premio Nobel, nació en la
  Ciudad de México.* (*valer* + noun = to earn someone something)
- *Trabajó en un laboratorio. En ese laboratorio se sintetizó la noretisterona.* → *Trabajó en el
  laboratorio en el cual se sintetizó la noretisterona.*

### The passive

When the discovery matters more than who made it, Spanish uses the *ser* passive
(B1 12), the *se* passive, or the third-person plural:

- *La noretisterona fue sintetizada en 1951.* — Norethisterone was synthesized in 1951.
- *El premio fue compartido con dos colegas.* — The prize was shared with two colleagues.
- *Se le concedió el premio Nobel en 1970.* — He was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1970.

The *ser* passive agrees with its subject (*fue sintetizada*, *fueron galardonados*) and names
the agent with *por*: *fue galardonado por la Academia*. The participle *galardonado* (from
*galardonar*, to give an award to) is very common in the press: *la científica galardonada*.

## Six lives

> Bernardo Houssay (Buenos Aires, 1887–1971) fue un médico argentino cuya especialidad era la
> fisiología. En 1947 recibió la mitad del Premio Nobel de Fisiología o Medicina por descubrir el
> papel que desempeña una hormona del lóbulo anterior de la hipófisis en el metabolismo del
> azúcar. Se le considera el
> primer latinoamericano galardonado con un Nobel en una ciencia.
>
> Luis F. Leloir (París, 1906 – Buenos Aires, 1987), quien se formó como médico en Argentina,
> obtuvo en 1970 el Premio Nobel de Química, el cual no compartió con nadie. Fue premiado por
> descubrir los nucleótidos de azúcar y su papel en la formación de los carbohidratos. Trabajó en
> un instituto de investigación de Buenos Aires.
>
> Luis E. Miramontes (Nayarit, 1925 – Ciudad de México, 2004) era todavía estudiante de química
> cuando, el 15 de octubre de 1951, logró en los laboratorios de la empresa Syntex la síntesis de la
> noretisterona, un compuesto que se usaría en algunas de las primeras píldoras anticonceptivas.
> La patente fue registrada a nombre de Miramontes, George Rosenkranz y Carl Djerassi. La UNAM lo
> recuerda como el autor de una de las mayores contribuciones de la ciencia mexicana.
>
> Guillermo González Camarena (Guadalajara, 1917 – Puebla, 1965) fue un ingeniero cuyo sistema
> tricromático secuencial de campos, desarrollado hacia 1939, fue patentado en México en 1940 y en
> Estados Unidos dos años después. En México suele presentarse como el creador de la televisión a
> color, aunque otros inventores habían hecho demostraciones de televisión en color antes que él.
> En los años sesenta desarrolló un sistema bicolor más sencillo.
>
> Mario Molina (Ciudad de México, 1943 – 2020) fue un químico que en 1974, junto con Sherwood
> Rowland, publicó un estudio según el cual ciertos gases de uso industrial dañaban la capa de
> ozono. En 1995 compartió el Premio Nobel de Química con Rowland y Paul Crutzen por sus trabajos de
> química atmosférica. Trabajaba entonces en el MIT, en Estados Unidos.
>
> Rodolfo Neri Vela (Chilpancingo, Guerrero, 1952), ingeniero egresado de la UNAM, viajó en el
> transbordador Atlantis en la misión STS-61-B, que despegó el 26 de noviembre de 1985 y aterrizó el
> 3 de diciembre. Durante la misión, en la cual se pusieron en órbita tres satélites, entre ellos
> el Morelos II, el segundo satélite mexicano de comunicaciones, dio 109 vueltas a la Tierra. Fue
> el primer mexicano en participar en una misión espacial de la NASA.

Summary: Houssay, an Argentine physician and physiologist, received half of the 1947 Nobel Prize
in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the role of a pituitary hormone in sugar metabolism; he
is considered the first Latin American Nobel laureate in a science. Leloir won the 1970 Nobel in
Chemistry alone, for sugar nucleotides. Miramontes, still a chemistry student, synthesized
norethisterone at Syntex on October 15, 1951; the compound went into some of the first birth
control pills. González Camarena patented a color television system in Mexico in 1940, though
others had shown color television before him. Molina's 1974 study with Rowland warned that
industrial gases harmed the ozone layer; he shared the 1995 Chemistry prize. Neri Vela flew on
the shuttle Atlantis in 1985, the first Mexican on a NASA space mission.

(*desempeñar un papel* — to play a role; *el lóbulo anterior de la hipófisis* — the anterior lobe of the pituitary gland; *formarse como* —
to train as; *el compuesto* — compound; *la síntesis* — synthesis, lesson 23; *el estudio* — study, research
paper, lesson 18; *la capa de ozono* — ozone layer; *el transbordador* —
space shuttle; *despegar / aterrizar* — to take off / to land; *dar vueltas a* — to go around.
*Egresado de la UNAM* uses lesson 02's *el egresado*, a graduate.)

## Comparison table

| Name | Country | Field | Key date | What the sources say |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bernardo Houssay | Argentina | physiology | 1947 | half of the Nobel in Physiology or Medicine |
| Luis F. Leloir | Argentina (born in Paris) | biochemistry | 1970 | the whole Nobel in Chemistry |
| Luis E. Miramontes | Mexico | chemistry | October 15, 1951 | synthesis of norethisterone; patent with Rosenkranz and Djerassi |
| Guillermo González Camarena | Mexico | electronic engineering | 1940 | Mexican patent for a color TV system |
| Mario Molina | Mexico | atmospheric chemistry | 1995 | a third of the Nobel in Chemistry |
| Rodolfo Neri Vela | Mexico | communications engineering | November 26, 1985 | first Mexican on a NASA space mission |

![A timeline from 1940 to 2000 with six markers. 1940: González Camarena, Mexican patent for color television. 1947: Houssay, Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. 1951: Miramontes synthesizes norethisterone. 1970: Leloir, Nobel Prize in Chemistry. 1985: Neri Vela flies on the shuttle Atlantis. 1995: Molina, Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Argentine names are marked with a triangle and Mexican names with a circle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reporting a claim exactly

"First" and "inventor" are where science writing goes wrong. Three habits keep you accurate:

1. Keep the source's qualifier. The UNAM article on Neri Vela calls him *el primer mexicano en
   participar en una misión espacial de la NASA*. That's narrower than "the first Mexican in
   space", and it's what the source says.
2. Say who makes the claim. *En México suele presentarse como el creador de la televisión a
   color* reports the claim and its setting without making it yours. Other useful frames: *se le
   atribuye* (it is attributed to him), *se le considera* (he is considered), *según la UNAM*, *de
   acuerdo con el comité Nobel*.
3. Prefer the precise verb. Miramontes *sintetizó* a compound; he didn't "invent the pill",
   which needed other people's work, tests and a company to sell it. Molina *compartió* the prize;
   Leloir *no lo compartió*.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: one sentence from three facts

Facts: *Houssay era argentino. Houssay estudió la fisiología de las glándulas. Por ese trabajo
recibió el premio Nobel en 1947.*

1. Choose the main fact for the main clause: *Houssay recibió el premio Nobel en 1947.*
2. Attach the nationality as a non-restrictive clause or an apposition: *Houssay, un médico
   argentino, …*
3. Attach the work with a relative after a preposition: *por un trabajo sobre la fisiología de las
   glándulas* or, more formally, *por el trabajo sobre las glándulas gracias al cual se hizo
   famoso*.
4. Result: *Bernardo Houssay, un médico argentino cuyo campo era la fisiología, recibió en 1947 el
   premio Nobel por sus trabajos sobre una hormona de la hipófisis.* (*cuyo* agrees with *campo*.)

### Example 2: from active to passive, with the claim intact

Active, from a museum label: *En 1940, el gobierno mexicano le otorgó a Guillermo González
Camarena una patente por un sistema de televisión a color.* (*otorgar* = to grant)

1. Make the patent the subject: *una patente… fue otorgada*. The participle agrees: *otorgada*,
   feminine like *patente*.
2. Keep the date and the beneficiary: *En 1940 le fue otorgada a González Camarena una patente por
   un sistema de televisión a color.*
3. Or use the *se* passive, more common in speech: *En 1940 se le otorgó una patente por un sistema
   de televisión a color.*
4. Check the claim: the label says *una patente por un sistema*, not *la invención de la
   televisión a color*. Don't let the passive change "a patent for a system" into "he invented
   color television".

## Words for science and awards

- *el físico, la física* (physicist; *la física* also means physics, and *el físico* also means
  physique); *el astrónomo, la astrónoma*; *el astronauta, la astronauta*; *la fisiología*.
- *el premio Nobel*: as the name of a prize, style guides capitalize it (*el Premio Nobel de
  Química*), and the press also writes *el premio Nobel*; for a laureate, lowercase (*Molina es
  premio nobel*, *los nobel*);
  *galardonar* and *el galardón* (award), formal words of the press.
- *la píldora anticonceptiva*; *la órbita* (*poner en órbita*); *el satélite*.

None of the six was a physicist or an astronomer: Houssay and Leloir trained as physicians,
Miramontes and Molina were chemists, González Camarena and Neri Vela were engineers. A learner who
writes *el físico Mario Molina* makes the kind of slip this lesson warns about.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*Houssay, cuya trabajos…*~~ → *cuyos trabajos*. *Cuyo* agrees with the thing possessed.
- ~~*La patente fue registrado*~~ → *fue registrada*. The participle agrees with the subject of a
  *ser* passive.
- Capitals: *el Premio Nobel de Química* is the prize; *un premio nobel* (lowercase) is a person
  who won it. *Nobel* is never written with an accent.
- Turning *se le atribuye* (it is attributed to him) into a certainty in your own summary.
- Saying *astronauta* changes for gender: it doesn't; only the article does (*la astronauta*).

## Key points

- Dense biographies join facts with *cuyo, el cual, quien* and relatives after prepositions.
- The *ser* passive agrees with its subject; the agent goes with *por*; the *se* passive is the
  everyday alternative.
- Report claims as the source makes them: keep qualifiers, say who claims it (*se le considera,
  según…*), choose precise verbs.
- Facts: Houssay 1947 and Leloir 1970 (Argentina); Miramontes 1951, González Camarena 1940, Neri
  Vela 1985, Molina 1995 (Mexico).

lessons.title: Recalcó que no habría cambios: reporting at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module is about passing on what other people say. It starts with **[[reported speech]]**.

In B1 (lesson 16) you learned the basic shifts after a past verb such as *dijo que*: present →
imperfect, preterite → pluperfect, future → conditional, command → imperfect subjunctive. Since
then this course has added the **[[perfect subjunctive]]** (lesson 02), the **pluperfect
subjunctive** (03) and the **conditional perfect** (04). That completes the set: now any sentence
can be reported, whatever its tense or mood.

The second half of the lesson is about **[[reporting verbs]]**: the verbs that tell your reader *how*
something was said (*recalcó, sostuvo, insinuó, le reprochó*). Choosing the right verb
summarizes the speaker's intention in one word, and each verb brings its own pattern: *que* + indicative, *que* + subjunctive, *a* + infinitive or *con* +
infinitive. The theme is interviews and press conferences; every person in the lesson is
fictional.

## Every shift, including the subjunctive

After a reporting verb in the past (*dijo, explicó, aseguró…*), each tense in the original words
moves one step back. Here are the B1 shifts and the new ones together:

| Original words | Reported after *dijo que…* |
|---|---|
| present: *"Estoy lista."* | imperfect: *estaba lista* |
| preterite or perfect: *"Lo firmé." / "Lo he firmado."* | pluperfect: *lo había firmado* (the preterite *lo firmó* is also common) |
| future: *"Habrá pipas."* | conditional: *habría pipas* |
| future perfect: *"Habremos terminado."* | conditional perfect: *habrían terminado* |
| present subjunctive: *"Quiero que vengas."* | imperfect subjunctive: *quería que fuera* |
| *ojalá* + present subjunctive: *"Ojalá llueva."* | *ojalá* + imperfect subjunctive: *ojalá lloviera* |
| perfect subjunctive: *"No creo que lo hayan visto."* | pluperfect subjunctive: *no creía que lo hubieran visto* |
| command: *"Llámenme."* | imperfect subjunctive: *que la llamaran* |
| imperfect, pluperfect, conditional, conditional perfect, imperfect and pluperfect subjunctive | no change |

The subjunctive follows the **[[sequence of tenses]]** from lesson 03: once the main verb is past,
a present subjunctive becomes imperfect and a perfect subjunctive becomes pluperfect.

- *"Espero que hayan entendido."* → *Dijo que esperaba que hubieran entendido.* — She said she
  hoped they had understood.
- *"Ojalá no sea grave."* → *Dijo que ojalá no fuera grave.* — He said he hoped it wasn't serious.
- *"Si hubiera llovido, habríamos cancelado."* → *Explicó que si hubiera llovido, habrían
  cancelado.* — She explained that if it had rained, they would have canceled. (Nothing can move
  further back, so a past condition stays as it is.)

As in B1, the shift is optional when what was said is still true or still ahead: *Dijo que el
museo abre los lunes* (it still does). And in Latin America a request that is still pending
often keeps the present subjunctive: *Me pidió que la llame mañana* is normal Mexican Spanish
when "tomorrow" hasn't come yet. For a finished past situation, use the imperfect subjunctive:
*Me pidió que la llamara.* All the *-ra* forms in this lesson also have *-se* forms (*fuese,
hubiesen visto*), which are just as correct.

## Reporting verbs and their patterns

![A chart of reporting verbs in four groups. Que plus indicative, for statements: afirmar, asegurar, sostener, alegar, recalcar, subrayar, puntualizar, revelar, insinuar, replicar, jurar que. Que plus subjunctive, for influence and reproach: pedir, sugerir, recomendar, aconsejar, suplicar, reprochar. Verbs that take either mood with a change of meaning: advertir que, insistir en que, decir que, convencer de que. Verbs with a preposition or infinitive: animar a, prometer, jurar, amenazar con.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Que + indicative: passing on a statement

These verbs report information and add a nuance:

| Verb | What it adds | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *sostener* | to maintain a view, often against others | *El abogado sostuvo que el contrato era válido.* |
| *alegar* | to give as a reason or excuse | *Alegó que no había visto la señal.* |
| *recalcar, subrayar* | to stress a point | *Recalcó que no habría cambios.* |
| *puntualizar* | to add a precise detail or correct one | *Puntualizó que la cifra (lesson 19: the figure) era provisional.* |
| *revelar* | to make something secret known | *Reveló que había recibido amenazas.* |
| *insinuar* | to hint without saying it outright | *Insinuó que alguien había filtrado el documento.* |
| *replicar* | to answer back | *Replicó que eso no era cierto.* |

*Recalcó que no habría cambios.* — She stressed that there would be no changes. *Insinuó que
alguien había filtrado el documento* (filtrar = to leak). — He hinted that someone had leaked
the document.

### Que + subjunctive: influence, pleading and reproach

*Pedir, sugerir, recomendar* and *aconsejar* (B1) take the subjunctive because they try to make
someone act. So do *suplicar* (to beg) and *reprochar* (to reproach): *Le suplicó que no lo
publicara.* — She begged him not to publish it. *Me reprochó que no lo hubiera llamado.* — He
reproached me for not having called him. (*Reprochar* can also take the indicative for a plain
fact, *le reprochó que llegaba siempre tarde*, but the subjunctive is the usual choice.)

### One verb, two moods, two meanings

Some verbs report either a fact or an instruction, and the mood tells you which:

- *advertir*: *Advirtió que habría retrasos* (warned that: indicative). *Advirtió que no
  saliéramos* (warned us not to: subjunctive).
- *insistir en*: *Insistió en que era inocente* (insisted it was true). *Insistió en que lo
  acompañara* (insisted that I go with him).
- *decir*: *Dijo que venían* (said they were coming). *Dijo que vinieran* (told them to come).
- *convencer de*: *La convencí de que era verdad* (convinced her it was true). *La convencí de que
  viniera* (persuaded her to come).

Neither mood is wrong here: they say different things. The nouns are *la advertencia* (warning)
and, for *amenazar* below, *la amenaza* (threat).

### Prepositions and infinitives

- *animar a* + infinitive, or *a que* + subjunctive for another person's action: *Me animó a
  postularme / Me animó a que me postulara.* — She encouraged me to apply (*postularse*, lesson 17:
  to apply for a job).
- *prometer* + infinitive, or *que* + conditional: *Prometió volver / Prometió que volvería.* — He
  promised to come back.
- *jurar* + infinitive (a promise) or *que* + indicative (a statement): *Juró decir la verdad.
  Juró que no sabía nada.* — He swore to tell the truth. He swore he knew nothing.
- *amenazar con* + infinitive or noun: *El equipo amenazó con abandonar el torneo.* — The team
  threatened to pull out of the tournament.

## Reported questions and the echo *que*

Questions work as in B1: *preguntar si* for yes / no questions, and the question word with its
accent for the rest. *"¿Habrá pipas?" → Preguntó si habría pipas.* In conversation, when you
repeat a question someone didn't hear, Spanish puts *que* in front: *¿Que si vienes mañana?* —
(I said) are you coming tomorrow? *¿Que qué hora es?* — (I asked) what time it is. This echo
*que* belongs to speech; don't write it in a report.

## Reading: a press conference and the story that reports it

The director of a city water utility announces repairs. The speakers are fictional. *Las pipas*
are water trucks (Mexico), *el acueducto* is the aqueduct and *repartir* (lesson 06) is to hand
out.

![A press conference. A spokesperson stands at a podium with three microphones, a banner behind her; a stack of printed press releases lies on a side table; two reporters raise their hands, one holding a recorder; a TV camera on a tripod films from the right. Labels name the spokesperson, the microphone, the press release and the camera.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the picture: *el vocero / la vocera* (A2: spokesperson) at the podium, *el micrófono*
(microphone), *el comunicado* on the table, and *la cámara* filming the reporters' questions.

> Directora: Buenos días. Como dice el comunicado que les repartimos, el sábado empezará la reparación del acueducto norte. Les pido a todos que guarden agua desde el jueves.
>
> Reportera: ¿Cuánto durará el corte?
>
> Directora: Unas treinta y seis horas. Si todo sale bien, el domingo por la noche ya habremos terminado.
>
> Reportero: Extraoficialmente se habla de una semana. ¿Lo puede confirmar?
>
> Directora: No, eso no es cierto. Quiero que quede claro: oficialmente son treinta y seis horas.
>
> Reportera: ¿Van a subir las tarifas para pagar la obra?
>
> Directora: Este año no habrá ningún cambio en las tarifas. Se lo puedo asegurar.
>
> Reportero: Los vecinos de la colonia Las Palmas dicen que nadie les avisó.
>
> Directora: Les recomiendo que consulten nuestra página. Y no creo que nadie se haya quedado sin información: hemos repartido volantes durante dos semanas.
>
> Reportera: ¿Habrá pipas?
>
> Directora: Sí, veinte. Ojalá no las necesitemos.

The next day's story:

> Corte de agua de 36 horas a partir del sábado
>
> La directora del organismo municipal de agua, Marta Ruelas, anunció ayer que el sábado empezaría la reparación del acueducto norte y pidió a la población que guardara agua desde el jueves. Según explicó, el corte duraría unas treinta y seis horas y, si todo salía bien, el domingo por la noche ya habrían terminado los trabajos.
>
> Ruelas negó que la obra fuera a durar una semana, como se había dicho extraoficialmente, y recalcó que este año no habría cambios en las tarifas. A los vecinos de Las Palmas, que se quejaron de no haber recibido aviso, les recomendó que consultaran la página del organismo. Sostuvo que no creía que nadie se hubiera quedado sin información, ya que se habían repartido volantes durante dos semanas. Por último, puntualizó que habría veinte pipas disponibles y dijo que ojalá no fueran necesarias.

Translation:

> Director: Good morning. As the press release we handed out says, repairs on the north aqueduct will begin on Saturday. I'm asking everyone to store water from Thursday on.
>
> Reporter: How long will the outage last?
>
> Director: About thirty-six hours. If all goes well, we'll have finished by Sunday night.
>
> Reporter: Unofficially, there's talk of a week. Can you confirm that?
>
> Director: No, that isn't true. I want to be clear: officially it's thirty-six hours.
>
> Reporter: Are you going to raise rates to pay for the work?
>
> Director: There will be no change in rates this year. I can assure you of that.
>
> Reporter: Residents of the Las Palmas neighborhood say nobody warned them.
>
> Director: I recommend they check our website. And I don't think anyone has been left without information: we've been handing out flyers for two weeks.
>
> Reporter: Will there be water trucks?
>
> Director: Yes, twenty. I hope we won't need them.
>
> 36-hour water outage starting Saturday. The director of the city water utility, Marta Ruelas, announced yesterday that repairs on the north aqueduct would begin on Saturday and asked the public to store water from Thursday. According to her, the outage would last about thirty-six hours and, if all went well, the work would be finished by Sunday night. Ruelas denied that the work would last a week, as had been said unofficially, and stressed that there would be no changes in rates this year. To the residents of Las Palmas, who complained that they hadn't been warned, she recommended checking the utility's website. She maintained that she didn't think anyone had been left without information, since flyers had been handed out for two weeks. Finally, she specified that twenty water trucks would be available and said she hoped they wouldn't be needed.

Look at how each line was turned into one sentence of the story: *empezará → empezaría; les pido que
guarden → pidió que guardara; habremos terminado → habrían terminado; no creo que se haya quedado
→ no creía que se hubiera quedado; hemos repartido → se habían repartido; ojalá no las
necesitemos → ojalá no fueran necesarias.* The reporter also chose verbs that summarize:
*negó* for "No, eso no es cierto", *recalcó* for "Se lo puedo asegurar".

## Summarizing a whole interview

When you report a long conversation you don't shift every line; you compress it. Three habits
help:

1. Name the act, not the words. *"¿Por qué no me avisaste? Me enteré por otros"* → *Le
   reprochó que no le hubiera avisado.*
2. Group what belongs together. Three answers about prices become *Insistió en que los
   precios no subirían.*
3. Quote (*citar*) only what matters. Keep a short, striking phrase in quotation marks and report the
   rest: *Dijo que la obra era "urgente, no opcional".* Spanish puts the period after the closing
   quotation mark.

What a source says *extraoficialmente* (off the record) isn't quoted with a name. *La primicia* is a scoop and *la exclusiva* an exclusive: *El diario dio la
primicia* (broke the story first); *la entrevista en exclusiva* (the exclusive interview).

## Pronunciation

- *Insinúo, insinúe*: the written accent breaks the diphthong: *in-si-NÚ-o* (four syllables),
  *in-si-NÚ-e*. Compare *insinuamos* (*in-si-nua-mos*, four syllables, stress on *-nua-*).
- *Recalqué, puntualicé, supliqué*: stress on the last syllable, as in every regular *yo*
  preterite: *re-cal-QUÉ, pun-tua-li-CÉ, su-pli-QUÉ*.
- *Extraoficialmente*: seven syllables, *ex-tra-o-fi-cial-men-te*; *-cial-* is one syllable, and
  like every *-mente* adverb it keeps the stress of the adjective (*-CIAL-*) and adds a second one on
  *-MEN-*.
- *Entrevistador, entrevistado*: five syllables each: *en-tre-vis-ta-DOR, en-tre-vis-TA-do*.

## Common mistakes

- An indicative after a verb of influence: ~~*Me recomendó que tomo el metro*~~ → *Me recomendó
  que tomara el metro.*
- *Amenazar* with the wrong preposition: ~~*Amenazó de renunciar*~~ → *Amenazó con renunciar.*
- *Animar* without *a*: ~~*Me animó que participara*~~ → *Me animó a que participara* (or *a
  participar*).
- A future kept after *prometió* when the moment has passed: ~~*Prometió que lo hará*~~ (about last
  month's promise) → *Prometió que lo haría.* (If the promised time is still ahead, *lo hará* is
  heard too.)
- Missing the second shift: ~~*Dijo que no creía que lo hayan visto*~~ → *no creía que lo
  hubieran visto.*
- Reading *advertir que* + subjunctive as "warn that": *Advirtió que no saliéramos* means "warned
  us not to go out".

## Key points

- After a past reporting verb: present subjunctive → imperfect subjunctive, perfect subjunctive →
  pluperfect subjunctive, future perfect → conditional perfect, plus all the B1 shifts; past
  conditions and the past subjunctives don't change.
- *-ra* and *-se* are both correct (*hubieran / hubiesen*).
- *sostener, alegar, recalcar, subrayar, puntualizar, revelar, insinuar, replicar* + *que* +
  indicative; *suplicar, reprochar* (and *pedir, sugerir, recomendar*) + *que* + subjunctive.
- *advertir, insistir en, decir, convencer de*: indicative for a fact, subjunctive for an
  instruction.
- *animar a* + infinitive / *a que* + subjunctive; *prometer* + infinitive / *que* + conditional;
  *amenazar con* + infinitive.
- The echo *que* (*¿Que si vienes?*) is for conversation only.
