lessons.title: Fue detenido, se detuvo, detuvieron: passive and impersonal sentences
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 reported what people said. News also reports what *happened*, and often the person who
did it is unknown, unimportant or deliberately left out. Spanish has several ways to say that:
the **[[passive voice]]** with *ser*, the **[[passive se]]**, the **[[impersonal se]]**, the third-person
plural, and the compressed grammar of headlines.

In B1 (lesson 12) you met the *ser* passive in the preterite (*La ciudad fue fundada por los
mexicas*), *estar* + participle for a state, the *se* passive and *Restauraron la iglesia* (an
unnamed "they"). This lesson takes the *ser* passive into every tense, separates the two kinds of
*se*, and shows how one event changes shape in a headline, a news story, a sensationalist
version and a radio bulletin. The theme is the news media: newspapers, TV, radio and press
freedom.

## The *ser* passive in every tense

The passive is *ser* in any tense + the **[[participle]]**, which agrees with the subject. The person
who did it, the **[[agent]]**, comes with *por*.

| Tense of *ser* | Example |
|---|---|
| present | *El noticiero es visto por millones de personas.* |
| preterite | *La ley fue aprobada en marzo.* |
| imperfect | *Las noticias eran revisadas por dos editores.* |
| present perfect | *La reforma ha sido aprobada.* |
| pluperfect | *El puente ya había sido cerrado.* |
| future | *El museo será inaugurado en mayo.* |
| conditional perfect | *El accidente habría sido evitado con una señal.* |
| present subjunctive | *Esperan que el caso sea investigado.* |
| pluperfect subjunctive | *Si hubiera sido avisada, la población habría salido antes.* |

Only the participle agrees; *sido* never changes: *La reforma ha sido aprobada; los acuerdos han
sido firmados.*

- *La reforma ha sido aprobada por el Congreso.* — The reform has been approved by Congress.
- *El accidente habría sido evitado con una señal.* — The accident would have been avoided with a
  sign.

In news you'll also read *estar siendo* + participle for something in progress: *El caso está
siendo investigado* (the case is being investigated). Recognize it; in your own Spanish *se está
investigando el caso* or *están investigando el caso* is more natural.

*Estar* + participle (B1) describes the resulting state, not the action: *El puente fue cerrado
el lunes* (the event) / *El puente está cerrado* (how it is now).

The *ser* passive belongs to writing: news, history, reports. In conversation it sounds stiff, and
Spanish speakers use the alternatives below.

## The transformations

![A chart showing one sentence in four forms. Active: La policía detuvo a dos hombres. Ser passive: Dos hombres fueron detenidos por la policía, with a note that the participle agrees and the agent comes with por. Impersonal se: Se detuvo a dos hombres, with a note that the verb stays singular before a plus a person. Third person plural: Detuvieron a dos hombres, meaning someone did it. A second example row with a thing: El Senado aprobó la ley; La ley fue aprobada por el Senado; Se aprobó la ley, with a note that the verb agrees with the thing; Aprobaron la ley.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Passive *se* and impersonal *se*

Both have no visible doer, but they are built differently.

**[[Passive se]]** is used with things (or people not specified). The thing is the grammatical
subject, so the verb agrees with it:

- *Se publicaron los resultados.* — The results were published.
- *Se vende una casa. Se venden casas.* — House for sale. Houses for sale.

You'll see *se vende casas* on signs, but the *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (DPD, entry
*se*) says the verb must agree with the plural subject: *se venden casas*. Write it that way.

**[[Impersonal se]]** has no subject at all, so the verb is always third-person singular. It is used
in two cases:

1. With a specific person introduced by *a*: *Se detuvo a los sospechosos.* — The suspects were
   arrested. The *a* is what tells you they were arrested by someone; *Se detuvieron los
   sospechosos* would sound as if they stopped themselves. Because there's no subject, the verb
   stays singular even with plural people: ~~*Se detuvieron a los sospechosos*~~ mixes the two
   constructions, and the DPD rejects it.
2. With verbs that have no object: *Se vive bien aquí. En esta redacción se trabaja mucho.* —
   People live well here. In this newsroom people work hard. (*La redacción*, B1's composition,
   is also a newsroom.)

A reflexive verb can't take one more *se*: for "people get up early here" say *Aquí la gente se
levanta temprano* or *Aquí uno se levanta temprano*.

## Other ways to leave the doer out

| Structure | Example | Use |
|---|---|---|
| third-person plural | *Dicen que va a llover. Me robaron la cartera.* | an unknown "they", never including the speaker |
| *uno / una* | *Uno nunca sabe.* | a general statement that includes the speaker; women often say *una* |
| generic *tú* | *Si trabajas de noche, duermes mal.* | very common in speech for "you, anyone" |
| *la gente* | *La gente ya no lee el periódico.* | people in general (singular verb) |

For one unknown thief, the third-person plural is the natural choice: *Me robaron la cartera*
(someone stole my wallet).

## Headlines and attribution

Headlines save words. Three patterns appear every day in Mexican and other Spanish-language papers:

- **Participle without *ser***: *Detenido el presunto responsable del robo.* (*Presunto* =
  alleged, the word journalists use before guilt is proven.)
- Present tense, third-person plural, no article: *Aprueban nueva ley de vivienda.*
  *Recuperan campana robada.* The present reports a past event, and "they" are the authorities.
- A noun instead of a verb: *Aprobación de la reforma. Fuerte aumento de precios.* Lesson 18
  returns to this nominal style.

To say where information comes from, use *según* (according to): *según la policía, según fuentes
oficiales, según informó la agencia.* After *según*, a pronoun takes the subject form: *según ella,
según tú.*

![The front page of a newspaper called El Diario del Valle, dated Thursday, November 12, 2026. A large headline, Recuperan campana robada en San Telmo, with a subheadline; a photo of a bronze bell in a scrapyard; two lines of small text under the photo; and on the right an opinion column with a small portrait of its author. Labels point to the headline, the photo, the caption and the column.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

On a front page (B1 honors' *la primera plana*): *el titular* (A2: headline), *la foto* and its
*pie de foto* (caption), and on the side *la columna* (B1 honors: column) with its columnist.

## Reading: one event, four versions

A bronze bell is stolen from a small town. All names are fictional. *La campana* is a bell, *el
deshuesadero* a scrapyard (Mexico), *la chatarra* scrap metal, *la parroquia* the parish church
and *la fiscalía* the prosecutor's office; *una vez que* (lesson 11) means "once".

> Titular. Recuperan campana robada en San Telmo; detenidos dos hombres
>
> Nota informativa. La campana de bronce de la parroquia de San Telmo, que había sido robada el pasado domingo, fue recuperada ayer en un deshuesadero de la capital del estado. Según la fiscalía, se detuvo a dos hombres de 24 y 31 años, que habrían vendido la pieza como chatarra. La campana, de unos trescientos kilos, será devuelta a la comunidad el viernes, una vez que haya sido revisada por especialistas. Los vecinos habían organizado guardias desde el robo.
>
> Versión sensacionalista. ¡Se robaron la campana! ¡Qué sacrilegio! Unos sinvergüenzas se llevaron la joya de San Telmo para venderla por kilo. Indignados, los vecinos no dormían. Ahora los ladrones tendrán que dar la cara.
>
> Boletín de radio. Son las siete de la mañana. En San Telmo ya se escucha otra vez la campana… bueno, casi. Fue recuperada ayer en un deshuesadero y se espera que regrese el viernes. Dos hombres fueron detenidos. Seguiremos informando.

Translation:

> Headline. Stolen bell recovered in San Telmo; two men arrested
>
> News story. The bronze bell of the San Telmo parish church, which had been stolen last Sunday, was recovered yesterday at a scrapyard in the state capital. According to the prosecutor's office, two men aged 24 and 31 were arrested; they allegedly sold the piece as scrap metal. The bell, weighing about three hundred kilos, will be returned to the community on Friday, once it has been inspected by specialists. Residents had organized watches since the theft.
>
> Sensationalist version. They stole the bell! What a sacrilege! Some shameless crooks made off with San Telmo's jewel to sell it by the kilo. Outraged, the residents couldn't sleep. Now the thieves will have to face the music.
>
> Radio bulletin. It's seven in the morning. In San Telmo the bell can already be heard again… well, almost. It was recovered yesterday at a scrapyard, and it's expected back on Friday. Two men have been arrested. We'll keep you posted.

What to notice:

- *Nota informativa* is a straight news story: in Mexico *una nota* is a news story (a new sense
  of A2's *la nota*, a grade).
- The headline uses a third-person plural present (*Recuperan*) and a participle (*detenidos*).
- The news story uses the *ser* passive in four tenses (*había sido robada, fue recuperada, será
  devuelta, haya sido revisada*), impersonal *se* with people (*se detuvo a dos hombres*), and
  *según*. *Habrían vendido* is a conditional perfect that news uses for a claim not yet proven
  ("allegedly sold"), like *presunto*. The RAE's glossary calls it the *condicional de rumor*:
  recognize it, but don't use it yourself, since some newsroom style guides advise against it.
- The sensationalist version has no facts the story doesn't have; it adds emotion (*qué sacrilegio,
  unos sinvergüenzas, la joya, indignados*), an exclamation and a judgment (*los ladrones*: no court has
  said so). That's *el sensacionalismo*, and the appetite for gory or shocking details it feeds is
  *el morbo*. In Mexico, crime and accident reporting is called *la nota roja*, a section some
  papers live on.
- *Se robaron la campana* is the everyday *se* of involvement (lesson 15: *robarse algo*), not a
  passive: the subject is an unnamed "they".
- The radio bulletin is spoken: shorter sentences, the present, a passive or two (*fue recuperada,
  fueron detenidos*) and passive *se* (*se escucha*).

## Freedom of the press

The words of the trade: a reporter (*el reportero, la reportera*) or a correspondent abroad (*el
corresponsal*) *cubre* (covers; participle *cubierto*) a story, and the outlet's *cobertura*
(coverage) may also use material from *una agencia de noticias* (a news agency). Each *medio de
comunicación* (media outlet: a paper, a radio station or *una cadena*, a TV network) *difunde*
(spreads) the news; *la difusión* of a story is how far it travels, and a paper's *tirada* is its
print run.

A TV network lives on its *audiencia* (ratings) and counts it for every *transmisión* (broadcast).

*La libertad de prensa* lets reporters cover what powerful people would rather hide; *la censura*
is its opposite, and a government that *censura* (censors) a story cuts it before it reaches the
public. Reporters Without Borders (*Reporteros sin Fronteras*) has published a World
Press Freedom Index every year since 2002, covering 180 countries and territories; check its
site for the current ranking, which changes yearly. A media outlet's *línea editorial* (editorial
line) decides what it covers and how, while *la imparcialidad* is the standard reporters are held
to.

## Pronunciation

- *Transmisión*: three syllables, *trans-mi-SIÓN*; the *ns* before *m* is often reduced to an *s*
  in speech (*tras-mi-sión*), and the DPD (entry *tras-*) accepts both spellings of
  *tra(n)smitir*, so *trasmisión* is also correct.
- *Audiencia*: three syllables, *au-DIEN-cia*: both *au* and *ie* are diphthongs.
- *Corresponsal*: *co-rres-pon-SAL*, with a trilled *rr*.
- *Sensacionalismo*: six syllables, *sen-sa-cio-na-LIS-mo*; *-cio-* is one syllable.

## Common mistakes

- No agreement in the passive *se*: ~~*Se vende casas*~~ → *Se venden casas*.
- A plural verb with *a* + people: ~~*Se detuvieron a los sospechosos*~~ → *Se detuvo a los
  sospechosos* (or *Los sospechosos fueron detenidos*).
- Agreeing *sido*: ~~*La ley ha sida aprobada*~~ → *ha sido aprobada*.
- *De* for the agent: ~~*fue escrito de una reportera*~~ → *por una reportera*.
- Overusing the *ser* passive in speech. *¿Viste? Fue detenido el alcalde* is understood, but a
  Mexican speaker would more often say *Detuvieron al alcalde* (*Se detuvo al alcalde* is news
  style).
- A pronoun after *según* in the wrong form: ~~*según mí*~~ → *según yo* or *en mi opinión*.

## Key points

- The *ser* passive works in every tense: *ha sido aprobada, había sido cerrado, será inaugurado,
  habría sido evitado*; the participle agrees, *sido* doesn't; the agent takes *por*.
- *Estar siendo* + participle is news style (recognize it).
- Passive *se* agrees with the thing: *se venden casas* (DPD).
- Impersonal *se* stays singular: with *a* + person (*se detuvo a los sospechosos*) or without an
  object (*se vive bien*).
- Other impersonals: *dicen que…, me robaron…, uno, tú, la gente*.
- Headlines: participle (*Detenido…*), present plural (*Aprueban…*), nouns (*Aprobación de…*);
  attribute with *según*.

lessons.title: Se me quemó el arroz: se and object pronouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 14 used *se* for the passive and the impersonal. But *se* has other jobs too: by B2 you've
met it as a reflexive (*se lava*), as a stand-in for *le* (*se lo di*), in verbs like *irse*, and
in accidents (*se me cayó*). This lesson puts all of them on one map so you can tell them apart,
then extends the **[[accidental se]]** and looks at **[[clitic doubling]]**: why Spanish says *Le di la
receta a mi tía*, with both *le* and *a mi tía*. It ends with three regional points you'll hear
in real kitchens: Latin America's *se los*, Spain's **[[leísmo]]**, and Mexico's *se me hace que*.

The theme is food and cooking, with a cooking show where everything goes wrong.

## The values of *se* in one map

![A map of the values of se in seven boxes around a central se. Reflexive: Se lava las manos. Reciprocal: Se escriben cada semana. Se for le or les before lo, la: Se lo di. Pronominal verb with its own meaning: irse, llevarse, quedarse, ponerse. Involvement with eating and drinking: Se comió todo el pastel. Accidental: Se me quemó el arroz. Passive and impersonal, lesson 14: Se venden tamales; Se vive bien aquí.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Kind | Example | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Reflexive | *Se lava las manos.* | the subject does it to itself |
| Reciprocal | *Se escriben cada semana.* | "each other" fits |
| *se* for *le / les* | *Se lo di.* | *se* comes before *lo, la, los, las* |
| Pronominal verb | *Se fue. Se llevó la olla.* | the verb means something different without *se* |
| Involvement | *Se comió todo el pastel.* | you can drop *se* and the facts stay the same |
| Accidental | *Se me quemó el arroz.* | *se* + *me / te / le…* + a verb agreeing with the thing |
| Passive / impersonal | *Se venden tamales. Se vive bien.* | no doer is mentioned |

Two of these deserve a closer look.

Pronominal verbs that change meaning. *Ir* is to go, *irse* to leave; *llevar* to carry,
*llevarse* to take away (or to get along: *Nos llevamos bien*); *quedar* to be located or to fit,
*quedarse* to stay; *poner* to put, *ponerse* to put on or to become (*Se puso rojo*). These are
separate verbs to learn, not grammar to work out.

Involvement. With verbs of eating, drinking, reading and learning, *se* (or *me, te, nos*)
adds a sense of completeness or enjoyment: *Se comió todo el pastel* (he ate up the whole cake);
*Me tomé un café* (I had myself a coffee); *Me leí el libro en un día* (I read the whole book in a day). Without the pronoun the
facts are the same: *Comió todo el pastel*. It usually needs a specific object: *Se comió el
tamal*, but not ~~*Se come mucho*~~ in this sense (that's the impersonal *se*: people eat a lot).

## The accidental *se*

When something goes wrong without anyone meaning it to, Spanish makes the *thing* the subject and
puts the unlucky person in an indirect-object pronoun:

| *se* | person | verb (agrees with the thing) | thing |
|---|---|---|---|
| *se* | *me* | *quemó* | *el arroz* |
| *se* | *nos* | *olvidó* | *la sal* |
| *se* | *le* | *cayeron* | *los huevos* |
| *se* | *te* | *echó a perder* | *la leche* |

- *Se me quemó el arroz.* — I burned the rice (it got burned on me).
- *Se le cayeron los huevos.* — She dropped the eggs.
- *Se te va a echar a perder la leche.* — Your milk is going to go bad.

The verb agrees with the thing, not the person: *se me cayó el plato, se me cayeron los platos*.
To name the person, add *a* + noun: *A Toño se le olvidaron los chiles.* It works in every tense:
*Se me había olvidado* (I had forgotten); *Ojalá no se nos acabe el gas* (I hope we don't run out
of gas).

*Quemé el arroz* is also correct; it simply doesn't soften your responsibility. Common verbs:
*caerse, olvidarse, quemarse, romperse, perderse, acabarse, descomponerse* (to break down) and
*echarse a perder*.

## Clitic doubling

**[[Clitic doubling]]** means using a pronoun and the noun it refers to in the same sentence. In
Spanish it is normal, and sometimes required:

- Indirect objects usually take *le / les* even when the noun is there: *Le di la receta a
  mi tía. A los niños les encanta el mole.* With *gustar*-type verbs the pronoun is required.
- A direct object placed first takes *lo, la, los, las*: *A Juan lo vi ayer. El mole lo hace
  mi abuela. Las tortillas las compramos en la esquina.* — My grandmother makes the mole. We buy
  the tortillas on the corner.
- A + stressed pronoun always needs the clitic too: *Te lo dije a ti, no a él* (I told *you*,
  not him); never ~~*Dije a ti*~~.

### Pronoun order with periphrases and commands

Indirect before direct, and *le / les* become *se* before *lo, la, los, las*. The pair goes
before a conjugated verb or attaches to an infinitive, a gerund or an affirmative command:

- *Se la voy a pedir a Mari. / Voy a pedírsela a Mari.* — I'm going to ask Mari for it.
- *Te lo estoy explicando. / Estoy explicándotelo.*
- *Pásamela. Dáselo. No se lo des.* — Pass it to me. Give it to him. Don't give it to him.

Count the syllables before you add an accent: *pide → pídesela*, *dar → dárselo*.

### *Se lo* and *se los*

*Se* never shows the plural, so many Latin Americans move it onto the next pronoun: *Se los dije*
for "I told them (it)". The DPD (entry *pronombres personales átonos*) describes this as frequent
in many American countries, especially in colloquial speech and spreading among educated
speakers in some, and recommends *se lo* in careful speech. You'll hear *se los* constantly in
Mexico; recognize it, but write *Se lo dije (a ellos)*.

### Leísmo (Spain)

In much of Spain, *le* is used as a direct object for a man: *A Juan le vi ayer*. The RAE accepts
this for a masculine singular person, but not for women or things, and the Latin American
standard, like this course, uses *lo*: *A Juan lo vi ayer*. Recognize it when you read Spanish
from Spain.

### *Se me hace que*

In Mexico *se me hace que* is an everyday way to say "I think, it seems to me": *Se me hace que va
a llover.* — I think it's going to rain. *¿No se te hace muy caro?* — Doesn't it seem very
expensive to you? It takes the indicative like *creo que*. In other countries it's less usual; *me
parece que* is understood everywhere.

## Mexican cuisine

In 2010 UNESCO added "La cocina tradicional mexicana: una cultura comunitaria, ancestral y viva y el
paradigma de Michoacán" to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of
Humanity. Its description names corn, beans and chili as the base, and nixtamalization:
corn is cooked with lime (*cal*) to make *el nixtamal*, which is ground (traditionally on a
stone *metate*) into *la masa* for tortillas and *tamales*. Mexican *gastronomía* also gives the
world *el mole*, a thick sauce of chilies, spices and seeds, and countless *guisados* (home-style
stews, often eaten in tacos). In Mexico a prepared dish is *un platillo*: *un platillo típico*.

![A Mexican kitchen. On the stove, a flat round griddle with two tortillas on it; on the counter, a three-legged stone mortar with a pestle; a tall clay pot steaming on a back burner; a large ladle hanging on the wall. Labels name the four objects.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the picture: *el comal* (griddle), *el molcajete* (stone mortar), *la olla* (A2: pot) and *el
cucharón* (lesson 21: ladle).

## Reading: a cooking show and its recipe

Lupita and her assistant Toño are recording an episode of a cooking show. Both are fictional.
*Voltear* is to turn over, and *los jitomates* are tomatoes (Mexico).

> Lupita: Bienvenidos a *La sazón de Lupita*. Hoy vamos a preparar una salsa de molcajete. Toño, ¿me pasas los jitomates?
>
> Toño: Ya los puse en el comal, como me dijo.
>
> Lupita: ¡Ay, Toño! Se te quemaron. Mira, están negros de un lado.
>
> Toño: Perdón, se me olvidó voltearlos. Es que estaba buscando los chiles.
>
> Lupita: No pasa nada; un poco quemados le dan sabor. ¿Y los chiles?
>
> Toño: Se me cayeron al piso, pero ya los lavé.
>
> Lupita: Bueno. Ahora el ajo al molcajete, con una pizca de sal. ¿Dónde está la sal?
>
> Toño: Se nos acabó. Se la pido a Mari, la del programa de al lado.
>
> Lupita: Pídesela, y dile que se la devolvemos mañana.
>
> Toño: Listo, aquí está. Dice que nos la presta. Oiga, se me hace que las tortillas también se están quemando.
>
> Lupita: ¡Toño! Bueno, amigos, así es la cocina de verdad. Si a ustedes se les quema algo, no se preocupen.

The recipe shown at the end:

> Salsa de molcajete. Para cuatro personas: 4 jitomates, 2 chiles serranos, 1 diente de ajo, ¼ de cebolla, una pizca de sal y 2 cucharadas de cilantro picado.
>
> 1. Calienta el comal y asa los jitomates, los chiles y el ajo. Voltéalos para que no se quemen.
> 2. Pela el ajo y muélelo en el molcajete con la sal.
> 3. Agrega los chiles y después los jitomates, poco a poco.
> 4. Por último, agrega la cebolla y el cilantro y revuelve. Prueba y sazona al gusto.
>
> Se sirve con tortillas recién hechas.

Translation:

> Lupita: Welcome to *Lupita's Touch*. Today we're going to make a molcajete salsa. Toño, will you pass me the tomatoes?
>
> Toño: I already put them on the griddle, like you told me.
>
> Lupita: Oh, Toño! You burned them. Look, they're black on one side.
>
> Toño: Sorry, I forgot to turn them over. I was looking for the chilies.
>
> Lupita: No problem; a little burned, they give it flavor. And the chilies?
>
> Toño: I dropped them on the floor, but I've washed them.
>
> Lupita: OK. Now the garlic into the molcajete, with a pinch of salt. Where's the salt?
>
> Toño: We've run out. I'll ask Mari for it, from the show next door.
>
> Lupita: Ask her for it, and tell her we'll give it back tomorrow.
>
> Toño: OK, here it is. She says she'll lend it to us. Hey, I think the tortillas are burning too.
>
> Lupita: Toño! Well, friends, that's real cooking. If something burns on you, don't worry.
>
> Molcajete salsa. Serves four: 4 tomatoes, 2 serrano chilies, 1 clove of garlic, ¼ onion, a pinch of salt and 2 tablespoons of chopped cilantro. 1. Heat the griddle and roast the tomatoes, chilies and garlic. Turn them so they don't burn. 2. Peel the garlic and grind it in the molcajete with the salt. 3. Add the chilies and then the tomatoes, a little at a time. 4. Finally, add the onion and cilantro and stir. Taste and season as you like. Serve with freshly made tortillas.

Toño speaks to his boss with *usted* (*como me dijo, oiga*); Lupita uses *tú* with him. *Se la
pido a Mari* is *se* for *le*: *le pido la sal a Mari → se la pido*. *Se sirve* is the passive
*se* of recipes. Instructions in recipes use either the *tú* command (*asa, voltéalos*), as here,
or the impersonal *se* (*se asan los jitomates*). Other words for the kitchen: *hornear* (to bake),
*a la parrilla* (grilled), *rallar* (to grate) and, on every package, *la fecha de caducidad*
(expiration date); food past it is *caducado* (or B1's *vencido*).

## Pronunciation

- *Molcajete*: *mol-ca-JE-te*; the *j* is the Spanish *j*, from the throat.
- *Nixtamal*: in Mexico the *x* here is usually said like *s*: *nis-ta-MAL* (some speakers use an
  English *sh* sound, as in Nahuatl).
- *Maíz*: two syllables, *ma-ÍZ*; the accent breaks the diphthong. Plural *maíces*.
- *Rallar* and *rayar* (to scratch) sound the same for most Spanish speakers (yeísmo): the
  spelling tells them apart.
- *Pídesela, dárselo*: the attached pronouns don't move the stress: *PÍ-de-se-la, DAR-se-lo*.

## Common mistakes

- Making the verb agree with the person: ~~*Se me cayeron el plato*~~ → *Se me cayó el plato*.
- *Le lo* for *se lo*: ~~*Le lo di*~~ → *Se lo di*.
- Leaving out the doubled pronoun with *gustar*: ~~*A los niños encanta*~~ → *A los niños les
  encanta*.
- A fronted object without its pronoun: ~~*El mole hace mi abuela*~~ → *El mole lo hace mi
  abuela*.
- Forgetting the accent when pronouns attach: ~~*pidesela, dandoselo*~~ → *pídesela,
  dándoselo*.
- Writing *se los* for one thing in a formal text: → *Se lo expliqué a ellos*.

## Key points

- *se* can be reflexive, reciprocal, a stand-in for *le / les*, part of a pronominal verb, the
  *se* of involvement, accidental, passive or impersonal.
- Accidental *se*: *se* + *me / te / le / nos / les* + verb agreeing with the thing: *Se me
  quemaron las tortillas.*
- Clitic doubling: *Le di la receta a mi tía; El mole lo hace mi abuela; Te lo dije a ti.*
- Pronouns go before the conjugated verb or attach to infinitive, gerund and affirmative command
  (*Se la voy a pedir / Voy a pedírsela*).
- *Se los* for *se lo* is very common in Latin America; the DPD recommends *se lo* in careful
  speech. Spain's *leísmo* (*le vi* for a man) is for recognition.
- *Se me hace que* = *me parece que* (Mexico).

lessons.title: Llevo un año entrenando: verbal periphrases
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last three lessons were about reporting what others say and do. This one gives you the tools
to tell how an action unfolds: how long it has lasted, whether it is starting, continuing,
stopping or happening again, and whether it built up gradually.

You already know several **[[verbal periphrases]]**: *estar* + **[[gerund]]** (*estoy corriendo*, A2), *ir
a* + infinitive, *acabar de*, *soler* and *tener que*. A periphrasis is a conjugated auxiliary verb
plus an infinitive, a gerund or a participle, where the auxiliary has lost its literal meaning:
in *Llevo un año entrenando*, nobody is carrying anything. This lesson adds the rest of the set
that B2 needs. The theme is fitness, habits and willpower (general information only, not
medical advice).

Three earlier words get new senses here: A2's *la carrera* (degree course) is also a race (*una
carrera de diez kilómetros*); B1's *la constancia* (written proof) is also perseverance; and
*el calentamiento* (from B1's *calentamiento global*) is a warm-up before exercise.

![A chart of verbal periphrases in five groups. Beginning: ponerse a plus infinitive, echarse a reír, llorar or correr. Continuing and duration: seguir or continuar plus gerund, seguir sin plus infinitive, llevar plus time plus gerund. Over time: ir plus gerund, venir plus gerund, andar plus gerund. Ending: dejar de plus infinitive, acabar plus gerund, acabar por plus infinitive. Repeating: volver a plus infinitive. A box of others: llegar a, alcanzar a, estar por, tener plus participle. Each with an example sentence.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## How long: *llevar* + time + gerund

*Llevar* + a period of time + gerund says how long something has been going on up to now:

- *Llevo un año entrenando.* — I've been training for a year.
- *¿Cuánto tiempo llevas estudiando español?* — How long have you been studying Spanish?
- *Llevaba tres meses corriendo cuando se lesionó.* — She'd been running for three months when she
  got injured.

For something that has *not* happened in a while, use *sin* + infinitive: *Llevo dos semanas sin
ir al gimnasio* (I haven't been to the gym for two weeks). The same ideas can be said with *hace*
(*Hace un año que entreno*) or *desde hace* (*Entreno desde hace un año*); *llevar* is the most
conversational.

*Llevar* + participle, which agrees with the object, counts what has been done so far: *Llevo
corridos diez kilómetros* (I've run ten kilometers so far). Recognize it; *Ya corrí diez
kilómetros* is the everyday equivalent.

## Continuing: *seguir* + gerund, *seguir sin* + infinitive

*Seguir* (or the more formal *continuar*) + gerund means "to keep on, still": *Sigue lloviendo.
¿Sigues entrenando con Marta?* — It's still raining. Are you still training with Marta? The
negative uses *sin* + infinitive: *Sigo sin entender la rutina* (I still don't understand the
routine). Never use an infinitive after *seguir* alone: ~~*sigo entrenar*~~.

## Over time: *ir, venir, andar* + gerund

- *ir* + gerund: a change that builds up step by step. *Poco a poco voy mejorando.* — Little by
  little I'm getting better. *La motivación se fue perdiendo.* — Motivation gradually faded.
- *venir* + gerund: something repeated or growing over a period up to now, often with *desde*.
  *Vengo notando el cansancio desde hace semanas.* — I've been noticing the tiredness for weeks.
- *andar* + gerund: going around doing something, often with a critical tone. *Anda diciendo
  que va a correr un maratón.* — He's going around saying he'll run a marathon.

## Beginning, ending and repeating

| Meaning | Periphrasis | Example |
|---|---|---|
| to start (deliberately) | *ponerse a* + infinitive | *Me puse a estirar.* (I started stretching.) |
| to burst out | *echarse a* + *reír, llorar, correr* | *Se echó a llorar en la meta.* (She burst into tears at the finish line.) |
| to stop | *dejar de* + infinitive | *Dejé de comer azúcar.* (I stopped eating sugar.) |
| to do again | *volver a* + infinitive | *Volví a correr después de la lesión.* (I started running again after the injury.) |
| to end up | *acabar / terminar* + gerund; *acabar por* + infinitive | *Acabé cambiando de entrenador. Acabó por aceptar.* (I ended up changing coaches. He ended up accepting.) |

*Echarse a* is used with a few verbs only: *reír, llorar, correr, temblar*. In written Spanish
you'll also see *romper a llorar* (to burst into tears): recognize it.

## Reaching a point and being about to

- *llegar a* + infinitive: to go so far as, or to manage after effort. *Llegué a correr
  veinte kilómetros.* — I managed to run twenty kilometers. *Llegó a pensar que nunca se
  recuperaría.* — She even came to think she'd never recover.
- *alcanzar a* + infinitive: to manage to (in time), common in Latin American speech: *No
  alcancé a estirar antes de la clase.* — I didn't manage to stretch before class.
- *estar por* + infinitive: in Mexico and some other Latin American countries, "to be about to":
  *La carrera está por empezar* (the race is about to start), like B1's *estar a punto de*.
  Everywhere, including Mexico, it can also mean "still to be done" (*La cocina está por limpiar*:
  the kitchen still needs cleaning), and in Spain that is the sense you'll meet; for "about to",
  the DPD (entry *estar*) notes that *estar para* is more usual there. *Quedar por* also means "still to
  do": *Quedan tres kilómetros por recorrer.*
- *tener* + participle: something already done or decided, with the participle agreeing with
  the object. *Tengo pensado inscribirme en la carrera.* — I'm planning to sign up for the race.
  *Ya tengo escritas tres páginas del diario.* — I've already got three pages of the diary written.

And A2's *soler* for habits: *Suelo entrenar temprano* (I usually train early); *Solía correr en el
parque* (I used to run in the park).

## Where the pronouns go

With a periphrasis, an object or reflexive pronoun goes before the conjugated verb or after the
infinitive or gerund, with no difference in meaning:

- *Lo sigo intentando. / Sigo intentándolo.* — I keep trying.
- *Me voy a poner en forma. / Voy a ponerme en forma.* — I'm going to get in shape.
- *Lo dejé de hacer. / Dejé de hacerlo.* — I stopped doing it.

The pronoun never goes between the two parts: ~~*Sigo lo intentando*~~. Attaching it to a gerund
moves nothing but needs an accent: *intentando → intentándolo*.

## Reading: a training diary

Renata, a fictional office worker from Puebla, keeps a diary while she trains for a 10 km race.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Renata's six weeks
  accDescr: A timeline of Renata's six weeks of training, each step with its periphrasis. Week 1, she starts running: se puso a correr. Week 2, she is gradually improving: va mejorando. Week 3, she stalls and stops for a few days: se estancó, dejó de correr. Week 4, she runs again: volvió a correr. Week 5, she has been training for five weeks: lleva cinco semanas entrenando. Week 6, she manages to run 10 kilometers: llegó a correr diez kilómetros.
  A["Semana 1: se puso a correr"] --> B["Semana 2: va mejorando"]
  B --> C["Semana 3: se estancó; dejó de correr"]
  C --> D["Semana 4: volvió a correr"]
  D --> E["Semana 5: lleva cinco semanas entrenando"]
  E --> F["Semana 6: llegó a correr 10 km"]
```

> Semana 1. Llevo años con un trabajo sedentario y ya se me nota en la báscula. Hoy me puse a correr: quince minutos y acabé sudando como nunca. Mi entrenadora dice que la constancia vale más que la fuerza de voluntad.
>
> Semana 2. Voy mejorando poco a poco. Ya no me duelen tanto los músculos, sobre todo si hago estiramientos al terminar.
>
> Semana 3. Me estanqué. Sigo sin pasar de cinco kilómetros y el cansancio no se me quita. Dejé de correr unos días.
>
> Semana 4. Volví a entrenar. El secreto era el calentamiento: antes no lo hacía. También me hidrato mejor.
>
> Semana 5. Llevo cinco semanas entrenando y ya tengo pensado inscribirme en la carrera del domingo. Mi hermano anda diciendo que no voy a terminarla.
>
> Semana 6. ¡Llegué a correr diez kilómetros! En la meta me eché a llorar. Mi hermano no alcanzó a verme llegar, pero vio las fotos. Ahora estoy por empezar otro reto: la dieta. Esa sí me va a costar.

Translation:

> Week 1. I've had a desk job for years and it's starting to show on the scale. Today I started running: fifteen minutes, and I ended up sweating like never before. My coach says perseverance is worth more than willpower.
>
> Week 2. I'm getting better little by little. My muscles don't hurt as much anymore, especially if I stretch when I finish.
>
> Week 3. I've stalled. I still can't get past five kilometers and the tiredness won't go away. I stopped running for a few days.
>
> Week 4. I started training again. The secret was the warm-up: I didn't do it before. I'm also drinking more water.
>
> Week 5. I've been training for five weeks and I'm already planning to sign up for Sunday's race. My brother is going around saying I won't finish it.
>
> Week 6. I managed to run ten kilometers! At the finish line I burst into tears. My brother didn't make it in time to see me finish, but he saw the photos. Now I'm about to start another challenge: the diet. That one is really going to be hard.

In *ya se me nota*, *me* marks the person it shows on (*notarse* = to show); *el cansancio no se
me quita* has the same *se* + *me* shape as lesson 15's accidental *se*; *la meta* (A2) is both a goal and a finish line.

## Habits and health

*Un hábito* is a habit (A2's *la costumbre* is a near synonym that also means a custom); *el sedentarismo* is a
sedentary lifestyle; *ponerse en forma* is to get in shape. *Una lesión* is an injury, and to get
injured is *lesionarse*. *El agotamiento* is exhaustion, stronger than *el cansancio*. *El
sobrepeso* is excess weight. *El progreso* is progress, and to make progress is *progresar*: *Voy
progresando poco a poco* (I'm making progress little by little). This lesson gives language, not advice: ask a doctor or a qualified
trainer before starting a new routine.

## Pronunciation

- *Báscula, músculo*: stress on the first syllable, hence the written accents: *BÁS-cu-la,
  MÚS-cu-lo*.
- *Estiramiento*: five syllables, *es-ti-ra-MIEN-to*; *-mien-* is one syllable.
- *Sedentarismo*: *se-den-ta-RIS-mo*.
- *Hidrátate*: the attached pronoun keeps the stress on *-drá-*: *hi-DRÁ-ta-te*.
- *Entrenamiento*: *en-tre-na-MIEN-to*, five syllables.

## Common mistakes

- The infinitive after *llevar* or *seguir*: ~~*Llevo un año entrenar*~~ → *Llevo un año
  entrenando*; ~~*Sigo entrenar*~~ → *Sigo entrenando*.
- *Volver de* for "again": ~~*Volví de correr*~~ means "I came back from running"; "I ran again" is
  *Volví a correr*.
- *Dejar* without *de*: ~~*Dejé fumar*~~ → *Dejé de fumar*.
- A pronoun in the middle: ~~*Sigo lo intentando*~~ → *Lo sigo intentando* or *Sigo
  intentándolo*.
- Reading *estar por* only as "still to be done" in Mexico: with an event, *El camión está por
  salir* means it's about to leave.
- Overusing *estar* + gerund for long durations. *Estoy entrenando desde hace un año* is correct,
  but *Llevo un año entrenando* is the more natural choice.

## Key points

- *llevar* + time + gerund (*Llevo un año entrenando*), *llevar* + time + *sin* + infinitive
  (*Llevo dos meses sin correr*); *llevar* + participle for recognition.
- *seguir / continuar* + gerund; *seguir sin* + infinitive.
- *ir* + gerund (gradual), *venir* + gerund (up to now), *andar* + gerund (going around).
- *ponerse a, echarse a* (start); *dejar de* (stop); *volver a* (again); *acabar* + gerund /
  *acabar por* (end up).
- *llegar a* (go so far as), *alcanzar a* (manage to, Latin America), *estar por* (about to in
  much of Latin America), *tener* + participle (already done or planned).
- Pronouns before the conjugated verb or attached to the infinitive or gerund.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: La entrevista: from conversation to profile
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 13 turned a press conference into a news story. A press conference gives you short,
public statements; an interview gives you an hour of conversation with one person, full of
anecdotes, digressions and half-finished sentences. Out of that a journalist writes un
perfil, a profile: a portrait of the person that mixes description, summary and a few
carefully chosen quotations.

Here you'll read a long, fictional interview (summarized in English: read the Spanish first) and
the profile written from it, and see what the journalist quoted, what she reported with lesson
13's **[[reporting verbs]]**, and what she left out. The last part is about the ethics of quoting.

## The interview

Itzel Cárdenas is a fictional volcanologist (*vulcanóloga*) from Puebla who explains volcanoes on
a video channel. A journalist interviews her for a weekend magazine. *El Popo* is the everyday
name for Popocatépetl, the active volcano near Puebla and Mexico City; *la ceniza* is ash and *la
fumarola* the plume of gas and steam a volcano gives off.

> Entrevistador: Usted tiene casi un millón de seguidores y le dicen "la señora de los volcanes". ¿Cómo empezó todo?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: Por una pregunta de mi sobrina. Tenía seis años y un día, mientras veíamos la fumarola del Popo desde la azotea, me preguntó si el volcán estaba enojado. Le expliqué lo que pasaba adentro y me pidió que se lo volviera a contar al día siguiente, con dibujos. Ahí me di cuenta de que la curiosidad de una niña de seis años es la misma que la de un científico. Grabé un video para ella, lo subí y, para mi sorpresa, lo vieron miles de personas.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Siempre supo que su vocación era la ciencia?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: No, para nada. En la prepa yo quería ser actriz. Lo que pasa es que tuve una maestra de geografía, la maestra Ofelia, que nos llevaba de excursión a las faldas del volcán. Ella me inspiró. Nos hacía tocar las rocas y nos preguntaba qué historia contaban. Si no la hubiera conocido, seguramente estaría haciendo telenovelas.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Fue su mentora?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: Más que eso: fue mi primer referente. Después, en la universidad, tuve un mentor formal, el doctor que dirigió mi tesis, que me enseñó a dudar de todo, incluso de mis propios datos. Pero la pasión me la contagió Ofelia. Todavía le mando mis videos antes de publicarlos; es mi crítica más dura.
>
> Entrevistador: Muchos científicos piensan que la divulgación es una pérdida de tiempo. ¿Qué les diría?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: Que los entiendo, pero que se equivocan. Hacer ciencia y contarla son dos trabajos distintos y los dos son necesarios. Si la gente no entiende lo que hacemos, ¿por qué lo va a financiar? Además, explicar algo con palabras sencillas te obliga a entenderlo mejor. Yo he aprendido muchísimo preparando videos para niños.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Qué es lo más difícil de ser divulgadora?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: No exagerar. El algoritmo premia el miedo: si pongo en el título "¡El Popo va a explotar!", tengo el triple de visitas. Pero sería mentir. Mi regla es no decir nada que no le diría a un colega en un congreso. Cuando hay actividad, le pido a la gente que siga las indicaciones de Protección Civil y no los rumores. Y cuando no sé algo, lo digo.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Ha recibido críticas?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: Muchas. Algunos colegas dicen que simplifico demasiado; algunos seguidores, que soy demasiado técnica. Supongo que eso significa que estoy en el lugar correcto. Lo que sí me dolió fue que un periódico publicara una frase mía sacada de contexto. Yo había dicho "no hay que tenerle miedo al volcán, sino respeto", y apareció como "no hay que tenerle miedo al volcán". Esa media frase podía poner a alguien en peligro. Les escribí y la corrigieron, pero el daño ya estaba hecho.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Cómo es un día normal para usted?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: No hay días normales. Por la mañana reviso los datos de las estaciones que vigilan el volcán; por la tarde doy clases en la universidad, y por la noche, cuando mi casa por fin está en silencio, grabo. Un video de diez minutos me lleva unas doce horas de trabajo: leer, escribir el guion, dibujar, grabar y editar. Mi pareja dice que vivo con tres: con él, con el volcán y con la cámara.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Alguna vez la han tratado distinto por ser mujer?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: Sí, sobre todo al principio. En las salidas de campo, algunos daban por hecho que yo era la estudiante y mi compañero el investigador, aunque fuera al revés. Todavía hay quien me pregunta en los comentarios si de verdad soy doctora. Ya no me enoja: le mando el enlace de mi tesis y sigo grabando. Lo que sí me importa es que las niñas que me ven sepan que las vulcanólogas existen.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Qué consejo le daría a una joven que quiere dedicarse a la ciencia?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: Que no espere a sentirse lista. Yo llevo quince años estudiando volcanes y todavía me pongo nerviosa antes de cada grabación. Y que busque a su Ofelia: alguien que la anime cuando todo salga mal. La inspiración está muy bien, pero lo que te saca adelante es la gente.
>
> Entrevistador: ¿Y después de los volcanes?
>
> Itzel Cárdenas: Tengo pensado hacer una serie sobre los sismos, porque en México todos tenemos una historia de un temblor. Pero sin prisa. Primero quiero terminar un libro para niños. Se llama *¿Está enojado el volcán?*, y está dedicado a mi sobrina, que ya tiene dieciséis años y, por cierto, quiere ser actriz.

Summary in English. Cárdenas, who has almost a million followers, says it all began when
her six-year-old niece, watching the volcano's plume, asked whether it was angry; the video she
made to explain it was seen by thousands. In high school she wanted to act, until a geography
teacher, Ofelia, took the class to the volcano and asked what stories the rocks told. Ofelia was
her first role model; her thesis advisor, her formal mentor, taught her to doubt everything, but
the passion came from Ofelia, who still sees every video first. To scientists who call outreach a
waste of time she says that doing science and telling it are two necessary jobs. The hardest part
is not exaggerating when the algorithm rewards fear: she says nothing she wouldn't tell a
colleague, sends people to Civil Protection's instructions and admits what she doesn't know. Her
days mix data, teaching and filming; a ten-minute video takes about twelve hours. People once
assumed she was the student rather than the researcher, and commenters still doubt her doctorate.
What hurt most was a newspaper printing half her sentence about fear, leaving out "but respect".
Her advice to young women: don't wait to feel ready, and find someone who will encourage you.
Next come a series on earthquakes and a children's book for her niece, who now wants to act.

Hard phrases: *las faldas del volcán* (the lower slopes), *me la contagió* (passed it on to me,
like a contagious thing), *sacada de contexto* (taken out of context), *lo que te saca
adelante* (what keeps you going), *por cierto* (lesson 17: by the way), *la tesis* (lesson 02:
thesis), *un congreso* (a conference) and *el algoritmo* (16h2: the algorithm).

## The profile

> La señora de los volcanes
>
> Apasionada de los volcanes, Itzel Cárdenas habla del Popocatépetl como quien habla de un vecino difícil. Lleva quince años estudiando volcanes y casi un millón de personas siguen sus videos, pero insiste en que todo empezó con una pregunta de su sobrina de seis años: si el volcán estaba enojado.
>
> No siempre quiso ser científica. En la prepa soñaba con ser actriz, hasta que una maestra de geografía, Ofelia, empezó a llevar a su grupo a las faldas del volcán. "Fue mi primer referente", recuerda. Cárdenas reconoce que, si no la hubiera conocido, "seguramente estaría haciendo telenovelas".
>
> Sus días son largos: por la mañana revisa los datos del volcán, por la tarde da clases y por la noche graba. Calcula que cada video de diez minutos le lleva unas doce horas. Más de una vez ha tenido que demostrar que era la investigadora y no "la estudiante"; hoy contesta esas dudas con el enlace de su tesis.
>
> Defiende la divulgación frente a los colegas que la consideran una pérdida de tiempo: sostiene que contar la ciencia es tan necesario como hacerla. Su regla contra el sensacionalismo es sencilla: no decir en un video nada que no le diría a un colega. Por eso le dolió tanto que un periódico la citara a medias. "No hay que tenerle miedo al volcán, sino respeto", puntualiza.
>
> A las jóvenes que quieren dedicarse a la ciencia les aconseja que no esperen a sentirse listas y que busquen a alguien que las anime. Ella ya tiene el siguiente proyecto: un libro para niños dedicado a su sobrina, que, como ella a su edad, quiere ser actriz.

Summary in English. The profile opens with Cárdenas talking about the volcano "like a
difficult neighbor" and with her niece's question. It tells how a teacher turned a would-be actress
into a scientist, quoting two lines (her first role model; "I'd probably be making soap operas").
It sums up her long days and the doubts she faced as a woman researcher, her defense of outreach
and her rule against sensationalism, quotes her full sentence about fear and respect, and ends with
her advice to young women and the children's book for her niece. *Como quien habla de* = the way
someone talks about; *la citara a medias* = quoted her by halves.

## How the profile was built

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: From interview to profile
  accDescr: The steps a journalist follows. Record the interview. Transcribe it. Choose a central idea for the portrait. Pick a few quotations that only this person could have said. Report the rest with reporting verbs, in the present tense. Check facts and names. Optionally, read the quotations back to the interviewee to confirm them, without letting her rewrite the piece.
  A["Grabar la entrevista"] --> B["Transcribir"]
  B --> C["Elegir una idea central"]
  C --> D["Escoger pocas citas: lo que solo ella diría"]
  D --> E["Resumir el resto con verbos de habla, en presente"]
  E --> F["Verificar datos y nombres"]
  F --> G["Confirmar las citas (opcional)"]
```

### Example 1: the present tense of profiles

The news story in lesson 13 reported with *anunció, recalcó, sostuvo*, and every tense shifted.
A profile describes a person as she is now, so it usually reports in the present: *insiste en que
todo empezó…, recuerda, reconoce, sostiene, aconseja.* With a present reporting verb nothing
shifts: *insiste en que todo empezó* keeps the preterite she used. Only the subjunctive follows the main verb:
*les aconseja que no esperen* (present → present subjunctive), where lesson 13's past report
would give *les aconsejó que no esperaran*.

### Example 2: choosing what to quote

Out of more than 600 words of answers, the profile quotes three phrases. Each passes one test:
only this person could have said it this way. *"Seguramente estaría haciendo
telenovelas"* is funny and personal; *"no hay que tenerle miedo al volcán, sino respeto"* is the
sentence she cares about most. Plain facts (fifteen years, a million followers) are
reported, not quoted: quotation marks are for voice, not information.

### Example 3: one answer, three summaries

Her answer about outreach can be reported several ways, each with a different verb and pattern:

- *Sostiene que contar la ciencia es tan necesario como hacerla.* (que + indicative: her view)
- *Les reprocha a algunos colegas que vean la divulgación como una pérdida de tiempo.* (que +
  subjunctive: a reproach; too strong for what she said, which began *los entiendo*)
- *Admite que los entiende, pero insiste en que se equivocan.* (fair, but longer)

The profile chose the first: a reporting verb is an interpretation, so it must match the tone.

## Quoting accurately

The interview shows what goes wrong: half a sentence said the opposite of the whole. Journalism
ethics codes generally agree on these rules:

- Quotation marks mean her words. Inside them, change nothing that alters meaning. Dropping
  fillers (*este…, o sea*) is common practice; changing tenses or words is not.
- Cuts must not change the meaning. Spanish marks a cut inside a quotation with *[…]*.
- Report fairly what you don't quote. *Insinúa* or *alega* where she *explica* is a quiet
  distortion.
- Corrections are public. A wrong quote is corrected where readers will see it.

Spanish punctuation: for printed texts the RAE recommends angle quotation marks (« ») first, with
double quotation marks (" ") inside them; most Mexican media use double quotation marks. The
period goes after the closing mark: *…sino respeto".*

## Common mistakes

- Shifting tenses after a present reporting verb: ~~*Recuerda que había sido su primer
  referente*~~ when the source said *fue* → *Recuerda que fue su primer referente*.
- A reporting verb stronger than the original: *Exige que…* for a polite suggestion.
- Quoting a plain fact: ~~*"Llevo quince años estudiando volcanes", dice*~~ → *Lleva quince años
  estudiando volcanes.* Save quotation marks for her voice.
- The period inside the closing quotation mark, English style: ~~*respeto."*~~ → *respeto".*

## Key points

- *Un perfil* is a portrait built from an interview: description, summary and a few quotations.
- Profiles usually report in the present (*cuenta, recuerda, sostiene, aconseja que* + present
  subjunctive); news stories report in the past, with every shift.
- Quote what only that person could say; report facts.
- Each reporting verb is an interpretation: match it to the tone of the original.
- Never let a cut or a summary change the meaning; correct publicly when it does.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: ¿Es verdad? Fact-checking and disinformation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 14 showed how one event turns into a headline, a news story and a sensationalist version.
On social media there's a fourth version: the post that spreads faster than anyone can check it.
This honors lesson is about checking: how fact-checkers decide whether a claim is true, and the
Spanish they use to report what they found. You'll use lesson 13's reporting verbs to say who
claimed what, lesson 14's passive and impersonal *se* to report findings without making them
personal, and a set of hedges for claims nobody has confirmed yet.

The words first. B1 taught *las noticias falsas* (fake news), which is what you'll usually hear
in Mexico, along with the English *fake news*. In Spain the everyday word for a false story spread
on purpose is *el bulo*, which the DLE defines as a false piece of news spread for some purpose.
*La desinformación* is false information spread deliberately; Spanish often uses the same word where
English sometimes distinguishes misinformation (spread by mistake).

## How a claim is checked

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to check a viral claim
  accDescr: Five questions in order. Who published it first, and is that source reliable? When was it published, and is the date the one the post claims? Is there an original context, such as a full speech, a full document or the first place a photo appeared? For images, a reverse image search finds where and when the picture appeared before. Do other reliable sources confirm it? The answer leads to a verdict: true, misleading or false.
  A["¿Quién lo publicó primero? ¿Es una fuente fiable?"] --> B["¿Cuándo se publicó? ¿Coincide la fecha?"]
  B --> C["¿Cuál es el contexto original?"]
  C --> D["¿La imagen ya había aparecido antes? (búsqueda inversa)"]
  D --> E["¿Lo confirman otras fuentes fiables?"]
  E --> F["Veredicto: verdadero, engañoso o falso"]
```

The five questions:

1. The source. Who said it first? An official account, a news outlet with a name and an
   address, or an anonymous chain message? *Una fuente fiable* (in Latin America often *confiable*) is
   a reliable source; A2's *la fuente* (fountain) also means "source".
2. The date. Old news recirculates as new. A real photo with a false date is still
   disinformation.
3. The original context. Find the full speech, the whole document, the complete video. A
   sentence cut in half can say the opposite (16h1).
4. Images. A reverse image search (*una búsqueda inversa de imágenes*) shows where a picture
   appeared before. *Una captura de pantalla* (screenshot) is easy to fake: look for the original
   page, not the image of it. To doctor an image is *manipular*; the result shows *manipulación*.
5. Confirmation. Do other reliable sources report the same thing independently?

*El algoritmo* of a social network shows people more of what they react to, and fear and anger get
reactions. That's one reason a false story can *viralizarse* (go viral) before any correction.

## The language of unconfirmed claims

News and fact-checks keep a distance from what they haven't confirmed:

| Hedge | Example |
|---|---|
| *supuestamente* (B1) | *El video muestra supuestamente una inundación de hoy.* |
| *al parecer, por lo visto* (B1) | *Al parecer, la foto es de 2017.* |
| *según* + source | *Según fuentes del ayuntamiento, el corte es parcial.* |
| *presunto* (alleged) | *el presunto autor de la publicación* |
| conditional (recognition) | *El mensaje habría sido creado por una cuenta falsa.* |
| *circula en redes* | *Circula en redes un mensaje que asegura que…* |

The conditional in the last but one line (*habría sido creado*: "was allegedly created") is the
same one you saw in lesson 14's news story. Recognize it; when you write, *según* + source or
*supuestamente* says the same thing more plainly.

Findings are reported impersonally, with lesson 14's structures: *Se trata de un montaje* (it's a
fake, a composite image). *La imagen fue tomada en 2017. No se encontró ninguna publicación
(lesson 18: publication, post) oficial. Se consultó al organismo, que desmintió el mensaje.* Corrections use the same style: *En
una versión anterior de esta nota se afirmaba que…; el dato fue corregido.*

## Warning signs

Before you share a post, look for the marks of disinformation. It asks you to share it at once
(*¡Compártelo ya!*) or warns that "they" will delete it. It names no source, or a vague one (*un
amigo que trabaja en el gobierno*). It is written in capital letters with many exclamation marks.
It shows a screenshot instead of a link. It makes you angry or afraid, and that's the point: a
message built to provoke a reaction is built to travel. None of these proves a post is false, but
each is a reason to check before you pass it on.

## Three viral posts

All three posts and their checks are fictional.

### Example 1: an exaggeration

> Publicación. ¡URGENTE! Desde mañana cortan el agua en TODA la ciudad durante una semana. Lo dijo la directora del organismo. ¡Compártelo antes de que lo borren!
>
> Verificación. Engañoso. El organismo municipal de agua anunció en un comunicado un corte de treinta y seis horas, a partir del sábado y solo en las colonias del norte. La directora negó que la obra fuera a durar una semana. El mensaje, que se viralizó el jueves, exagera la duración y el área afectada. Se recomienda consultar la página oficial del organismo.

> Post. URGENT! Starting tomorrow they're cutting off the water in the WHOLE city for a week. The utility's director said so. Share before they delete it!
>
> Check. Misleading. The city water utility announced in a press release a thirty-six-hour outage, starting Saturday and only in the northern neighborhoods. The director denied that the work would last a week. The message, which went viral on Thursday, exaggerates the length and the area affected. Checking the utility's official website is recommended.

The post takes a real announcement (lesson 13's press conference) and inflates it. The clues:
capital letters, *¡Compártelo antes de que lo borren!* (urgency plus a hint of censorship), and no
link to the source. The check reports the claim with *negó que* + subjunctive and gives its
advice impersonally (*Se recomienda…*).

### Example 2: a real photo, a false date

![A fictional social media post. A profile icon and the name Noticias Ya Ya, the text "Así amaneció hoy la estación Centro", a photo of a flooded subway platform, and counters for likes and shares. A red stamp across the photo reads FALSO, and a note below says the photo was first published in 2017.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Publicación. Así amaneció hoy la estación Centro del metro. ¡Nadie nos avisó!
>
> Verificación. Falso. Una búsqueda inversa muestra que la foto fue publicada por primera vez en 2017 por una agencia de noticias, durante unas lluvias en otra ciudad. Hoy la estación funciona con normalidad, según confirmó el sistema de transporte. La imagen es real, pero se usó fuera de contexto.

> Post. This is what Centro metro station looked like this morning. Nobody warned us!
>
> Check. False. A reverse image search shows the photo was first published in 2017 by a news agency, during heavy rains in another city. Today the station is operating normally, the transit system confirmed. The image is real, but it was used out of context.

Nothing in the picture was manipulated: the lie is the date and the place. *Fue publicada por
primera vez* (ser passive) and *se usó* (passive *se*) keep the report about the image, not about
whoever shared it.

### Example 3: surprising, but true

> Publicación. Video: un cocodrilo pasea por una playa de Oaxaca y los turistas lo graban como si nada.
>
> Verificación. Verdadero. El video fue grabado el martes, según testigos localizados por este medio, y la Protección Civil municipal confirmó que el animal fue reubicado esa tarde. Las autoridades recordaron que no hay que acercarse a la fauna silvestre.

> Post. Video: a crocodile strolls along a beach in Oaxaca and the tourists film it as if it were nothing.
>
> Check. True. The video was filmed on Tuesday, according to witnesses this outlet tracked down, and the municipal Civil Protection office confirmed the animal was relocated that afternoon. The authorities reminded people not to approach wild animals.

Checking isn't only debunking. *La verificación* (fact-checking) also confirms true stories, and a
check that a claim is accurate is as useful as one that it's false. *Como si nada* (as if it were
nothing) is B1's *como si* in a fixed phrase.

## Who checks

Fact-checking is now a branch of journalism. In 2016, fact-checking organizations from many
countries agreed on a code of principles through the International Fact-Checking Network:
nonpartisanship, transparency about sources, funding and methods, and open corrections. In Mexico,
*Verificado 2018*, organized by Animal Político, AJ+ Español and Pop-Up Newsroom with about 90
partner organizations, checked claims during the campaign for the federal election of July 1,
2018, including a WhatsApp line where people could send messages to *verificar* (to fact-check).
Sites change their names and methods, so look up who is checking today in the country whose news
you read.

## Common mistakes

- *Verificar* in the preterite: ~~*verificé*~~ → *verifiqué* (c → qu before e).
- *Viralizarse* without its pronoun: ~~*El video viralizó*~~ → *El video se viralizó*.
- Stating a rumor as fact: ~~*El autor del mensaje es un político*~~ → *Según el organismo, el
  mensaje habría sido creado por…* or *El presunto autor…*
- *Bulo* in Mexican Spanish: understood by many readers, but *noticia falsa* sounds more natural
  there.
- Using a plural verb in an impersonal finding about people: ~~*Se consultaron a dos expertos*~~
  → *Se consultó a dos expertos*.

## Key points

- Check the source, the date, the original context and the image, then look for confirmation; the
  verdict can be *verdadero, engañoso* or *falso* (true, misleading or false).
- *El bulo* is Spain's word; in Mexico *noticia falsa* or *fake news* is usual.
- Hedges: *supuestamente, al parecer, según…, presunto*, and the news conditional (*habría sido
  creado*) for recognition.
- Report findings impersonally: *Se trata de…, La imagen fue tomada…, Se consultó a…*
- *Fiable / confiable, manipular, la captura de pantalla, el algoritmo, viralizarse.*

lessons.title: Es más, para colmo…: discourse markers at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This module is about arguing with precision: saying exactly how one idea relates to the next,
writing in the formal style of reports and research, describing data, and defending a proposal.
It starts with small words.

In B1 (lesson 19) you learned the **[[discourse markers]]** that organize a text: *en primer lugar,
además, por un lado… por otro, sin embargo, en conclusión*. At B2 you
need the markers that do finer jobs: correcting yourself in mid-sentence, saying "in fact" or
"actually", piling one complaint on another, slipping in a side remark, and closing a topic with
a shrug.

The theme is the job market: applying for jobs, contracts, freelancing and automation. B1
lesson 15 covered life at work; here the question is how work is changing. A2's *las
prestaciones* (benefits), *el aguinaldo* (year-end bonus) and *la vacante* (vacancy) come back.

## What a discourse marker does

A **[[connector]]** such as *porque* or *aunque* joins two clauses into one sentence. A discourse
marker doesn't: it stands outside the grammar of the sentence and tells the listener how to
take what comes next ("I'm correcting myself", "this is a stronger point", "by the way").
Most markers can move, and they are set off with commas:

- *De hecho, la empresa no despidió a nadie.* — In fact, the company didn't lay anyone off.
- *La empresa, de hecho, no despidió a nadie.*

Connectors and markers give a text **[[cohesion]]**: its sentences visibly hang together. That is
different from **[[coherence]]**, which is whether the ideas themselves make sense in that order; no
marker can rescue an argument that jumps around.

![A chart titled Marcadores del discurso por función with five colored columns. Reformular: es decir, o sea, mejor dicho, dicho de otro modo. Corregir y matizar: de hecho, en realidad, más bien. Añadir y reforzar: además, es más, encima, para colmo, with an arrow showing they get stronger downward. Hacer un paréntesis: por cierto, a propósito. Concluir o restar importancia: al fin y al cabo, de todos modos, en cualquier caso, en fin, total. Markers used mostly in conversation are marked with a speech bubble: o sea, encima, para colmo, en fin, total.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Reformulating: saying it another way

You know *es decir* (that is) and *o sea* (I mean, that is) from A2. Two more:

- *Mejor dicho* (or rather) corrects what you just said with a more accurate word: *La entrevista
  es el lunes, mejor dicho, el martes.* — The interview is on Monday, or rather on Tuesday.
- *Dicho de otro modo* (in other words, put another way) explains the same idea in plainer terms:
  *La empresa va a automatizar la nómina. Dicho de otro modo, ya no necesita a tres personas para
  calcular los sueldos.* — The company is going to automate payroll. In other words, it no longer
  needs three people to work out the salaries.

*Es decir* works in any text; *o sea* belongs to speech.

## Correcting and nuancing: in fact, actually, rather

- *De hecho* (in fact) backs up what was said with a fact, often a stronger one: *Las habilidades
  blandas importan mucho. De hecho, son lo primero que reviso.* — Soft skills matter a lot. In
  fact, they're the first thing I look at. It can also contradict with a fact: *Dicen que nadie
  contrata en diciembre; de hecho, a mí me contrataron el 15 de diciembre.*
- *En realidad* (actually, really) sets the reality against an appearance or a belief: *Parece un
  trabajo fácil, pero en realidad tiene mucha presión.* — It looks like an easy job, but actually
  there's a lot of pressure.
- *Más bien* (rather) swaps a word for a more exact one: *No es un mal sueldo; es más bien un
  sueldo bajo para la ciudad.* — It isn't a bad salary; it's rather a low salary for the city. After
  a negative it often means "more like": *—¿Estás nervioso? —No, más bien emocionado.*

Watch the false friend: *actualmente* (A2) means "currently", not "actually". *Actualmente
trabajo desde casa* = I currently work from home.

## Adding and building up

*Además* (A1) adds a point. Three markers add a point that weighs more than the last:

- *Es más* (what's more) adds a stronger argument for the same side, in speech or writing: *El
  proyecto es viable. Es más, ya funciona en otras dos ciudades.*
- *Encima* (on top of that) is colloquial and usually piles up complaints: *Me bajaron el sueldo y,
  encima, me cambiaron de horario.* — They cut my salary and, on top of that, changed my
  schedule. As an adverb or with *de* it still means "on top (of)": *encima de la mesa*.
- *Para colmo* (to top it all off) is also colloquial and marks the last straw: *Llovía, perdí el
  camión y, para colmo, la entrevista era en otro edificio.*

So *además* → *es más* → *encima* / *para colmo* climbs from neutral to exasperated. In a formal
e-mail, *además* or *asimismo* (B1) is the safe choice; *encima* and *para colmo* sound like a
complaint over coffee.

## Digressing: by the way

*Por cierto* (by the way) opens a side remark, often a question: *Por cierto, ¿ya enviaste tu
currículum?* *A propósito*, which you learned in A2 as "on purpose" (*no lo hice a propósito*),
can open a side remark in the same way: *A propósito, ¿ya enviaste tu currículum?*

## Concluding and dismissing

These close a topic, but each with its own attitude:

- *Al fin y al cabo* (after all) gives the reason that settles the matter: *No me molesta trabajar
  los sábados; al fin y al cabo, me pagan el doble.*
- *De todos modos* (anyway), also *de todas formas* or *de todas maneras*, says that what came before
  doesn't change the conclusion: *No sé si me van a contratar. De todos modos, voy a seguir
  buscando.* — I don't know if they'll hire me. Anyway, I'm going to keep looking.
- *En cualquier caso* (in any case) does the same job and is a little more formal: *Puede que la
  empresa cierre o que se mude. En cualquier caso, habrá despidos.*
- *En fin* (well, anyway; in short) wraps up, often with a sigh of resignation: *En fin, así son
  las cosas.*
- *Total* (so in the end) is colloquial and introduces the outcome of a story, usually a
  disappointing one, often as *total, que…*: *Me hicieron cuatro entrevistas. Total, que le dieron
  el puesto a otra persona.* *Total* is also an ordinary adjective (*el precio total*, the total
  price); here it is a marker.

| Marker | Speech | Writing |
|---|---|---|
| *es decir, mejor dicho, de hecho, en realidad, más bien, es más, por cierto, al fin y al cabo, de todos modos, en cualquier caso* | yes | yes |
| *dicho de otro modo* | yes | yes (a little formal) |
| *o sea, encima, para colmo, en fin, total* | yes | informal texts only (chats, personal e-mails) |

## Work words for this lesson

To apply for a job in Mexico is *postularse* (*me postulé a una vacante*); Spain usually says
*presentarse a un puesto*. You'll also hear *aplicar a una vacante*, a calque of English "apply",
which is very common in Mexican speech; in careful writing, use *postularse* or B1's *solicitar*.
The ad itself is *una oferta de empleo* (a job posting; Spain also *oferta de trabajo*).

A permanent position is *un puesto de planta* (*Busco trabajo de planta* = I'm looking for a
permanent job), with benefits; *un trabajador independiente* (a freelancer, also *un freelance*)
works by project. *La nómina* is the payroll, *el despido* a dismissal or layoff, and
*sustituir* means to replace (*sustituyo, sustituyó*: a *y* appears, as in *construir*).

A fact worth knowing: a 2021 reform of Mexico's labor laws (published in the *Diario Oficial de
la Federación* on April 23, 2021) banned *la subcontratación de personal* (supplying
workers to another company); outside firms may still provide specialized services outside the
client's main business if they are registered with the labor ministry (STPS).

## Podcast: *Talento en línea*

Two recruiters talk about automation.

> Daniela: Bienvenidos a *Talento en línea*. Hoy hablamos de automatización. Arturo, ¿la
> inteligencia artificial nos va a quitar el trabajo?
>
> Arturo: No todo el trabajo. Mejor dicho, va a cambiar muchas tareas, pero no
> necesariamente puestos completos. De hecho, las empresas que conozco que automatizaron la
> nómina no despidieron a todo el equipo: lo reorganizaron.
>
> Daniela: Pero sí hay despidos.
>
> Arturo: Claro que los hay. En realidad, lo que más me preocupa es que la gente no se esté
> preparando.
>
> Daniela: Coincido. Yo leo cientos de solicitudes al mes, y lo que distingue a un candidato
> ya no es tanto el título, sino más bien las habilidades blandas: comunicarse, resolver
> problemas, trabajar en equipo. Es más, algunas ofertas de empleo que publicamos ya no piden
> carrera.
>
> Arturo: Lo mismo pasa con los trabajadores independientes. Se postulan a proyectos en
> plataformas internacionales y, encima, compiten con gente de todo el mundo.
>
> Daniela: Y, para colmo, sin prestaciones. Por cierto, ¿qué recomiendas: un puesto de planta
> o trabajar por proyecto?
>
> Arturo: Depende de la etapa de tu vida. Al fin y al cabo, un puesto de planta te da seguro
> social, aguinaldo y vacaciones pagadas. Dicho de otro modo, estabilidad.
>
> Daniela: ¿Y algún consejo práctico para los que se están postulando ahora?
>
> Arturo: Que no se postulen a cien vacantes con el mismo currículum. Más vale adaptar cada
> solicitud a la oferta de empleo, aunque tome más tiempo.
>
> Daniela: ¿Y qué les dices a los que temen que un programa los sustituya?
>
> Arturo: Que aprendan a usar esas herramientas antes que nadie. En cualquier caso, ninguna
> máquina hace una entrevista como tú.
>
> Daniela: Eso espero. En fin, se nos acabó el tiempo. Total, que el futuro del trabajo no
> está escrito. ¡Gracias, Arturo!

Summary: Daniela asks whether AI will take our jobs. Arturo corrects himself: it will change
tasks more than whole jobs, and the firms he knows that automated payroll reorganized their staff
instead of firing everyone. There are layoffs, he admits, but what worries him is that people
aren't preparing. Daniela says soft skills now count more than degrees, and some of her postings
don't require one. Arturo adds that freelancers compete worldwide; Daniela adds that they have no
benefits. Arturo says a permanent job means stability, advises adapting each application to the posting
instead of sending the same CV everywhere, and says that people afraid of being replaced should
learn the new tools first. Daniela closes: nobody knows the future of work.

*Quitar el trabajo* = to take (someone's) job away; *coincido* = I agree (*coincidir*, to agree,
to coincide); *antes que nadie* = before anyone else; *más vale* = it's better to; *el seguro social* = social security
(health care and a pension, in Mexico through the IMSS); *se nos acabó el tiempo* = we've run out
of time. *Lo que me preocupa es que* takes the subjunctive (*se esté preparando*), as B1's *me
preocupa que* does.

## Punctuation

A marker takes a comma after it at the start of a sentence (*Por cierto, ¿viste la oferta?*) and
commas on both sides in the middle (*El sueldo, en realidad, no es malo*). After a full clause,
writers put a semicolon or period before it: *Es caro; de todos modos, lo voy a comprar.*

## Pronunciation

- *De hecho*: the *h* is silent, so the two *e*'s merge into one long *e*: *de-e-cho*.
- *Al fin y al cabo* links into one breath: *al-fi-nyal-ca-bo*.
- *Automatización* has six syllables: *au-to-ma-ti-za-ción*, stress on the last; *z* sounds like
  *s* in Latin America.
- *Sustituir* has three syllables, *sus-ti-tuir*, with the stress on the last; *sustituyo* has
  four, *sus-ti-tu-yo*.

## Common mistakes

- *En fin* as "finally": the DLE lists that sense, but today *en fin* mostly closes a topic,
  often with resignation. For the last item of a list, use *por último* or *finalmente*.
- Saying *actualmente* for "actually". "Actually, I'm a freelancer" is *En realidad, soy
  trabajador independiente*.
- Using *o sea* as a filler between every few words (*o sea, fui, o sea, y…*). A few are normal
  in casual speech; in an interview or a presentation, too many sound careless.
- Using *encima* or *para colmo* for good news. They usually pile up problems; for a positive
  extra point, *además* or *es más* is the natural choice.
- Leaving out the commas. *De hecho la empresa…* is easy to misread; write *De hecho, la
  empresa…*.

## Key points

- Discourse markers tell the listener how to take what follows; they are movable and go between
  commas.
- Reformulate with *es decir, o sea, mejor dicho* (correcting yourself) and *dicho de otro modo*.
- *De hecho* backs up with a fact; *en realidad* sets reality against appearance; *más bien* swaps
  in a more exact word.
- *Además → es más → encima / para colmo* builds up, from neutral to exasperated.
- *Por cierto* (also *a propósito*) opens a side remark.
- *Al fin y al cabo* settles; *de todos modos* and *en cualquier caso* dismiss; *en fin* and *total*
  wrap up, colloquially.
