lessons.title: La mejora de la calidad: nominal style in formal writing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Compare two sentences that say the same thing:

- *Los participantes consumieron menos azúcar, y por eso les bajó la presión.* — The
  participants ate less sugar, and that's why their blood pressure went down.
- *La reducción del consumo de azúcar provocó una disminución de la presión arterial.* — The
  reduction in sugar consumption led to a decrease in blood pressure.

The first is how you'd tell a friend. The second is how a research paper, a news report or an
official document says it: the actions have become nouns (*reducir → la reducción, consumir →
el consumo, disminuir → la disminución*). That process is **[[nominalization]]**, and a text built
on it is written in the **[[nominal style]]**. You need to read it for the DELE B2 reading texts and
the news, and to use some of it in formal writing; you also need to unpack it into verbs when
you explain the same idea aloud.

The theme is science and research: how studies are designed, written and read. Lesson 14's
**[[passive se]]** and **[[impersonal se]]** and lesson 05's **[[neuter lo]]** come back. (*La presión
arterial* = blood pressure; *el consumo* = consumption, from lesson 05.)

## From verb to noun

Most nominalizations add a suffix to the verb's stem. The suffix tells you the gender, which
saves a lot of guessing:

| Suffix | Gender | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-ción / -sión* | feminine | *publicar → la publicación, comprobar → la comprobación, observar → la observación, reducir → la reducción* |
| *-miento* | masculine | *conocer → el conocimiento, comportarse → el comportamiento, financiar → el financiamiento, descubrir → el descubrimiento* |
| *-dad* (from adjectives) | feminine | *posible → la posibilidad, estable → la estabilidad* |
| *-ura, -dura* | feminine | *quemar → la quemadura* (burn), *picar → la picadura* (sting); from adjectives, *alto → la altura* |
| *-aje* | masculine | *aprender → el aprendizaje* (learning), *aterrizar → el aterrizaje* |
| *-anza* | feminine | *enseñar → la enseñanza* (teaching), *confiar → la confianza* |
| *-eza* (from adjectives) | feminine | *rico → la riqueza, triste → la tristeza* |
| no suffix: *-a, -o, -e* | varies | *mejorar → la mejora, aumentar → el aumento, debatir → el debate* |

Some nouns come from Greek or Latin and don't follow the pattern: *analizar → el análisis*
(masculine, plural *los análisis*), *investigar → la investigación* but *el estudio* from
*estudiar*. When you're not sure, check the dictionary: *mejorar* gives *la mejora*, not
*mejoración*.

![A chart with three columns: Verbo, Sustantivo and Terminación. Rows: mejorar, la mejora, -a; analizar, el análisis, -is; comprobar, la comprobación, -ción; conocer, el conocimiento, -miento; financiar, el financiamiento, -miento; observar, la observación, -ción; aprender, el aprendizaje, -aje; enseñar, la enseñanza, -anza. Feminine nouns are on a pink background and masculine nouns on a blue one, with a key at the bottom.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Unpacking the nominal style

A nominal sentence packs a lot into a few nouns joined by *de*. To understand it, or to say it
aloud, unpack it in three steps:

1. Find the nouns that hide verbs (*la reducción, el consumo, la disminución*).
2. Ask who does each action: who reduced? who consumed?
3. Rebuild the sentence with those people as subjects and the nouns as verbs.

*La mejora de la calidad del agua tras la instalación de filtros redujo las enfermedades
gastrointestinales.* → *Instalaron filtros, el agua mejoró y la gente se enfermó menos del
estómago.* — They installed filters, the water got better and people got fewer stomach
illnesses.

Going the other way is how you make your own writing more formal: *Analizamos los datos y
comprobamos que…* → *El análisis de los datos permitió comprobar que…* Don't overdo it. A text
in which every sentence is a chain of four nouns is hard to read, even for experts.

Two more nominal forms to recognize:

- The infinitive as a noun, with *el*: *el ir y venir de los estudiantes* (the comings and
  goings of the students), *El fumar está prohibido* (smoking is banned). In everyday Spanish
  you'd say *fumar está prohibido* or *se prohíbe fumar*; the version with *el* sounds formal or
  literary. Recognize it; you don't need to produce it.
- Lo + participle names "the thing that was done": *lo ocurrido* (what happened), *lo dicho*
  (what was said), *lo observado* (what was observed), *lo expuesto* (what has been set out). It is
  lesson 05's neuter *lo* with a participle: *Según lo observado, el fenómeno se repite cada año.*

## Support verbs

Formal Spanish often replaces a simple verb with a **[[support verb]]** and a noun: the verb carries
the tense and the noun carries the meaning.

| Simple verb | Support verb + noun | |
|---|---|---|
| *estudiar* | *llevar a cabo un estudio* | to carry out a study |
| *analizar* | *realizar un análisis* | to perform an analysis |
| *medir* | *efectuar una medición* | to take a measurement (formal) |
| *decidir* | *tomar una decisión* | to make a decision |
| *preguntar* | *hacer una pregunta* | to ask a question |
| *explicar* | *dar una explicación* | to give an explanation |

Some style guides warn against using *realizar* for everything (*realizar una visita, realizar
una llamada*): *visitar* and *llamar* are shorter and clearer. Use the support verb where it is the
normal phrase (*tomar una decisión, llevar a cabo un estudio*), not to make a sentence look
important.

## How research is written

Research papers often avoid naming the people who did the work, so they use the **[[passive se]]** and the
**[[impersonal se]]** from lesson 14: *Se analizaron 300 muestras* (300 samples were analyzed); *Se
observó que el consumo bajaba en verano* (it was observed that…); *Se recomienda repetir el
estudio.*

They also **[[hedge]]**: a careful paper says what the data suggest, not what they prove.

- *Los datos sugieren que…* — The data suggest that…
- *Los resultados parecen indicar que…* — The results seem to indicate that…
- *Esto podría deberse a…* — This could be due to…
- *Es posible que otros factores influyan en…* — Other factors may influence…

The biggest reason to hedge is the difference between a correlation and a cause. If two
things rise together (*una correlación*), one doesn't necessarily cause the other. Ice cream sales
and drownings both go up in summer, but ice cream doesn't drown anyone: heat drives both. A
researcher would write *La correlación no implica causalidad* (correlation doesn't imply
causation). To test a cause, you need an experiment such as *un ensayo clínico* (a clinical
trial), where one group gets the real treatment and another a *placebo* (a dummy pill), and,
ideally, nobody knows who got which.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The research cycle
  accDescr: A simplified research cycle in nine steps, top to bottom. Observación y pregunta (observation and question); revisión de lo publicado (review of what has been published); hipótesis (hypothesis); diseño del estudio: método y variables (study design: method and variables); recolección de datos (data collection); análisis (analysis); conclusiones (conclusions); revisión por pares (peer review); publicación (publication). An arrow from publication goes back to the first step, labeled nuevas preguntas (new questions).
  A["Observación y pregunta"] --> B["Revisión de lo publicado"]
  B --> C["Hipótesis"]
  C --> D["Diseño del estudio: método y variables"]
  D --> E["Recolección de datos"]
  E --> F["Análisis"]
  F --> G["Conclusiones"]
  G --> H["Revisión por pares"]
  H --> I["Publicación"]
  I -- "nuevas preguntas" --> A
```

Real research loops back at every step, but this is the shape most method courses teach.
Before a paper (*un artículo científico*) is published, other experts check it: that is *la
revisión por pares* (peer review). *El financiamiento* (funding; Spain usually *la
financiación*) often comes before all of it.

## Evidence, proof and pattern

Two words you know have a science sense:

- A1's *la prueba* (test) also means evidence or proof: *No hay pruebas de que el celular cause
  insomnio* (there's no evidence that…).
- *La evidencia* traditionally meant obviousness, and the DLE gives a legal sense, a decisive
  proof. In science writing across Latin America, *la evidencia* (often *las evidencias*) for
  "evidence" is now very common (*la evidencia científica*), though some style guides prefer
  *pruebas* or *indicios* (signs). Both will be understood.

*El patrón* is a pattern (*un patrón de comportamiento*, a pattern of behavior); it also means
boss, and a sewing pattern. *El estudio* is a study here; it can also be a studio.

## Text: one study, two readers

The abstract, as a journal would publish it:

> Resumen. El objetivo del presente estudio fue analizar la relación entre el uso nocturno del
> celular y la calidad del sueño en estudiantes universitarios. Se llevó a cabo una encuesta a 412
> estudiantes de entre 18 y 24 años y se realizó un seguimiento de sus horas de sueño durante
> cuatro semanas. El análisis de los datos mostró una correlación negativa entre el tiempo de
> pantalla después de las 23:00 horas y la duración del sueño. Asimismo, se observó una
> disminución del rendimiento académico en el grupo con mayor exposición. No obstante, dado el
> carácter observacional del estudio, los resultados no permiten establecer una relación de
> causalidad. Otros factores, como el estrés o la carga de trabajo, podrían explicar el fenómeno
> observado. Se recomienda la realización de ensayos controlados para comprobar dicha relación.

> Abstract. The aim of this study was to analyze the relationship between nighttime cell phone
> use and sleep quality in university students. A survey of 412 students aged 18 to 24 was carried
> out, and their hours of sleep were tracked for four weeks. Analysis of the data showed a negative
> correlation between screen time after 11 p.m. and sleep duration. Likewise, a decline in academic
> performance was observed in the group with the greatest exposure. However, given the
> observational nature of the study, the results do not allow a causal relationship to be
> established. Other factors, such as stress or workload, could explain the phenomenon observed.
> Controlled trials are recommended to test that relationship.

The same study for a general reader:

> ¿Dormimos menos por culpa del celular? Unos investigadores les preguntaron a 412 universitarios
> cómo usaban el celular en la noche y midieron cuánto dormían durante un mes. Los que más usaban
> la pantalla después de las once dormían menos y tenían peores calificaciones. Pero ojo: eso no
> quiere decir que el celular sea la causa. Puede que los estudiantes más estresados, o con más
> tarea, usen más el celular y además duerman peor. Para saberlo, habría que hacer un experimento.

> Do we sleep less because of our phones? Some researchers asked 412 university students how they
> used their phones at night and measured how much they slept for a month. Those who used the
> screen most after eleven slept less and got worse grades. But careful: that doesn't mean the
> phone is the cause. It may be that the most stressed students, or those with more homework, use
> their phones more and also sleep worse. To find out, you'd have to do an experiment.

Compare: *se llevó a cabo una encuesta* became *les preguntaron*; *se realizó un seguimiento*
(tracking) became *midieron*; *una disminución del rendimiento académico* became *peores
calificaciones*. *Dicha relación* is formal for "that relationship" (*dicho, dicha* = the
aforementioned). Both versions hedge: *no permiten establecer
una relación de causalidad* and *eso no quiere decir que… sea la causa*.

## Pronunciation

- *Análisis*: four syllables, *a-ná-li-sis*, stressed on the second. *Fenómeno*: four,
  *fe-nó-me-no*. Both carry a written accent because the stress falls three syllables from the end.
- *Correlación*: four syllables, *co-rre-la-ción*, with a trilled *rr*.
- *Investigación*: five syllables, *in-ves-ti-ga-ción*.
- *Placebo*: three syllables, *pla-ce-bo*, with *ce* said like *se*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*La análisis*~~ → *el análisis*; it's masculine, and the plural is *los análisis* (no change), like *la
  crisis → las crisis* but masculine.
- Saying *demuestra* about a correlation. An observational study *sugiere* or *muestra una
  relación*; only a well-designed experiment allows *demuestra*, and careful writers still hedge.
- Speaking in the nominal style. *Procedo a la realización de la compra* sounds like a parody
  of a bureaucrat. In conversation, use verbs: *Voy a comprarlo.*
- Inventing nouns by rule. *Mejoración* and *analización* don't exist. If a noun sounds odd,
  look it up.
- Using *realizar* for everything. Prefer the plain verb or the usual support verb (*tomar una
  decisión*, not *realizar una decisión*).

## Key points

- Nominalization turns verbs into nouns: *-ción* and *-dad* are feminine, *-miento* and *-aje*
  masculine. *El análisis* is masculine and doesn't change in the plural.
- The nominal style packs actions into nouns joined by *de*; unpack it by asking who did what.
- Recognize *el* + infinitive (*el fumar*); use *lo* + participle (*lo ocurrido, lo dicho*).
- Support verbs: *llevar a cabo un estudio, realizar un análisis, tomar una decisión*.
- Research writing uses *se* (*Se observó que…*) and hedges (*los datos sugieren, parece
  indicar*). A correlation is not a cause.
- *La prueba* also means evidence; *el patrón* is a pattern.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: El 40 % de los encuestados: data, trends and the formal e-mail
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Numbers turn an opinion into an argument. In this lesson you learn to describe data in Spanish:
percentages and fractions, rising and falling trends, comparisons between groups or years. Then
you put the data to work in a formal e-mail that passes on information and gives an opinion.

Both skills are tested in the DELE B2 writing paper. The official guide (2014) describes a first
task in which you write a letter or e-mail based on a short recording, passing on its content and
giving your view, and a second task with two options, one of which is commenting on a graph or
table. Lesson 18 gave you the formal nominal style; B1 lesson 20 gave you the formulas of a formal
letter and the idea of **[[register]]**, the level of formality you keep all the way through. The theme is society in numbers: surveys, the census
and how Mexican households are changing.

## Percentages and agreement

In Spanish a percentage normally takes an article: *el 40 %* for a precise figure, *un 40 %* for
an approximate or newly introduced one. Both are common in the press.

When a percentage is followed by *de* + a plural noun, the verb can be singular (agreeing with *el
40 %*) or plural (agreeing with *los encuestados*, the respondents). The *Diccionario panhispánico
de dudas* (DPD, 2005, entry *concordancia*, 4.8) accepts both and notes that the plural is
generally more frequent:

- *El 40 % de los encuestados opina que…* / *El 40 % de los encuestados opinan que…* — 40% of
  respondents think that…
- *La mayoría de los jóvenes vive / viven con sus padres.* — Most young people live with their
  parents.

There is one case where only the plural sounds normal: when the verb has an adjective or another
description of the subject, the DPD says the plural is the norm. *La mayoría de los encuestados
están satisfechos* (satisfied), *el 14 % de los jóvenes viven solos* (live alone).

*La minoría* works the same way. *La estadística* is both "statistics" (the science) and "a
statistic": *Según las estadísticas oficiales…* *La cifra* is a figure: *una cifra récord*.

## Fractions and "x out of y"

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| *la mitad (de)* | half |
| *un tercio, dos tercios* | a third, two thirds |
| *la cuarta parte, tres cuartas partes* | a quarter, three quarters |
| *tres de cada diez* | three out of ten |
| *uno de cada cinco* | one in five |

*Tres de cada diez mexicanos viven…* takes a plural verb (the subject is *tres*). *Uno de cada cinco
encuestados vive solo* takes a singular one. *La cuarta parte* is usual in formal writing; *un
cuarto* is also correct, and the everyday choice for "a quarter of an hour" (*un cuarto de hora*).

## Describing trends

| To go up | To go down | No change |
|---|---|---|
| *aumentar, subir, crecer* | *disminuir, bajar, descender* | *mantenerse estable* |
| *registrar un incremento / un aumento* | *registrar un descenso / una disminución* | *no variar* |
| *duplicarse* (×2), *triplicarse* (×3) | *reducirse a la mitad* (to halve) | |

The prepositions do the work:

- *pasar de… a…*: *La cifra pasó del 7 % al 14 %.* — The figure went from 7% to 14%.
- *aumentar / disminuir en*: *El desempleo aumentó en dos puntos.* — Unemployment rose by two
  points.
- *alcanzar*: *El porcentaje alcanzó su punto más alto en 2020.* — It reached its peak in 2020.
- *hasta*: *subió hasta el 30 %* — it rose to 30%.

Be precise about points and percent. If a share goes from 20% to 25%, it rose *cinco puntos
porcentuales* (five percentage points), which is *un 25 %* more than before (5 is a quarter of 20).

*Incrementar* (to step up, to increase) is formal and usually takes an object: *El municipio
incrementó el presupuesto.* For something that increases by itself, use *aumentar* or
*incrementarse*: *Las ventas se incrementaron.* *Descender* changes its stem like *entender*
(*desciende, descendió*). *Disminuir* adds a *y* like *construir* (*disminuye, disminuyó*).
*Duplicarse* and *triplicarse* are used mostly in the third person: *La población se triplicó.*

## Comparing and approximating

- *frente a*: *el 41 % en 2026 frente al 52 % en 2016* — 41% in 2026 against 52% in 2016
- *en comparación con*: *Hay menos hogares grandes en comparación con el año 2000.*
- *respecto a* (also *con respecto a*): *un aumento notable respecto al censo anterior* — a
  considerable rise compared to the previous census
- *mientras que*: *Los hombres votaron más, mientras que las mujeres…* — whereas

To soften a number: *casi* (almost), *cerca de* (nearly), *alrededor de* (around), *poco más de*
(just over), *aproximadamente*.

## Writing numbers

The DPD (entry *números*, provisional 2nd edition) recommends grouping digits in threes with a
space and not with a point or comma (*126 014 024*), with no space in four-digit numbers (*2020,
1200*), and accepts both the comma and the point for decimals, according to each country's
preference. Mexico uses the point for decimals (*3.6 ocupantes*), and everyday Mexican writing
usually groups thousands with commas (*126,014,024*), though INEGI's own reports use spaces.
Spain uses the decimal comma (*3,6*). In Spanish text, the RAE's *Ortografía* (2010) leaves a space
before the sign: *el 40 %*.

## Mexico in numbers: the census

INEGI (Mexico's national statistics institute) carries out a census (*un censo*) every ten
years. The 2020 census counted 126 014 024 inhabitants, 51.2% of them women. Two trends stand out:

![A line chart titled Edad mediana de la población de México with the years 2000, 2010 and 2020 on the horizontal axis and age in years from 0 to 35 on the vertical axis. The line rises from 22 in 2000 to 26 in 2010 and 29 in 2020. Source: INEGI, Censo de Población y Vivienda 2020.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- Aging (*el envejecimiento*): the median age rose from 22 in 2000 to 29 in 2020, and 12.0%
  of the population was 60 or older.
- Smaller households: the average number of occupants per home fell from 4.4 in 2000 to 3.9
  in 2010 and 3.6 in 2020.

Behind both lie a lower birth rate (*la tasa de natalidad*) and a lower death rate (*la tasa de
mortalidad*). *La tasa* is a rate here; it also means a fee (lesson 24).

## Model 1: a survey report

The survey and its figures are invented for this lesson.

![A grouped bar chart titled ¿Con quién viven los jóvenes de 18 a 34 años? Encuesta Vivir en San Andrés, 2016 y 2026 (datos ficticios). Five categories, with 2016 and 2026 bars: con sus padres 52 % and 41 %; en pareja, con o sin hijos 24 % and 27 %; solos 7 % and 14 %; con amigos o compañeros 11 % and 12 %; otra situación 6 % and 6 %.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Vivir en San Andrés 2026: con quién viven los jóvenes
>
> La encuesta, realizada en mayo de 2026 a 1200 personas de entre 18 y 34 años, muestra cambios
> notables respecto a 2016. Aunque la opción más frecuente sigue siendo vivir con los padres, el
> porcentaje de los que lo hacen descendió del 52 % al 41 %, es decir, once puntos porcentuales.
> En cambio, la proporción de jóvenes que viven solos se duplicó: pasó del 7 % al 14 %. Vivir en
> pareja registró un ligero incremento (del 24 % al 27 %), mientras que compartir vivienda con
> amigos se mantuvo prácticamente estable. En conjunto, las cifras apuntan a una tendencia clara:
> los jóvenes se independizan más, pero en hogares más pequeños, lo cual coincide con el descenso
> del número de ocupantes por vivienda que registra el censo.

> Living in San Andrés 2026: who young people live with
>
> The survey, carried out in May 2026 among 1,200 people aged 18 to 34, shows considerable changes
> compared to 2016. Although the most common option is still living with one's parents, the
> percentage of those who do so fell from 52% to 41%, that is, eleven percentage points. By
> contrast, the share of young people who live alone doubled: it went from 7% to 14%. Living with
> a partner showed a slight increase (from 24% to 27%), while sharing a home with friends remained
> practically stable. Taken together, the figures point to a clear trend: young people are moving
> out more, but into smaller households, which matches the drop in the number of occupants per
> home recorded by the census.

The report opens with who was asked, when and how many; it describes the biggest changes first;
it uses *es decir* to translate a figure into points; and it ends with an interpretation linked
to another source.

## Model 2: a formal e-mail

Mariana heard the survey discussed on local radio and writes to the municipal housing office,
passing on the data and giving her opinion.

![A formal e-mail divided into seven numbered blocks, top to bottom, each with a label on the left: el asunto (Datos de la encuesta Vivir en San Andrés y una propuesta); el saludo (Estimada licenciada Herrera:); el motivo (Me dirijo a usted para hacerle llegar…); los datos (Según la encuesta…); la opinión (Desde mi punto de vista…); la petición (Le agradecería que…); la despedida y la firma (Quedo a su disposición… Atentamente, Mariana Solís Treviño).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Asunto: Datos de la encuesta *Vivir en San Andrés* y una propuesta
>
> Estimada licenciada Herrera:
>
> Me dirijo a usted como vecina del municipio para hacerle llegar algunos datos que escuché ayer
> en la radio municipal y que pueden interesar a la Dirección de Vivienda.
>
> Según la encuesta *Vivir en San Andrés 2026*, el 14 % de los jóvenes de 18 a 34 años viven solos,
> el doble que hace diez años, mientras que el porcentaje de los que viven con sus padres descendió
> del 52 % al 41 %. Dicho de otro modo, cada vez más jóvenes buscan una vivienda pequeña.
>
> Desde mi punto de vista, estas cifras muestran que la oferta actual no responde a la demanda:
> casi todas las viviendas nuevas del municipio tienen tres recámaras. Por ello, le agradecería que
> la Dirección estudiara la posibilidad de incluir departamentos de una recámara en sus próximos
> proyectos.
>
> Quedo a su disposición para cualquier aclaración.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Mariana Solís Treviño

> Subject: Data from the *Living in San Andrés* survey and a proposal
>
> Dear Ms. Herrera,
>
> I am writing to you as a resident of the municipality to pass on some figures I heard yesterday
> on the municipal radio station, which may be of interest to the Housing Department.
>
> According to the *Living in San Andrés 2026* survey, 14% of young people aged 18 to 34 live alone,
> twice as many as ten years ago, while the percentage of those who live with their parents fell
> from 52% to 41%. In other words, more and more young people are looking for a small home.
>
> In my view, these figures show that the current supply does not meet demand: almost all new homes
> in the municipality have three bedrooms. I would therefore be grateful if the Department would
> consider including one-bedroom apartments in its upcoming projects.
>
> I remain available for any clarification.
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Mariana Solís Treviño

*Licenciada* is the usual title in Mexico for a woman with a bachelor's degree (A1); *la
recámara* is the everyday Mexican word for a bedroom; *hacerle llegar* = to pass on to you; *por
ello* = therefore (formal, like *por eso*). After *le agradecería que* (conditional) comes the
imperfect subjunctive, *estudiara*, the safest choice in a formal letter (B1 lesson 20).

## Pronunciation

- *Porcentaje*: four syllables, *por-cen-ta-je*; *Estadística*: five, *es-ta-dís-ti-ca*.
- *Envejecimiento*: six syllables, *en-ve-je-ci-mien-to*; the *ie* is one syllable.
- *Disminuir*: three, *dis-mi-nuir*; *disminuye*: four, *dis-mi-nu-ye*.
- Read *el 40 %* as *el cuarenta por ciento*, and *3.6* as *tres punto seis* in Mexico (*tres coma
  seis* in Spain).

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out the article: *40 % de los encuestados* sounds like a headline. In a sentence,
  write *el 40 %* or *un 40 %*.
- Mixing up points and percent: from 20% to 25% is five points, not "5% more".
- *Incrementó* with no object: *Las ventas incrementaron* is heard, but in careful writing
  prefer *las ventas aumentaron* or *se incrementaron*.
- A singular verb with an adjective: write *la mayoría de los encuestados están satisfechos*,
  not *está satisfecha*.
- Comma for thousands in a Spain-facing text: in Spain *1,5* means one and a half. When writing
  for an international reader, a space (*10 000*) avoids the confusion.

## Key points

- *El / un 40 % de los encuestados* + singular or plural verb; plural when an adjective follows.
- Fractions: *un tercio, la cuarta parte, tres de cada diez*.
- Trends: *aumentar / disminuir en, pasar de… a…, duplicarse, mantenerse estable, registrar un
  descenso*. Points are not percent.
- Compare with *frente a, en comparación con, respecto a, mientras que*.
- A formal e-mail: subject, greeting with a colon, purpose, data, opinion, request, closing.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Yo propondría que…: debating and proposing solutions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last three lessons gave you tools for precise argument: discourse markers (17), the formal
nominal style (18) and the language of data (19). This lesson puts them into a live debate,
where you have to agree with part of what someone says, refute the rest, and propose something
better. B1's honors lesson on discussions taught you to take the floor and disagree politely;
here the focus is on proposals: making them, weighing them and reaching a compromise.

The theme is public problems and their solutions: water supply, public transportation and
awareness campaigns, the kind of everyday issue a neighborhood assembly argues about. It's also
the skill behind the first task of the DELE B2 speaking test, described at the end.

## Agreeing and disagreeing, with nuance

*Estar de acuerdo* is followed by different things depending on what you agree with:

- With a person or an idea: *Estoy de acuerdo contigo. Estoy de acuerdo con la propuesta.*
- With a fact you accept as true, the indicative, usually with *en que*: *Estoy de acuerdo en
  que el agua es el problema principal.* — I agree that water is the main problem.
- With a proposal (something someone should do), the subjunctive, often with *con que*: *Estoy
  de acuerdo con que se cobre más a quien más consume.* — I agree with charging more to whoever
  uses most.
- In the negative, the subjunctive is usual: *No estoy de acuerdo en que el problema sea tan
  grave. No estoy de acuerdo con que gastemos todo en pipas.*

Speakers use both *en que* and *con que* in both meanings, so the meaning, not the preposition,
chooses the mood: a fact you accept takes the indicative; a proposal, or a claim you reject,
takes the subjunctive. In careful writing, keep the preposition (*de acuerdo en que*, not *de
acuerdo que*).

*Tener razón en que* + indicative concedes a point before you turn it: *Tienes razón en que las
fugas son un problema, pero repararlas tarda años.* — You're right that the leaks are a problem,
but fixing them takes years.

## Conceding and refuting

A good refutation first gives the other side its due, then answers it. To concede: *Es cierto
que* (it's true that), *Reconozco que* (I admit that), *Admito que*, all + indicative. Then turn
with *sin embargo, pero, aun así*. To refute (*refutar*) or rebut (*rebatir*) the point:

- *Eso no quiere decir que* + subjunctive: *Es cierto que la campaña costó poco; eso no quiere
  decir que haya funcionado.* — That doesn't mean it worked.
- *No es que* + subjunctive, *es que* + indicative (lesson 05): *No es que las pipas sean malas, es
  que no resuelven nada.* — It's not that the water trucks are bad; it's that they don't solve
  anything.
- *El problema es que…, Lo que no se dice es que…*: then your counterargument (*el
  contraargumento*), ideally with a fact or a figure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Four moves to refute an argument
  accDescr: Four boxes in a column. First, sum up the other argument fairly: Si entiendo bien, usted propone que... Second, concede what is reasonable: Es cierto que... Third, rebut with a counterargument and a fact: Sin embargo, eso no quiere decir que... Fourth, propose an alternative: Yo propondría que...
  A["1. Resume el argumento: Si entiendo bien, usted propone que…"] --> B["2. Concede lo razonable: Es cierto que…"]
  B --> C["3. Rebate con un contraargumento: Sin embargo, eso no quiere decir que…"]
  C --> D["4. Propón una alternativa: Yo propondría que…"]
```

## Proposing

A proposal in Spanish is often softened with the conditional, and a conditional in the main
clause is usually followed by the imperfect subjunctive (the **[[sequence of tenses]]**, lesson 03):

- *Yo propondría que el municipio invirtiera en reparar la red.* — I'd suggest that the
  municipality invest in repairing the network.
- *Sería conveniente que / Convendría que* + imperfect subjunctive: *Sería conveniente que la
  campaña empezara antes del verano.*
- *Lo ideal sería que* + imperfect subjunctive: *Lo ideal sería que cada escuela tuviera su propio
  sistema de captación de lluvia* (rainwater harvesting).
- *Habría que* + infinitive (one ought to, we'd need to): *Habría que medir el consumo de cada
  calle.*
- *¿Y si…?* + imperfect subjunctive (what if we…?): *¿Y si pidiéramos una reunión con el
  municipio?*
- More direct, with the present: *Propongo que* + present subjunctive: *Propongo que votemos hoy.*

You'll also hear *Yo propondría que el municipio invierta*, with the present subjunctive after the
conditional; it's common in Latin America, and not wrong, but the imperfect is the safe choice in
formal speech and writing.

To present a problem or an approach, use *plantear*: *Quiero plantear un problema* (I want to raise
an issue); the noun is *el planteamiento* (approach, proposal): *Su planteamiento es interesante,
pero…*

## Weighing proposals

| Question | Useful words |
|---|---|
| Can it be done? | *viable* (viable), *factible* (feasible), *realista* |
| Does it work? | *eficaz* (effective; plural *eficaces*), *la eficacia* |
| When does it pay off? | *a corto plazo* (in the short term), *a largo plazo* (in the long term) |
| What's against it? | *el inconveniente* (drawback), *los pros y los contras* |
| Who pays? | *el subsidio* (subsidy), *la subvención* (a grant), *el presupuesto* (B1) |

*Eficaz* means that something achieves its effect; B1's *eficiente* means it does so without waste.
A campaign can be *eficaz* (people save water) without being *eficiente* (it cost a fortune).
*El inconveniente* is a close synonym of B1's *la desventaja*: *El principal inconveniente es el
costo.* (*El costo* is the usual word in Mexico; Spain usually says *el coste*.)

A *subsidio* usually lowers a price for users (*el subsidio al transporte público*); a *subvención*
is money a government grants to an organization or project. In practice, Mexican usage often says
*subsidio* for both.

Comparing proposals uses the superlative: *la propuesta más viable, la menos costosa, la más eficaz
de todas*.

## Dialogue: the neighborhood assembly

In the Las Palmas neighborhood, water arrives only three days a week. The neighbors' association
has a card with five proposals.

![A card headed Colonia Las Palmas: el agua solo llega tres días por semana. ¿Qué proponen? with five numbered proposals, each with a small icon. 1. Reparar las fugas de la red (a wrench on a pipe). 2. Más pipas en los días sin servicio (a water truck). 3. Captación de lluvia con subsidio municipal (a roof gutter filling a tank). 4. Campaña para concientizar sobre el ahorro (a megaphone). 5. Tarifa más alta para quien más consume (a water meter).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

> Presidenta: Bueno, vecinos, tenemos cinco propuestas. ¿Cuál les parece la más viable?
>
> Lucía: Yo propondría que el municipio invirtiera primero en reparar las fugas. Es lo más eficaz a
> largo plazo: no sirve de nada traer más agua si la mitad se pierde en el camino.
>
> Ernesto: Tienes razón en que las fugas son un problema, pero repararlas tarda años. Mientras
> tanto, la gente necesita agua. Habría que pedir más pipas ya.
>
> Lucía: No estoy de acuerdo con que gastemos el presupuesto en pipas. Es una solución a corto
> plazo y, encima, cara.
>
> Ramiro: A ver, no es que las pipas sean malas, es que no resuelven nada. Yo apoyo la captación de
> lluvia. Es factible: la escuela ya la tiene y funciona.
>
> Ernesto: Es cierto que funciona en la escuela; sin embargo, en una casa pequeña no hay espacio
> para un tanque grande.
>
> Ramiro: Eso no quiere decir que no se pueda hacer. Muchas casas ya tienen tinaco.
>
> Presidenta: ¿Y la campaña para concientizar?
>
> Lucía: Sería conveniente que acompañara a las otras medidas, pero sola no basta.
>
> Presidenta: Entonces, ¿qué les parece esto? A corto plazo, pipas los días sin servicio; a largo
> plazo, reparar la red. Y lo ideal sería que el municipio subsidiara la captación de lluvia.
>
> Ernesto: Me parece razonable, siempre y cuando el plan tenga fechas.
>
> Ramiro: De acuerdo. Que quede en el acta.

> President: Well, neighbors, we have five proposals. Which one seems most viable to you?
>
> Lucía: I'd propose that the municipality invest first in repairing the leaks. It's the most
> effective thing in the long term: there's no point bringing in more water if half of it is lost
> on the way.
>
> Ernesto: You're right that the leaks are a problem, but fixing them takes years. Meanwhile,
> people need water. We'd need to ask for more water trucks now.
>
> Lucía: I don't agree with spending the budget on water trucks. It's a short-term solution and,
> on top of that, an expensive one.
>
> Ramiro: Look, it's not that the trucks are bad; it's that they don't solve anything. I support
> rainwater harvesting. It's feasible: the school already has it and it works.
>
> Ernesto: It's true that it works at the school; however, in a small house there's no room for a
> big tank.
>
> Ramiro: That doesn't mean it can't be done. Lots of houses already have a rooftop tank.
>
> President: And the awareness campaign?
>
> Lucía: It would be a good idea for it to go along with the other measures, but on its own it's
> not enough.
>
> President: So, what do you think of this? In the short term, water trucks on the days without
> service; in the long term, repairing the network. And ideally the municipality would subsidize
> rainwater harvesting.
>
> Ernesto: That seems reasonable to me, as long as the plan has dates.
>
> Ramiro: Agreed. Let it go in the minutes.

In Mexico, *la pipa* is the usual word for a water truck and *el tinaco* for the water tank on a
rooftop; *la fuga* (A2) is the leak, and *la red* the network of pipes. *Razonable*
(reasonable) is lesson 05's word, *siempre y cuando* (as long as) lesson 12's, and *el acta* (the
minutes; feminine, with *el* like *el agua*) is new. Notice how the president ends the debate: she
sums up and combines proposals into a compromise.

## Another problem: getting around the city

The same tools work for any public issue, such as public transportation (*el transporte
público*) and mobility (*la movilidad*, how people get around):

- *Lo ideal sería que hubiera un carril exclusivo para el camión.* — Ideally there'd be a dedicated
  lane for the bus.
- *Habría que implementar el pago con tarjeta en todas las rutas.* (*implementar* = to implement;
  *la implementación*)
- *La iniciativa de la ciclovía es interesante, pero el principal inconveniente es la
  infraestructura: faltan estacionamientos para bicicletas.*
- And back to water: *Más que una campaña de concientización, propongo que se mejore el
  abastecimiento de agua en toda la ciudad.* (*el abastecimiento* = supply)

*Concientizar* (to raise awareness) and *la concientización* are the usual forms in Mexico and
much of Latin America; Spain says *concienciar* and *la concienciación*.

## The DELE B2 speaking task 1, in general terms

According to the official guide (2014), the first speaking task is prepared in advance: you choose
one of two topics, each presenting a problem and a set of proposals to solve it. You then talk
about the proposals, saying which seem best and why, with their pros and cons, and discuss them
with the examiner, who may challenge your choice. The guide gives six to seven minutes for
it; check the current guide on the Instituto Cervantes site before your exam, since details can
change. Everything in this lesson applies: evaluate (*la más viable a corto plazo*), concede
(*Es cierto que…*), refute (*Eso no quiere decir que…*) and propose (*Yo propondría que…*).

## Pronunciation

- *Infraestructura*: six syllables, *in-fra-es-truc-tu-ra*: *a* and *e* are said separately.
- *Contraargumento*: six syllables, *con-tra-ar-gu-men-to*, with both *a*'s heard, though they
  often merge in fast speech.
- *Eficaz*: three syllables, stress on the last; *eficaces*: four, *e-fi-ca-ces*.
- *Abastecimiento*: six syllables, *a-bas-te-ci-mien-to*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*Habría que pidamos más pipas*~~ → *Habría que pedir más pipas.* *Habría que* takes an
  infinitive.
- Using *eficaz* and *eficiente* as if they were the same: effect vs. economy of means.
- Repeating the noun: *Es la propuesta más factible de todas las propuestas que hay* is clumsy;
  *Es la más factible de todas* is enough.
- Attacking the person (*Usted no sabe nada*) instead of the argument (*Ese argumento no
  considera el costo*).

## Key points

- *Estar de acuerdo en / con que* + indicative for an accepted fact, + subjunctive for a
  proposal; subjunctive in the negative.
- Concede (*Es cierto que, Tienes razón en que* + indicative), then refute (*Eso no quiere decir
  que, No es que…, es que…*).
- Propose with *Yo propondría que, Sería conveniente que, Lo ideal sería que* + imperfect
  subjunctive, or *Habría que* + infinitive.
- Weigh proposals: *viable, factible, eficaz, a corto / largo plazo, el principal inconveniente*.
- End a debate with a compromise that combines the best proposals.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Escribir en la universidad: summarizing, quoting and paraphrasing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 18 showed you how research is written; this lesson shows you how to write *about* other
people's research, the core skill of any university paper in Spanish. You'll summarize a source,
put it in your own words without copying it (*el plagio*, plagiarism, is lesson 02's word), quote
it correctly with a **[[reporting verb]]**, and give references in one consistent style. Lesson 13's
reported speech and lesson 18's nominal style are the grammar behind all of it.

We'll work with one short source, invented for this lesson, and three students' attempts to use
it.

## The source

> Durante buena parte del siglo XX, las ciudades latinoamericanas se diseñaron para el automóvil.
> Las avenidas se ensancharon, las banquetas se redujeron y el peatón pasó a ser un obstáculo para
> el tráfico. Sin embargo, en las últimas dos décadas varias ciudades han comenzado a revertir esta
> tendencia. La peatonalización de calles céntricas, lejos de arruinar el comercio, suele atraer a
> más visitantes, aunque también puede elevar las rentas de los locales y expulsar a los negocios
> tradicionales. Por ello, una política de movilidad que solo piense en el peatón corre el riesgo
> de olvidar a quienes viven y trabajan en esas calles. La ciudad caminable no es únicamente una
> cuestión de diseño urbano, sino también de justicia social.
>
> — Lucía Ferrer, *Ciudades que caminan* (Editorial Ejemplo, 2019), p. 45. (Author and book
> invented.)

> For much of the twentieth century, Latin American cities were designed for the car. Avenues
> were widened, sidewalks were narrowed and the pedestrian became an obstacle to traffic. However,
> in the last two decades several cities have begun to reverse this trend. Pedestrianizing
> downtown streets, far from ruining business, tends to attract more visitors, although it can
> also raise the rents of commercial premises and push out traditional businesses. For that
> reason, a mobility policy that thinks only of the pedestrian runs the risk of forgetting those
> who live and work on those streets. The walkable city is not only a matter of urban design, but
> also of social justice.

*Ensancharse* = to be widened; *la peatonalización* = pedestrianization; *revertir* = to reverse;
*el local* = commercial premises, a store space; *expulsar* = to push out; *correr el riesgo de*
= to run the risk of.

## Summarizing

*Un resumen* (A2) keeps the main idea and the line of argument and drops examples and details. A
reliable method:

1. Find the thesis (*la tesis*, the central claim, lesson 02's word): here, the last sentence.
2. Mark the steps that lead to it: cities were built for cars → some are changing → but
   pedestrianizing has a social cost → so it's also a question of justice.
3. Close the source and write the summary from your notes, in your own sentences.
4. Check it against the source: same meaning, nothing added, nothing distorted.

A summary is usually about a quarter or a third of the original's length. In a report for decision
makers, the opening summary is *el resumen ejecutivo* (executive summary): one page or less that
states the problem, the findings and the recommendation, so that a busy reader can stop there.

## Paraphrasing

To paraphrase (*parafrasear*) is to restate one idea in your own words and structure; the result
is *una paráfrasis* (plural *las paráfrasis*). A real paraphrase changes more than words:

- Structure: turn nouns into verbs or the reverse (lesson 18): *la peatonalización de calles
  céntricas* → *cuando se cierran al tráfico las calles del centro*.
- Order: start with a different element: *Atraer visitantes no garantiza que…*
- Voice: active ↔ passive or *se* (lesson 14): *las ciudades se diseñaron* → *los urbanistas
  diseñaron las ciudades*.
- Words: synonyms only where they are exact (*el sinónimo*, synonym, is lesson 23's word); a
  technical term like *peatonalización* can stay.

A paraphrase still needs a reference: the idea isn't yours, even if the words are.

## Quoting

Use a direct quotation (*una cita textual*) when the exact wording matters: a definition, a
striking phrase, a claim you are about to dispute. Keep it short and introduce it with a reporting
verb, which also tells the reader how the author makes the claim:

| Verb | Nuance | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *afirma* | states | *Ferrer afirma que la ciudad caminable es una cuestión de justicia.* |
| *señala* | points out | *Señala que las rentas pueden subir.* |
| *sostiene* | maintains, argues (lesson 13) | *Sostiene que…* |
| *advierte* | warns | *Advierte que una política así corre el riesgo de…* |
| *plantea* | raises (lesson 20) | *Plantea una pregunta incómoda.* |
| *reconoce* | acknowledges | *Reconoce que el comercio no se arruina.* |
| *propone* | proposes + subjunctive | *Propone que se piense también en los vecinos.* |

These verbs report a statement, so they take the indicative; *propone que* and *sugiere que* (in
the sense of recommending) take the subjunctive because they report an influence. *Según Ferrer
(2019)…* and *De acuerdo con Ferrer…* need no *que*. The person you quote is *el autor citado*
(*la autora citada*).

A short quotation goes inside your sentence, in quotation marks: *Para Ferrer, la ciudad caminable
"no es únicamente una cuestión de diseño urbano, sino también de justicia social" (2019, p. 45).*
The RAE recommends angle quotes (« ») as the first choice in printed texts, but in Mexico double
quotes (" ") are far more common in print and online; either is fine if you use one
consistently. A long quotation (APA style, for instance, sets the limit at 40 words) goes in a
separate indented block, without quotation marks.

## References in one consistent style

Every source you use, quoted or paraphrased, gets a reference (*una referencia*) in the text and
a full entry in the list at the end: *la bibliografía* (bibliography; some styles call the list
*Referencias* and include only the works cited). Styles differ, and your school or journal will
tell you which to use. Two common ones, as examples:

- APA (7th edition, 2019), widely used in the social sciences: author and year in the
  text, *(Ferrer, 2019, p. 45)*, and in the list *Ferrer, L. (2019). Ciudades que caminan.
  Editorial Ejemplo.*
- Chicago, common in history and the humanities: a footnote (*una nota al pie*, plural *las
  notas al pie*) with the full reference the first time, and a short form after that.

The rule that matters more than any style: pick one and use it everywhere. A paper whose references
switch styles looks careless even when every source is right.

A long paper also opens with *el índice* (table of contents; at the back of a book, *el índice* is
also the index) and ends with *el párrafo de cierre* (closing paragraph), which sums up and looks
ahead without adding new sources.

![Three pages of a student paper side by side, with five parts numbered. Page 1 shows a list of chapters with page numbers: el índice. Page 2 shows a paragraph with a sentence in quotation marks followed by a small raised number, the quotation labeled la cita textual; at the bottom of the page, below a short line, the matching numbered note labeled la nota al pie. The last paragraph of the page is labeled el párrafo de cierre. Page 3, headed Bibliografía, lists three entries in alphabetical order: la bibliografía.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Academic voice: *nosotros* and *se*

Spanish academic prose rarely says *yo*. Writers use either the "plural of modesty" (*plural de
modestia*: one author writing *nosotros*) or the impersonal and passive *se*:

- *En este trabajo analizamos tres casos.* — In this paper we analyze three cases.
- *En este trabajo se analizan tres casos.* — Three cases are analyzed in this paper.

Both are correct; some fields and journals prefer one. Don't mix them in the same paper, and don't
switch to *yo* in the conclusion.

## Three attempts

Three students summarize Ferrer's paragraph for a paper on mobility.

### Example 1: plagiarized

> Durante gran parte del siglo XX, las ciudades de América Latina se diseñaron para el carro. Las
> avenidas se hicieron más anchas y las banquetas más pequeñas. Pero en las últimas dos décadas
> algunas ciudades han empezado a revertir esta tendencia.

> For much of the twentieth century, the cities of Latin America were designed for the car. Avenues
> were made wider and sidewalks smaller. But in the last two decades some cities have started to
> reverse this trend.

This is the source with a few words swapped (*gran parte* for *buena parte*, *empezado* for
*comenzado*), the same sentences in the same order, and no reference. Changing words doesn't make
it yours: it's plagiarism.

### Example 2: weak

> Ferrer dice que "las avenidas se ensancharon, las banquetas se redujeron y el peatón pasó a ser
> un obstáculo para el tráfico". También dice que "la peatonalización de calles céntricas, lejos de
> arruinar el comercio, suele atraer a más visitantes" (2019).

> Ferrer says that "avenues were widened, sidewalks were narrowed and the pedestrian became an
> obstacle to traffic." She also says that "pedestrianizing downtown streets, far from ruining
> business, tends to attract more visitors" (2019).

Nothing is stolen, but nothing is done either: two long quotations strung together with *dice*,
no page number, and the main point (social justice) missing. The reader learns what Ferrer wrote,
not what the student understood.

### Example 3: good

> Ferrer (2019) sostiene que varias ciudades latinoamericanas, construidas durante el siglo XX en
> función del automóvil, empiezan a recuperar sus calles para los peatones. Reconoce que cerrar el
> centro al tráfico suele atraer visitantes, pero advierte que también puede encarecer los locales y
> desplazar a los negocios de siempre. De ahí su conclusión: la ciudad caminable es "también [una
> cuestión] de justicia social" (p. 45).

> Ferrer (2019) argues that several Latin American cities, built during the twentieth century around
> the car, are beginning to reclaim their streets for pedestrians. She acknowledges that closing the
> center to traffic tends to attract visitors, but warns that it can also make commercial premises more
> expensive and push out long-standing businesses. Hence her conclusion: the walkable city is
> "also [a matter] of social justice" (p. 45).

The structure is the student's own; three reporting verbs show how Ferrer argues (*sostiene,
reconoce, advierte*); the thesis and the source's hedges (*varias, suele*) are kept; and the quotation is short, exact and referenced.
Square brackets mark words the student added to make the quotation fit. *Encarecer* = to make more
expensive; *desplazar* = to displace; *de siempre* = long-standing.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that synonyms make a paraphrase. Change the structure, and cite anyway.
- Quoting instead of thinking: a paper that is half quotations shows no understanding.
- Using *dice* for every source. Choose the verb that matches what the author does: states, warns,
  acknowledges, proposes.
- ~~*Propone que se piensa en los vecinos*~~ → *Propone que se piense…*: a proposal reports an
  influence and takes the subjunctive.
- Mixing styles: a footnote reference on one page and *(Ferrer, 2019)* on the next.
- Writing *yo* in one paragraph and *nosotros* in the next.

## Key points

- Summarize from your notes, not from the page; keep the thesis and the line of argument.
- *Parafrasear* means new structure and words, with the meaning intact and a reference.
- Quote briefly, with a reporting verb that shows the author's stance; indicative after *afirma,
  señala, sostiene, advierte*; subjunctive after *propone que*.
- One reference style throughout (APA, Chicago or whatever your institution asks for); a
  bibliography at the end, footnotes if the style uses them.
- Academic voice: the plural of modesty (*analizamos*) or impersonal *se* (*se analizan*), not
  both.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Conferencias y discursos: listening to and giving a talk
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A lecture is the longest stretch of Spanish you'll have to follow without being able to ask
"sorry?": in a class, at a conference, in a podcast, and in the last task of the DELE B2
listening test. The good news is that speakers who give talks signpost them: they announce the
plan, mark each step, and sum up at the end. Lesson 17's discourse markers are the small signals;
this lesson adds the large ones, shows you how to take notes while listening, and then turns the
tables: you'll see how to give a short talk and an acceptance speech yourself.

## The words of a talk

At a conference (*un congreso*; note that *una conferencia* is a single lecture, not the event),
each speaker (*el ponente*, *la ponente*; in much of Latin America also *el expositor*) gives a
talk (*una ponencia*) in an auditorium (*el auditorio*, which also means the audience), usually
with slides (*las diapositivas*). At the end comes the Q&A session (*el turno de preguntas*). To
present ideas is *exponer* (*expongo, expuse*; participle *expuesto*: *las ideas expuestas*). A
formal speech is *un discurso*, the person giving it *el orador* (*la oradora*), and the art of
public speaking *la oratoria*.

![A conference room seen from the back. On a stage, a woman stands behind a lectern with a microphone; behind her, a large screen shows a slide titled Pictogramas del Metro with a simple bar chart. In the foreground, rows of seats with an audience seen from behind; one person raises a hand.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(*El atril* = the lectern; *el micrófono* = the microphone.)

## How a talk is built

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The structure of a lecture
  accDescr: Six steps from top to bottom. Saludo y presentación (greeting and introducing yourself); anuncio del tema y del plan (announcing the topic and the plan); desarrollo: punto 1, punto 2, punto 3 (development in points); recapitulación (recap); conclusión (conclusion); turno de preguntas (Q&A session). A dotted side note on the development step says that digressions are opened and closed explicitly: abro un paréntesis, cierro el paréntesis.
  A["Saludo y presentación"] --> B["Anuncio del tema y del plan"]
  B --> C["Desarrollo: punto 1, punto 2, punto 3"]
  C --> D["Recapitulación"]
  D --> E["Conclusión"]
  E --> F["Turno de preguntas"]
  N["Digresión: abro un paréntesis… cierro el paréntesis"] -.- C
```

Each step has its own phrases. When you're listening, these are the moments to write a new
heading in your notes.

| Job | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Announce the topic | *Hoy voy a hablarles de… / El tema de mi ponencia es…* |
| Announce the plan | *Mi ponencia tiene tres partes. En primer lugar voy a…, después…, y por último…* |
| Move on | *Paso ahora a… / Vamos al segundo punto. / Esto nos lleva a…* |
| Go back | *Como decía… / Como ya mencioné… / Volviendo a lo de antes…* |
| Highlight | *Lo importante aquí es… / Quiero subrayar que…* |
| Digress | *Abro un paréntesis. / Por cierto…* (and *Cierro el paréntesis*) |
| Recap | *Recapitulando… / En resumen…* |
| Conclude | *Para concluir… / Para terminar…* |
| Open the Q&A | *Con esto termino. Quedo atento / atenta a sus preguntas.* |

In Mexico the preterite is usual for what the speaker said a few minutes ago (*como ya mencioné*);
a speaker from Spain would more often say *como ya he mencionado* (lesson 01).

## Taking notes while listening

You can't write everything, so write the skeleton: headings when you hear a signpost, key words
(nouns and numbers), and arrows for the links between ideas. Common abbreviations in Spanish notes:

| Note | Means |
|---|---|
| *q* | *que* |
| *xq* | *porque* |
| *tb* | *también* |
| *c/* , *s/* | *con, sin* |
| *ej.* | *por ejemplo* |
| *aprox.* | *aproximadamente* |
| *EE. UU.* | *Estados Unidos* |
| *s. XX* | *siglo XX* |
| → , ↑ , ↓ | leads to, rises, falls |

Dates in Spanish go day / month / year: *4/9/1969* is September 4, 1969, not April 9.

According to the official DELE B2 guide (2014), the last task of the listening test is a long
monologue, such as a lecture or a speech, which you hear twice, with questions on its main ideas
and details. The skills in this lesson (following the plan, separating the main point from a
digression, catching dates and figures) are exactly what it needs.

## Transcript: a talk at a design conference

The speaker is fictional; the facts about the Metro are real and sourced in this module's notes.

> Buenas tardes a todos y gracias a los organizadores del congreso por la invitación. Me llamo Elena
> Vázquez, soy diseñadora gráfica y hoy voy a hablarles de unos dibujos que muchos de ustedes ven
> todos los días sin mirarlos: los pictogramas del Metro de la Ciudad de México.
>
> Mi ponencia tiene tres partes. En primer lugar, voy a contar brevemente cómo nació el sistema de
> señales del Metro. Después, voy a explicar cómo funciona un pictograma. Y, por último, quiero
> plantear una pregunta: ¿qué nos dicen hoy esos dibujos sobre la ciudad?
>
> Empiezo por la historia. El Metro se inauguró el 4 de septiembre de 1969, con un primer tramo de la
> línea 1 entre Zaragoza y Chapultepec. Pero no bastaba con trenes y túneles: hacía falta que
> millones de personas, muchas de ellas recién llegadas a la capital, se orientaran bajo tierra. La
> señalización se le encargó a un equipo en el que destacaba el diseñador estadounidense Lance Wyman,
> que un año antes había trabajado en la imagen de los Juegos Olímpicos de 1968. Según se suele
> contar, el estilo olímpico, con sus líneas limpias y sus colores planos, pasó casi directamente al
> Metro.
>
> Paso ahora al segundo punto: cómo funciona un pictograma. Un pictograma es un dibujo muy simple que
> representa una idea. En el Metro, cada estación tiene el suyo, y casi siempre hace referencia al
> lugar: a su historia, a un edificio cercano o al significado de su nombre. El ejemplo más conocido
> es Chapultepec. El nombre, de origen náhuatl, se suele traducir como "cerro del chapulín", así que
> el pictograma es, sencillamente, un chapulín. Dicho de otro modo, el dibujo traduce el nombre.
>
> Abro un paréntesis. Se suele decir que los pictogramas se pensaron para las personas que no sabían
> leer. Es una idea muy extendida, y tiene parte de verdad: en 1969 una parte de la población no
> sabía leer, y los dibujos les permitían orientarse. Pero no eran solo para ellas: un dibujo se
> reconoce más rápido que un nombre, también para quien no conoce la ciudad. Cierro el paréntesis.
>
> Como decía, cada pictograma cuenta algo. Y a veces la estación cuenta más que el pictograma. En
> Pino Suárez, por ejemplo, durante las obras apareció un pequeño templo mexica dedicado a Ehécatl,
> el dios del viento, que hoy se puede ver dentro de la estación. Y en Talismán se exhibe uno de los
> mamuts encontrados durante la construcción. El Metro, al fin y al cabo, se construyó encima de
> varias ciudades anteriores.
>
> Vamos al tercer punto. Hoy la red tiene doce líneas y alrededor de 195 estaciones, y los
> pictogramas siguen ahí, aunque la ciudad ha cambiado muchísimo. Esto nos lleva a la pregunta que
> planteé al principio: ¿qué nos dicen esos dibujos sobre la ciudad? Yo diría que dos cosas. Primero,
> que una ciudad puede explicarse a sí misma con imágenes: quien viaja de Chapultepec a Pino Suárez
> recorre, sin saberlo, cinco siglos de historia. Y segundo, que un buen diseño puede durar: medio
> siglo después, ese lenguaje visual sigue guiando a millones de personas.
>
> Recapitulando: el sistema nació con el Metro en 1969, con la huella del diseño olímpico; cada
> pictograma resume un lugar; y ese lenguaje visual sigue vivo más de cincuenta años después.
>
> Para concluir, les propongo un pequeño ejercicio. La próxima vez que tomen el Metro, miren el
> pictograma de su estación y pregúntense por qué es ese y no otro. Les aseguro que van a descubrir
> algo de su ciudad. Con esto termino. Muchas gracias, y quedo atenta a sus preguntas.

Summary: Elena Vázquez, a graphic designer, announces a talk in three parts on the pictograms
of the Mexico City Metro. First, history: the Metro opened on September 4, 1969, with a stretch of
Line 1 between Zaragoza and Chapultepec; millions of people, many of them new to the city, had to
find their way underground, and the signage was given to a team that included the US designer
Lance Wyman, who had worked on the 1968 Olympics, whose style is said to have passed to the Metro.
Second, how pictograms work: each station's drawing refers to the place, as Chapultepec's
grasshopper translates its Nahuatl name. In a digression, she qualifies the popular idea that the
pictograms were designed for people who couldn't read: partly true, but a drawing is recognized
faster than a name by everyone. Some stations tell even more: a small Mexica temple to the wind god Ehécatl at Pino
Suárez and a mammoth at Talismán. Third, with twelve lines and about 195 stations today, the
drawings show that a city can explain itself in images and that good design lasts. She recaps,
invites the audience to look at their own station's pictogram, and opens the Q&A.

*El tramo* = stretch, section; *orientarse* = to find one's way; *encargar* = to commission;
*destacar* = to stand out; *el chapulín* = grasshopper (Mexico); *la huella* = mark, trace;
*las obras* = construction works.

Notice the signposts: the plan (*En primer lugar… Después… Y, por último…*), the transitions
(*Paso ahora al segundo punto; Vamos al tercer punto; Esto nos lleva a…*), the digression opened
and closed, the recap and the conclusion. If you had only those sentences, you could still
reconstruct the talk.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: notes from the third paragraph

While listening to the history section, a good note-taker writes something like this:

- *Historia*
- *Metro inaug. 4/9/1969: L1 Zaragoza–Chapultepec*
- *problema: orientar a millones bajo tierra (muchos recién llegados)*
- *señalización → equipo c/ L. Wyman (diseñador EE. UU.)*
- *1 año antes: JJ. OO. 1968 → estilo (líneas limpias, colores planos) → Metro*

The heading comes from the signpost (*Empiezo por la historia*); the date and names are copied
exactly; arrows replace whole clauses; *JJ. OO.* is the usual abbreviation of *Juegos Olímpicos*.

### Example 2: from notes to a summary

From those notes, without looking at the transcript:

> *El Metro se inauguró en 1969 y necesitaba un sistema de señales que orientara a millones de
> usuarios. El diseñador Lance Wyman, que venía de trabajar en los Juegos Olímpicos de 1968,
> formó parte del equipo, y el estilo olímpico pasó al Metro.*

> The Metro opened in 1969 and needed a signage system that would guide millions of users. The
> designer Lance Wyman, who had just worked on the 1968 Olympics, was part of the team, and the
> Olympic style passed to the Metro.

Two sentences, the speaker's facts, your structure. Notice what was left out: the exact stations
of the first stretch, and the hedge *según se suele contar*, which a careful summary might keep.

### Example 3: opening your own talk

A talk of five minutes still needs a plan, said aloud:

> *Buenos días. Hoy quiero exponer una idea sencilla: que el transporte público también es
> cultura. Primero voy a presentar un caso, después voy a explicar qué lo hace especial y, por
> último, voy a proponer algo para nuestra ciudad.*

> Good morning. Today I want to present a simple idea: that public transportation is also culture.
> First I'll present a case, then I'll explain what makes it special and, finally, I'll propose
> something for our city.

Use few words per slide and don't read them aloud; the audience reads faster than you speak.

## A short acceptance speech

At the end of the conference, Elena's talk wins a prize.

> Muchas gracias. Es un honor recibir este premio, y más en un congreso con ponencias tan buenas.
> Quiero agradecerle al jurado su generosidad y a los organizadores su trabajo. No puedo terminar
> sin mencionar a quienes hicieron posible esta investigación: los trabajadores del Metro que me
> abrieron sus archivos y me contaron sus historias. Este premio también es suyo. Decía en mi
> ponencia que una ciudad puede explicarse con imágenes; hoy añadiría que también se explica con
> la gente que la hace funcionar todos los días. Dedico este reconocimiento a mi papá, que me llevó
> en Metro por primera vez. Muchas gracias.

> Thank you very much. It's an honor to receive this prize, especially at a conference with such
> good talks. I want to thank the jury for its generosity and the organizers for their work. I
> can't finish without mentioning those who made this research possible: the Metro workers who
> opened their archives to me and told me their stories. This prize is theirs too. I said in my
> talk that a city can explain itself through images; today I would add that it also explains
> itself through the people who make it work every day. I dedicate this award to my dad, who took
> me on the Metro for the first time. Thank you very much.

The shape of a good acceptance speech: thanks, a compliment to the others, the people behind the
work, one link back to the talk, a dedication, thanks again. Under a minute.

## Pronunciation

- *Ponencia*: three syllables, *po-nen-cia*. *Diapositiva*: five, *dia-po-si-ti-va*.
- *Auditorio*: four, *au-di-to-rio*. *Oratoria*: four, *o-ra-to-ria*.
- *Expuse* and *expuso* (not *exponí*): the stress falls on *pu*, as in *puse*.

## Common mistakes

- Calling the whole event *una conferencia*. A conference is *un congreso*; *una conferencia* is
  one lecture.
- ~~*Exponí mis ideas*~~ → *Expuse mis ideas.* *Exponer* is conjugated like *poner*.
- Writing down every word. Write headings, names, numbers and arrows.
- Reading the date *4/9* as April 9.
- Treating a digression as the main point: what comes between *abro un paréntesis* and *cierro el
  paréntesis* is rarely what the questions ask about.
- Reading your slides aloud instead of talking to the audience.

## Key points

- A talk has a predictable shape: greeting, plan, points, recap, conclusion, Q&A. Its signposts
  are your note headings.
- *Un congreso* is the event, *una ponencia* a talk at it, *el ponente* the speaker.
- Notes: headings, key words, numbers, arrows and abbreviations (*q, xq, tb, c/, s/*).
- *Exponer* goes like *poner*: *expongo, expuse, expuesto, expón*.
- An acceptance speech: thanks, the people behind the work, a dedication; under a minute.
