lessons.title: Abrelatas y portazos: word formation, diminutives and augmentatives
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Up to B1 you learned words one at a time. At B2 you meet thousands you have never studied, in
articles, ads and conversations, and many of them are built from parts you already know:
*des-* + *conectar*, *abre* + *latas*, *casa* + *-ita*. This lesson, the first of the course's
last module, shows the main building blocks of Spanish words: **[[prefixes]]** at the front,
**[[suffixes]]** at the end, **[[compound words]]** made of a verb and a noun, and the endings that make
things small or big, the **[[diminutive]]** and the **[[augmentative]]**. Taking a word apart lets you
guess what it means; putting parts together lets you describe an object whose name has slipped
your mind (*una cosa para abrir botellas*). The theme is the house: tools, gadgets and fixing
things yourself.

![A word-building tree. At the root, the verb hacer (to do, to make). One branch adds the prefix des- to give deshacer (to undo); another adds re- to give rehacer (to redo). A second root, the noun la lata (can), joins the verb form abre to give the compound el abrelatas (can opener). A third root, la cuchara (spoon), grows two branches: the diminutive la cucharita (teaspoon) and the augmentative el cucharón (ladle). A fourth, la puerta (door), gives el portazo (slam of a door) with the suffix -azo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Prefixes: changing the meaning from the front

A **[[prefix]]** is a piece added to the start of a word. It changes the meaning but usually not
the kind of word: *hacer* and *deshacer* are both verbs.

| Prefix | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *des-* | the opposite, undoing | *hacer → deshacer* (to undo), *conectar → desconectar* (to unplug), *armar → desarmar* (to take apart) |
| *in- / im- / i-* | not | *útil → inútil* (useless), *posible → imposible*, *legal → ilegal*, *regular → irregular* |
| *re-* | again | *hacer → rehacer* (to redo), *leer → releer*, *calentar → recalentar* (to reheat) |
| *pre-* | before | *ver → prever* (to foresee, lesson 04), *calentar → precalentar* (to preheat), *la venta → la preventa* (presale) |
| *anti-* | against | *el virus → el antivirus*, *adherente → antiadherente* (nonstick) |
| *sobre-* | over, too much | *cargar → sobrecargar* (to overload), *el peso → el sobrepeso* (excess weight) |
| *sub-* | under | *subterráneo* (underground), *subrayar* (to underline) |
| *co-* | together | *el autor → el coautor* (coauthor), *el fundador → el cofundador* (cofounder) |
| *auto-* | self | *la estima → la autoestima* (B1), *el retrato → el autorretrato* (A2) |
| *multi-* | many | *el uso → multiusos* (multipurpose: *una navaja multiusos*, a multipurpose pocketknife), *multinacional* |

The "not" prefix changes its spelling with the next sound: *im-* before *p* and *b*
(*imposible, imbatible*), *i-* before *l* and *r*, and the *r* is then doubled (*ilegal,
irregular, irresponsable*). The RAE's *Ortografía* (2010) writes a prefix joined to its word,
with no hyphen (*antivirus, cofundador*); it uses a hyphen before a capital letter or a number
(*anti-OTAN, sub-21*) and writes the prefix apart when it goes with a phrase of several words
(*ex primer ministro*).

A word that starts with these letters isn't always a prefix plus a word, though. *Recordar*
doesn't mean "to *cordar* again", and *desayunar* hides a nice surprise: it is *des-* +
*ayunar* (to fast), so breakfast is "un-fasting". Treat a prefix as a strong hint, then check
that the meaning fits the sentence.

One prefix explains a Mexican word in this lesson. *Desarmar* is to take apart, and *-dor*
names the tool that does it: *el desarmador* is the screwdriver in Mexico (Spain says *el
destornillador*, from *des-* + *el tornillo*: the "unscrewer").

## Suffixes: changing the kind of word

A **[[suffix]]** goes at the end, and it often changes the kind of word: *reparar* (to repair, a
verb) → *la reparación* (a noun) → *reparable* (an adjective).

| Suffix | Makes | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-ción* | nouns from verbs (feminine) | *instalar → la instalación*, *reparar → la reparación* |
| *-dad* | nouns from adjectives (feminine) | *útil → la utilidad*, *seguro → la seguridad* |
| *-ero, -era* | jobs; containers and holders | *el zapato → el zapatero* (shoemaker); *la sal → el salero* (saltshaker), *el café → la cafetera* (coffee maker), *la llave → el llavero* (key ring) |
| *-ería* | shops | *el zapato → la zapatería*, *la ferretería* (hardware store, from Latin *ferrum*, iron, the root of *el hierro*) |
| *-ble* | adjectives: "can be done" | *lavar → lavable* (washable), *recargar → recargable* (rechargeable), *desechar → desechable* (disposable) |
| *-oso* | adjectives: "full of" | *el ruido → ruidoso* (A2), *el peligro → peligroso* (A2), *el cariño → cariñoso* |
| *-ista* | attitudes and jobs (same form for both genders) | *optimista, el electricista* (A2), *la dentista* |
| *-ivo* | adjectives: "tending to" | *crear → creativo*, *el deporte → deportivo* |
| *-izar, -ificar* | verbs: "make it so" | *moderno → modernizar*, *simple → simplificar*, *la clase → clasificar* |
| *-ear* | verbs from nouns | *el golpe* (blow) → *golpear* (to hit), *el pedal → pedalear* |

There is one more pattern, with a prefix and an ending added at the same time to an adjective:
*gordo → engordar* (to gain weight, B1), *frío → enfriar* (to cool), *blando* (soft) →
*ablandar* (to soften), *largo → alargar* (to lengthen), *corto → acortar* (to shorten). There is no verb
~~*gordar*~~ and no adjective ~~*engordo*~~: the two pieces come together.

## Compound words: *el abrelatas*

The most useful Spanish **[[compound word]]** for objects joins a verb, in its *él* form, to a
plural noun: the thing that does that action to those things.

| Compound | Parts | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *el abrelatas* | *abre* (opens) + *latas* (cans) | can opener |
| *el sacacorchos* | *saca* (pulls out) + *corchos* (corks) | corkscrew |
| *el sacapuntas* | *saca* + *puntas* (points) | pencil sharpener |
| *el paraguas* | *para* (stops) + *aguas* | umbrella |
| *el parabrisas* | *para* + *brisas* (breezes) | windshield |
| *el rascacielos* | *rasca* (scratches) + *cielos* (skies) | skyscraper |
| *el portafolios* | *porta* (carries) + *folios* (sheets) | briefcase, portfolio |
| *el salvavidas* | *salva* (saves) + *vidas* (lives) | life jacket, lifebuoy; lifeguard |
| *el cortaúñas* | *corta* (cuts) + *uñas* (nails) | nail clippers |
| *el lavatrastes* | *lava* (washes) + *trastes* (dishes, Mexico) | kitchen sink (Mexico) |

Three rules hold for this pattern:

- As names of things they're masculine, even when the noun inside is feminine: *las latas*, but
  *el abrelatas*. One that names a person takes *la* for a woman: *la salvavidas* (lifeguard).
- The plural doesn't change: *un sacacorchos, dos sacacorchos*; *los rascacielos de Monterrey*.
- They're written as one word, with one stress, on the noun part: *a-bre-LA-tas*.

Not every tool has a compound name, of course. Here are the other Mexican words you'll need in
a toolbox, with Spain's where they differ: *el martillo* (hammer), *el clavo* (nail), *el
tornillo* (screw), *el taladro* (power drill), *la manguera* (hose), *el pegamento* (glue), *el
trapeador* (mop; from *trapear*, to mop; Spain *la fregona*), *la cubeta* (bucket; Spain *el
cubo*) and *el destapador* (bottle opener; from *destapar*, to uncap; Spain *el abrebotellas*,
another compound, or *el abridor*).

![A toolbox (la caja de herramientas) with a bucket (la cubeta) beside it, and in front of them, labeled in Spanish: el martillo (hammer), el desarmador (screwdriver), el taladro (power drill), el clavo (nail) and el tornillo (screw).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## *-azo*: a blow, or something sudden

Added to a noun, *-azo* names a blow with that thing, or a sudden, forceful act:

- *la puerta → el portazo*: the slam of a door. *Se fue dando un portazo* (She left, slamming
  the door). Notice that *puerta* becomes *port-*.
- *el freno* (brake) *→ el frenazo*: sudden braking. *El chofer dio un frenazo* (The driver braked suddenly).
- *el martillo → el martillazo*: a blow with a hammer. *el codo* (elbow) *→ el codazo*.
- *la flecha* (arrow) *→ el flechazo*: an arrow's hit, and, figuratively, love at first sight,
  as if Cupid's arrow had struck. *Fue un flechazo: nos casamos al año.*

In informal speech *-azo* also means "great, huge": *un golazo* (a great goal), *un exitazo* (a
huge hit).

## The diminutive: small, warm and polite

The **[[diminutive]]** ending makes a word smaller, but in everyday Spanish it does much more.

| Ending | Usually for | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *-ito, -ita* | words ending in *-o, -a* and most consonants | *la casa → la casita*, *el libro → el librito*, *el árbol → el arbolito* |
| *-cito, -cita* | words ending in *-n, -r*, and many in *-e* | *el camión → el camioncito*, *la mujer → la mujercita*, *el café → el cafecito* |
| *-ecito, -ecita* | many one-syllable words | *el pan → el panecito*, *la flor → la florecita* (Mexico also *el pancito*) |

The spelling keeps the sound: *poco → poquito*, *amigo → amiguito*, *taza → tacita*.

What the diminutive does:

- Size: *una casita* is a small house; *la cucharita* is a teaspoon.
- Affection: *mi abuelita, mi hijito*.
- Politeness and softening: *¿Me da un vasito de agua? Espéreme un momentito. ¿Un cafecito?*
  A small request sounds less demanding.
- Intensity, on adverbs and adjectives: *cerquita* (really close), *rapidito* (nice and quick),
  *calientito* (nice and warm), *tempranito* (nice and early).

The diminutive is used all over the Spanish-speaking world, but visitors often notice how much
it is used in Mexico, especially in requests and on adverbs. A1's *ahorita* is the famous case:
it can mean right now, in a moment, a little while ago, or a polite "later" that may not come
soon. A 2021 study of Mexico City speech in El Colegio de México's journal *Cuadernos de
Lingüística* found younger speakers using *ahorita* more and more where it doesn't mean "right
now". Context and tone tell you which is meant: *Ahorita voy* can mean "I'm coming" or "in a
bit".

Some diminutives became words of their own, and their link to the base word is now only
historical: *la ventana → la ventanilla* (A2: a car or ticket window), *el bolso → el bolsillo*
(pocket), *la manteca* (lard) *→ la mantequilla* (butter). *-illo* is another diminutive ending,
more common in Spain than in Mexico for new diminutives.

![A scale from small to big in three rows. Spoons: la cucharita (teaspoon), la cuchara (spoon), el cucharón (ladle). Dogs: el perrito, el perro, el perrazo. Houses: la casita, la casa, la casona. Above the small end: diminutive, -ito; above the big end: augmentative, -ón, -azo.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The augmentative: big, clumsy or impressive

The **[[augmentative]]** makes a word bigger, often with a tone of admiration, mockery or
criticism:

- *-ón, -ona*: *la cuchara → el cucharón* (ladle), *la casa → la casona* (a big old house).
  Feminine nouns often turn masculine with *-ón*: *la silla → el sillón* (armchair), *la caja →
  el cajón* (drawer). These three are now simply the names of things.
- With verbs, *-ón* names a person who does something too much: *mandar → mandón* (bossy),
  *llorar → llorón* (crybaby), *preguntar → preguntón* (nosy).
- *-ote, -ota*: *grande → grandote* (huge, informal), *la palabra → la palabrota* (swearword).
- *-azo, -aza*: *el perro → el perrazo* (a big dog).

## Text 1: a DIY video

Mariela has a YouTube channel called *Arréglalo tú* (Fix It Yourself). This is the start of her
video on a leak under the kitchen sink.

> ¡Hola, hola! Bienvenidos a otro video de *Arréglalo tú*. Hoy les enseño a reparar una fuga
> chiquita debajo del lavatrastes. Si ven gotitas en el piso del mueble, no se preocupen: casi
> siempre es una conexión floja. Primero, cierren la llave de paso, que normalmente está
> cerquita, abajo, en la pared. Pongan una cubeta debajo del tubo, por si cae agua. Ahora, con
> un desarmador, quiten los dos tornillos de la tapa. ¿Ven esta tuerca? Está floja. Nada de
> herramientas raras ni martillazos: se aprieta con la mano, despacito, sin forzarla. Si el
> tubo tiene la rosca gastada, le ponen un poquito de cinta de teflón antes de apretarlo. Abran
> la llave otra vez y esperen un ratito. ¿Ya no gotea? ¡Listo! Sequen el piso con el
> trapeador, y si les sirvió este video, regálenme un "me gusta".

> Hi, hi! Welcome to another *Fix It Yourself* video. Today I'll show you how to repair a tiny
> leak under the kitchen sink. If you see little drops on the floor of the cabinet, don't worry:
> it's almost always a loose connection. First, close the shutoff valve, which is usually close
> by, down low on the wall. Put a bucket under the pipe, just in case water comes out. Now, with
> a screwdriver, take out the two screws of the cover. See this nut? It's loose. No fancy tools,
> and no hammering: you tighten it by hand, gently, without forcing it. If the pipe's thread is
> worn, put a little bit of Teflon tape on it before you tighten it. Open the valve again and
> wait a little while. Not dripping anymore? Done! Dry the floor with the mop, and if this video
> helped you, give me a "like".

*La llave de paso* = shutoff valve (A1's *la llave*, key, also means faucet or valve); *la tuerca*
= nut (for a bolt); *flojo* = loose; *la rosca* = thread (of a screw or pipe); *gotear* = to drip
(from *la gota*, drop). Count the diminutives: *chiquita, gotitas, cerquita, despacito,
poquito, ratito*. Not one of them is about real size alone: they make the job sound small and
easy. *Regálenme un "me gusta"* uses *regalar* (to give as a gift) for a friendly request.

## Text 2: an ad

> *Caja de herramientas Maestro, 40 piezas.* Todo lo que necesitas para los arreglos de la
> casa: martillo, cuatro desarmadores, taladro inalámbrico con batería recargable, clavos y
> tornillos de varios tamaños, y un destapador de regalo. Ligera, resistente e irrompible.
> ¡Arréglalo tú mismo y ahórrate la visita del plomero! Solo 999 pesos.

> Maestro toolbox, 40 pieces. Everything you need for repairs around the house: a hammer,
> four screwdrivers, a cordless drill with a rechargeable battery, nails and screws in several
> sizes, and a free bottle opener. Light, sturdy and unbreakable. Fix it yourself and save
> yourself the plumber's visit! Only 999 pesos.

*Irrompible* is *in-* (spelled *i-* before *r*, with *rr*) + *romper* + *-ble*: "that can't be
broken". *Ligera* is light in weight; *resistente*, sturdy. *Ahórrate la visita del plomero* means
"save yourself (the cost of) a plumber's visit".

## Pronunciation

- Compounds carry one stress, on the noun part: *a-bre-LA-tas* (4 syllables), *sa-ca-COR-chos*
  (4), *ras-ca-CIE-los* (4), *pa-RA-guas* (3: *guas* is one syllable).
- *Cortaúñas*: *cor-ta-Ú-ñas*, 4 syllables. The accent on *ú* shows that *a* and *u* are
  pronounced separately.
- *Desarmador*: *de-sar-ma-DOR*, 4 syllables: the *s* goes with the next vowel, as in
  *desayunar*.
- *Cucharón*: *cu-cha-RÓN*; the plural *cucharones* has no written accent.
- *Taladro*: *ta-LA-dro*, with a soft single *r* after *d*.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*La abrelatas*~~, ~~*los abrelatases*~~ → *el abrelatas*, *los abrelatas*.
- ~~*Inlegal*~~, ~~*inposible*~~ → *ilegal*, *imposible*.
- Reading every diminutive as "small": *ahorita* and *un cafecito* are about tone, not size.
- Adding *-ito* to anything in formal writing: diminutives are warm and friendly, so a formal
  letter or an exam essay uses few of them.
- Guessing from false parts: *recordar* isn't "re-" + a Spanish verb, and *la ventanilla* isn't just
  "a small window".

## Key points

- Prefixes change the meaning (*des-, in-, re-, pre-, anti-, sobre-, sub-, co-, auto-,
  multi-*); suffixes often change the kind of word (*-ción, -dad, -ero, -ería, -ble, -oso,
  -ista, -ivo, -izar, -ear, -ificar*).
- Verb + plural noun = an object: masculine, plural unchanged (*el abrelatas, los abrelatas*).
- *-azo*: a blow or a sudden act (*portazo, frenazo, flechazo*).
- Diminutives (*-ito, -cito, -ecito*) add affection, politeness and intensity, and they're very
  frequent in Mexico; augmentatives (*-ón, -ote, -azo*) add size and attitude, and some became
  words of their own (*el cucharón, el cajón*).
- Mexican tool words: *el desarmador, el trapeador, la cubeta, el destapador, el lavatrastes*.

lessons.title: Por la sierra, para el mirador: por and para at B2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You've used *por* and *para* since A1, and B1 sorted out the basics: *para* + infinitive for a
purpose, *por* for a cause. At B2 the two words carry finer meanings, and a learner's choice is
one of the quickest signs of level: *Trabajo por mi familia* and *Trabajo para mi familia* are
both correct, and they don't mean the same. This lesson puts every use in one system, adds the
fixed phrases you'll meet in texts, and practices them with the language of nature: national
parks, landscapes, the seasons and ecotourism in Mexico. Lesson 16's *estar por* and lesson
14's passive with *por* come back here.

## One idea for each word

A picture helps more than a list. *Para* looks at the end point: the goal, the destination,
the deadline, the person something is for. *Por* looks at the path: the route you go along,
the cause that pushes you, the means, the exchange. Most uses follow from that.

![A chart of por and para in two panels. Left, POR: the path, drawn as a winding dashed line, with its uses: cause (por la lluvia), through or along (por la sierra), means (por teléfono), exchange (por 200 pesos), duration (por dos horas), passive agent (por los guardaparques), still to do (quedan 2 km por recorrer). Right, PARA: the end point, drawn as an arrow pointing to a flag, with its uses: purpose (para ver aves), destination (para el mirador), deadline (para el viernes), opinion (para mí), comparison (para ser enero), recipient (para ti), employer (para el gobierno).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### *Para*: the goal

| Use | Example | Translation |
|---|---|---|
| purpose (+ infinitive, or *para que* + subjunctive) | *Madrugamos para ver las aves.* | We got up early to see the birds. |
| destination | *Mañana salimos para el cañón.* | Tomorrow we leave for the canyon. |
| deadline | *Tenemos que reservar para el viernes.* | We have to book by Friday. |
| opinion | *Para mí, es el parque más bonito.* | In my view, it's the prettiest park. |
| comparison with what's expected | *Para ser enero, hace mucho calor.* | For January, it's very hot. |
| recipient | *Estos binoculares son para ti.* | These binoculars are for you. |
| employer | *Trabaja para el gobierno estatal.* | She works for the state government. |
| *estar para* | *No estoy para bromas.* | I'm not in the mood for jokes. |

*Estar para* + infinitive can also mean "to be about to" (*El tren está para salir*), but in
Mexico the everyday form is lesson 16's *estar por* + infinitive (*El tren está por salir*).

### *Por*: the path and the cause

| Use | Example | Translation |
|---|---|---|
| cause, reason | *Cerraron el sendero por la lluvia.* | They closed the trail because of the rain. |
| through, along, around | *Caminamos por la orilla del río.* | We walked along the riverbank. |
| a rough place or time | *El cenote está por aquí. Llegamos por la tarde.* | The cenote is around here. We arrived in the afternoon. |
| means | *Nos avisaron por mensaje.* | They let us know by text. |
| exchange, price | *Pagamos 90 pesos por persona.* | We paid 90 pesos per person. |
| duration | *Estuvimos en la cima por dos horas.* | We were at the top for two hours. |
| agent of the passive (14) | *La reserva es vigilada por los guardaparques.* | The reserve is watched over by the rangers. |
| on behalf of, in favor of | *Lucha por los manglares.* | She fights for the mangroves. |
| still to be done | *Quedan tres kilómetros por recorrer.* | There are three kilometers still to go. |
| about to (16) | *Está por llover.* | It's about to rain. |

Two notes on these. For duration, Mexican Spanish often leaves *por* out or uses *durante*:
*Estuvimos dos horas en la cima* is the most natural of the three. And *el sendero* (trail) is
lesson 08's word.

## Pairs that change the meaning

These are the sentences where both words are correct and the choice is the message:

- *Trabajo por mi familia* (because of my family, on their behalf) / *Trabajo para mi familia*
  (my family is my employer, or my work is meant for them).
- *¿Por qué viniste?* (Why: what caused it?) / *¿Para qué viniste?* (What for: what's your
  purpose?)
- *Por mí, podemos ir mañana* (As far as I'm concerned, we can go tomorrow) / *Para mí, el
  mejor día es mañana* (In my opinion, the best day is tomorrow).
- *Lo hice por ti* (for your sake, because of you) / *Lo hice para ti* (as something for you).
- *Pasamos por Oaxaca* (we went through Oaxaca) / *Vamos para Oaxaca* (we're heading to Oaxaca).
- *Te lo cambio por el mapa* (I'll trade it for the map) / *Te lo compré para el viaje* (I
  bought it for you, for the trip).

## Fixed phrases

| Phrase | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *por si acaso* | just in case | *Lleva impermeable, por si acaso.* |
| *por excelencia* | par excellence, the quintessential | *El cenote es el paisaje yucateco por excelencia.* |
| *por lo visto* (B1) | apparently | *Por lo visto, ya abrieron el mirador.* |
| *por poco* + present | almost (in the past) | *Por poco me caigo en la barranca.* (I almost fell.) |
| *por fin* | at last | *¡Por fin llegamos!* |
| *para colmo* (17) | to top it all | *Se nos acabó el agua y, para colmo, empezó a llover.* |
| *para siempre* (A1) | forever | *Algunas especies desaparecen para siempre.* |
| *para nada* | not at all (informal) | *¿Estás cansado? Para nada.* |

*Por si* also works with a whole clause, usually with the present indicative (*Lleva agua por si
tienes sed*), or with the imperfect subjunctive for a less likely case (*por si hiciera frío*),
never the present subjunctive; and *por poco* uses the present to tell a past near-miss, which surprises English
speakers.

## Places in nature

Lesson 01 gave you *a lo largo de* (along, throughout). Four more phrases place things in a
landscape:

- *a orillas de* (on the shores of, on the banks of): *un pueblo a orillas del lago*;
- *en lo alto de* (at the top of, high on): *una cruz en lo alto del cerro*;
- *al pie de* (at the foot of): *acampamos al pie del volcán*;
- *en el fondo de* (at the bottom of): *peces en el fondo del cenote*.

## Mexico's natural spaces

Mexico has deserts, high plateaus, volcanoes, cloud forests, jungles, reefs and two long coasts.
*El altiplano* is the high plateau of central and northern Mexico; *la barranca* is the
Mexican word for a deep ravine (the canyons of Chihuahua are known as the Barrancas del Cobre,
the Copper Canyon); *el cráter* is the mouth of a volcano. In the north of the Yucatán Peninsula, where there
are almost no surface rivers, water collects underground, and *el cenote*, a natural
sinkhole that opens onto it, was a main source of water for the Maya there. The word comes from
a Maya word. In the lakes and canals of Xochimilco lives *el ajolote*, an axolotl, a salamander that
keeps its gills all its life; it is endemic to the Valley of Mexico, and the IUCN lists it as critically endangered.

Two protected areas with dates:

- Desierto de los Leones, on the edge of Mexico City, became Mexico's first national park
  in 1917, under President Venustiano Carranza. Despite its name it's a conifer forest: it was
  called a *desierto* because nobody lived there, and Carmelite monks had a convent in it from
  1611 to 1814.
- Sian Ka'an, in Quintana Roo, is a biosphere reserve and has been a UNESCO World Heritage
  Site since 1987. It takes in forests, mangrove swamps, marshes, lagoons and part of the
  Mesoamerican Barrier Reef.

In much of central and southern Mexico the year has two halves: *la temporada de lluvias*,
roughly from late spring to early fall, and *la temporada seca*, the rest of the year. Check a
park's own page before you go: trails close for rain, fires or nesting seasons.

![A map of an invented coastal park, labeled in Spanish: el sendero (a dashed trail winding through the forest), el mirador (a viewpoint tower on a hill), el cenote (a round pool), el manglar y la laguna (mangrove trees around a lagoon), la playa (a beach, with a sea turtle on it) and el arrecife (a coral reef in the sea).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Text: a ranger's talk

Julián is a *guardaparques* at the Laguna del Venado National Park, a park invented for this
lesson on the coast of Quintana Roo. He's speaking to a group at the start of a guided hike.

> Buenos días a todos y bienvenidos. Me llamo Julián y soy guardaparques aquí desde hace diez
> años. Hoy vamos a caminar por el sendero de la selva para llegar al mirador. Son cuatro
> kilómetros; pararemos un par de veces para descansar y para ver la flora y la fauna. Les pido
> que no salgan del sendero, por su seguridad y por las plantas. Muchas de las especies que van a
> ver son endémicas: solo existen en esta región. Desde el mirador se ven el manglar, la laguna
> y, si el día está despejado, el arrecife. Para ser temporada seca, hay bastante agua en la
> laguna, porque llovió mucho en septiembre. De regreso pasaremos por un cenote; quien quiera
> nadar, puede hacerlo, pero sin bloqueador, para no contaminar el agua. Un último aviso: de
> mayo a octubre, las tortugas marinas vienen a esta playa a poner sus huevos, así que por la
> noche la playa está cerrada. Lleven agua y gorra, por si acaso. ¿Alguna pregunta? ¿No? Pues
> vámonos, que nos quedan muchas cosas por ver.

> Good morning, everyone, and welcome. My name is Julián and I've been a ranger here for ten
> years. Today we're going to walk along the jungle trail to get to the viewpoint. It's four
> kilometers; we'll stop a couple of times to rest and to see the plants and wildlife. Please
> don't leave the trail, for your safety and for the plants' sake. Many of the species you'll
> see are endemic: they exist only in this region. From the viewpoint you can see the mangrove
> swamp, the lagoon and, if the day is clear, the reef. For the dry season, there's quite a lot
> of water in the lagoon, because it rained a lot in September. On the way back we'll go past a
> cenote; anyone who wants to swim can, but without sunscreen, so as not to pollute the water.
> One last notice: from May to October, sea turtles come to this beach to lay their eggs, so the
> beach is closed at night. Bring water and a cap, just in case. Any questions? No? Then let's
> go, because we still have lots of things to see.

*Despejado* = clear (sky); *el bloqueador* = sunscreen (Mexico; Spain *la crema solar*); *poner
huevos* = to lay eggs. Every *por* and *para* in the talk fits the chart: *por el sendero*
(path), *para llegar* (purpose), *por su seguridad* (on behalf of), *para ser temporada seca*
(comparison), *pasaremos por un cenote* (through, past), *por la noche* (rough time), *por si
acaso*, *por ver* (still to do). The nesting months are part of the invented park's rules; real
seasons vary by beach and species.

## Pronunciation

- *Guardaparques*: *guar-da-PAR-ques*, 4 syllables; *gua* is one syllable.
- *Biodiversidad*: *bio-di-ver-si-DAD*, 5 syllables (*bio* is one).
- *Endémico*: *en-DÉ-mi-co*; *ecoturismo*: *e-co-tu-RIS-mo*.
- *Ajolote*: *a-jo-LO-te*, with the Spanish *j*; *cenote*: *ce-NO-te* (with seseo, *se-NO-te*).
- *Arrecife*: *a-rre-CI-fe*, with a trilled *rr*; *manglar*: *man-GLAR*, 2 syllables.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*Gracias para todo*~~ → *Gracias por todo*: you thank someone *for* a cause.
- ~~*Estudio por aprender*~~ → *Estudio para aprender*: purpose takes *para*.
- ~~*Lo necesito por el lunes*~~ → *Lo necesito para el lunes* (deadline).
- ~~*Fue fundada para los monjes*~~ → *por los monjes* when the monks founded it: the agent of
  the passive takes *por* (*para los monjes* would mean "for the monks").
- Forcing *por* into every duration: *Viví dos años en Puebla* is the usual way to say it.
- Turning a real difference into a mistake: *¿Por qué?* and *¿Para qué?* are both correct
  questions; they ask for different things.

## Key points

- *Para* looks at the end point: purpose, destination, deadline, opinion, comparison,
  recipient, employer; *estar para* = in the mood for (or about to).
- *Por* looks at the path: cause, route, rough place or time, means, exchange, duration, the
  agent of the passive, on behalf of, *quedar / estar por* + infinitive.
- Pairs change the meaning: *por / para mí, ¿por qué? / ¿para qué?, trabajar por / para*.
- Fixed phrases: *por si acaso, por excelencia, por poco, por fin, para colmo, para siempre*.
- Nature words: *el parque nacional, la reserva de la biosfera, el manglar, el arrecife, el
  cenote, la barranca, endémico, la temporada de lluvias / seca*.

lessons.title: Writing at B2: the formal letter and the opinion article
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

B1's lesson 23 taught short e-mails, posts and reviews. At B2 you write longer texts for
readers you don't know: a letter to an institution, an opinion piece for a newspaper or a blog.
This lesson gives you a method, the layout of a formal letter, paragraphing, B2 punctuation and
three original models, using the connectors of lessons 07, 10 and 17 and the nominal style of
lesson 18. It also prepares the DELE B2 writing test (lesson 24).

## The two DELE B2 writing tasks, in general terms

The official *Guía del examen DELE B2* (Instituto Cervantes, 2014) describes two tasks, written
in 80 minutes in all:

- Task 1: a letter or e-mail, formal or informal, of 150 to 180 words. You first listen to
  a short informative recording (the guide mentions things like news, an ad or an offer) and
  take notes; your letter passes on what you heard and gives your opinion of it.
- Task 2: an *artículo de opinión* (opinion piece), also of 150 to 180 words. You choose one
  of two options, each introduced by a short news item: an article commenting on a graph, or
  a blog article or a review.

Formats can change: check the current guide on the Instituto Cervantes site before an exam.
In every task, cover each point, stay in the word range and keep one register.

## A method in six steps

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: A method for writing a B2 text
  accDescr: Six steps from top to bottom. One, read the task and underline every point it asks for. Two, decide who the reader is and choose the register, formal or informal. Three, make an outline of three or four paragraphs, with the main idea of each and one example or piece of data. Four, write the draft. Five, edit it with a checklist of content, connectors, agreement, accents and punctuation. Six, count the words and check every point is covered.
  A["1. Read the task: underline every point"] --> B["2. Who reads it? Choose the register"]
  B --> C["3. Outline: 3-4 paragraphs, one main idea each"]
  C --> D["4. Write the draft"]
  D --> E["5. Edit: content, connectors, agreement, accents, punctuation"]
  E --> F["6. Count the words; tick off every point"]
```

## Structure: three parts, one idea per paragraph

A good *estructura* for both genres has three parts:

- *La introducción* presents the topic and why you're writing. In an opinion piece it also
  states your *tesis* (lesson 02's thesis, in a new sense): the one-sentence statement of what
  you will argue.
- *El desarrollo* (the body) gives one *idea principal* (B1) per paragraph, each backed by
  *ideas secundarias*: supporting ideas, examples, data. To *ilustrar* or *ejemplificar* a
  point, give a concrete case (*Por ejemplo, en mi colonia…*); to *enumerar* several, use
  *en primer lugar, en segundo lugar, por último*.
- *La conclusión* sums up (*sintetiza*) your position in a short *síntesis*, or makes a
  proposal. It adds no new argument.

A text is *coherente* when its ideas follow a logical order without contradictions; it has
*cohesión* when connectors, pronouns and synonyms join its sentences. Avoid *la reiteración*
(repeating one word again and again): use a *sinónimo* (*la medida, la propuesta*), a pronoun,
or lesson 18's nominal style (*la construcción del puente* for *que construyan el puente*). An
*antónimo* (opposite) sharpens a contrast: *no es un gasto, es una inversión*.

## The formal letter

A *carta formal* has a fixed *formato*:

| Part | Formal | Informal |
|---|---|---|
| *El saludo* (greeting), followed by a colon | *Estimados señores: / Estimada señora Ruiz:* | *Querida Ana: / Hola, Daniel:* |
| Opening line | *Me dirijo a ustedes en relación con…* | *Te escribo porque…* |
| Body | *usted / ustedes*, full sentences, connectors | *tú*, a more personal tone |
| Closing | *Quedo a la espera de su respuesta. Atentamente,* | *Un abrazo, / Saludos,* |
| *La posdata* (P. D.) | rare in formal letters | *P. D. ¿Ya viste la foto?* |

After the greeting's colon, the next line starts with a capital letter. An e-mail's *asunto* is its
subject line.

## Punctuation at B2

The RAE's *Ortografía de la lengua española* (2010) is the reference for all of this.

- The comma. Never put one between a subject and its verb, however long the subject:
  ~~*La propuesta del ayuntamiento de cerrar la calle, me parece excelente*~~ → *La propuesta
  del ayuntamiento de cerrar la calle me parece excelente*. Use commas around an aside (*Mi
  hermana, que trabaja ahí, me lo dijo*), after a connector that opens a sentence (*Sin
  embargo, …*) and before the name of the person you address (*Hola, Daniel*).
- *El punto y coma* (semicolon) separates items in a list that already contain commas, and
  joins two closely linked sentences, often before a connector: *La idea es buena; sin embargo,
  llega tarde.*
- *Los dos puntos* (colon) go after a letter's greeting and before a list, an example or an
  explanation. In running text the word after them begins with a
  *minúscula* (lowercase letter): *Tenía una razón: no había presupuesto.*
- Capitals. The title of a book, a film or an article capitalizes only its first word and
  proper names (*Cien años de soledad*). Days, months, languages and nationalities take lowercase: *el
  sábado 3 de septiembre*, *el español*, *una autora mexicana*.
- Accents. Question words keep their accent in indirect questions (*No sé qué decir*); *el /
  él, tu / tú, si / sí, mas / más* differ by the accent; *solo* and the demonstratives *este,
  ese* are normally written without one; *fue, dio, vio* never take one. Write *porque* (because), *por qué* (why), *el porqué* (the reason).

*Una errata* is a typo: the editing step is there to catch them.

## Model 1: a formal e-mail

Rosa Elena heard a radio report about a plan to close a downtown street to cars on Sundays.
She writes to the city government (162 words from greeting to postscript).

> Asunto: Propuesta de cerrar la calle Hidalgo los domingos
>
> Estimados señores:
>
> Me dirijo a ustedes en relación con la propuesta del ayuntamiento, que escuché ayer en la
> radio, de cerrar la calle Hidalgo a los autos los domingos por la mañana. Según el reportaje,
> la medida empezaría en marzo, y la calle se usaría para bicicletas, puestos de artesanía y
> actividades para niños.
>
> En primer lugar, quisiera expresar mi apoyo a la iniciativa. Vivo en el centro desde hace doce
> años y creo que un espacio sin ruido ni tráfico mejoraría la convivencia entre los vecinos.
> Además, los comercios de la zona podrían beneficiarse de la llegada de visitantes.
>
> Sin embargo, me preocupa el acceso de las personas mayores y de los servicios de emergencia.
> Por lo tanto, les sugiero que se mantenga un carril libre para las ambulancias y que se
> amplíe el transporte público ese día.
>
> Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Rosa Elena Vargas
>
> P. D. Con gusto participaría en una reunión vecinal sobre el tema.

> Subject: Proposal to close Hidalgo Street on Sundays
>
> Dear Sir or Madam,
>
> I am writing to you about the city government's proposal, which I heard on the radio
> yesterday, to close Hidalgo Street to cars on Sunday mornings. According to the report, the
> measure would start in March, and the street would be used for bicycles, craft stalls and
> activities for children.
>
> First of all, I would like to express my support for the initiative. I have lived downtown for
> twelve years, and I think a space without noise or traffic would improve life together among
> neighbors. In addition, the area's shops could benefit from the arrival of visitors.
>
> However, I am concerned about access for older people and for emergency services. I therefore
> suggest that a lane be kept free for ambulances and that public transportation be increased on
> that day.
>
> I look forward to your reply.
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Rosa Elena Vargas
>
> P.S. I would be glad to take part in a neighborhood meeting on the subject.

Paragraph 1 reports what she heard; 2 gives her opinion and two reasons; 3, a reservation and
a proposal. *La medida, la iniciativa* and *la propuesta* avoid repeating one word.

## Model 2: an opinion article for a blog

A1's *la entrada* (entrance) is also a blog post. This one reacts to an invented news item
(160 words, title not counted).

> ¿Siguen siendo necesarias las bibliotecas públicas?
>
> Hace unos días se publicó que una ciudad del norte cerrará dos de sus bibliotecas porque cada
> vez reciben menos visitantes. Muchos piensan que, con internet, ya no las necesitamos. Yo no
> estoy de acuerdo.
>
> En primer lugar, una biblioteca no es solo un lugar para pedir libros prestados. Es uno de los
> pocos espacios públicos, gratuitos y tranquilos que quedan en una ciudad: allí estudian
> jóvenes que no tienen dónde hacerlo en casa, y allí aprenden a usar una computadora muchas
> personas mayores. En segundo lugar, el acceso a internet no es igual para todos, y la
> información en línea no siempre es de calidad.
>
> Ahora bien, es cierto que las bibliotecas deben cambiar. La modernización de sus servicios,
> con talleres, actividades para niños y préstamo de libros electrónicos, podría atraer a un
> público nuevo.
>
> En definitiva, cerrar una biblioteca es ahorrar poco y perder mucho. Antes de hacerlo, valdría
> la pena preguntarles a los vecinos qué biblioteca quieren.

> Are public libraries still necessary?
>
> A few days ago it was reported that a city in the north will close two of its libraries
> because they get fewer and fewer visitors. Many people think that, with the internet, we
> don't need them anymore. I don't agree.
>
> First, a library isn't just a place to borrow books. It's one of the few public, free and
> quiet spaces left in a city: young people who have nowhere to study at home study there, and
> many older people learn to use a computer there. Second, access to the internet isn't the
> same for everyone, and information online isn't always good.
>
> That said, it's true that libraries must change. Modernizing their services, with workshops,
> activities for children and e-book lending, could attract a new audience.
>
> In short, closing a library saves little and loses a lot. Before doing it, it would be worth
> asking the neighbors what kind of library they want.

The *tesis* ends the introduction (*Yo no estoy de acuerdo*); *ahora bien* (that said)
concedes a point (lesson 17); *en definitiva* opens the conclusion; *la modernización de sus
servicios* is lesson 18's nominal style.

## Model 3: editing a draft

A hurried first draft of an informal e-mail to Daniel, with nine problems (78 words):

> Hola Daniel: ¿Como estás? Te escribo porque el Sábado 14 de Septiembre es la inauguración de
> la nueva biblioteca del barrio. Mi hermana, que trabaja ahí me dijo que habrá un taller de
> escritura, una exposición de fotos y un concierto. Va a ser muy interesante. El concierto es
> de un grupo de jazz muy interesante. No se si quieres venir, pero si vienes, te va a encantar.
> Avísame antes del jueves, porque hay que inscribirse ¿Te late?

The corrections:

1. *Hola, Daniel:* (a comma before the name of the person addressed).
2. *¿Cómo estás?* (a question word takes its accent).
3. *el sábado* and 4. *septiembre* (lowercase days and months).
5. *Mi hermana, que trabaja ahí, me dijo…* (an aside takes two commas).
6. *muy interesante… muy interesante*: a reiteration. Second time: *un grupo de jazz buenísimo*.
7. *No sé si quieres venir* (*sé*, from *saber*, takes an accent; *se* is the pronoun).
8. *…hay que inscribirse. ¿Te late?* (end the sentence before the question).
9. *Va a ser muy interesante* adds nothing after the list: cut it, or make it specific.

> Hi, Daniel! How are you? I'm writing because Saturday, September 14, is the opening of the
> neighborhood's new library. My sister, who works there, told me there'll be a writing
> workshop, a photo exhibition and a concert. The concert is by a really great jazz band. I
> don't know if you want to come, but if you do, you'll love it. Let me know before Thursday,
> because you have to sign up. Are you in?

*¿Te late?* (Mexico, informal) = Are you up for it? / Sound good?

## Pronunciation

- *Coherente*: *co-he-REN-te*, 4 syllables, silent *h*; *cohesión*: *co-he-SIÓN*, 3.
- *Síntesis*: *SÍN-te-sis*, stressed on the first syllable.
- *Posdata*: *pos-DA-ta*; the RAE prefers it to *postdata*.
- *Errata*: *e-RRA-ta*, with a trilled *rr*.

## Common mistakes

- Writing 120 or 220 words when the task asks for 150–180: stay in range.
- A comma between subject and verb: ~~*El problema principal, es el tráfico*~~.
- English-style capitals: ~~*El Lunes*~~, ~~*Los Mexicanos*~~, ~~*Cien Años de Soledad*~~.
- Mixing *tú* and *usted* in one letter (*le escribo… te sugiero*): choose one and keep it.
- A conclusion with a new argument, or no conclusion at all.

## Key points

- Plan, draft, edit, count; one main idea per paragraph, with supporting ideas.
- Introduction with your *tesis*, development with examples, a conclusion that sums up or
  proposes.
- Formal letter: *Estimados señores:*, *Me dirijo a ustedes…*, *Atentamente,*.
- No comma between subject and verb; *punto y coma* in long lists and before connectors;
  lowercase after a colon in running text and for days, months and nationalities.

lessons.title: The DELE B2 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This last core lesson of Spanish B2 explains what B2 means, describes the Instituto Cervantes'
DELE B2 exam in general terms, gives a strategy for each of its four tests, and reviews the
course's grammar in four charts. You don't have to take the exam, but knowing its format is a
good way to measure your level, and its tasks are the kinds of things a B2 speaker does
anyway: read an opinion piece, follow a lecture, write a formal letter, defend a proposal.

## What B2 means

B2 is the fourth of the six levels of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), the
upper "independent user". In plain words, at B2 you can:

- understand the main ideas of complex texts, concrete or abstract, including discussions in
  your own field, and follow long talks and arguments on familiar topics;
- talk with native speakers fluently and spontaneously enough that neither side has to strain;
- write clear, detailed texts on a wide range of subjects, explain your view on a current
  issue, and set out the advantages and disadvantages of different options;
- write letters that show what events and experiences mean to you personally.

At B2 you still make mistakes, but they rarely cause misunderstandings, and you often notice and
correct them yourself.

## The DELE B2

The DELE (*Diplomas de Español como Lengua Extranjera*) are the Instituto Cervantes' official
diplomas. The figures below come from the official *Guía del examen DELE B2* (© 2014 Instituto
Cervantes), in this course's own words. Formats, dates and fees can change: check the
Instituto Cervantes site before you register.

| Test | Time | Tasks | Items or length | Points |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reading (*Comprensión de lectura*) | 70 minutes | 4 | 36 items | 25 |
| Listening (*Comprensión auditiva*) | 40 minutes | 5 | 30 items | 25 |
| Writing (*Expresión e interacción escritas*) | 80 minutes | 2 | 150–180 words each | 25 |
| Speaking (*Expresión e interacción orales*) | 20 minutes, plus 20 minutes to prepare | 3 | 6–7, 5–6 and 3–4 minutes | 25 |

![A diagram of the DELE B2. Four boxes: reading, 70 minutes, 4 tasks; writing, 80 minutes, 2 tasks; listening, 40 minutes, 5 tasks; speaking, 20 minutes after 20 minutes of preparation, 3 tasks; each worth 25 points. Reading and writing form group 1, listening and speaking group 2, each of 50 points, and each needs at least 30. At the bottom: 30 or more in both groups gives Apto.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

How it's scored. The 100 points form two groups of 50: group 1 is reading + writing, group 2
is listening + speaking. You need at least 30 in each group to be *apto*; a strong group can't
make up for a weak one. In reading and listening each correct item scores 1, and the total is
converted to the test's 25 points (20 of 36, for example, gives about 13.9); there is no
*penalización* (penalty) for a wrong answer, so answer everything. Writing and speaking are
marked by trained examiners on scales from 0 to 3, where band 2 corresponds to B2: a
*holístico* (overall) score counts 40% and an *analítico* (detailed) score 60%. The detailed
score looks at four things: for writing, *adecuación* (fit to the genre and task),
*coherencia*, *corrección* (accuracy) and *alcance* (range); for speaking, *coherencia*,
*fluidez*, *corrección* and *alcance*.

### What each test asks, in general terms

- Reading. Four tasks on texts of about 400–450 words, or several shorter ones: a complex
  informative text with three-option questions; four short texts in which people give opinions
  or tell experiences, to match with statements; a text with short passages taken out, to put
  back (there are more options than gaps); and a literary, historical or biographical text with
  gaps, each with three options.
- Listening. Short conversations; a longer conversation in which you decide who said which
  idea; a radio or TV interview; short monologues or conversations matched with statements;
  and a lecture, speech or long monologue. Every recording is played twice.
- Writing. Lesson 23 described the two tasks: a letter or e-mail written from notes on a short
  recording, and an opinion piece chosen from two options, each introduced by a short news
  item: an article commenting on a graph, or a blog article or a review.
- Speaking. Task 1, prepared: a problem with a card of proposals; you weigh their pros and
  cons, then discuss them with the examiner. Task 2, prepared: an imagined situation shown in a
  photo; you describe it and talk about it. Task 3, not prepared: a short conversation about
  survey results or news on a current trend. Each time you choose one of two options. You may
  use the notes and outline you made while preparing. Two examiners are present: one talks with
  you; the other doesn't take part in the conversation and listens to mark you.

Which Spanish? The guide says the texts come from varied sources and varieties of Spanish, and
that in your answers any Hispanic norm is accepted if you apply it consistently and it is
backed by large groups of educated speakers. Write and speak the Mexican Spanish of this course
and recognize the rest (honors 24h1 helps).

- [DELE B2 exam guide (PDF, Instituto Cervantes)](https://agenda.cervantes.es/sites/default/files/guia_examen_dele_b2_0.pdf)

## The words of the exam

| Word | Meaning | Where you'll meet it |
|---|---|---|
| *la tarea* | task (A1's homework, in a new sense) | *La prueba tiene cuatro tareas.* |
| *el ítem, los ítems* | item, question | *36 ítems de selección múltiple* |
| *el estímulo* | prompt, stimulus | the text, photo or graph a task starts from |
| *el fragmento* | excerpt, fragment | a piece cut out of a text |
| *el hueco* | gap, blank | *Complete los huecos.* |
| *seleccionar, emparejar* | to select, to match | *Seleccione la opción correcta. Empareje los textos con los enunciados.* |
| *la audición* | the playing of a recording | *Escuchará cada audición dos veces.* |
| *la hoja de respuestas* | answer sheet | where you mark your answers |
| *el baremo, la ponderación* | marking scheme, weighting | how points are calculated |
| *la inscripción, la tasa* | registration, fee | 19's *la tasa* (rate), in a new sense: *la tasa de inscripción* |

*La comprensión lectora* (reading comprehension) and *la comprensión auditiva* (listening
comprehension) are the general names for the two skills; *la escucha* is listening as an
activity. *La prueba escrita* and *el examen oral* are the written and spoken parts. *La banda*
is a score level, as in "band 2".

## Strategies for each test

Reading. Time matters: 70 minutes for 36 items is under two minutes each, so work
*contrarreloj* (against the clock) with a *cronómetro* (timer) when you practice. Read the
questions first. In *selección múltiple* (multiple choice), the wrong options often repeat the
text's words with one change (*siempre / a veces*, *causa / consecuencia*). To put sentences
back into a text, look at both sides of each gap: a connector, a pronoun or a tense usually
decides it.

Listening. Use the pause before each recording to read the statements and predict. Get the
main idea the first time and check details the second. Listen for changes of mind and for
concessions (*Es verdad que…, pero…*): the speaker's final position is what counts.

Writing. Follow lesson 23's method, and keep 10 minutes at the end for editing.

Speaking. In the 20 minutes of preparation, write *notas de apoyo* (prompt notes: key words, not full
sentences) for tasks 1 and 2. Show range: hypotheses (*Si yo fuera el alcalde…*), concessions
(*Aunque la propuesta es cara…*), probability (*Estarán celebrando algo*). If you lose the
thread, say so and go on (*Lo que quería decir es que…*). Honors 24h2 has full models.

And *los nervios* (nerves, plural in this sense)? Practice with a timer until the format
holds no surprises, sleep well, and arrive early.

## Grammar review

### Which subjunctive tense?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which subjunctive tense?
  accDescr: A decision chart for a verb that needs the subjunctive. First question: is the main verb in the present, the future, the present perfect or a command? If yes, the second question is whether the action in the subjunctive happens at the same time or later, or before. Same time or later: present subjunctive, as in Espero que vengas. Before: perfect subjunctive, as in Espero que hayas aprobado. If the main verb is in a past tense or the conditional, ask the same question. Same time or later: imperfect subjunctive, as in Quería que vinieras. Before: pluperfect subjunctive, as in Me dolió que no me lo hubieras dicho. A note: a present main verb can also take a past subjunctive for a past event, as in No creo que lo dijera ayer.
  A["The verb needs the subjunctive"] --> B{"Main verb: present, future, perfect or command?"}
  B -- yes --> C{"Subjunctive action: same time or later, or before?"}
  C -- "same time or later" --> P1["Present: Espero que vengas. (B1)"]
  C -- before --> P2["Perfect: Espero que hayas aprobado. (02)"]
  B -- "no: past or conditional" --> D{"Same time or later, or before?"}
  D -- "same time or later" --> P3["Imperfect: Quería que vinieras. (B1)"]
  D -- before --> P4["Pluperfect: Me dolió que no me lo hubieras dicho. (03)"]
  B -.- N["A present can take a past subjunctive for a past event: No creo que lo dijera ayer. (03)"]
```

The *-se* forms (*viniese, hubiese dicho*) are correct too, more common in writing and in Spain.

### Conditions

| Kind | Condition | Result | Example | Lesson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Real, possible | *si* + present | present, future, command | *Si llueve, nos quedamos.* | B1 |
| Unreal now | *si* + imperfect subjunctive | conditional | *Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría.* | B1 |
| Unreal in the past | *si* + pluperfect subjunctive | conditional perfect (or *hubiera*) | *Si hubiera salido antes, no habría perdido el vuelo.* | 04 |
| Mixed: past cause, present result | *si* + pluperfect subjunctive | conditional | *Si hubiera estudiado medicina, ahora sería médica.* | 04 |
| With *de* + infinitive | *de* + infinitive | as above | *De haberlo sabido, te habría avisado.* | 04 |
| With a connector | *siempre que, a menos que, en caso de que* + subjunctive | any fitting tense | *Iré siempre que me acompañes.* | 12 |

### Connectors and mood

| Indicative | Subjunctive | Either, with a change of meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *ya que, puesto que, dado que* (cause, 10) | *para que, a fin de que* (purpose, 11) | *aunque*: indicative for a fact, subjunctive for a possibility or a point you grant (07) |
| *así que, por lo tanto* (consequence, 10) | *antes de que* (11) | *cuando, en cuanto, hasta que*: indicative for habits and the past, subjunctive for the future (11) |
| *como* first in the sentence = since (10) | *a menos que, con tal de que, siempre y cuando* (12) | *de modo que*: indicative for a result, subjunctive for a purpose (10) |
| *sin embargo, no obstante* (sentence connectors, 07, 17) | *sin que* (11) | *por mucho que*: indicative for a fact, subjunctive for a hypothesis or a point you grant (07) |

### Reporting in the past

| Direct speech | After *dijo que* | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| present: *"Está cerrado."* | imperfect: *estaba cerrado* | 13 |
| preterite or perfect: *"Lo vi." / "Lo he visto."* | pluperfect: *lo había visto* (a preterite often stays: *lo vio*) | 13 |
| future: *"Llegaré tarde."* | conditional: *llegaría tarde* | 13 |
| future perfect: *"Habré terminado."* | conditional perfect: *habría terminado* | 13 |
| command: *"Llámame."* | imperfect subjunctive: *que la llamara* | 13 |
| *aquí, hoy, mañana* | *allí, ese día, al día siguiente* | 13 |

If what was said is still true, the tense can stay: *Dijo que el museo abre los lunes* (13).

## Dialogue: dos semanas antes

Camila, from Monterrey, is helping her Canadian friend Ethan, who has registered for the DELE B2.

> Camila: ¿Ya te llegó la confirmación de la inscripción?
>
> Ethan: Sí, ya pagué la tasa. Hago la prueba escrita el sábado por la mañana, y el examen oral, por la tarde.
>
> Camila: ¿Y cómo vas con la comprensión auditiva?
>
> Ethan: Mejor. Antes me ponía nervioso si no entendía una palabra, y perdía el resto de la audición. Ahora sigo escuchando.
>
> Camila: Eso es lo más importante. ¿Y la expresión escrita?
>
> Ethan: Me cuesta no pasarme de 180 palabras. Si hubiera practicado con cronómetro desde el principio, ya lo tendría resuelto.
>
> Camila: Pues todavía tienes dos semanas. Te propongo algo: cada día, una tarea contrarreloj.
>
> Ethan: Va. Y el oral, ¿me ayudas? Necesito a alguien que me haga preguntas que no espero.
>
> Camila: Claro. Pero no me pidas que sea amable: los examinadores no lo son.
>
> Ethan: ¡Bueno, eso no lo sabes! Ojalá me toque una examinadora tan buena onda como tú.

> Camila: Has the confirmation of your registration arrived yet?
>
> Ethan: Yes, I've already paid the fee. I take the written test on Saturday morning, and the oral exam in the afternoon.
>
> Camila: And how's the listening comprehension going?
>
> Ethan: Better. Before, I'd get nervous if I didn't understand a word, and I'd lose the rest of the recording. Now I keep listening.
>
> Camila: That's the most important thing. And the writing?
>
> Ethan: I find it hard not to go over 180 words. If I had practiced with a timer from the start, I'd have it sorted by now.
>
> Camila: Well, you still have two weeks. Here's an idea: every day, one task against the clock.
>
> Ethan: OK. And the oral, will you help me? I need someone to ask me questions I don't expect.
>
> Camila: Sure. But don't ask me to be nice: the examiners aren't.
>
> Ethan: Well, you don't know that! I hope I get an examiner as nice as you.

*Pasarse de* = to go over (a limit); *buena onda* (Mexico, informal) = nice, cool. Ethan's
*Si hubiera practicado…, ya lo tendría resuelto* is a mixed condition (04), and *alguien que me
haga preguntas* is a relative clause about someone not yet known. The guide doesn't say when the
speaking test is held; check with your exam center, since it may be on another day.

## What comes next

At C1 you'll handle more kinds of subordinate clause, the full range of *se*, idiomatic and
literary register, and long texts in which the argument is implicit. Keep your reviews and
drills going, read the books on the course's reading list, and above all, keep talking.

## Pronunciation

- *Ítem*: *Í-tem*, plural *ítems* (both with the accent).
- *Holístico*: *o-LÍS-ti-co*, silent *h*; *analítico*: *a-na-LÍ-ti-co*.
- *Contrarreloj*: *con-tra-rre-LOJ*, trilled *rr*; the final *j* is soft and often barely heard.
- *Baremo*: *ba-RE-mo*; *ponderación*: *pon-de-ra-CIÓN*, 4 syllables.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking the total decides: each group needs 30 of its 50 points.
- Leaving items blank: a wrong answer costs nothing.
- Learning model answers by heart: examiners mark how you handle the task you're given.
- Mixing Mexican and Spain's Spanish in one answer: choose one norm and keep it.
- *Presentar un examen* (Mexico) or *hacer un examen*, not ~~*tomar un examen*~~ for the
  candidate (B1 24).

## Key points

- B2: you understand complex texts and long arguments, talk fluently with native speakers,
  and write clear, detailed texts that weigh options.
- DELE B2: reading 70 min (4 tasks, 36 items), listening 40 min (5 tasks, 30 items, each
  recording twice), writing 80 min (2 tasks of 150–180 words), speaking 20 min after 20 to
  prepare (3 tasks); 25 points each; two groups of 50, at least 30 in each for *apto*.
- Any educated norm of Spanish is accepted if you use it consistently.
- Grammar: the four subjunctive tenses follow the main verb; *si* + pluperfect subjunctive for
  the past; connectors fix or change the mood; tenses shift back after *dijo que*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson. ¡Felicidades! You have finished the core of Spanish B2.

lessons.title: Honors: Vos, usted y tú across the Americas
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since A1 you've used *tú* with friends, *usted* with people you treat formally, and *ustedes*
for "you all", as most Mexicans do. You've also known since A1 that Argentines and Uruguayans
say *vos*. Lesson 24 told you that the DELE accepts any educated norm of Spanish, and in a
Buenos Aires podcast or a Costa Rican series you'll hear *vos tenés, ¿viste?* and parents who
call their children *usted*. This lesson explains how address works in several countries, so
that you understand it when you hear it.

It is for recognition only. This course's norm stays Mexican: keep using *tú* and *usted*.
Nothing here is drilled or asked of you in an answer, and the *vos* forms are shown so you can
recognize them, not to replace yours. B1's honors lesson 24h1 covered regional words; this one
is about grammar: pronouns and verb forms.

## Three ways to say "you" to one person

Spanish has three singular pronouns of address, and countries combine them in different
systems. The facts below follow the RAE's *Diccionario panhispánico de dudas* (DPD, 2005,
entry *voseo*) and a survey of address in the Americas by Miguel Calderón Campos (in *La lengua
española en América: normas y usos actuales*, Universitat de València, 2010).

| Country or region | Familiar | Formal | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mexico (most of it) | *tú* | *usted* | The DPD notes that *vos* survives in parts of Chiapas and Tabasco. |
| Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay | *vos* | *usted* | The DPD calls *voseo* general there, used by every social class. In Montevideo you also hear *tú* with *vos* verb forms (*tú llegás*). |
| Central America | *vos* (with some *tú*) | *usted* | *Voseo* is the general familiar form, according to the DPD. |
| Costa Rica | *vos* | *usted* | *Usted* reaches almost every situation, even among family and friends (Calderón Campos). |
| Chile | *tú* + verb forms of *vos* | *usted* | In familiar speech: *tú sabís*; more careful speech uses ordinary *tú* forms. |
| Colombia | *tú*, *vos* or *usted*, by region | *usted* | *Vos* predominates in Antioquia and the west (DPD); *usted* between friends is frequent, for example in Bogotá. |
| Spain | *tú* | *usted* | Plural *vosotros* (familiar) / *ustedes* (formal). |

So there are names for each habit. *El tuteo* is addressing someone as *tú* (A1's *tutear*);
*el voseo* is using *vos* or its verb forms; and *el ustedeo* is using *usted* where you might
expect *tú*, as a sign of closeness rather than distance. In every country of the Americas the
plural is *ustedes*, for friends and strangers alike.

## The voseo of Argentina and Uruguay

**[[Voseo]]** in the Río de la Plata changes the pronoun and some verb forms. The rest of the
grammar is the same as yours.

![A chart comparing Mexican tú with Río de la Plata vos. Present: tú hablas, vos hablás; tú tienes, vos tenés; tú eres, vos sos; tú vives, vos vivís; tú puedes, vos podés. Commands: ven, vení; di, decí; siéntate, sentate. At the bottom: the same for tú and vos are the preterite (hablaste), the object pronoun te and the possessive tu. Stressed syllables are underlined.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- The present. The stress moves to the ending, and stem changes disappear, because the
  stem is no longer stressed: *vos hablás, comés, vivís*; *tenés, querés, podés, dormís*. Three
  very common verbs are irregular: *vos sos* (*ser*), *vas* (*ir*) and *has* (*haber*).
- The command. Drop the *-r* of the infinitive and stress the last vowel: *hablá, comé,
  viví; vení, decí, poné, salí*. With a pronoun the stress stays put, and no written accent is
  needed: *sentate, fijate, decime*. The DPD notes that *andá* is used for *ir*: *Andá a
  dormir*.
- The preterite is the same as for *tú* in educated speech: *vos hablaste*. A final *-s*
  (*hablastes*) is heard, but the DPD doesn't consider it standard.
- The present subjunctive. The DPD says the educated norm uses the *tú* forms (*Quiero que
  vengas*), even though *vos* forms (*que vengás*) are heard, especially in negative commands
  (*no te preocupés*).
- Pronouns. *Vos* is the subject and follows prepositions (*para vos, con vos*: there is no
  *contigo* form), while the object pronoun is *te* and the possessives are *tu, tuyo*: *Vos
  sabés que tu hermana te quiere.*

## Voseo elsewhere

- Central America. The forms are close to those of the Río de la Plata: *vos tenés, vos
  sos*. *Vos* is familiar; *usted* is used much more widely than in Mexico.
- Chile. In familiar speech many Chileans use the pronoun *tú* with *vos*-type verb endings,
  often with the *-s* weakened: *¿Tú sabís?, ¿Cómo estái?* The DPD describes this as accepted in
  educated familiar speech, while the pronoun *vos* itself is avoided in educated speech there
  and can sound rude.
- Colombia. In Medellín and the rest of Antioquia, *vos* predominates in familiar speech; on the
  Caribbean coast, *tú* dominates.

Why does Spanish have *vos* at all? In medieval Spanish *vos* was a respectful form; over the
centuries it became familiar, and *tú* won out in Spain. A widely repeated explanation for the
map is that regions in close contact with the colonial capitals, Mexico City and Lima, followed
Spain's use of *tú*, while more distant regions kept *vos*. Historians of the language add
other factors, so treat that as a simplification.

## *Ustedeo*: usted as closeness

In Costa Rica, *usted* is used in almost every situation: with a stranger, with a boss, and also
with a brother, a child or a friend. Colombia also has a strong *ustedeo*: a study of
university students in Bogotá cited by Calderón Campos found young men often using *usted* with
male friends of their own age. For a Mexican, *usted* between friends can sound cold; in those
places it can be warm. Listen for the tone, not only the pronoun.

## Regional words that go with the grammar

- *Che* (Argentina, Uruguay): hey; it calls someone's attention or fills a pause. *Che, ¿venís
  mañana?*
- *¿Viste?* (Río de la Plata): you know?, see?, a tag at the end of a sentence. Literally "did
  you see?" (*viste* is the preterite of *ver*).
- *El lunfardo*: the slang of Buenos Aires, usually said to have grown in the late 19th and early 20th centuries in
  the working-class neighborhoods where many immigrants lived. B1's *laburar* (to work) and *el
  pibe* (kid, guy) belong to it.
- *El mate*: an infusion of the dried leaves of *yerba mate*, drunk from a gourd, also called *el
  mate*, through a metal straw. In Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay it is often shared in a circle:
  the same gourd goes from hand to hand.
- *¡Pura vida!* (Costa Rica): all good, great; also hello, thanks or goodbye.
- *El tico, la tica*: a Costa Rican, informally; Costa Ricans use the word themselves. It is
  usually explained by their fondness for the diminutive *-ico* (*chiquitico*).
- *La tonada*: the lilt or melody of a regional accent. Argentines talk about *la tonada
  cordobesa*; Mexicans hear a *tonada* in the speech of the north or of Yucatán.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: reading a message in *voseo*

Martina, from Rosario, sends a voice note to her Mexican friend Lupita. Read it, then see how it
would sound in Mexican Spanish.

> *Che, Lupita, ¿cómo andás? ¿Ya llegaste a Buenos Aires? Si querés, el sábado te paso a buscar
> y vamos a la feria de San Telmo. Traé ropa cómoda, ¿viste?, que se camina mucho. Y no te
> olvidés del protector solar. Avisame cuando puedas.*

Step by step:

1. Find the *vos* verbs: *andás, querés, traé, olvidés, avisame*. *Llegaste* is a preterite: the
   same as for *tú*.
2. Change each one to *tú*: *andas, quieres, trae, olvides, avísame*. Notice the stem change
   that comes back in *quieres*, and the written accent that *avísame* needs once the stress
   falls on *vi*.
3. Change the regional words: *Che* → *Oye*; *¿viste?* → *¿sabes?*; *te paso a buscar* → *paso
   por ti*; *el protector solar* → *el bloqueador* (Mexico).

> *Oye, Lupita, ¿cómo andas? ¿Ya llegaste a Buenos Aires? Si quieres, el sábado paso por ti y
> vamos a la feria de San Telmo. Trae ropa cómoda, ¿sabes?, porque se camina mucho. Y no te
> olvides del bloqueador. Avísame cuando puedas.*

> Hey, Lupita, how's it going? Have you arrived in Buenos Aires yet? If you want, I'll pick you
> up on Saturday and we'll go to the San Telmo market. Bring comfortable clothes, you know,
> because there's a lot of walking. And don't forget your sunscreen. Let me know when you can.

### Example 2: choosing how to address people when you travel

Task: you're spending a semester in San José, Costa Rica, then a month in Montevideo. Which
forms should you use?

1. Keep your own system. Your Mexican *tú* and *usted* are understood everywhere, and an
   educated foreigner who speaks one variety consistently sounds natural.
2. Follow the other person's lead with *usted*. If a Costa Rican friend calls you *usted*, it
   isn't distance. Your *tú* will be understood, but the DPD notes that Costa Ricans can hear
   *tuteo* as affected, so *usted* often fits in better.
3. Don't build your own mixture. Some mixtures are local norms (*tú llegás* in Montevideo, *tú
   sabís* in Chile), but a learner who mixes sounds undecided.
4. Imitate *vos* only if you learn it fully. A half-learned *voseo* (*vos tienes, vos eres*)
   is worse than a good *tuteo*.

## Conversation: tres maneras de decir "tú"

Lupita, from Guadalajara, is studying in San José, Costa Rica. In a café she meets her
classmate Andrés, a Costa Rican, and Martina, an Argentine on an exchange.

> Andrés: ¡Hola, Lupita! ¿Cómo está? Le presento a Martina, una compañera de Argentina.
>
> Lupita: ¡Mucho gusto! Oye, Andrés, ¿por qué me hablas de usted? ¿Estás enojado conmigo?
>
> Andrés: ¡Para nada! Aquí en Costa Rica uno le dice "usted" hasta a la mamá. Es de cariño.
>
> Martina: ¡Qué lindo! En Argentina es al revés: a mi abuela le hablo de vos. ¿Y vos, Lupita, de dónde sos?
>
> Lupita: De Guadalajara. Espera, ¿"sos" es "eres"?
>
> Martina: Claro. Y "tenés" es "tienes", ¿viste? Es fácil: el acento va al final.
>
> Andrés: Los ticos también usamos "vos", pero más con los amigos. Con desconocidos, usted.
>
> Lupita: ¡Qué enredo! En México es más sencillo: tú para los amigos y usted para los mayores o los jefes.
>
> Martina: Che, ¿y ustedes quieren probar un mate? Traje la yerba desde Rosario.
>
> Andrés: ¡Pura vida! Yo traigo el agua caliente.
>
> Lupita: Bueno, pero ustedes me enseñan cómo se toma. ¡No quiero quedar mal!

> Andrés: Hi, Lupita! How are you? Let me introduce Martina, a classmate from Argentina.
>
> Lupita: Nice to meet you! Hey, Andrés, why are you calling me "usted"? Are you mad at me?
>
> Andrés: Not at all! Here in Costa Rica people say "usted" even to their mom. It's affectionate.
>
> Martina: How sweet! In Argentina it's the other way around: I call my grandma "vos". And you, Lupita, where are you from?
>
> Lupita: From Guadalajara. Wait, is "sos" "eres"?
>
> Martina: Sure. And "tenés" is "tienes", see? It's easy: the stress goes at the end.
>
> Andrés: We Ticos use "vos" too, but more with friends. With strangers, "usted".
>
> Lupita: What a tangle! In Mexico it's simpler: "tú" for friends, and "usted" for older people or bosses.
>
> Martina: Hey, do you two want to try some mate? I brought the yerba from Rosario.
>
> Andrés: Great! I'll bring the hot water.
>
> Lupita: OK, but you'll have to show me how to drink it. I don't want to make a fool of myself!

*Hablarle de usted / de vos* = to address someone as *usted* / *vos*; *el enredo* = tangle, mess;
*quedar mal* = to look bad, to make a bad impression. Lupita's *En México es más sencillo* is her
impression: Mexicans also adjust their *tú* and *usted* by family, region and age.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking *voseo* is incorrect or uneducated: in the Río de la Plata every social class uses
  it, and the DPD notes that the Academia Argentina de Letras recognizes it as legitimate.
- Mixing *vos* with *tú* forms (~~*vos tienes*~~) when you imitate it.
- Reading *usted* in Costa Rica or Bogotá as coldness.
- Forgetting that *vos* forms have their own stress: *sentate* is *sen-TA-te*, *tenés* is
  *te-NÉS*.

## Key points

- *Tuteo*, *voseo* and *ustedeo*: Mexico uses *tú / usted*; the Río de la Plata *vos / usted*;
  Costa Rica *vos / usted*, with *usted* almost everywhere; Chile mixes *tú* with *vos* endings
  in familiar speech.
- Río de la Plata forms: present *hablás, tenés, sos*; command *hablá, vení, decí*; preterite as
  for *tú*; object *te*, possessive *tu*; after prepositions *vos*.
- The plural is *ustedes* in all of the Americas.
- Recognition only: keep your Mexican *tú* and *usted*, and use one system consistently.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: DELE B2 writing and speaking in practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 23 gave you a method for writing and lesson 24 described the DELE B2. This lesson puts
both to work: two original writing tasks in the exam's general format, each with a plan, a
model answer and the edits that turned a first draft into a second one, then plans and models
for the three speaking tasks, with a way to manage the 20 minutes of preparation. Every task
here was written for this course: none is taken from the exam or its model papers. Read the
models for their structure, not to learn them by heart: examiners mark how you handle the task
in front of you.

## Writing

### Example 1: a letter from notes

Task (in the style of writing task 1): *You heard a short radio report about your city's new
program to collect food waste from homes. Write an e-mail of 150–180 words to the city's
environment office: say what you heard, give your opinion, and ask one question.*

Lupe's notes while listening were short, as yours should be: *recolección de residuos
orgánicos — desde el 1 de junio — martes y viernes — bote café gratis — composta para parques —
multa si se mezcla*. Her plan: paragraph 1, what she heard; paragraph 2, her opinion with two
reasons; paragraph 3, a doubt and a question; a formal closing.

> Estimados señores:
>
> Les escribo en relación con el nuevo programa de recolección de residuos orgánicos que se
> presentó ayer en la radio. Según la información, a partir del 1 de junio pasarán por las
> casas los martes y los viernes, cada familia recibirá un bote café gratuito, y los residuos se
> convertirán en composta para los parques de la ciudad.
>
> Me parece una iniciativa excelente. Por un lado, casi la mitad de lo que tiramos en mi casa es
> comida, de modo que el volumen de basura se reducirá mucho. Por otro, me gusta que lo que
> sale de nuestras cocinas vuelva a la ciudad en forma de áreas verdes.
>
> No obstante, tengo una duda. En la radio se dijo que habrá multas para quien mezcle los
> residuos. ¿Habrá algún periodo de aprendizaje antes de aplicarlas? Muchos vecinos mayores
> necesitarán tiempo para acostumbrarse.
>
> Les agradezco de antemano su respuesta.
>
> Atentamente,
>
> Guadalupe Torres

> Dear Sir or Madam,
>
> I am writing about the new organic waste collection program that was presented on the radio
> yesterday. According to the information, from June 1 they will come by people's homes on
> Tuesdays and Fridays, each family will receive a free brown bin, and the waste will be turned
> into compost for the city's parks.
>
> I think it is an excellent initiative. On the one hand, almost half of what we throw away in
> my house is food, so the volume of garbage will go down a lot. On the other, I like the fact
> that what leaves our kitchens comes back to the city as green spaces.
>
> However, I have a question. On the radio it was said that there will be fines for anyone who
> mixes the waste. Will there be a learning period before they are applied? Many older
> neighbors will need time to get used to it.
>
> Thank you in advance for your reply.
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Guadalupe Torres

The model has 152 words from greeting to signature. It reports (paragraph 1), gives an opinion
with reasons (2) and asks (3), so every point of the task is covered. Lupe's first draft had
four problems, and her second draft fixed them:

1. It ran to 196 words. She cut a sentence about her own garden: interesting, but not asked
   for.
2. *En la radio dijeron* became *se dijo*: more formal, and the impersonal *se* (lesson 14)
   fits a letter to an office.
3. She had written *la mitad de lo que tiramos es comida, entonces…*; *de modo que* is the
   written connector of consequence.
4. *Creo que habrá multas* became a question: the task asked for one, and her draft had none.

### Example 2: an opinion piece from data

Task (in the style of the graph option of task 2): *A news item reports that more and more
young people get their news from social media. Write an opinion piece of 150–180 words for a
youth magazine commenting on the data below and giving your opinion.*

| Main source of news, people aged 18–25 (invented data) | 2016 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Social media | 38% | 64% |
| TV | 35% | 14% |
| News websites and apps | 19% | 17% |
| Print and radio | 8% | 5% |

> ¿Nos informan las redes o nos entretienen?
>
> Según los datos del estudio, en diez años el porcentaje de jóvenes que se informan
> principalmente por redes sociales ha pasado del 38 % al 64 %, mientras que la televisión ha
> caído del 35 % al 14 %. Los sitios de noticias se mantienen casi igual.
>
> A mi modo de ver, el cambio no es sorprendente: las redes son rápidas, gratuitas y están en
> el bolsillo de todos. Lo preocupante es que sus algoritmos no distinguen entre información y
> entretenimiento, y premian lo que provoca emociones fuertes, no lo que es cierto.
>
> Eso no significa que debamos abandonarlas. Lo que propongo es aprender a usarlas mejor:
> seguir a medios con periodistas profesionales, comprobar una noticia antes de compartirla y
> leer de vez en cuando algo más largo que una publicación.
>
> En definitiva, las redes pueden informarnos, siempre y cuando no les dejemos todo el trabajo
> a ellas. La responsabilidad de estar bien informados sigue siendo nuestra.

> Do social networks inform us or entertain us?
>
> According to the study's data, in ten years the percentage of young people who get their news
> mainly from social media has gone from 38% to 64%, while television has fallen from 35% to
> 14%. News websites have stayed almost the same.
>
> As I see it, the change isn't surprising: social media is fast, free and in everyone's pocket.
> What's worrying is that their algorithms don't tell information from entertainment, and they
> reward what provokes strong emotions, not what's true.
>
> That doesn't mean we should abandon it. What I propose is learning to use it better: following
> outlets with professional journalists, checking a news story before sharing it, and reading
> something longer than a post now and then.
>
> In short, social media can inform us, as long as we don't leave all the work to it. The
> responsibility for being well informed is still ours.

The article has 153 words, title not counted. Its first paragraph describes the data without
opinion; the second interprets it; the third proposes; the fourth concludes with *siempre y
cuando* + subjunctive (lesson 12). *El algoritmo* is a word from honors 16h2 (algorithm). In
the second draft the writer changed *muchísimo* to the figures themselves and replaced a
repeated *las redes sociales* with *las redes* and *las*, which avoids reiteration (lesson 23).

## Speaking

### The 20 minutes of preparation

You prepare tasks 1 and 2 together, so *la gestión del tiempo* (time management) starts before
you say a word.

![Two bars. The first shows the 20 minutes of preparation: minutes 0 to 10 for task 1 (read, weigh, notes), minutes 10 to 18 for task 2 (photo, key words), and minutes 18 to 20 to review. The second shows the test itself, about 20 minutes: task 1, 6 to 7 minutes; task 2, 5 to 6 minutes; task 3, 3 to 4 minutes, with no preparation for task 3.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Write *notas de apoyo* (prompt notes): key words and connectors, never full sentences, because
you can't read sentences aloud naturally. A *mapa conceptual* (concept map) works well for task
1: the problem in the middle, the proposals around it, a plus or a minus by each.

### Example 3: task 1, weighing proposals

Problem (invented): *In many cities, traffic around schools at 8 a.m. is chaotic.* The card lists
six proposals: a school bus, staggered start times, closing the street for an hour, a "walking
bus" of parents, fines for double parking, and a campaign to come by bike.

Notes: *problema → 3 caras: seguridad, contaminación, tiempo / (+) camión escolar: menos autos
(−) caro / (+) horarios escalonados: fácil, barato / (−) multas: no educan / elijo: horarios +
camión*.

> Bueno, el problema tiene tres caras: la seguridad de los niños, la contaminación y el tiempo
> que perdemos todos. De las propuestas, la que me parece más fácil de aplicar es la de los
> horarios escalonados: si unos grupos entraran a las siete y media y otros a las ocho y cuarto,
> el tráfico se repartiría sin gastar un peso. El camión escolar sería la mejor solución a
