> largo plazo, aunque saldría caro. En cambio, las multas no me convencen: castigan, pero no educan.
> Así que yo combinaría las dos primeras.

> Well, the problem has three sides: the children's safety, pollution and the time we all waste.
> Of the proposals, the one that seems easiest to put into practice is staggered start times: if
> some groups came in at seven thirty and others at a quarter past eight, the traffic would be
> spread out without spending a peso. The school bus would be the best solution in the long
> run, although it would be expensive. On the other hand, the fines don't convince me: they punish, but
> they don't educate. So I'd combine the first two.

After the monologue comes the conversation. Wait for your *turno de palabra* (turn to speak),
answer the examiner's objection directly, and give a reason: *Entiendo lo que dice, pero…*.

### Example 4: task 2, an imagined situation

The photo (described here in words): *in an airport, a woman sits on a suitcase looking at her
phone; behind her, a departures board full of red letters.*

> En la foto veo a una mujer de unos treinta años en un aeropuerto. Está sentada sobre su
> maleta y mira el celular con cara de preocupación. Al fondo hay una pantalla de salidas con
> muchos vuelos en rojo, así que supongo que han cancelado vuelos, quizás por el mal tiempo.
> Me imagino que tenía una reunión importante y que ahora está escribiéndole a su jefe. Si yo
> estuviera en su lugar, buscaría primero un vuelo para el día siguiente y después un hotel.

> In the photo I see a woman of about thirty in an airport. She's sitting on her suitcase and
> looking at her phone with a worried face. In the background there's a departures screen with
> lots of flights in red, so I suppose flights have been canceled, maybe because of bad weather.
> I imagine she had an important meeting and that she's now writing to her boss. If I were in
> her place, I'd first look for a flight for the next day and then a hotel.

The order is general → detail → hypothesis → what you would do: *Al fondo, supongo que,
me imagino que, si yo estuviera…*.

### Example 5: task 3, survey results

Invented survey: *62% of people say they check their phone within five minutes of waking up.*
Task 3 has no preparation, so *la improvisación* is part of the task: *improvisar* well means
reacting, giving one example and asking back.

> Examinadora: ¿Le sorprende el dato?
>
> Candidato: La verdad, no. Bueno… yo mismo lo hago: lo primero que veo es la alarma, y ya que
> tengo el celular en la mano, reviso los mensajes.
>
> Examinadora: ¿Y le parece un problema?
>
> Candidato: Depende. Si es un minuto, no. Lo malo es cuando… a ver, ¿cómo lo digo?… cuando
> uno empieza el día respondiendo a los demás en lugar de pensar en lo suyo. ¿Usted también
> lo hace?

> Examiner: Does the figure surprise you?
>
> Candidate: Honestly, no. Well… I do it myself: the first thing I see is the alarm, and since
> the phone is in my hand, I check my messages.
>
> Examiner: And do you think it's a problem?
>
> Candidate: It depends. If it's a minute, no. The bad thing is when… let's see, how do I put
> it?… when you start the day answering other people instead of thinking about your own
> things. Do you do it too?

## Fluency: pauses and hesitation

*La soltura* (ease, fluency) doesn't mean speaking without stopping. Native speakers make a
*pausa* (pause) to think and show *vacilación* (hesitation) too; what matters is filling the gap
with Spanish, not with silence or English.

| To gain time | To rephrase | To pick up the thread |
|---|---|---|
| *Bueno… / A ver… / Pues…* | *Lo que quiero decir es que…* | *Como decía…* |
| *¿Cómo lo diría?* | *Mejor dicho…* | *Volviendo a lo de antes…* |
| *Es una buena pregunta.* | *O sea…* | *Retomando lo que decía usted…* |

If you lose your place, *retomar el hilo* (pick up the thread) with one of the phrases in the
third column. Practice the whole speaking test with a timer and record yourself: you'll hear
where you stop and which phrases you overuse.

## Common mistakes

- Writing full sentences in the 20 minutes and then reading them aloud.
- Describing the photo for five minutes without imagining anything: task 2 asks you to imagine
  the situation.
- Agreeing with everything in task 1's conversation: a reasoned disagreement shows more range.
- Answering task 3 in one word. React, explain, give an example, ask back.
- Learning a model answer by heart: an off-topic answer scores poorly however correct it is.

## Key points

- Writing: notes → plan → draft → second draft. Cut what the task doesn't ask for, raise the
  register, check that every point is covered and count the words.
- Speaking: about 10 minutes of preparation for task 1 and 8 for task 2, with prompt notes in
  key words or a concept map.
- Task 1: weigh the proposals, say which you prefer and why, then debate. Task 2: describe, imagine, hypothesize. Task 3:
  react, explain, ask back.
- Pauses are normal: fill them with *bueno, a ver, lo que quiero decir es que*, and pick up the
  thread with *como decía*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Cine latinoamericano
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

B1's lesson 23 taught you to write a review: did you like the film, and should others see it?
This lesson is about film history and analysis: how Mexican cinema became one of the strongest
in the Spanish-speaking world, which directors you should know, and how to talk about a film's
plot, its shooting and its reception. It uses two tools from this course: the passive (*fue
rodada en…, fue nominada a…*, lesson 14) and relative clauses (*la película cuyo guion…, el
director, quien…*, lesson 09).

No film dialogue is quoted here: scripts are protected by copyright, so you'll find titles,
names and facts only, and the plots are told in this course's own words. Look the films up and
watch them, with Spanish subtitles if you can.

## A timeline

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1936 | *Allá en el Rancho Grande*, directed by Fernando de Fuentes, premieres; it is usually taken as the start of the Golden Age. |
| 1944 | *María Candelaria*, directed by Emilio Fernández and photographed by Gabriel Figueroa, with Dolores del Río, is released (it was shot in 1943). |
| 1946 | *María Candelaria* is among the films given the top award at the first Cannes festival. |
| 1950 | Luis Buñuel's *Los olvidados* premieres in Mexico on December 9. |
| 1951 | Buñuel wins the award for best director at Cannes for *Los olvidados*. |
| 1957 | Pedro Infante dies (April 15), one of the events that mark the end of the Golden Age. |
| 1991 | María Novaro's *Danzón*. |
| 2001 | Lucrecia Martel's *La ciénaga* wins the Alfred Bauer Prize at the Berlin festival. |
| 2014–2019 | Mexican directors win five Oscars for best director in six years (details below). |
| 2023 | Guillermo del Toro's *Pinocho* (*Pinocchio*) wins the Oscar for best animated feature. |

## The Golden Age of Mexican cinema

The *Época de Oro* (Golden Age) is usually dated from 1936 to the mid-1950s; one common account
runs it from *Allá en el Rancho Grande* to 1956. During the Second World War, the film
industries of the United States and Europe produced less for Latin American audiences, and
Mexico's studios filled the gap with comedies, melodramas and musical films about the
countryside, sold across the continent. Stars such as Dolores del Río and Pedro Infante, the
director Emilio "el Indio" Fernández and the cinematographer Gabriel Figueroa, famous for his
skies and clouds in black and white, became known far beyond Mexico. The period's end is
usually linked to the spread of television in the 1950s, the closing of several studios in
1957 and 1958, and the death of Pedro Infante in 1957.

## Buñuel and *Los olvidados*

Luis Buñuel was a Spanish director who had settled in Mexico, where he made most of his films
of the 1940s and 1950s. *Los olvidados* (The Forgotten Ones, 1950) was shot in the poor
neighborhoods on the edge of Mexico City. In this course's own words: it follows a group of
boys who live on the street, led by an older one who has escaped from a reform school, and a
younger boy who tries to stay out of trouble and is dragged down with them. It refuses the
comforting endings of the melodramas of its time.

The film caused an uproar in Mexico: it premiered on December 9, 1950, and was pulled from
theaters after a few days. The next year Buñuel won the award for best director at Cannes, and
the film's reputation changed. In 2003 UNESCO added the film to its Memory of the World
register.

## Directors of today

Three Mexican directors born in the 1960s are often mentioned together:

| Director | Oscars (ceremony year) |
|---|---|
| Alfonso Cuarón | best director for *Gravity* (*Gravedad*, 2014); best director, best cinematography and best foreign-language film for *Roma* (2019) |
| Alejandro G. Iñárritu | best picture, best director and best original screenplay for *Birdman* (2015); best director for *The Revenant* (*El renacido*, 2016) |
| Guillermo del Toro | best director for *The Shape of Water* (*La forma del agua*, 2018), which also won best picture; best animated feature for *Pinocho* (2023) |

The Oscars are given early in the year after a film's release, so *Roma*, released in 2018,
won at the 2019 ceremony. Between 2014 and 2019 a Mexican-born director won the Oscar for best
director five times. The cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, also Mexican, won three Oscars in a
row for best cinematography (2014, 2015 and 2016), for *Gravity*, *Birdman* and *The Revenant*.

Two women directors to know:

- María Novaro (born in Mexico City in 1951) made *Danzón* (1991), in which a telephone operator
  from Mexico City who lives for the *danzón* dance halls travels to Veracruz to look for her
  missing dance partner, and finds something else: herself. The film was shown at Cannes in
  1991.
- Lucrecia Martel, from Salta, Argentina, made *La ciénaga* (The Swamp, 2001), her first feature:
  two middle-class families in decline spend a hot, heavy summer together. It won the Alfred
  Bauer Prize at the Berlin festival in 2001.

## The words of film

![A film set, labeled in Spanish. A camera on a tripod (la cámara) points at an actress sitting at a table, with a script (el guion) on the table. A boom microphone (el micrófono) hangs over her head; a studio light (el reflector) stands to one side; a clapperboard (la claqueta) lies on a folding chair.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *El largometraje* is a feature film; *el cortometraje* (or informally *el corto*) a short.
- *El guionista, la guionista* writes *el guion* (B1), the script.
- *El rodaje* is the shooting of a film; *rodar* is to shoot it: *La película se rodó en
  Veracruz.* *Rodar* has the *o → ue* stem change: *ruedo, ruedas, rueda, rodamos, ruedan*. It
  also means to roll: *La pelota rodó por la calle.*
- *La cinematografía* is the art of photographing a film, and also the cinema of a country as a
  whole: *la cinematografía mexicana*.
- *La cartelera* lists what's showing: *¿Qué hay en cartelera?* A film *está en cartelera*
  while it's in theaters.
- *Un éxito de taquilla* is a box-office hit (A2's *la taquilla*).
- *Nominado* (nominated): *Fue nominada a cinco premios.* *La nominación* is the nomination.

On the set in the picture you can see *la cámara* (camera), *el micrófono* (microphone), *el
reflector* (studio light), *la claqueta* (clapperboard) and *el guion*.

## Talking about a film: plot, shooting, reception

A short analysis usually covers three things, and B2 grammar makes each one precise.

- The plot (*la trama*, B1): use the present, as for any story, and relatives to add
  information: *una madre cuyo hijo desaparece*, *un pueblo en el que nunca pasa nada*.
- The shooting: the *ser* passive and the *se* passive, because what matters is the film, not
  who held the camera: *Fue rodada en blanco y negro. Se filmó en exteriores reales.*
- The reception: the passive again, with dates: *Fue estrenada en 1950 y retirada de la
  cartelera a los pocos días. Fue nominada a diez premios.*

### Example 1: *Roma* in three sentences

Task: present *Roma* with one passive, one relative clause and one fact about its reception.

1. *Roma (2018) fue escrita, dirigida y fotografiada por Alfonso Cuarón.* (Roma was written,
   directed and photographed by Alfonso Cuarón.) Three participles, all feminine to agree with
   *la película*.
2. *Es una película en blanco y negro, ambientada en la colonia Roma de la Ciudad de México a
   principios de los años setenta, cuya protagonista es una trabajadora del hogar.* (It's a
   black-and-white film set in the Roma neighborhood of Mexico City in the early seventies,
   whose main character is a domestic worker.) *Cuya* agrees with *protagonista*, the thing
   possessed.
3. *En 2019 ganó tres premios Óscar, entre ellos el de mejor director.* (In 2019 it won three
   Oscars, among them best director.)

Check: *fue escrita* agrees with *Roma*; *cuya* follows the noun after it; the ceremony year,
not the release year, goes with the award.

### Example 2: a critical paragraph

Task: write a short critical paragraph (history and analysis, not "I liked it") about a film.
The short film below is invented, so the analysis can be original (115 words).

> *Agua de mayo* es un cortometraje de quince minutos que fue rodado en una sola semana en un
> pueblo de la sierra de Puebla. Su guionista y directora, que debutó con este trabajo, cuenta
> la historia de una niña cuyo padre se fue a trabajar al norte. La película se apoya casi por
> completo en la imagen: la cinematografía, con largos planos fijos y luz natural, sustituye a
> los diálogos, lo cual exige paciencia al espectador. Aunque el final es previsible, el corto
> fue seleccionado en varios festivales y nominado a un premio Ariel, algo poco común para una
> primera obra. Es, sobre todo, una mirada honesta a las familias que la migración deja atrás.

> *Agua de mayo* (May Rain) is a fifteen-minute short film that was shot in a single week in a
> village in the mountains of Puebla. Its screenwriter and director, who made her debut with
> this work, tells the story of a girl whose father has gone north to work. The film relies
> almost entirely on images: the cinematography, with long still shots and natural light,
> takes the place of dialogue, which demands patience from the viewer. Although the ending is
> predictable, the short was selected at several festivals and nominated for an Ariel award,
> something unusual for a first work. It is, above all, an honest look at the families that
> migration leaves behind.

*Debutar* = to make one's debut; *el plano fijo* = a still shot; *previsible* = predictable. The
paragraph combines the *ser* passive (*fue rodado, fue seleccionado*), *cuyo*, *lo cual* for a
whole idea, *aunque* + indicative for a fact, and a final judgment based on what the film does.
The Ariel is the award of Mexico's film academy, the Academia Mexicana de Artes y Ciencias
Cinematográficas.

## Common mistakes

- ~~*La película fue dirigido por…*~~ → *fue dirigida*: the participle agrees with the subject.
- ~~*Rodo una película*~~ → *ruedo* (stem change); but *rodamos, rodé, rodaba* have no change.
- Confusing the release year with the award year: *Roma* came out in 2018 and won its Oscars in
  2019.
- English capitals in Spanish titles: *Los olvidados*, *La forma del agua*, not ~~*Los
  Olvidados*~~.
- Quoting dialogue in a text you publish: describe the scene instead (*En la escena final, la
  protagonista…*).

## Key points

- Golden Age: from 1936 (*Allá en el Rancho Grande*) to the mid-1950s; Fernández, Figueroa,
  Dolores del Río, Pedro Infante.
- Buñuel's *Los olvidados* (1950): pulled from theaters at first, best director at Cannes in
  1951.
- Cuarón, Iñárritu and del Toro: five Oscars for best director between 2014 and 2019; Lubezki,
  three for cinematography; Novaro's *Danzón* (1991) and Martel's *La ciénaga* (2001).
- Analyze a film with the passive (*fue rodada, se estrenó*), relatives (*cuyo, lo cual*) and
  the film words *el largometraje, el rodaje, la cartelera, el éxito de taquilla, la
  nominación*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: El cuento latinoamericano: the short story
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Spanish A2 taught *el cuento* (short story) and B1 the words for discussing one: *el narrador, la
trama, el desenlace*. This lesson reads the short story as a Latin American strength. You'll meet
seven writers through facts and short retellings, learn what makes a story **[[fantastic literature]]**,
and practice three reading strategies on an original story that uses every past
tense of this course, the subjunctive and the tenses of probability.

## Seven writers

Look for them in anthologies (*antologías*) or in the free Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes
(cervantesvirtual.com).

- Horacio Quiroga (Salto, Uruguay, 1878 – Buenos Aires, 1937) set many stories in the jungle of
  Misiones, Argentina, where he lived for years. In "El almohadón de plumas" (in *Cuentos de amor
  de locura y de muerte*, 1917) a young wife weakens day by day, and after her death a creature is
  found in her feather pillow. In 1927 he published ten pieces of advice for story writers.
- Jorge Luis Borges (Buenos Aires, 1899 – Geneva, 1986): labyrinths, mirrors and infinite libraries, in
  *Ficciones* (1944) and *El Aleph* (1949). In "El Aleph" a man is shown, in a cellar, a tiny
  point that contains every place in the universe.
- Julio Cortázar (Brussels, 1914 – Paris, 1984; Argentine). In "Casa tomada" (1946, collected in
  *Bestiario*, 1951) a brother and sister lose their old house, room by room, to something never
  named.
- Juan Rulfo (Jalisco, 1917 – Mexico City, 1986) is known for two books: *El llano en llamas* (1953,
  fifteen stories in the first edition) and the novel *Pedro Páramo* (1955). In "¡Diles que no me
  maten!" an old man who killed someone decades ago begs for his life; the colonel who holds him
  is the dead man's son.
- Juan José Arreola (Ciudad Guzmán, Jalisco, 1918 – Guadalajara, 2001): short, ironic pieces in
  *Confabulario* (1952). In "El guardagujas" (the switchman), his most anthologized story, an old
  railway employee describes to a traveler a train system so absurd that a ticket guarantees
  nothing.
- Elena Garro (Puebla, 1916 – Cuernavaca, 1998): the novel *Los recuerdos del porvenir* (1963,
  Premio Xavier Villaurrutia) and the stories of *La semana de colores* (1964). In "La culpa es
  de los tlaxcaltecas" a woman keeps slipping into the time of the Spanish conquest.
- Augusto Monterroso (Tegucigalpa, Honduras, 1921 – Mexico City, 2003; Guatemalan, in Mexico
  from 1944), master of *el microrrelato*. *El dinosaurio*, in *Obras completas (y otros
  cuentos)* (1959), is one sentence of seven words about waking up; the reader imagines the rest.
  Premio Príncipe de Asturias, 2000.

## Realism, the fantastic and magical realism

*El realismo* shows a world that works like ours: the violence and poverty in most of *El llano en
llamas* are *verosímiles* (believable). In fantastic literature (*lo fantástico*), something
*inverosímil* (impossible by the rules of our world) breaks into an ordinary setting, and neither
the characters nor the reader can explain it: Cortázar's house, Quiroga's pillow. **[[Magical realism]]**
(B1's *el realismo mágico*), the label made famous by Gabriel García Márquez, tells impossible
events calmly, as if they were normal. Critics often call Garro a forerunner of it, though she
rejected the label. The labels
are used loosely: take them as tendencies, not boxes.

A fantastic story works through *la ambientación* (the setting, made concrete), *la atmósfera*
(the mood the details create) and *la intriga* (the suspense that keeps you reading). Many feel
*oníricos*, dreamlike. The picture shows a common shape.

![A rising line in five steps, from left to right. Step 1, low on the left: el mundo cotidiano, a small house. Step 2: la primera señal, a question mark. Step 3: la tensión crece, three stacked arrows going up. Step 4, at the top: el clímax, a star. Step 5, the line drops a little to the right: el final ambiguo, a key with a question mark, because an object or clue remains.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Three reading strategies

1. Time. Map the tenses: the imperfect sets the background (*olía a café*), the preterite
   moves the plot (*bajó un muchacho*), the pluperfect jumps back (*la habían llamado del
   hospital*). The future and conditional of probability (lesson 08) show a character guessing:
   *Tendría unos veinte años* (He must have been about twenty).
2. The narrator. Who tells the story, and what does that voice know? An **[[omniscient narrator]]**
   knows everything; a third-person narrator may stay with one character and know only what she
   sees; a first-person narrator (*yo*) may be wrong.
3. Inference. Fantastic stories rarely explain. Collect the text's clues and draw your
   own conclusion (an **[[inference]]**), then check it against every detail.

## The story

Read it once for the plot, then for the tenses and clues. *El camión* is the usual word for a bus
in much of Mexico.

> #### La sala de espera
>
> El autobús se descompuso a las diez y media de la noche, en medio de un valle que Julia no
> conocía. El chofer revisó el motor con una linterna, habló por teléfono y anunció que el camión
> de reemplazo no llegaría hasta las seis de la mañana. Algunos pasajeros se acomodaron para
> dormir; otros salieron a fumar bajo la llovizna. Julia no podía quedarse quieta. Esa tarde la
> habían llamado del hospital de San Gabriel: su padre, que había trabajado cuarenta años en el
> ferrocarril, estaba muy grave.
>
> —Allá adelante está la vieja estación —le dijo el chofer, señalando una luz entre los
> árboles—. Hace años que no pasan trenes, pero por lo menos tiene techo.
>
> Julia caminó por la orilla de la carretera hasta un edificio de ladrillo con un reloj redondo
> sobre la puerta. Le sorprendió que la sala de espera estuviera iluminada. Adentro olía a café y
> a madera húmeda. Detrás de una ventanilla, un empleado de bigote blanco escribía en un cuaderno
> con una pluma de las antiguas.
>
> —Buenas noches —dijo Julia—. ¿Todavía pasan trenes por aquí?
>
> —Todas las noches, señorita —contestó el empleado, sin levantar la vista—. El de las once
> cuarenta va a San Gabriel. ¿Le doy su boleto?
>
> Julia pensó que sería una broma, pero sacó la cartera. El hombre no quiso aceptar su dinero. Le
> entregó un boleto de cartón amarillo, como los que su padre guardaba en una caja de galletas, y
> volvió a su cuaderno.
>
> En las bancas había una docena de pasajeros. Una señora con un rebozo gris tenía en las piernas
> una canasta de pan dulce. Un niño con uniforme escolar y una gorra de otra época leía una
> historieta. Un señor de sombrero miraba la puerta como si esperara a alguien que llevaba mucho
> tiempo sin llegar. Nadie hablaba por teléfono; nadie miraba una pantalla. Julia sacó su celular
> para llamar al hospital y vio que no tenía señal.
>
> Se sentó junto a la señora del rebozo. El reloj de la pared marcaba las once y cuarto. Julia
> esperó un rato largo, se levantó, caminó hasta la ventana, regresó. Cuando volvió a mirar el
> reloj, seguía marcando las once y cuarto.
>
> —Ese reloj está descompuesto —comentó.
>
> —No, mija —le dijo la señora, y le ofreció una concha—. Aquí el tiempo camina distinto. Todos
> estamos esperando a alguien.
>
> —¿A quién espera usted?
>
> —A mi hijo. Se fue al norte en un tren como este y me prometió que volvería en uno igual.
>
> Julia habría querido preguntarle cuánto tiempo llevaba esperando, pero algo en la voz de la
> señora se lo impidió. Mordió la concha, que estaba tibia, como recién salida del horno.
>
> Entonces se oyó a lo lejos un silbato largo. Los pasajeros se pusieron de pie al mismo tiempo,
> sin prisa, como si hubieran ensayado ese movimiento muchas veces. Una luz blanca entró por las
> ventanas y el piso empezó a temblar. Julia salió al andén. El tren, negro y brillante, soltaba
> un vapor que ocultaba las ruedas. No se parecía a ningún tren que ella hubiera visto, salvo en
> las fotos de la caja de galletas.
>
> De uno de los vagones bajó un muchacho con uniforme de ferrocarrilero. Tendría unos veinte
> años. Julia lo reconoció antes de verle bien la cara: tenía la misma manera de ladear la cabeza
> que su padre, la misma cicatriz en la ceja, cuyo origen él nunca había querido contar. El
> muchacho caminó hacia ella, se quitó la gorra y sonrió.
>
> —No te preocupes, flaca —le dijo. Así la llamaba su padre cuando ella era niña—. Ya me toca
> irme. Y tú ya llegaste lejos.
>
> Julia quiso contestar, pero no le salió la voz. El muchacho le puso algo frío en la mano, le
> cerró los dedos con cuidado y subió de nuevo al vagón. La señora del rebozo, el niño de la
> historieta y el señor del sombrero subieron detrás de él. El tren se fue alejando sin ruido,
> hasta que solo quedó la neblina.
>
> La despertó el chofer, sacudiéndole el hombro.
>
> —Señorita, ya llegó el camión. ¿Qué hacía aquí? Este lugar está cerrado desde hace veinte
> años.
>
> Julia miró a su alrededor. La sala de espera no tenía techo; entre las bancas rotas crecía la
> hierba, y donde había estado el reloj solo quedaba un círculo más claro en la pared. No había
> ventanilla, ni empleado, ni olor a café. Habrá sido un sueño, pensó. Habré caminado dormida.
>
> En el teléfono tenía una llamada perdida del hospital, de las once cuarenta.
>
> Julia abrió la mano. Sobre la palma tenía un reloj de bolsillo, viejo, con una locomotora
> grabada en la tapa. Las manecillas estaban detenidas en las once cuarenta. En la otra mano
> todavía apretaba el boleto amarillo, el cual no tenía fecha ni destino, sino una sola palabra
> escrita con pluma: *Llegada*.

Glosses: *la ventanilla* (ticket window), *el rebozo* (traditional shawl), *la historieta* (comic
book), *mija* (my dear, from *mi hija*), *la concha* (a sweet roll with a shell-patterned top),
*el silbato* (whistle), *el ferrocarrilero* (railway worker), *ladear* (to tilt), *flaca* (an
affectionate nickname, "skinny"), *ya me toca* (it's my turn), *las manecillas* (clock hands), *la llegada* (arrival).

In brief: Julia's bus breaks down at night while she is traveling to see her dying father, a
retired railway worker. She shelters in an old station, which is lit; a clerk gives her a yellow
ticket for the 11:40 train, and the passengers seem to come from other decades. The clock never
moves past 11:15. A woman with sweet bread says that everyone there is waiting for someone. A steam
train arrives; a young railway worker gets off, and Julia recognizes her father at twenty by his
scar and his way of tilting his head. He calls her by her childhood nickname, says it's his turn to
go, presses something into her hand and boards with the others. At dawn the driver wakes her in a
roofless station closed for twenty years. She guesses it was a dream, but the hospital called at
11:40, and she holds her father's pocket watch, stopped at 11:40, and the ticket, which says only
"Arrival".

### Example 1: time and narrator

*Esa tarde la habían llamado del hospital* is pluperfect: the call came before the night the story
tells. *Tendría unos veinte años* and *Habrá sido un sueño* express probability: Julia guesses,
and the narrator doesn't confirm. The narrator speaks in the third person but stays with Julia: we
know her thoughts (*pensó*) and nobody else's.

### Example 2: building an inference

Clues: the call at 11:40, the watch stopped at 11:40, the young man who says it's his turn to go,
the passengers "waiting for someone". Inference: the father died at 11:40, and the station is a
place between life and death. The text never says so, and the ending keeps the doubt. The watch in
her hand is what makes the story fantastic rather than a dream.

## Three microstories

A *microrrelato* tells a whole story in a few lines and lets the reader write the rest. These three
are original.

> *Mudanza.* Cuando terminamos de subir las cajas al camión, mi madre volvió a entrar en la casa
> vacía para despedirse. Todavía no ha salido. A veces, desde la calle, la vemos saludar por la
> ventana.
>
> *Insomnio.* Contó ovejas hasta el amanecer. La número mil trescientos doce se detuvo, lo miró a
> los ojos y le preguntó, con mucha educación, si ya podía irse a dormir.
>
> *Herencia.* El abuelo me dejó en su testamento una llave y ninguna puerta. Llevo treinta años
> probándola en todas las cerraduras de la ciudad. Anoche, por fin, una puerta me reconoció.

*Moving*: my mother went back into the empty house to say goodbye and still hasn't come out; we
see her wave from the window. *Insomnia*: sheep number 1,312 politely asked him if it could go to
sleep now. *Inheritance*: my grandfather left me a key and no door; after thirty years of trying
locks, a door recognized me last night. Each sets up something normal and breaks it in the last
sentence.

## Pronunciation

*Verosímil* has four syllables (*ve-ro-sí-mil*), *inverosímil* five; both stress *sí*.
*Atmósfera* (*at-mós-fe-ra*) and *onírico* (*o-ní-ri-co*) stress the third syllable from the end.
*Antología* has five (*an-to-lo-gí-a*): the accent breaks the *ía*.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing *verosímil* (believable) with *verdadero* (true): an invented story can be
  *verosímil*.
- *El cuentista* for a woman: say *la cuentista*, like *la periodista*.
- Reading every strange story as a dream: look for the clue that resists that explanation.

## Key points

- Quiroga, Borges, Cortázar, Rulfo, Arreola, Garro and Monterroso: masters of the short story.
- *Realismo*: believable; *lo fantástico*: the inexplicable breaks into the ordinary; magical
  realism: the impossible told as normal.
- Read for time (map the tenses), narrator (who knows what) and inference (clues, then a
  conclusion).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: El ensayo: the essay and Mexican essayists
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In B1 you learned *el ensayo* as a rehearsal, and lesson 18 taught *el ensayo clínico* (clinical
trial). Its third sense is the one this lesson is about: the essay. The **[[literary essay]]** is a short prose text in
which a writer thinks in public about a subject, with a personal voice and no obligation to prove
everything like a scientist. It is the genre Mexican writers used to think about their country.
You'll meet four of them, follow the moves an essay makes, read an original essay, and plan one of
your own with the connectors of this course.

## An attempt, not a treatise

The name comes from Michel de Montaigne, whose *Essais* (1580) were "attempts" or "trials": a mind
trying out an idea. An essay is closer to *la reflexión* (reflection) than to a report. It can
wander, tell an anecdote, change its mind, and it is judged by the quality of its *pensamiento*
(thought) and its prose. In Latin America, *el ensayista* or *la ensayista* has often been a public
figure, and *el pensador* (thinker) a writer as much as a philosopher.

## Four Mexican essayists

- Alfonso Reyes (Monterrey, 1889 – Mexico City, 1959) belonged to the Ateneo de la Juventud, a
  circle of young intellectuals founded in 1909. His *Visión de Anáhuac* (1917) is a prose evocation
  of the Valley of Mexico and its great city before the conquest. He wrote on Greek literature,
  Spanish poetry and almost everything else with the same curiosity.
- José Vasconcelos (Oaxaca, 1882 – Mexico City, 1959) was the first head of the Secretaría de
  Educación Pública (1921–1924), where he launched the mural program of lesson 92. In *La raza
  cósmica* (1925) he argued that the mixing of peoples in Latin America would produce a new
  "cosmic race". The essay is historically important and much criticized today, partly because it
  treated Indigenous cultures as something to be absorbed.
- Octavio Paz (Mexico City, 1914–1998) published *El laberinto de la soledad* in 1950 (revised in
  1959): essays on what he called *la mexicanidad* (Mexicanness), including a chapter on the
  *máscaras* (masks) that, in his view, Mexicans wear to protect themselves. His generalizations
  about "the Mexican" are debated now, but the book is still widely read. He received the Nobel
  Prize in Literature in 1990.
- Rosario Castellanos (Mexico City, 1925 – Tel Aviv, 1974) grew up in Chiapas. Her master's thesis,
  *Sobre cultura femenina* (1950), asked why women had been kept outside culture, and her essays
  in *Mujer que sabe latín…* (1973), whose title plays on a saying about educated women, read
  women's lives with irony. She was Mexico's ambassador to Israel from 1971 until her death.

## The moves of an essay

An essay doesn't follow a fixed plan, but most move through the same steps. *La premisa* is the
idea everything else rests on. Examples make it concrete. A **[[digression]]** (*la digresión*) steps
aside from the main line, and good essayists make it pay off when they come back. An argumentative
essay (*un ensayo argumentativo*) also answers an objection before concluding.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The moves of an argumentative essay
  accDescr: Six steps from top to bottom. A hook, then the premise, then examples, then a digression that returns to the theme, then an objection answered, and finally a conclusion that opens outward.
  A["Gancho: a scene or a question"] --> B["La premisa: the idea to defend"]
  B --> C["Ejemplos: two or three concrete cases"]
  C --> D["La digresión: a step aside that returns"]
  D --> E["La objeción: Se dirá que... answered"]
  E --> F["La conclusión: a proposal or an open question"]
```

Each move has typical phrases:

| Move | Phrases |
|---|---|
| Premise | *Esta es mi premisa: …; Sostengo que…; Me propongo mostrar que…* |
| Examples | *Pensemos en…; Basta mirar…; Un ejemplo:* |
| Digression | *Permítame el lector una digresión; Vale la pena detenerse en…; Vuelvo al tema.* |
| Objection | *Se dirá que…; Es cierto que…, pero…; No pretendo… sino…* |
| Conclusion | *En conclusión…; No propongo…, sino algo más modesto: …* |

## The essay

This essay is original. Its subject, waiting, is one none of the four writers above is known for.
Read it once for the argument, then again to find the moves.

> #### Elogio de la espera
>
> Pasamos una parte enorme de la vida esperando: el camión, la quincena, el resultado de un
> examen, la respuesta a un mensaje que alguien ya leyó. Nadie suma esas horas, porque nadie cree
> que valga la pena sumarlas. Sin embargo, sospecho que la espera dice más de nosotros que muchas
> de las cosas que hacemos con prisa. Esta es mi premisa: la espera no es tiempo perdido, sino el
> tiempo en que descubrimos qué nos importa.
>
> Pensemos en la fila de la tortillería a la una de la tarde. Nadie la ha elegido y, sin embargo,
> en ella se aprende más sobre un barrio que en cualquier encuesta: quién saluda a quién, quién le
> cede su lugar a la señora del bebé, quién se queja del precio y quién del gobierno. La fila nos
> obliga a convivir con desconocidos sin la excusa de estar ocupados. O pensemos en la sala de
> espera de un hospital, donde las horas pesan de otra manera. Ahí nadie mira el reloj para saber
> la hora, sino para medir la angustia. Quien haya esperado toda una noche noticias de un ser
> querido sabe que hay esperas que nos cambian.
>
> También hay esperas que elegimos. El campesino que siembra maíz en junio sabe que no cosechará
> hasta el otoño, y nadie diría que pierde el tiempo mientras tanto: cuida la milpa, mira el cielo,
> hace cuentas. Quien espera un hijo no está detenido nueve meses; se prepara. Incluso el lector
> que no se salta páginas para saber cómo termina una novela practica una paciencia que es, en el
> fondo, una forma de respeto. En todos estos casos, esperar no significa quedarse quieto, sino
> dejar que algo madure a su propio ritmo. Lo que convierte la espera en sufrimiento no es su
> duración, sino nuestra incapacidad de habitarla.
>
> Permítame el lector una digresión. En español, *esperar* significa a la vez aguardar, tener
> esperanza y contar con que algo ocurra; el inglés necesita tres verbos donde nosotros usamos uno.
> No sé si la lengua refleja una manera de ver el mundo o si es una casualidad, pero me gusta
> pensar que entre esperar el tren y esperar que el tren llegue hay menos distancia de la que
> parece: quien espera, de algún modo, ya confía. Mi abuela, que esperó durante once años las
> cartas de un hermano que se había ido al norte, decía que la esperanza era la espera con los ojos
> abiertos.
>
> Vuelvo al tema. Se dirá que esta defensa de la espera es un lujo, y que para muchas personas
> esperar significa perder un día de salario en una oficina pública o tres horas diarias en un
> transporte lento. Es cierto, y no pretendo idealizar la injusticia: una cosa es la espera
> inevitable y otra muy distinta la que nos imponen la mala organización o el desprecio. Esa
> segunda espera no se elogia: se combate. Pero precisamente porque la espera injusta nos indigna,
> deberíamos reconocer el valor de la otra, la que no depende de nadie.
>
> Hoy la tecnología nos promete eliminar la espera. Las series empiezan cuando queremos, la comida
> llega a la puerta y los mensajes viajan en un segundo. No obstante, nunca habíamos sido tan
> impacientes. Una aplicación nos dice en cuántos minutos llegará el camión, y aun así miramos la
> pantalla cada diez segundos, como si nuestra mirada pudiera acelerarlo. Si la respuesta tarda un
> minuto, sentimos que el otro nos ignora; si una página tarda tres segundos en cargarse, la
> cerramos. Hemos ganado velocidad, pero hemos perdido la capacidad de estar sin hacer nada, la cual era, quizá, una forma de pensar.
>
> En conclusión, no propongo que volvamos a las cartas que tardaban meses ni que celebremos las
> filas interminables. Propongo algo más modesto: que la próxima vez que nos toque esperar, no
> saquemos el teléfono de inmediato. Que miremos alrededor. Tal vez descubramos que la espera, como
> la esperanza, es una manera de prestarle atención al futuro sin dejar de vivir el presente.

Glosses: *elogio* (praise, in praise of), *la quincena* (B1: payday, twice a month), *ceder su
lugar* (to give up one's place), *convivir con* (to spend time with), *la milpa* (cornfield, in
Mexico and Central America), *habitar* (to inhabit, to live in), *aguardar* (to wait, formal), *contar con que* (to count on something happening), *idealizar*
(to idealize), *el desprecio* (contempt), *nos toque* (it falls to us).

In brief: the writer's premise is that waiting isn't lost time but the time when we find out what
matters to us. Examples: the line at the tortilla shop, where you learn more about a neighborhood
than from any survey, and a hospital waiting room, where waiting changes people. Some waits we
choose: the farmer between sowing and harvest, the reader who doesn't skip ahead; what makes
waiting painful is not its length but our inability to live in it. Then a digression: Spanish *esperar* means to wait, to hope and to expect, as if waiting already held some hope; the
writer's grandmother called hope "waiting with your eyes open". Back to the theme, an objection:
for many people waiting is an injustice (lost wages, slow transport). The writer agrees that unfair
waiting must be fought, not praised. Technology promised to end waiting, yet we have never been so
impatient (we stare at the app that tells us when the bus will come), and we have lost the
ability to do nothing, which may have been a way of thinking. The conclusion proposes something modest: next time, don't take out your phone at once; look around.

### Example 1: finding the moves

Paragraph 1 opens with a list of everyday waits (the hook) and states the premise outright (*Esta
es mi premisa…*). Paragraph 2 gives two examples, each introduced by *pensemos en*, and paragraph 3
adds chosen waits. Paragraph 4 is the digression, announced and closed by formulas. Paragraph 5 answers an
objection with *Se dirá que… Es cierto, y no pretendo…*. Paragraph 6 adds a second argument, and
paragraph 7 concludes with a modest proposal in the subjunctive (*propongo… que no saquemos*). Notice *Quien haya esperado*,
a perfect subjunctive after *quien* for anyone at all, and *la cual*, a relative pronoun after a
comma.

### Example 2: planning a short argumentative essay

Topic: *¿Vale la pena leer a los clásicos?* (Is it worth reading the classics?) A plan of about
250 words:

1. Hook: a scene (*En la mesa de mi abuelo siempre había un libro viejo…* There was always an old
   book on my grandfather's table…).
2. Premise: *Sostengo que los clásicos no son obligación, sino conversación.* (I maintain that the
   classics are not an obligation but a conversation.)
3. Two examples: a classic that still explains the present; one you read at the wrong age.
4. Objection: *Se dirá que son difíciles y lejanos. Es cierto que…, pero…* (It will be said that
   they're difficult and distant. It's true that…, but…)
5. Conclusion: *No propongo que leamos solo clásicos, sino que…* (I'm not proposing that we read
   only classics, but that…) + subjunctive.

Keep one idea per paragraph and let the connectors show the moves. A good essay reads as a
*reflexión*, not a list: *reflexionar sobre algo* is to think it through.

## Pronunciation

*Reflexión* and *reflexionar*: the *x* sounds like *ks* (*re-flek-sión*, three syllables).
*Digresión* has three (*di-gre-sión*), *premisa* three, stressed on *mi*.

## Common mistakes

- *Ensayo* has three senses: essay, rehearsal and trial (*un ensayo clínico*). Context decides.
- *Reflexionar* (to think over) is not *reflejar* (to reflect light or show).
- *El pensamiento* is the thought; *el pensador*, the person who thinks.
- *Argumentativo* describes a text that argues, not a person who likes to argue.

## Key points

- An essay is a personal, reasoned *reflexión* in prose; Montaigne's *Essais* (1580) named it.
- Reyes, Vasconcelos, Paz and Castellanos used the essay to think about Mexico, culture and
  women's lives.
- Moves: hook, premise, examples, digression, objection, conclusion.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: El muralismo y el arte mexicano: describing a work of art
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

A1 gave you *el mural*, A2 *el pintor*, and A2's honors lesson on art *el cuadro, el retrato,
el autorretrato, el boceto* and *el muralista*. This lesson tells the story of *el muralismo*,
Mexico's best-known contribution to twentieth-century art, and of Frida Kahlo beside it. Then it
teaches the language of describing a work of art: where things are, what they represent, and how
to say it with the passive and relative clauses of this course.

## Walls for everyone

After the Revolution (1910–1920), the new government wanted an art that belonged to the public.
In 1921 José Vasconcelos (lesson 91) became the first head of the Secretaría de Educación Pública
(SEP), and he invited painters to cover the walls of public buildings. The idea was that a wall
in a school or a ministry could be seen by everyone, including people who couldn't read, while a
canvas in a private collection could not.

UNAM's *Gaceta* dates the movement's oldest mural, Roberto Montenegro's *El árbol de la vida*, to
1921. The first great site was the former Escuela Nacional Preparatoria, today the Antiguo Colegio
de San Ildefonso in Mexico City: Diego Rivera began *La creación* there in 1922, and about forty
more murals were painted in the building through 1926. The state was the movement's great
*mecenas* (patron).

## Three painters, and a fourth

| Artist | Life | Works and places (as museum and official sources date them) |
|---|---|---|
| Diego Rivera | Guanajuato, 1886 – Mexico City, 1957 | SEP murals (1923–1928); Palacio Nacional staircase (from 1929); *Detroit Industry*, Detroit Institute of Arts (1932–1933) |
| José Clemente Orozco | Zapotlán el Grande (today Ciudad Guzmán), Jalisco, 1883 – Mexico City, 1949 | San Ildefonso (mid-1920s); Hospicio Cabañas, Guadalajara (late 1930s; a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997) |
| David Alfaro Siqueiros | Chihuahua, 1896 – Cuernavaca, 1974 | *La marcha de la humanidad*, Polyforum Cultural Siqueiros, Mexico City (1971) |
| Frida Kahlo | Coyoacán, Mexico City, 1907–1954 | *Las dos Fridas* (1939), Museo de Arte Moderno; her house, the Casa Azul, a museum since 1958 |

Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros are called *los tres grandes*. Rivera painted crowded, colorful
scenes of history and work; Orozco's figures are darker and more tragic; Siqueiros experimented
with industrial paints and with compositions meant to be seen while walking past them. A private patron could
also be a problem: in 1933 Rivera painted a mural for the Rockefeller Center in New York, his
patrons objected to its content, and it was destroyed in 1934. He painted a new version at the
Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City that same year.

Frida Kahlo was not a muralist. After a bus accident in 1925 she began to paint, mostly small
*óleos* (oil paintings) on canvas and metal, many of them self-portraits. She married Rivera in
1929. Her first solo exhibition was at a New York *galería* in 1938, and today many people consider
*Las dos Fridas* one of her masterpieces.

## Fresco, oil and the brush

A mural is often painted *al fresco*: the painter applies pigment mixed with water to fresh lime
plaster, and as the plaster dries the color becomes part of the wall. Only the area that can be
finished in one day is plastered, so the work is planned in sketches (*bocetos*) first. That's a
**[[fresco]]**. Easel painting is *el óleo sobre lienzo*: oil paint on canvas, which can be corrected
for weeks. The tool is *el pincel*; each mark it leaves is *una pincelada*, and a line drawn with a
pencil or a brush is *un trazo*.

## Describing a picture

Describe from the general to the particular: what it is, the **[[composition]]** (how the parts are
arranged), then the details and what they may mean.

| To say | Spanish |
|---|---|
| where | *en primer plano* (in the foreground), *al fondo* (in the background), *en el centro*, *a la izquierda / a la derecha*, *en la parte superior / inferior* |
| what | *aparece, se ve, se representa a…, destaca…* |
| who made it | *fue pintado por…; se pintó en 1923* |
| how parts relate | *la figura central, en torno a la cual…; un paisaje cuyos colores…* |
| meaning, hedged | *parece simbolizar…, podría representar…, quizá aluda a…* |

![An original mural design for a school wall, in soft colors. In the center, a tall woman holds an open book. In the foreground, along the bottom, a row of children and adults read and write. In the background, at the top, two volcanoes and a large sun. On the left, a factory with a chimney and a small train. On the right, a field of corn and a farmer with a hoe.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 1: a model description

This mural design is original, drawn for this lesson; the text describes it as a museum guide
might.

> El mural fue diseñado para la pared principal de una escuela. En el centro destaca una mujer de
> gran tamaño que sostiene un libro abierto: es la figura central, en torno a la cual se organiza
> toda la composición. En primer plano aparece una fila de niños y adultos que leen y escriben,
> pintados con trazos sencillos y colores cálidos. Al fondo, en la parte superior, se ven dos
> volcanes y un sol enorme cuyos rayos parecen salir del libro. A la izquierda se representa una
> fábrica con una chimenea y un tren pequeño; a la derecha, una milpa y un campesino con su
> azadón. La obra parece decir que la educación une el campo y la ciudad, aunque, como en todo
> mural, cada espectador puede leerla a su manera.

The mural was designed for a school's main wall. In the center stands a large woman holding an open
book: she is the central figure around which the whole composition is organized. In the foreground
a row of children and adults read and write, painted with simple lines and warm colors. In the
background, at the top, there are two volcanoes and a huge sun whose rays seem to come out of the
book. On the left a factory with a chimney and a small train is shown; on the right, a cornfield and
a farmer with his hoe. The work seems to say that education unites the countryside and the city,
although, as with any mural, each viewer can read it in their own way.

Notice the passive (*fue diseñado*), the passive *se* (*se ven, se representa*), the relatives
*en torno a la cual* and *cuyos rayos*, and the hedge *parece decir*.

### Example 2: a museum label

A label (*la ficha técnica*; in Mexican museums often *la cédula*) gives the facts in a fixed order, without verbs: title, artist,
date, technique and support, size, place. For an invented work:

> *La lectura*. Ana Ruiz. 1968. Fresco sobre muro, 4 × 9 m. Escuela Primaria Los Volcanes,
> Puebla.

(*La lectura* "Reading". Ana Ruiz. 1968. Fresco on a wall, 4 × 9 m. Los Volcanes Primary School,
Puebla.) Then a short text in the present or the passive: *El mural fue pintado en tres meses. Se considera
la obra maestra de la artista.* (The mural was painted in three months. It is considered the
artist's masterpiece.) Note that *la obra maestra* keeps both words feminine, and the
plural is *las obras maestras*.

## Planning a mural

Two students at a *prepa* (high school, Mexico) plan a mural for their school with the art
teacher's sketch in front of them. Read it aloud, with two voices.

> ITZEL: Mira el boceto que nos dejó la maestra. Yo pondría a la abuela en el centro, como figura
> central, contándoles historias a los niños.
>
> MAURICIO: Me gusta, pero si la ponemos en el centro, ¿dónde va el mercado? Yo quería que se
> viera al fondo, con los puestos y los toldos de colores.
>
> ITZEL: Al fondo, en la parte superior, cabe perfectamente. Y en primer plano, los niños, pintados
> con pinceladas sueltas, como si se estuvieran moviendo.
>
> MAURICIO: ¿Lo vamos a pintar al fresco, como los muralistas?
>
> ITZEL: Ojalá, pero la maestra dice que el fresco exige preparar el muro y trabajar rapidísimo.
> Con pintura acrílica nos va a quedar bien, y podremos corregir.
>
> MAURICIO: Entonces hagamos primero los trazos con gis, para que todos opinen antes de que
> empecemos.
>
> ITZEL: Va. Y cuando lo terminemos, quiero que lleve una ficha técnica, como en los museos.

ITZEL: Look at the sketch the teacher left us. I'd put the grandmother in the center, as the central
figure, telling the children stories. MAURICIO: I like it, but if we put her in the center, where
does the market go? I wanted it to be seen in the background, with the stalls and the colorful
awnings. ITZEL: In the background, at the top, it fits perfectly. And in the foreground, the
children, painted with loose brushstrokes, as if they were moving. MAURICIO: Are we going to paint
it in fresco, like the muralists? ITZEL: I wish, but the teacher says fresco requires preparing the
wall and working very fast. With acrylic paint it'll turn out fine, and we can correct it.
MAURICIO: Then let's do the lines in chalk first, so everyone can give their opinion before we
start. ITZEL: OK. And when we finish it, I want it to have a label, like in museums.

*El gis* is chalk in Mexico (*la tiza* in many other countries); *Va* is a casual "OK, deal",
common in Mexico. Notice the sequence of tenses: *quería que se viera* (past → imperfect subjunctive), *para
que todos opinen antes de que empecemos* (present → present subjunctive).

## Seeing murals yourself

1. Find out the date, the patron and the building: a mural is made for one place.
2. Stand back and find the composition: the central figure, the foreground, the background.
3. Walk along it. Many murals are painted for a viewer who moves, up a staircase or along a
   corridor.
4. Look closely at the *pinceladas* and the *trazos*, and at how the painting meets doors and
   windows.
5. Only then read the label, and compare its reading with yours.

In Mexico City, the Antiguo Colegio de San Ildefonso, the SEP's historic building in the Centro and
the Palacio de Bellas Artes all show murals; in Guadalajara, the Hospicio Cabañas. Check opening
hours on their official pages before you go.

## Pronunciation

*Óleo* has three syllables, *ó-le-o*: in careful speech *e* and *o* stay in separate syllables. *Mecenas* is
*me-ce-nas*, stressed on *ce* (with the Latin American *s* sound for *c*). *Pincel* stresses the
last syllable: *pin-cel*.

## Common mistakes

- *El fresco* (a painting) is not the adjective *fresco* (fresh, cool): *un fresco de Orozco*.
- *El óleo* is oil paint or an oil painting; cooking oil is *el aceite*.
- *El mecenas* doesn't change: *los mecenas*, *la mecenas*.
- *Al fondo* is in the background, but *el fondo* alone can mean a fund (B1) or the bottom.
- A guide's or a critic's reading is an interpretation: hedge it (*parece, podría*).

## Key points

- *El muralismo* began in 1921–1922 with the SEP under Vasconcelos; the state was its patron.
- *Los tres grandes*: Rivera, Orozco, Siqueiros; Frida Kahlo painted mostly small oils, many of
  them self-portraits.
- *Al fresco* on wet plaster; *óleo sobre lienzo* with a *pincel*.
- Describe from general to particular: place (*en primer plano, al fondo*), the passive, relatives,
  hedged meaning.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Las lenguas de México: Mexico's many languages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Spanish is the language of this course, but it is not Mexico's only language. This lesson
presents Mexico's Indigenous languages through official facts and figures, the Nahuatl words you
already use when you speak Mexican Spanish, and the language of a careful, respectful report. In A2
you learned *el hablante* (speaker), *la variante* (variant) and *el préstamo*, which in
linguistics means a loanword. You'll need all three. The lesson ends with an original radio report
to listen to.

## How many languages?

*La lengua* means both "tongue" and "language"; in this topic it is more common than *el idioma*.
The official count comes from the Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI). Its *Catálogo
de las lenguas indígenas nacionales*, published in 2008, groups Mexico's Indigenous languages in
three levels:

| Level | Count | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| *familia lingüística* | 11 | languages descended from one ancestor | yuto-nahua, maya, oto-mangue |
| *agrupación lingüística* | 68 | what most people call "a language" | náhuatl, maya, zapoteco, tseltal |
| *variante lingüística* | 364 | a regional variety, often hard for speakers of other variants to understand | the Nahuatl of one region of Puebla |

So "68 languages" and "364 variants" are both correct answers, at different levels. A **[[language family]]**
is a set of languages that come from a common ancestor, as Spanish, Portuguese and Italian
come from Latin.

## What the law says

The Ley General de Derechos Lingüísticos de los Pueblos Indígenas was published in the *Diario
Oficial de la Federación* on March 13, 2003. In summary, it says that the Indigenous languages it
recognizes and Spanish are *lenguas nacionales* with the same validity in the places and contexts where they are spoken
(article 4); that every
Mexican may use his or her language in public and private life, speaking or writing (article 9);
and it created INALI (article 14). Spanish is the language of most of public life, but this law
makes it one national language among many.

## How many speakers?

In the 2020 census, INEGI (Mexico's statistics institute) counted 7,364,645 people aged 3 and over
who speak an Indigenous language, about 6.1% of that age group (the share INEGI reports and CONAPO, the
national population council, repeats). The census asks whether a person speaks the language, so it doesn't count
people who identify as Indigenous but grew up speaking only Spanish. The chart shows the six
languages with the most speakers.

![A horizontal bar chart titled Hablantes de 3 años y más, censo 2020 (INEGI). Náhuatl 1,651,958; maya 774,755; tseltal 589,144; tsotsil 550,274; mixteco 526,593; zapoteco 490,845. The Nahuatl bar is more than twice as long as any other.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Nahuatl, spoken by more than 1.6 million people, is the most widely spoken. Maya is spoken mostly
in the Yucatán Peninsula; Tseltal and Tsotsil in Chiapas; Mixtec and Zapotec mostly in Oaxaca and
neighboring states, and by migrants far from them.

### Talking about the figures

Census figures are a good place to practice the language of data (lesson 19). A few true
statements about the chart, worked out from INEGI's numbers:

- *Más de uno de cada cinco hablantes de lenguas indígenas habla náhuatl.* More than one in five
  speakers of Indigenous languages speaks Nahuatl (1,651,958 of 7,364,645 is about 22%).
- *Cerca de cuatro de cada diez hablan náhuatl, maya o tseltal.* About four in ten (41%).
- *El náhuatl tiene más del doble de hablantes que el maya.* More than twice as many as Maya.
- *El tsotsil y el mixteco tienen un número de hablantes parecido.* A similar number.

Keep the source's qualifiers when you report a figure: *según el censo de 2020*, *de 3 años y más*.
A statement without them may be true and still mislead.

## Choosing the right words

- *Lengua indígena* (Indigenous language) is the term the law and INALI use. *Lengua originaria*
  (native language of the Americas) is also common, especially in education and the media.
- *La lengua materna* is the first language a person learns at home. For many Mexicans it is
  Nahuatl, Maya or Zapotec, and Spanish is their second language.
- *El dialecto*. In linguistics a **[[dialect]]** is a regional variety of one language: the Spanish
  of Mexico and the Spanish of Spain are dialects of Spanish. Calling Nahuatl or Maya *dialectos*,
  as many people still do, suggests that they are not real languages. That is false, and it has
  long been used to look down on their speakers. Say *lenguas*.
- *Indígena* has one form for both genders: *una lengua indígena, un pueblo indígena*.

## Nahuatl in your Spanish

Nahuatl was the language of the Mexica (often called Aztecs) and a lingua franca of central Mexico
when the Spanish arrived. Hundreds of its words entered Mexican Spanish, and some passed into
general Spanish and English. A word of Nahuatl origin is *un nahuatlismo*, and the study of where a
word comes from is *la etimología*. The RAE's dictionary (DLE) gives the sources below.

| Spanish | From Nahuatl | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *el aguacate* | *ahuacatl* | English *avocado* came through Spanish |
| *el tomate* | *tomatl* | In central Mexico, *tomate* is often the green tomatillo, and the red one is *jitomate* (from *xitomatl*) |
| *el cacahuate* | *tlalcacahuatl* | Spain says *cacahuete* |
| *el papalote* | *papalotl* (butterfly) | a kite; Spain says *cometa* |
| *el guajolote* | *huexolotl* | a turkey; *el pavo* is the general word |
| *el chocolate* | debated | Nahuatl origin is generally accepted; the exact form is disputed |
| *el elote, el popote, el tianguis, el chapulín* | *elotl, popotl, tianquiztli, chapolin* | corn on the cob, drinking straw, street market, grasshopper |

Notice the pattern: the Nahuatl ending *-tl*, which Spanish speakers found hard at the end of a
word, often became *-te*.

Nahuatl is not the only source. *El cenote*, the natural well of the Yucatán Peninsula, comes from
Maya, according to the DLE. Older still are words from Taíno, a language of the Caribbean that the
Spanish met first, in 1492: *la canoa, el huracán, el maíz, la hamaca*. They spread to all of
Spanish, and several of them to English too (*canoe, hurricane, hammock*).

## Contact, loss and revitalization

Five centuries of contact produced *el mestizaje* (the mixing of peoples and cultures) and
widespread *bilingüismo* (bilingualism). Contact was not equal: for most of that time, school,
courts and jobs used Spanish, and many parents stopped speaking their language to their children so
that they would not face discrimination. Several languages in INALI's catalog now have very few
speakers.

*La revitalización* (revitalization) is the work of bringing a language back into daily use:
classes for children taught by speakers, books and dictionaries written by communities, radio
stations that broadcast in Indigenous languages, and social media, music and podcasts. The United
Nations declared 2022–2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages. Many linguists
stress that **[[language revitalization]]** succeeds when children speak the language at home, not
only in class.

## A radio report

Listen to the report with the words hidden first, then read along. The town and the people are
invented; the facts are those of this lesson.

```dialogue lang=es-MX
# Voces de la sierra: un reportaje radiofónico
Locutora: Buenas tardes. Hoy nos acompaña desde la sierra norte de Puebla nuestro reportero, Emiliano Vázquez. Emiliano, ¿qué encontraste?
= Good afternoon. Today our reporter, Emiliano Vázquez, joins us from the northern highlands of Puebla. Emiliano, what did you find?
Reportero: Buenas tardes. Estoy en una escuela primaria donde los niños aprenden a leer en náhuatl y en español. Según el censo de 2020, el náhuatl tiene más de un millón seiscientos mil hablantes, pero en muchas familias ya no se transmite a los hijos.
= Good afternoon. I'm at a primary school where the children learn to read in Nahuatl and Spanish. According to the 2020 census, Nahuatl has more than one million six hundred thousand speakers, but in many families it is no longer passed on to the children.
Reportero: Conmigo está la maestra Rosa Tepetla, cuya lengua materna es el náhuatl. Maestra, ¿por qué es importante esta escuela?
= With me is the teacher Rosa Tepetla, whose mother tongue is Nahuatl. Ms. Tepetla, why is this school important?
Maestra: Porque cuando yo era niña, en la escuela nos regañaban si hablábamos náhuatl. Mis papás decidieron no enseñárselo a mis hermanos menores para que no sufrieran lo mismo. Aquí queremos que los niños sepan que su lengua vale tanto como el español.
= Because when I was a girl, at school they scolded us if we spoke Nahuatl. My parents decided not to teach it to my younger brothers and sisters so they wouldn't suffer the same. Here we want the children to know that their language is worth as much as Spanish.
Reportero: ¿Y los niños lo hablan en casa?
= And do the children speak it at home?
Maestra: Algunos sí, con los abuelos. Otros lo están aprendiendo aquí y luego se lo enseñan a sus papás. Eso es la revitalización: que la lengua vuelva a la cocina, no solo al salón de clases.
= Some do, with their grandparents. Others are learning it here and then teach it to their parents. That's revitalization: the language going back into the kitchen, not just the classroom.
Reportero: Le pregunto a Joel, de diez años, qué palabra le gusta más.
= I ask Joel, ten years old, which word he likes best.
Joel: Papalotl. Es mariposa. Y en español decimos papalote, pero es otra cosa, es para volar en el viento.
= Papalotl. It's butterfly. And in Spanish we say papalote, but that's something else, it's for flying in the wind.
Locutora: ¡Qué bonito ejemplo de etimología! Emiliano, ¿qué dicen las autoridades?
= What a lovely example of etymology! Emiliano, what do the authorities say?
Reportero: La ley de derechos lingüísticos de 2003 reconoce el náhuatl y las demás lenguas indígenas como lenguas nacionales, igual que el español. Pero aquí nos dicen que faltan maestros bilingües y libros. Desde la sierra norte de Puebla, Emiliano Vázquez.
= The 2003 linguistic rights law recognizes Nahuatl and the other Indigenous languages as national languages, like Spanish. But here they tell us that bilingual teachers and books are lacking. From the northern highlands of Puebla, Emiliano Vázquez.
Locutora: Gracias, Emiliano.
= Thank you, Emiliano.
```

Notice the grammar of a report: the passive *se* (*ya no se transmite*), *cuya lengua materna*,
the imperfect subjunctive after a past verb (*decidieron no enseñárselo… para que no sufrieran*),
and *queremos que sepan* in the present.

### Example 1: guessing a source

*El mecate* (rope) and *el metate* (grinding stone) end in *-te*. Knowing the pattern, you can guess
that their Nahuatl sources ended in *-tl*: *mecatl* and *metlatl*. The pattern is a strong clue, not
a proof: *el chocolate* also ends in *-te*, and its exact source is still debated. Check a
dictionary before you state an etymology as fact.

### Example 2: rewriting a careless sentence

Careless: *En ese pueblo todavía hablan un dialecto, pero los jóvenes ya hablan bien.*

1. *Dialecto* treats the language as less than a language: write *una lengua indígena* or name it.
2. *Hablan bien* implies the other language is "bad": say what they speak.
3. Add facts instead of judgments.

Better: *En ese pueblo se habla tsotsil, y la mayoría de los jóvenes son bilingües en tsotsil y
español.* (In that town Tsotsil is spoken, and most young people are bilingual in Tsotsil and
Spanish.)

A second one: *Los indígenas no hablan español.* It treats millions of different people as one block and states a
false generalization. Better: *Según el censo de 2020, la mayoría de los hablantes de lenguas
indígenas también habla español; una minoría solo habla su lengua.* (According to the 2020 census,
most speakers of Indigenous languages also speak Spanish; a minority speak only their own
language.) The source and the qualifiers do the work that the stereotype was doing badly.

## Pronunciation

*Náhuatl* has two syllables, *ná-huatl*, stressed on the first. In Mexico *tl* is pronounced
together at the start of a syllable (*a-tlas, a-tle-ta*), while much of Spain splits it
(*at-las, at-le-ta*). The *x* of *México* sounds like *j*, but the *x* of *Xochimilco* sounds like *s*.
*Bilingüismo* has four syllables, *bi-lin-güis-mo*: the dieresis tells you to pronounce the *u*.

## Common mistakes

- Calling Indigenous languages *dialectos*. They are *lenguas*.
- *Los indígenas* as a noun for people is common, but it can sound distant: *los pueblos
  indígenas* or *las personas hablantes de náhuatl* is often preferred.
- Writing *el nahuatl* without the accent: *el náhuatl*.
- Saying Mexico has "one Indigenous language, Nahuatl": it has 68 *agrupaciones*.

## Key points

- INALI's 2008 catalog: 11 families, 68 language groupings, 364 variants.
- The 2003 law makes the Indigenous languages and Spanish *lenguas nacionales* with the same
  validity.
- INEGI, 2020: 7,364,645 speakers aged 3 and over; Nahuatl has the most.
- Many everyday Mexican words are *nahuatlismos*; *-tl* often became *-te*.
- Say *lengua indígena* or *lengua originaria*, not *dialecto*.

the lesson.

sections.name: Lo que pasó y lo que pudo pasar (what happened and what could have happened)
Opinar y matizar (giving and nuancing opinions)
Contar lo que se dice (reporting, the news and the media)
Los matices de la lengua y el DELE B2 (the fine points of the language and the B2 exam)
Honors: Literatura, arte y lenguas de México (literature, art and the languages of Mexico)

questions.stem: Which writer published the story collection "El llano en llamas" (1953) and the novel "Pedro Páramo" (1955)?
questions.explanation: Juan Rulfo (Jalisco, 1917 – Mexico City, 1986) is known above all for these two books. Arreola wrote Confabulario (1952), Cortázar was Argentine (Bestiario, 1951), and Monterroso is known for very short stories such as El dinosaurio.

questions.stem: Early in "La sala de espera" we read: "Esa tarde la habían llamado del hospital." What does the pluperfect tell you?
choices: The hospital will call her later that night.
The hospital calls her every afternoon.
The call came before the night the story tells.
She isn't sure whether the hospital called.
questions.explanation: The pluperfect (habían llamado) places an event before another past moment: the call came that afternoon, before the night of the story. It's how a narrator jumps back in time. A habit would need the imperfect (la llamaban), and doubt would need a hedge or the conditional.

questions.stem: When the young railway worker gets off the train, the narrator says: "Tendría unos veinte años." What does this sentence express?
choices: A guess about his age in the past
What his age would be under some condition
His age at some time in the future
questions.explanation: The conditional of probability expresses a guess about the past: "He must have been about twenty." Julia doesn't know his age; she estimates it. There is no "if" clause, so it isn't a condition, and nothing points to the future.

questions.stem: In "La sala de espera", which clues suggest that Julia's father died at 11:40 that night? Select all that apply.
choices: Julia has a missed call from the hospital at 11:40.
The pocket watch in her hand has stopped at 11:40.
The young man tells her that it's his turn to go.
The bus broke down at half past ten.
The clerk writes in a notebook with an old pen.
questions.explanation: The call, the watch and "Ya me toca irme" all point to the father's death at 11:40, though the story never says it. The breakdown sets the plot in motion and the clerk's old pen adds atmosphere; neither is a clue about the father.

questions.stem: Which description fits the narrator of "La sala de espera"?
choices: Julia herself, telling the story in the first person
An omniscient narrator who reports every character's thoughts
The father, remembering the night of his death
A third-person narrator who stays with Julia and knows her thoughts only
questions.explanation: The story says "Julia pensó…" and "Habrá sido un sueño, pensó": we enter Julia's mind and nobody else's. The narrator uses the third person (ella), so it isn't Julia speaking as "yo", and it never tells us what the clerk or the woman with the bread think.

questions.stem: Why does "La sala de espera" read as a fantastic story rather than a story about a dream?
choices: Because the station has been closed for twenty years
Because Julia wakes up holding her father's watch, an object from the "dream"
Because the bus driver wakes her at dawn
Because Julia guesses that it was a dream
questions.explanation: An object that crosses from the strange night into the real morning resists the "it was only a dream" explanation, and that doubt is what makes the story fantastic. The closed station and the driver could fit a dream, and Julia's own guess is exactly the explanation the watch puts in doubt.

questions.stem: Name the numbered steps in the shape of a fantastic tale.

image.alt: A rising line with five numbered steps from left to right: 1 low on the left by a small house, 2 by a question mark, 3 by three upward arrows, 4 at the top by a star, and 5 a little lower on the right by a key with a question mark.

questions.explanation: 1 is the everyday world (the bus, the valley), 2 the first strange sign (a lit station that should be closed), 3 the tension growing (the clock that doesn't move), 4 the climax (the father at twenty) and 5 the ambiguous ending, with an object that remains (the watch). A prólogo is a preface and a moraleja the moral of a fable.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Verosímil is believable and inverosímil its opposite; onírico is dreamlike (from the Greek for dream); la ambientación is the setting as the writer builds it; la intriga is the suspense that keeps you reading. An anthology is una antología.

questions.stem: Complete with the adjective that means "believable": "Los personajes son inventados, pero muy ___: parecen gente real."
questions.explanation: Verosímil has one form for masculine and feminine; with personajes it takes the plural: verosímiles. Remember the written accent on the í (ve-ro-sí-mi-les).

questions.stem: Why is Augusto Monterroso's "El dinosaurio" (1959) so often cited?
choices: It was the first fantastic story written in Mexico.
It is a long story told by a dinosaur.
It is a single sentence of seven words, and the reader imagines the rest.
It won the Premio Príncipe de Asturias.
questions.explanation: El dinosaurio is one of the shortest stories in Spanish: one sentence about waking up, seven words long, a model of the microrrelato. Monterroso himself won the Premio Príncipe de Asturias in 2000, for his whole work, not for that story.

questions.stem: Using the lesson's labels: in a story, everyone in a village calmly accepts that the grandmother floats above the table every Sunday, and nobody finds it strange. Which label fits best?
questions.explanation: The impossible told calmly, as if it were normal, is what the lesson calls magical realism. In fantastic literature the impossible disturbs the characters and can't be explained; realism keeps to what is believable; a microrrelato is a length, not a way of treating the impossible.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: It surprised her that the waiting room was lit.
questions.explanation: A reaction in the past (le sorprendió que) takes the imperfect subjunctive: estuviera. The subject can follow the verb (que estuviera iluminada la sala de espera), and the whole que clause can come first. Estaba iluminada, an indicative, is wrong after a verb of feeling.

questions.stem: In which story do a brother and sister lose their old house, room by room, to something that is never named?
choices: "¡Diles que no me maten!", by Juan Rulfo
questions.explanation: "Casa tomada" (1946, collected in Bestiario, 1951) is a classic fantastic story: the invader is never explained. "El guardagujas" is about an absurd railway, "El Aleph" about a point containing the universe, and Rulfo's story about an old man begging for his life.

questions.stem: Complete: "Elena Garro fue novelista, dramaturga y ___: sus cuentos están en La semana de colores."
questions.explanation: La cuentista is a short-story writer; the form is the same for a man and a woman, like la periodista. El cuento is the story itself, la contadora an accountant and la cuenta a bill or an account.

questions.stem: The genre's name comes from Montaigne's "Essais" (1580). What did the word mean?
questions.explanation: An essay is an attempt or trial: a mind trying out an idea, not a proof or a treatise. That's why Spanish ensayo also means a rehearsal and a trial (un ensayo clínico).

questions.stem: Who wrote "El laberinto de la soledad" (1950), with its chapter on Mexican "masks", and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1990?
questions.explanation: Octavio Paz (1914–1998). Reyes wrote Visión de Anáhuac (1917), Vasconcelos La raza cósmica (1925), and Castellanos the essays of Mujer que sabe latín… (1973).

questions.stem: Match each essayist to a fact from the lesson.
questions.explanation: Reyes evoked the Valley of Mexico before the conquest; Vasconcelos led the SEP and launched the murals; Paz won the Nobel; Castellanos's master's thesis asked why women had been kept out of culture. Pedro Páramo is Juan Rulfo's novel (lesson 90).

questions.stem: Put these parts of "Elogio de la espera" in the order the essay presents them.
choices: A list of everyday waits, then the premise
The tortilla line and the hospital waiting room
The three meanings of the verb esperar
An objection: some waiting is unjust
A modest proposal about the phone
questions.explanation: Hook and premise, examples, the digression on esperar, the objection (Se dirá que…), a second argument about technology, and the conclusion (Propongo algo más modesto…). The paragraph on waits we choose, between the examples and the digression, is left out here.

questions.stem: In the essay, what is the job of the sentence "Permítame el lector una digresión"?
choices: It announces a step aside from the main line.
questions.explanation: It announces a digression, which the writer closes later with "Vuelvo al tema". The premise is stated with "Esta es mi premisa", the objection begins with "Se dirá que", and the conclusion with "En conclusión".

questions.stem: "Se dirá que esta defensa de la espera es un lujo." What is the writer doing here?
choices: Introducing an objection in order to answer it
Admitting that the premise is false
questions.explanation: Se dirá que (it will be said that) raises a possible objection, which the writer then answers: Es cierto, y no pretendo idealizar la injusticia… pero… Answering an objection makes an argumentative essay stronger; it doesn't abandon the premise.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences from the essay contain a verb in the subjunctive? Select all that apply.
choices: Quien haya esperado toda una noche noticias de un ser querido sabe que hay esperas que nos cambian.
Nadie suma esas horas, porque nadie cree que valga la pena sumarlas.
Hoy la tecnología nos promete eliminar la espera.
Tal vez descubramos que la espera es una manera de prestarle atención al futuro.
questions.explanation: Haya esperado (perfect subjunctive after quien, "anyone who"), valga (after nadie cree que, a denied belief) and descubramos (after tal vez, a possibility) are subjunctive. Promete is present indicative and habíamos sido is pluperfect indicative.

questions.stem: Complete with reflexionar in the present subjunctive: "Es importante que los estudiantes ___ sobre lo que leen."
questions.explanation: Es importante que is a value judgment, so it takes the subjunctive: reflexionen (they). Reflexionar is a regular -ar verb, and it takes sobre: reflexionar sobre algo, to think something over.

questions.stem: What does "ensayo" mean in this sentence? "En 1925 Vasconcelos publicó un ensayo sobre el futuro de América Latina."
questions.explanation: Something a writer publishes about a subject is an essay. Un ensayo is a rehearsal in the theater (B1) and part of un ensayo clínico in medicine, but neither fits publishing "sobre el futuro de América Latina".

questions.stem: The essay plays on the meanings of esperar. What does it mean in "Espero que el tren llegue pronto"?
questions.explanation: Esperar que + subjunctive expresses a wish: I hope the train arrives soon. With a direct object (esperar el tren) it means to wait for. That one verb covers waiting, hoping and expecting is the digression of the essay.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Spanish.
questions.prompt: I propose that we don't take out our phones right away.
questions.explanation: Proponer que, a verb of influence, takes the subjunctive: no saquemos (sacar → saque, with c → qu). The time phrase can also come after the verb or before it (no saquemos de inmediato el teléfono; de inmediato no saquemos el teléfono). No sacamos, indicative, would report a fact instead of a proposal.

questions.stem: Which phrase would you use to state the premise of an essay?
questions.explanation: Sostengo que… (I maintain that…), like Esta es mi premisa or Me propongo mostrar que…, states the idea the essay defends. Vuelvo al tema closes a digression, Se dirá que introduces an objection, and Permítame una digresión opens a digression.

questions.stem: A teacher says: "Para el examen tienen que escribir un texto argumentativo." What kind of text is it?
choices: A text that defends a position with reasons
A text that tells a story in order
